en: Preface to Master Li’s *Comprehensive Treatise on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

This sūtra was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda under imperial decree during the Zhengsheng era of Empress Wu Zetian. The Preface by the Celestial Casket, Golden Wheel, Sage, and Divine Emperor [Zhongzong] states:
"I have heard that at the very beginning of the creative transformation of the universe, before the Way of Heaven had yet been differentiated, the tortoise..."
From the time the Dragon Tied the Elephant, human culture first emerged. Although eighteen thousand years have passed, all have remained within the same bounded realm;
yet among the seventy-two sovereigns, who could have known the meaning of the boundless? Consequently, people were deluded regarding the Four Patiences and transmigrated within the Six Realms;
families were entangled by the Five Hindrances and submerged beneath the Three Evil Paths. Then, when Vulture Peak rose in the west and the Elephant Vehicle [arrived]—

Driving eastward is the Sun of Wisdom, the Dharma King, who gazes loftily beyond the four great elements. The Tamer of Men from the Central Heaven dwells in supremacy, transcending the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Encompassing the Iron Ring Mountains, he stretches and contracts eons as vast as the sands of the Ganges; merging with the great void as his measure, how could numerical calculation ever exhaust him?
Entering the most minute regions of a single speck of dust, he cannot be described by names or words. As for that which is beyond attainment and beyond praise—its...
Is it not solely due to the Great Awakened One? In past kalpas, I planted the causes for this; I have humbly received the Buddha’s prophecy.
When the Golden Immortal descended with his decree, the verses of the *Mahāmegha* first manifested; when I opened the scrolls at the jade throne, the texts of the *Ratnavarṣa* later reached me.

Furthermore, through the accumulated blessings of my past merits, they have gathered upon my humble person. Thus, the earth is level and the heavens are perfected; the rivers are clear and the seas are tranquil. Extraordinary portents and rare auspicious signs arrive daily.

Furthermore, the sacred texts inscribed upon palm leaves arrived monthly and reached us year after year. From beyond the seas and across the deserts, the rites of presenting precious offerings were fully observed;
through perilous crossings and deep voyages, the words translated by successive interpreters were exhaustedly conveyed.

The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the Flower Ornament Scripture of the Great Vehicle, is the secret treasury of all Buddhas and the ocean of the Tathāgata’s nature. Reflecting deeply upon its profound meaning, it was translated as follows:
In the Jin Dynasty, more than six reigns have passed and nearly four hundred years have elapsed. Yet of this single collection of scriptures, we have obtained barely thirty thousand words;

we have merely uncovered half a pearl and have not yet beheld the complete treasure. I have heard that the Sanskrit original was previously in the kingdom of Khotan, so I dispatched envoys to welcome it, and it has only recently arrived here.
Having now beheld these hundreds of thousands of wondrous verses, I shall thus unfold these one hundred thousand authentic [words].
The Preface: In the first year of the Zhengsheng era, at Dàbiànkōng Monastery, I personally received the editorial revisions and reverently translated this text.
Consequently, the nectar of the Dharma began to flow; it was prefigured by a dream on the evening of the Gengshen day, when a drenching rain fell.

Subsequently, during the Renxu year, the gateway to the true nature (*dharmatā*) was opened, perfectly corresponding to the grace of the single flavor (*ekarasa*). How could one have known that in the final five hundred years [of the Dharma], such a thing would occur?
Suddenly, one encounters the words from the Golden Mouth; within the realm of Sahā, the secrets of the pearl casket are at once revealed.
It was during the Kaiyuan era that Li Tongxuan, the Elder of Fangshan, composed the *Comprehensive Treatise* (*He lun*). In his own preface, Tongxuan stated:
"The root of sentient beings relies upon the ocean of wisdom as its source; the stream of conscious beings takes the Dharma-body as their substance. It is only because..."

Afflictions give rise to the separation from wisdom, and conceptualizations transform the essence into something distinct. When one realizes the fundamental source, afflictions vanish; when one knows the essence of mind, it merges with the source.
This *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Flower Ornament Scripture of the Great Vaipulya, elucidates the primordial limit of sentient beings and reveals the fountainhead of the fruition of all Buddhas.

As for its being the fundamental source, it cannot be accomplished through effort; as for its being the fountainhead, it cannot be attained through practice. When effort ceases, one returns to the fundamental source.

The practice reaches its consummation and the source is perfected. That which is fundamentally without function yet acts with sovereign freedom according to conditions is none other than this Vairocana.

Thus, he takes up stations within the four heavens and manifests the eight phases of his life. Within the Bodhimaṇḍa, he appears in an *araṇya* (hermitage) to mark the beginning of his accomplishment;
in the Hall of Universal Radiance, he dwells in the great mansion of the *saṃbhogakāya*. The eldest son, Samantabhadra, brings forth the virtues of fruition from the treasury.
The Body: Mañjuśrī, the Youngest Son, first initiated his enlightenment at Mount Kāñcana. Through the *Sāgaramudrā-samādhi*, he manifested his spirit throughout the Dharma-realm;
by means of the *Samantacakṣu-dharmaparyāya*, he beheld oceans of lands within a single mote of dust. The two retributions—the primary and the secondary—interpenetrate body and land;
the two gates of cause and effect mutually penetrate essence and function. With the precious nets of the Śakras, he reveals the ten lands.

Layer upon layer, he grasps the stainless maṇi-jewel, illuminating the ten bodies in their profound majesty. Within the realms of infinite lands, self and other are not separated by even a hair’s breadth;
throughout the ten ages of past and present, beginning and end do not shift from the present moment. It is thus in this very place.
The same is true for the ten lands. The assembly of sages is like gathering clouds; they enter one another in a great ocean-like congregation.
Wisdom and ignorance do not obstruct one another, resembling many mirrors that reflect all forms without mutual interference, or like a thousand lamps illuminating a single room.

Within the "Chapter on Manifestation," the sequence of cause and effect is shown to mark the beginning and end. At the Jetavana Garden, the luminous Dharma-realm benefits humans and devas; Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra [are present].
While separated by sight and sound from those facing him, six thousand bhikṣus on the road were enlightened by the Ten Clarities.
At the eastern outskirts of the City of Awakening, the five groups of practitioners all arrived; before the temple of the Ancient Buddha, they collectively ascended to the Ten Wisdoms.

With Sudhana as the guide who illuminated the path, he manifested the brilliance of the assembly’s collective realization. Reaching the Dazhong era, the śramaṇa Zhining of Kaiyuan Temple in Fuzhou once again...

In his *Lunru Jing* (Discourse on Entering the Sūtras), he further states: "The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* was certainly not compiled by Arhats, nor was it transmitted and upheld by those of lesser saintly attainment.
The Great Version of the *Avataṃsaka* cannot be known or seen by anyone other than a Buddha. The Middle Version of the *Avataṃsaka* is known only by Bodhisattvas dwelling in the stages (*bhūmi*).
The Small Version of the *Avataṃsaka*, consisting of one hundred thousand verses, is what has been transmitted today; of this, only forty thousand verses have been obtained."

There are more than five thousand verses. The Sūtra says: "It is as if a person, through the power of transformation, were to manifest a Buddha; the manifested and the non-manifested are equal and without distinction.
All Buddhas who attain Bodhi—attainment and non-attainment are without differentiation. The youth Sudhana attained the Way in but a single lifetime;
six thousand bhikṣus developed wisdom without depending on many kalpas; the carriage of the white ox is about to awaken."
By this, one immediately transcends the Mahāyāna; the Golden World appears before one’s eyes, and the wisdom of Mañjuśrī is fully realized.

The Dragon Girl attaining Buddhahood in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* occurs in a mere instant. At Mount Wutai, one beholds the Buddha’s radiance and ascends to the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) at once.
During the Xinzhou period of the Great Tang, there was a lay elder named Li Tongxuan, who composed forty fascicles of a commentary on this sūtra. Zhi Ning read it.

This treatise captures the general meaning [of the sūtra]. Now, observing that the gentlemen of this land find it difficult to harmonize the treatise with the sūtra, I, Zhining, disregarding my own declining years, shall provide annotations to this treatise beneath the sūtra, so that those who read it in the future may [understand it clearly].

Without wasting his mental effort, as soon as he opened the sutra, he was able to see the treatise (*śāstra*). The commentary begins from the eighth fascicle of the treatise and is integrated into the sutra;
together, the treatise and the sutra comprise one hundred and twenty fascicles. Its seven fascicles of synoptic commentary are written and appended at the beginning.
Furthermore, in the year of Qiandé, the śramaṇa Huìyán composed a preface, stating: "This teaching is not [merely] that of the *Baiyan*..."
That which was compiled was the collection of Mañjuśrī, comprising three sections in total.
One section contains as many verses as there are atoms in thirteen thousand great thousandfold world systems and as many chapters as there are atoms in one four-continent world system.

Another section contains four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred verses and twelve hundred chapters. A third section contains one hundred thousand verses and forty-eight chapters. [These were] concealed.

It resided within the Dragon Treasury (Nāgārjuna’s collection) but had not yet spread throughout Jambudvīpa. When five hundred years remained from the end of the era of the True Dharma, the fourteenth patriarch, Nāgārjuna, accessed the divine ocean-treasury.
He observed that the first two sections were beyond the reach of worldly people, so he recited the latter section and brought it back to the Five Indias.
After being propagated for a thousand years, it was finally transmitted to China during the early Eastern Jin dynasty. The earth... [text fragment ends].
A miraculous spring gushed forth. During the Tang Dynasty, heavenly nectar descended. In the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong, there was a reclusive scholar named Li Tongxuan in Taiyuan.
He exhausted the true exegesis of the eighty-fascicle [Avataṃsaka Sūtra] and condensed the profound treatises of the forty scrolls.

By night, he wielded his divine pen, spreading the auspicious radiance of his jade-like teeth; by day, he explored the profound mysteries, moved by which a celestial youth provided him with meals. Zhang...
In the ocean of the Imperial Teaching, the heavens of its meaning are arrayed; within the Great Canon, there is no lack of anything.

There was the eminent monk Zhining, who, reflecting deeply upon the fact that later students find it difficult to fathom the abundance of the Dharma gates, combined the essential meanings of the sutras and treatises so they might complement one another.

However, as their categories were vast and prolific, he had not yet fully completed his critical appraisal. Having joined the itinerant community of monks to study with diligence, I have humbly examined his definitive conclusions. I venture...

I have sought out paper and brushes to rectify these omissions and oversights. I shall arrange the sūtras and śāstras to provide a clear overview, and manifest the teachings and principles so they may complement one another.

When the meaning is lucid and the prose refined, there is no need for a lion throne to embrace one’s volumes; when spiritual radiance and wisdom are ignited, why labor on Vulture Peak to seek a teacher?
Master Zhuo said: "The former Buddhas established the sūtras, and the later Buddhas composed the śāstras. Since the Buddha’s intent is unified, how could the sūtras and śāstras be at odds?"
He synthesized the treatises into a single work. The Buddha’s wisdom refined and categorized the sūtras and śāstras to establish their fundamental framework;
this was done solely for the convenience of future generations of Buddhists in their study and contemplation. How diligent he was in his efforts!

Yet, regarding the vastness of these one hundred and twenty fascicles, I fear that even all the worthy and saintly ones would never dare to treat them with casual ease. Since the end of the summer retreat, I have had the fortune to hear from Master Ning.

This is Yuan Wenwei. Having read the *Huayan He lun* (The Combined Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra) thoroughly once, he realized that no one explains the *Avatamsaka* as well as the Elder [Li Tongxuan].
Therefore, he has selected its most essential passages and recorded them here.

Should there be beings of great resolve who wish to ride the Tathāgata’s vehicle straight to the site of enlightenment, then these two hundred pages of concise and essential treatise are themselves the *Avatamsaka*.
The Dharma-realm is the treasury of all. One’s own mind is the wisdom of Vairocana Buddha; one’s own eyes are the fundamental wisdom of the Buddha Mañjuśrī;
one’s own body is the wisdom of Samantabhadra Buddha regarding the myriad differentiated practices; one’s own recitation is the voice of the Buddha;
one’s own hearing is the power of the Buddha Avalokiteśvara; one’s own speech is the Buddha opening the gate of non-duality; one’s own mindfulness...

These are the inconceivable supernormal powers of the Buddha; such sovereign merits belong entirely to the Buddha. How fortunate I am to have personally beheld him with my own eyes!—The Life and Deeds of the Venerable Li.
The Elder Li’s name was Tongxuan. His origins are not well known; when some inquired about his background, he would simply say he was a native of Cangzhou.
On the full moon day of the third month in the twenty-seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, carrying a staff and a satchel, he arrived at Tongying Township, forty *li* west of Yuxian in Taiyuan.
There was a village named Daxian where a man named Gao Shanu lived, who esteemed virtue and admired... [the text continues].
A gentleman, a senior official, visited his gate. Shan Nu gazed intently at the visitor’s majestic appearance and knew him to be no ordinary vessel.

He then bowed deeply with clasped hands to receive him, inviting him to return and dwell in peace. Every morning, he consumed nothing but ten dates and a single small cake made of cypress leaves, about the size of a spoon.
From then on, he did not associate with outsiders; he remained alone within his chamber. Holding his brush and facing his desk, he never let a moment pass in vain.
In this manner, three years passed. One day, he left Mount Shanu and traveled south for five or six *li* until he reached the ancient Buddhist hall of the Ma family.

There, he constructed a mud hut for himself and took up residence beside it. He remained there in quiet seclusion for another ten years. Later, once again carrying his scriptures and books in a sack, he set out along the road.
After traveling more than twenty *li*, he arrived at the secondary estate of the Han family, which is the present-day Guange Village.
Suddenly, he encountered a tiger blocking the path, crouching submissively as if waiting for something.
The Elder said to it, "I am about to compose a treatise to explain the Avataṃsaka Sūtra; you may choose a place for me to dwell. Having finished speaking, the tiger rose.
The Elder slowly stroked it and hung the bag he was carrying upon its back, letting it stay wherever it pleased. Thereupon, the tiger—
Looking toward the foothills of Mount Shenfu, he traveled directly downward for more than thirty li until he came before a clay grotto, where he immediately halted and crouched.
The elder then gathered his belongings and placed them inside the grotto; the tiger looked back several times, tucked its tail neatly, and departed.

This grotto was brilliant and pure, circular in shape, and measured ten to twelve feet in both width and length; it existed spontaneously and was not created by human labor. On all four sides of the grotto...
Originally, there were no springs or streams. On the very evening the Elder first arrived, a violent storm of wind and thunder broke out, uprooting an ancient pine tree over three hundred feet high.
By dawn, the spot beneath the roots of the pine had transformed into a pond, several fathoms deep and spanning more than fifty paces in circumference.
Its sweetness surpassed that of auspicious dew, and its color rivaled lapis lazuli. The people of the time called it the "Elder’s Spring. Until now...
Now, it is clear and bright, never having increased or diminished. In years as numerous as the suns and moons, prayers to it are invariably answered.

On the evening when the Elder composed his treatise, his mind plumbed the profound mysteries, and white light issued from his mouth, illuminating the interior of the niche in place of lamps and candles.
After he had resided in the mountains, two women suddenly appeared; their beauty was peerless in the world, both of marriageable age and both dressed in coarse cloth garments.
They all wrapped their heads with white cloths and said nothing regarding their surnames or dwellings. They constantly drew water and burned incense for the elder, providing paper and brushes.
At the juncture between the hours of the Rabbit and the Dragon, they would invariably prepare pure offerings, fully equipped with sweet delicacies, which they placed before the elder.

Once the meal was finished, they would remove the vessels and vanish, no one knowing where they went. This continued for five years without a single lapse in timing. When it came to [the time of] writing...
As the treatise was nearing its conclusion, [the monks] suddenly vanished from sight. I have carefully consulted the old records of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra:

when the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra of the Eastern Jin dynasty was translating the scriptures at Xie Sīkōng Monastery in Jiangdu, two youths dressed in green robes suddenly emerged from the pond in the courtyard.
They attended upon the foreign monk, burning incense and refilling the vases without leaving his side. Whenever evening approached, they would return.

He remained submerged in the marsh day after day, making this his constant practice. When the translation was completed and the manuscript had been transcribed with purity, he vanished silently without a trace.
The elder felt a profound resonance with this event, which accorded with what had occurred in the past. The elder stood seven chi and two cun tall; he had broad eyebrows and bright eyes.
His lips were vermilion and his flesh was purple-hued; his long beard was luxuriant and beautiful. His arms were long and straight, and the color of his hair was deep blue-black.

The tips of his body hairs curled to the right; his physical form was peerless, and his demeanor was extraordinary. There was no sublime mark that he did not fully possess. On his head he wore a crown of birch bark, and his body was draped in garments of hempen cloth.
He wore a long skirt with wide sleeves, which hung loosely from his waist as he walked, and he was without a leather belt. This was his usual appearance.
He walked barefoot and did not concern himself with welcoming or seeing off others. He roamed freely among humans and devas, unrestrained by any limitations.
One day, he suddenly left the mountain and visited a village at his former site. It happened that the villagers were gathered there for a communal feast and music.

The Elder addressed them all, saying, "May you dwell in peace; I am about to depart. The crowd then ceased their music and looked upon one another in startled alarm, all feeling deep compassion and sorrow, certain that—
The elder returned to Cangzhou. Shedding tears and speaking with one voice, they earnestly entreated him to remain.
The elder said, "Even if I were to live for a hundred years, I must eventually return. Thereupon, the entire assembly escorted him back into the mountains.

Upon reaching his meditation cell, he spoke to them again, saying, "Departing and staying are simply the natural course of things. You may each return home. As the multitude followed one after another, [the elder passed away].
A thick mist rose from all sides, obscuring the landscape so that the features of the scenery could not be distinguished. All those traveling on the road were struck with wonder and alarm.

On the following day, Chōso gathered his disciples and ascended the mountain to pay their respects; they found him sitting upright and solemn within his shrine, having already passed away through meditative transformation.
This occurred on the twenty-eighth day of the third month; he was ninety-six years of age. A giant serpent was coiled outside the shrine.
The serpent opened its eyes wide and gaped its mouth; it was not to be approached. The multitude then returned with sincere devotion and offered their prayers:
"We now wish to collect the entire body of the Elder and prepare for his interment. We beg that you withdraw your divine majesty so that we may complete this task.

Thereupon, the serpent withdrew its form and did not appear. The elders and the aged wept as they carried the remains on a litter. They selected a site on the northern slope of a great mountain and piled stones to form a tomb. This was the shrine.

The Fukuyama Jetavana Hermitage is the present-day Fangshan. When the Elder first passed away and his tomb was completed, smoke and clouds gathered and spread, and the cliffs and valleys shook and trembled.
Two white cranes wailed mournfully in the sky, and two deer called out to one another throughout the night;
other birds and beasts filled the mountains with their cries of grief. The people of the local villages led one another in transformation [of their ways].

In mourning, he pursued [the memory of his father] with childlike longing, as if he had lost his very lord of heaven. Whenever a ritual fast (*zhāi*) was established, clouds would immediately rise above the tomb;
this occurred thus for seven weeks. On the sixth day of the second month in the ninth year of the Dali era, there was a monk named Guangchao at the Jetavana Hermitage.
He obtained two treatises authored by the Elder [Xuanzang]: the first is the *Da fangguang fo xin huayan jing lun* (Treatise on the New Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha) in forty fascicles;

the second is the *Shier yuan sheng jie mi xian zhi cheng bei shi ming lun* (The Ten Illuminations: A Treatise on Resolving Delusion regarding Dependent Origination to Reveal Wisdom and Accomplish Compassion) in one fascicle.
He transcribed and propagated them throughout the regions of Bingzhou and Fenzhou. Guangchao’s disciple Daoguang was able to carry on his master’s legacy, shouldering these two works.

The treatise was circulated throughout Yan and Zhao and clearly displayed in the Huai and Si regions, enabling students of both the northern and southern traditions of later generations to fully engage with its critical arguments and receive its doctrinal transmission from these masters.
All of this was due to the merit of the two monks, Chao and Guang, in disseminating it. Recently, the monk Yuanjian has observed this.
He traveled specifically to Mount Fang to seek out the remains of the Elder. First, he paid homage at the stone tomb; next, he sought out the foundations of the meditation cave.
In front of the cave stood three pine trees, all of which had been planted by the Elder’s own hand. In the month preceding the Elder’s passing, one of the trees withered;
of the remaining two, sacred cranes have constantly nested upon their tops to this day. Furthermore, he visited Jiechou Village on the southern border of Shouyang.
I encountered Li Shiyuan, who was the younger cousin of the monk Guangchao, the compiler of the *Huayan jing helun*.
He showed me a true portrait of the Elder [Mañjuśrī]; having paid my respects and returned, my aspirations were fulfilled.
This concludes the first fascicle of the *Jianyao* (Essential Summary) of the *Dafangguang fo huayan jing helun*, compiled by Mazhi, the Recluse of Yunju.
The Comprehensive Treatise on the Harmony [of the Teachings] by Li Tongxuan, Elder of Cangzhou during the Tang Dynasty;
the Simplified Exposition by Li Zhi, Elder of Wenling;
and the Collated and Verified Edition by Dong Guangshu, a Later Scholar of Wuxing.
First, clarifying the classification of schools based on the teachings; second, clarifying the distinctions between schools based on the teachings;
third, clarifying the differences in the meaning of the teachings; fourth, clarifying the similarities and differences regarding the attainment of Buddhahood;
fifth, clarifying the differences in the vision of the Buddha; sixth, clarifying the temporal periods of the proclamation of the teachings.
Seventh, clarifying the provisional and the real regarding the Pure Land; eighth, clarifying the realm of gathering and transforming;
ninth, clarifying the extension and brevity of cause and effect; tenth, clarifying the beginning and end of the assembly’s teachings.

First, clarifying the classification of schools according to the teachings: Now, when the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, his essence corresponded to the true source, wherein principle and phenomena...
There are two gates. First, the mutual penetration of manifold aspects: when wisdom and its objects are perfectly quiescent, what dharma is not encompassed?

It is only because vessels differ in their capacities that their ritual protocols vary; because their beginnings and ends, gradual and sudden approaches, follow different faculties, the established teachings are appropriately distinct as Great and Small Vehicles.
The timing of causes and effects differs in their duration; the manifestations and essential bodies of transformation Buddhas differ in the means they employ for instruction;

and the lands differ in their purity, defilement, increase, or decrease. Regarding the stages and the causes and effects therein, each has its own natural affinity. For those who have newly begun their studies and are not yet familiar with the traces of the teachings, [this distinction must be understood].

By adhering to the provisional, one achieves the ultimate; yet those who are deluded do not advance in their cultivation. If one does not fully set forth the various schools to illustrate their respective benefits and harms, there will be no means by which to understand the stagnation of such delusion.

Now, I shall briefly divide the teachings into ten categories to clarify and expound them, so that students may come to know the fundamental principles, transition from the provisional to the ultimate, avoid stagnation in their practice, and swiftly realize Bodhi.
A certain Hīnayāna precept sūtra takes the existence of sentient beings as its primary tenet.

It was taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of ordinary people engaged in the creation of karma, stating what should be done and what should not be done, and that to abandon [unwholesome acts] is good while not abandoning them is unwholesome.
Such an established teaching is not [ultimately] real; such a teaching merely concerns the realm of the false and deluded sentiments of ordinary people. It is asserted arbitrarily...
One calculates all evils and restrains them through the teachings, causing beings to be reborn among humans and devas. Therefore, the preface to the *Śīla* states:
"If one desires to be born in the heavens or among humans, one should always protect the feet of the precepts and not allow them to be damaged.
Because the conditioned activities of sentient beings are performed in vain and are not truly attained, birth among humans and devas is impermanent; it is vain and unreal.

Not having yet attained the Dharma-body or Wisdom-body, this is not a school that asserts [the self] as substantially existent; rather, it is a school that asserts [it] as existing by way of conventional cognition.

Within the Śrāvaka vehicle, it serves as the standard for upholding the teachings. This is not the case for the *Upāli-paripṛcchā* in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. As the Sūtra asks: "Is the body the holy life (*brahmacarya*)?
Is bodily action, the four modes of deportment, and even the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, the ten assemblies, the seven obstacles, and the preceptor [the holy life]?"
"Are the *karmavācanā* rituals, the maṇḍala sites, and so forth, the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*)? Thus one should observe with discernment.
For one who seeks the Brahma-faring, it is found to be ultimately unobtainable; therefore, it is called the "pure Brahma-faring," as explained in the *Brahmacarya-parivarta*.

Such a pure practitioner is said to uphold the precepts of the Buddha-nature, because they attain the Dharma-body of the Buddha; this is true even from the very moment they first resolve their mind toward enlightenment.
One attains perfect enlightenment, becoming equal in essence to the Buddhas. Principle and phenomena are equal, merging into the true Dharma-realm.
Maintaining the precepts in this way, one does not perceive a self that can maintain the precepts, nor does one perceive another who breaks them.
It is neither the conduct of ordinary beings nor the conduct of sages; one does not perceive a self that gives rise to the bodhicitta, nor does one perceive the Buddhas attaining equality.
Perfect Enlightenment: if there were even the slightest dharma to be grasped, whether good or evil, it would not be called bodhi, nor would it be called pure conduct.
One should contemplate in this way. Such intrinsic morality is the Dharma-body; the Dharma-body is the wisdom of the Tathāgata;
the wisdom of the Tathāgata is perfect enlightenment. Therefore, it is not the same as the Lesser Vehicle. There is...

Because of the principles of acceptance and rejection, the second [system] follows the Bodhisattva Precepts of the Brahma Net Sūtra; it takes both the conventional (情有) and the ultimate (真) as its thesis.
This was taught by the Tathāgata for those among ordinary beings who possess the great resolve, who delight in practicing compassion, and who joyfully seek the fruit of Buddhahood.

It is taught that Vairocana Buddha is the original body (dharmakāya), while the thousands of billions [of manifestations] are transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya). This immediately causes the derivative consciousnesses to return to their source.
As the *Sutra on the Practice* states: "If a person receives the Buddha's precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas; having attained a rank equal to Great Enlightenment," and so forth.
Truly, you are the children of the Buddhas. This is because it constitutes the precepts of nature (*dharmatā-śīla*); this is the True Doctrine.
This is the sudden revelation of the *dharmakāya*-precepts of nature for sentient beings of great resolve; those of inferior capacity attain them gradually. One teaching responds to two faculties.
In this manner, thousands of billions [of emanations] each receive the dust-like multitude of beings. They all come to my abode, clearly abandoning the provisional to follow the ultimate.

Indeed, this constitutes the teaching of real existence (*dravyasat*). Nevertheless, although it establishes the doctrine of real existence, it differs from what is taught by Vairocana in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
This sūtra still proceeds according to the emanations of the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), only later arriving at the Original Body.

The principle of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*) is to suddenly reveal, all at once, the causal and resultant principles of the Great Wisdom Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), which is the original Dharmadhātu.
The facts are clearly manifest.
Regarding the teachings of the three types of *prajñā*, their primary purpose is to explain emptiness to reveal reality.

For those who, at the beginning, were taught the vehicles of the two *yānas* by the Tathāgata for the sake of ordinary beings among humans and devas, they remained attached to both principle and phenomena as being equally real; thus, they were unable to transcend hindrances. Therefore, the teaching of emptiness was expounded for them.
To destroy all attachments and fetters, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* teach eighteen kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

It is taught that all things—the Three Jewels of the world, the Four Noble Truths, the three periods of time, and so forth—are empty; even emptiness itself is empty, as explained at length in the sūtras.

This serves to clear away the obscurations such as ignorance and the karma produced by them. When ignorance is completely exhausted, all obstructions and karma cease to exist, and one attains the natural nirvāṇa (*prakṛti-nirvāṇa*).
It is naturally manifest; this constitutes true existence and is not termed the "School of Emptiness" (*śūnyavāda*).

Briefly citing ten categories will serve to understand the general outline.
First, the difference in the Teacher: this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* was preached by a Transformation Body Buddha (nirmāṇakāya-buddha), specifically one from the past.
The Buddha Prabhūtaratna has entered parinirvāṇa and come to bear witness to the realization of this sutra; thus, the Buddhas of the three periods of time all proclaim it together.

This is not the case with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, for its teaching lord is Vairocana himself—the true body of reality, wisdom, and principle—which is adorned by a body possessing the ocean-like merit of immeasurable marks.

The Buddhas of the three periods of time are of one and the same limit; they are at one and the same time within a single Dharma-realm. Their retributive marks are layered upon one another without obstruction.
Because the single limit of antiquity and the present is not comprised of the three periods of time, the ancient Buddha is not of the past and the present Buddha is not newly emerged.
As the nature and characteristics of fundamental wisdom are equal and its principle and phenomena are non-different from Suchness, this is the Original Buddha.

This explains the fundamental dharma. Because it involves the sudden reception of the great roots and is not a transformation Buddha, it is unlike the Lotus Sūtra, which features the parinirvāṇa of the ancient Buddha Prabhūtaratna and the appearance of the present Buddha to preach the Lotus Sūtra.

Second, regarding the distinction of emitting light: although the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* describes the emission of the fruit-light from the ūrṇā-kośa between the eyebrows, the realms it illuminates are stated to be only eighteen thousand lands, all appearing like gold;
thus, it remains limited and does not accord with the boundless, immeasurable, and inexhaustible.
It merely manifests the dharma of the fruit, without manifesting the stage of the cause. In the *Avataṃsaka*, however...
This scripture teaches the cause and effect of practice; it manifests the light of the Dharma, complete with the ten [stages] from beginning to end.

Regarding the distinctions between the three lands: when preaching the Lotus Sūtra, he transformed the world three times to make it a pure land, moved the devas and humans to other lands, and subsequently established the assembly gathered from other directions here, transforming this defiled [world].
Regarding the environment: it is made into a pure land. When the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is preached, this very Sahā world is itself the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmakośa-lokadhātu*).
Each and every world mutually contains and enters one another. As the sūtra says: "Each and every world fills the ten directions;
the ten directions enter into one without remainder. The worlds neither increase nor decrease."

It is thus because of incomparable merit. Furthermore, it is said that when the Buddhas attain enlightenment, they do so within the body of a single small sentient being and transform immeasurable multitudes;
yet that small sentient being neither knows nor perceives this. This is solely because ordinary beings and sages share the same essence (*dharmatā*) without any shifting or changing characteristics.
Within even a minute fraction [of a hair], self and other are of one essence, not a separate dharma.
The assembly of the *Avataṃsaka* shifts from the realms of humans and devas to reveal the pure lands.

Regarding the distinction between the four types of requests to the Dharma Master: when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was being taught, Śāriputra was the foremost among those who requested the teaching.
When the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* was being taught, the Buddha commanded Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra [to do so].
Bodhisattvas at each respective stage each proclaim the Dharma-gate of their own stage as the foremost of all teachings. The Buddha represents the dharma of fruition;
taking the fruition as the cause, he gives rise to the practice of great compassion and accomplishes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Since the essence of fruition is spontaneously realized, there is nothing that is not spoken. This is because the practice of great compassion arises from the non-conceptual fundamental wisdom. A.
The *Saṃghāṭa-dharmaparyāya* concerns the numerical laws of the world; it is vast and immeasurable, and is realized only by the Buddha.
It does not belong to the causal or resultant gates within the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*), but is a dharma-gate within the Buddha’s own stage, spoken by the Buddha himself.
The *Anuvyañjana-prabhāsa-guṇa-parivarta* is precisely the teaching of the Buddha-dharma that the Tathāgata himself proclaimed after having perfected his own cause and result.
Furthermore, it does not belong to the causal characteristics or the cause-and-effect within the five stages; this is called the "non-dual ignorance of the Buddha-fruit.
Apart from these two chapters of the sutra, all the remaining thirty-eight chapters are dharma-gates concerning the causal characteristics within the five stages.
Therefore, the Buddha did not speak of them himself, but rather entrusted them to the ten faiths, the ten abidings, and the ten... [practices].
Within the stages of the *caryā-pratipatti* (practice) and so forth, the Bodhisattvas speak for themselves, while the Buddha merely emits light to signify this.
When the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was being taught, there were no Śrāvakas or minor Bodhisattvas acting as the masters who requested the Dharma;

rather, it was entirely the great Bodhisattvas within the stage of Buddhahood who engaged in mutual question and answer to establish the characteristics and modes of the Dharma-gates of the fruit of Buddhahood.
For the sake of those with great faculties who seek awakening, the fruit of Buddhahood is directly taken as the cause all at once.

Thus, the cause takes the fruit as its cause, and the fruit takes the cause as its fruit. This is like various seeds; it can be seen by contemplating this through the power of concentration and wisdom.
The five great assemblies differ in their true and manifested aspects.
For example, at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the trichiliocosm is made pure and adorned, and all manifested beings fill it;
the Buddhas who come are all said to be manifestations. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* is not like this; rather, there are ten locations and ten assemblies, each filled with a multitude.
The ten directions, without shifting from their original locations, fill the Dharma-realm. Within each physical form and every pore of the body, world-systems multiply in successive layers;
the bodies of Bodhisattvas and Buddhas interpenetrate one another, and beings of various species likewise encounter no obstruction.
Body and land interpenetrate like reflections containing one another. The assembly that has come does not impair the Dharma-body.

Yet, the marks and embellishments of the body of marks and the marks and embellishments of the Dharma-body are of one limit and without difference; thus, the marks are entirely true and there is no transformation.
This is not like other teachings, which speak of both the transformed and the real, with their characteristics intermingled.
Within the sixfold introductory section, the various members of the assembly are enumerated. In the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, first the assembly of twelve thousand śrāvakas is listed;
next, Mahāprajāpatī with her retinue of six thousand is listed—these are the six thousand nuns who were her maternal aunt; and next, the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā is listed.
This refers to the consorts of the Buddha when he was a crown prince. When the Buddha was a crown prince, he had three consorts:
the first was named Gopī, the second Yaśodharā, and the third Manorathapriyā.
Following this, the eighty thousand bodhisattvas are listed together, followed by the various devas, nāgas, ghosts, and so forth. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, however, is not like this.
First, the foremost bodhisattvas are listed, numbering as many as the atoms in ten buddha-worlds, without counting their attendants.
Next, the assembly of Vajrapāṇi spirits is listed, followed by the various classes of deities, nāgas, devas, and so forth.
In total there are fifty-five assemblies. Each group follows [the Buddha], with numbers as vast as the atoms within a Buddha-world.
A single body takes the Dharma-realm as its measure; the distinction between self and other is entirely extinguished.
The Dharma-realm is itself the self, pervading everywhere; all conceptualizations of subject and object are severed.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* distinguishes itself by stating that the seven dragon girls transformed their bodies and attained Buddhahood;
in a single kṣaṇa, they changed from female bodies, perfected the bodhisattva practices, and became Buddhas in the southern direction. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, however, is not like this.

Provided that one is personally free from emotional views, great wisdom will become ever more luminous; thus, the essence of the myriad dharmas is true, devoid of any characteristic of transformation.
In the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, Śāriputra said to the goddess: "For what reason do you not transform this female body?"
The goddess said to Śāriputra, "For twelve years I have sought the mark of a woman, yet it is utterly unfindable.
What, then, is there to transform? As the daughter Antimatī said to Śāriputra: 'He is born as a man, and I am born as a woman.
One should know that all phenomena are from the beginning such in their essential nature; what is there to transform? [This concludes] the entry into the Dharma from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
In the "Chapter on the Realms" (Dhātuparivarta), there are fifty-three spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) encountered by the youth Sudhana:
Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, elders (gṛhapati), youths, upāsikās, maidens, sages (ṛṣi), and non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika).

Each and every one is fully endowed with the practices of a bodhisattva and is personally possessed of the Buddha-dharma. According to the various sentient beings who perceive his body differently, it is said that there is no transformation.
If one observes with the Dharma-eye, there is nothing mundane that is not true; if one observes with the worldly flesh-eye, there is nothing true that is not mundane.
By means of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, one contrasts this with the provisional teachings where the three faculties perceive only the superficial.

As for "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*): it causes the seeds of faith to be perfected; furthermore, by swiftly transforming the marks of a woman so that she attains Buddhahood, it inspires a sense of wonder, whereby one finally gives rise to the aspiration to advance toward true knowledge and vision.
Clearly, it employs the three provisional means to lead one back to the single reality.

Moreover, it shatters the fixed attachment to the time-periods of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, causing one to realize the nature of the three periods of time in a single *kṣaṇa*. It tears asunder...
He casts aside the net of views of the three vehicles and spreads the thatched hut of the bodhisattva, causing them to return to the gate of the *dharmadhātu* and enter the true abode of the Buddha.
Thus, he causes the dragon girl to attain Buddhahood, clarifying that this was not achieved through long cultivation in the past;
she was only eight years old. Furthermore, this signifies that it was not through ancient study, for the transformation from female to male occurred in no more than a single *kṣaṇa*. It is complete.
Practicing for the fruit of Buddhahood, not lacking even a hair’s breadth of thought—such is the nature of the Dharma. Its own essence is timeless;
yet those who study through provisional means are separated from it by their own views. Deluded regarding the reality of the Dharma, they conversely call it "transformative" (provisional).
Unaware that their own fundamental essence is thus, they remain entirely within the house, still harboring obstructed views. How can they point distantly toward the Sangha from outside the realm?

"Only [if you do so]. This view does not depart; it will certainly remain in opposition for eternal kalpas. Only when the mind turns back and the view is extinguished will one finally return to the original dwelling.
Why not now extinguish the karma of all views? It would be a waste to undergo the toil and hardship of many kalpas before turning back.

As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* explains in the Gate of the Dharmadhātu’s Dependent Origination: the single reality of ordinary beings and sages still exists as long as there is the separation of views. As long as views persist..."
In all cases, when deluded emotions cease, one is the Buddha; there is not a single dharma that possesses a characteristic of transformation.
Therefore, this is not like the Dragon Girl who transformed her body to become a Buddha.
Furthermore, the land where the eight dragon girls became Buddhas is distinct; it is called the Immaculate World in the South.

"This is not this Sahā world. The commentary explains: Because the mind has attained *āryasatya* (the truth of the noble ones), it is called "stainless" (*vimala*). Because it correctly accords with original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣā*), it is designated as the South.
The South represents *li* (separation); within *li* there is emptiness. Among the Eight Trigrams, *li* corresponds to the mind. Because the mind is empty and non-substantial, it is luminous.
If one were to actually dwell in the southern direction, self and other, this and that, would still remain separated. This, however—

It is like following the three vehicles (triyāna) to gradually guide those with provisional capacities toward faith and understanding, so that they may eventually return to the Buddha-vehicle (buddhayāna).
Because the force of their remaining attachments to the three vehicles is difficult to overcome, they first achieve a partial turning of the mind;

yet, as their attachment to self and others has not been severed, this differs from the *Avataṃsaka*, where self and others are mutually pervasive, such that within every single atom one abides in the cause [of Buddhahood].
This is the gateway of the Indra’s Net.
The assembly of nine thousand six hundred individuals distinguished themselves by generating the resolve for enlightenment.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that when the Dragon Girl attained Buddhahood, the Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas of the Sahā world—all members of the assembly—beheld from afar the Dragon Girl attaining Buddhahood, universally [benefiting all].
At that time, the humans and devas in the assembly listened to the Dharma and their hearts were filled with great joy; they all paid homage from afar.

This, however, merely accords with the provisional learning of the three vehicles regarding conditioned bodhi; they have not yet attained the universal gate of the dharma-realm, nor have they awakened to the fact that self and others are of one essence.
For this reason, there is such remote prostration. In the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, it is not so.

By means of the universal gate of the Dharma-realm, the Dharma-gate of universal vision, the sphere of the Tathāgata-garbha-body samādhi, and the Indra’s net-adorned Dharma-gate, they simultaneously attain the swirling world-oceans and the successive layers of wondrous wisdom.
This is because one realization is the realization of all, and one abandonment is the abandonment of all; thus, it is the realization of their own very selves.
Within, there are ten bodies of Buddha-lands as vast as oceans, adorned with all manner of splendors. Within the Buddha-body, the realms of one's own body appear and vanish in successive layers.
It is the natural law of the worlds of the ten directions to be thus; it is like the many rivers flowing toward the great ocean.
Although they have not yet entered the sea, their moistening nature does not differ; once they enter the great ocean, they all become equally salty.
Taste. All sentient beings are likewise thus. Although there is a distinction between delusion and awakening, the ocean of Buddhas from the very beginning is fundamentally no different.
Why is it that in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the multitude of this Sahā world offers respectful salutations from afar?
This matter of ritual and dharma-protocol is entirely distinct from that of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. It is just like the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Within this chapter, the assembly of six thousand attained tenfold clarity of vision in a single kṣaṇa; five hundred youths realized ten bodies in one lifetime.
Principle and phenomena pervade each other equally, such that there is no dharma that does not manifest. Since the dharma-realm resides within a single atom, [all things are revealed therein].
How could there be such remote veneration?

In the *Daśa-śrāvaka-vyākaraṇa*, the Śrāvakas receive distant prophecies. Within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Dragon Girl instantaneously seals the gate of the Dharma-realm that is timeless, fully manifesting the fruit of Buddhahood.
Although those of the three vehicles who follow provisional teachings possess hearts of faith and compliance, they remain [otherwise].

As the winds have not yet been extinguished, one cannot realize sudden enlightenment; it is only after distant kalpas that one ascends [to the fruit], and thus receives a prediction of future attainment.

This differs from the *Avataṃsaka*, where delusion is immediately the state of an ordinary person and awakening is immediately Buddhahood. Even if residual habits remain, they are treated by means of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
without the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, one merely achieves suppression and cannot enter the swift current of the Buddha.

[They] flow [on]. It is only after passing through distant kalpas that they are able to enter. Because the roots of faith of those who have newly set out on the three vehicles are inferior, they cannot free themselves from bondage;
their entrapment is manifold and they delight in attachment to birth and death. Although they seek transcendence from the world, [they remain bound].

Those of inferior faculties remain stagnant and regress. Thereupon, the Tathāgata causes them to contemplate through such observations as birth, old age, sickness, death, impermanence, impurity, momentary destruction, and the non-abiding of every thought-moment, so that they may give rise to wearying detachment (*nirveda*).
Once the mind of wearying detachment is accomplished, the mind abides amidst both the pure and the defiled. Thus does the Tathāgata act within his transformative teachings.
Within this [process], one further diligently cultivates compassion and wisdom to seek the fruit of Buddhahood.
Yet, because those of the three vehicles have not yet eliminated their discriminative views, they perceive this Sahā world as perpetually defiled;

thus, by explaining the causes and effects [of purification], their doubts are dispelled, and it is temporarily transformed into a pure land. Once the transformative power is withdrawn, they shall again see it as it truly is.

Defiled by this, their wisdom regarding the contemplation of impermanence is habitually difficult to redirect. Although the Dragon Girl was suddenly shown the Buddha-vehicle, despite her faith she was unable to realize it immediately.
For this reason, within the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, she received a prediction of future enlightenment.
All have been sheltered for distant eons, gradually drawn back by the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* until they return [to the truth].

Because the *Avataṃsaka* at that time directly bestowed [the teaching] such that those who resolve their minds become Buddhas immediately, the modes of practice differ for these reasons. Within this single scripture, there are two gateways:
first, the One Vehicle, the Tathāgata Vehicle, which leads directly to the site of enlightenment. The Tathāgata Vehicle is precisely the One Vehicle.
As stated in the "Bhadrapāla Chapter" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "Among all the various classes of sentient beings in the world, few desire to seek the Śrāvaka vehicle;
those who seek the Pratyekabuddha vehicle are even fewer still; those who seek the Mahāyāna are extremely rare.
While seeking the Mahāyāna is still considered easy, being able to have faith in this Dharma is exceedingly difficult. Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "If there should be..."
To those sentient beings whose minds are weary and submerged, he teaches the path of the śrāvaka to cause them to leave behind all suffering.

If there are further sentient beings whose minds possess slight clarity and sharpness, he teaches the Dharma of causes and conditions (pratītyasamutpāda) to cause them to attain the state of a pratyekabuddha.
If there are further sentient beings who delight in training in a heart of loving-kindness and compassion to extensively benefit other beings, for them...

He speaks of the Bodhisattva path. Furthermore, for those sentient beings who resolutely delight in the Great Matter and who turn the inexhaustible Buddha-dharma, he speaks of the path of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
This is the meaning of the division into four vehicles within the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
As in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the three chariots before the gate merely demonstrate the provisional gate; it is only with the white ox in the open space that the ultimate truth is clarified.
The True Teaching: The Buddha Vehicle is exclusively one; there is neither two nor three.
The provisional schools outside the gates of the "two and three" reveal the true teaching of the open ground. The four vehicles are in accord, and the two teachings are common;
yet their established methods of transformation each have their differences. Furthermore, the Lotus Sūtra says: "This alone is the one true reality; the other two are..."

This is not the ultimate truth. Based on this single passage, it appears that the Three Vehicles are established; yet when one examines their underlying convergence, they actually constitute four dharmas.
"Only this one thing is real" refers to the reality of the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*).

"The other two" refers to the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna and, by extension, the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas—these being the "other two. This is because the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas resemble [the Bodhisattvas] in their weariness with suffering.

Therefore, furthermore, in a single kṣaṇa, the Dragon Girl seals the nature of the three periods of time; from the state of an ordinary person, she immediately becomes a sage without shifting by even a hair’s breadth. This is roughly the same as the dharma-gate of entering the Way through understanding and practice as exemplified by the youth Sudhana. That Sudhana attained Buddhahood in a single lifetime does not mean he was apart from the kṣaṇa-limit; it means he realized the nature of the three periods of time within that very moment. Thus it has been said of old: [The text continues with verses: "The kṣaṇa is the ultimate limit; Within this kṣaṇa, there is no distinction between past, present, and future. If one can enter the Way within this kṣaṇa, One will attain the fruit of Buddhahood. This is the meaning. It is not that the Dragon Girl did not become a Buddha after her death; rather, she attained Buddhahood within that very kṣaṇa. It is simply that the kṣaṇa is extremely subtle and difficult to perceive. Therefore, it is said that she attained Buddhahood after seven days. Furthermore, the Dragon Girl is a female, while Sudhana is a male; thus, their capacities differ. Moreover, the Dragon Girl was already a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage, whereas Sudhana was a beginner. Consequently, the Dragon Girl’s realization was swift, while Sudhana’s was gradual. It is for these reasons that they differ. However, both have attained the fruit of Buddhahood within a single kṣaṇa. This is because the nature of the three periods of time is originally non-dual.
