Now, to summarize: returning to the dragon girl, within a single kṣaṇa, she undergoes the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti), perfects her practice, and attains Buddhahood—all at once and entirely completed.
This accords with the fundamental Dharma; for such is the nature of the Dharma. As for the establishment of "time" and "kalpas," these are the mental objects of sentient beings.
When Sudhana realizes this, it is called "one lifetime," because the time and kalpas of the three periods have already been exhausted. Furthermore...
Because there is no further birth, it is called "one birth.
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* takes the protection of the True Dharma as its primary theme.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* takes Buddha-nature as its primary theme. It differs from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in ten ways.

First, regarding the distinction of the locations where the teachings were spoken: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was taught at the twin śāla trees on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River in the kingdom of Kuśinagara.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was taught at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in the kingdom of Magadha, beneath the precious bodhi tree.
Second, the distinction between the adornment of the objective realm and the transformation-retribution [bodies].
When this *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* was being preached, the great bodhisattvas from all the Buddha-worlds all gathered for the assembly. Furthermore, the text states:
"At that time, by the spiritual power of the Buddha, the ground of the trichiliocosm became entirely soft and supple, without any mounds, ravines, sand, soil, or gravel."
[It is] free from stones, thorns, and poisonous weeds, and adorned with various jewels, just like the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha Amitāyus in the Western Quarter.
When the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was preached, there were ten seas of lotus-treasury worlds;
such extensive descriptions of adornment are precisely the adornments of the Tathāgata’s own true retribution-body (*vipākakāya*), and are not like—
In this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, by means of the Buddha’s supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), the assembly is temporarily transformed and purified for the sake of sentient beings.
The reason for this is that the assembly gathered for this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* consists of a mixture of those with the faculties of the three vehicles (*triyāna*).

If it were not sustained by the Buddha’s supernatural power, they would have no way to perceive it themselves. This is unlike the *Avataṃsaka*, where the faculties of the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) are pure and uniform.
There is a mixed assembly. Just as with the śrāvakas, because their faculties differ, they have originally not been seen within this gathering.

Although [they are not seen] in the sūtra, there is nonetheless the power of the Buddha’s spiritual transformations, and furthermore, as the text below shows, there is the power of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Regarding what is called "divine" (shen): an Arhat is called divine; it is not that they are actually ordinary beings who have been granted a temporary vision and thus named "divine.

One should know that the Adornments of the Flower Treasury (Huazang zhuangyan), the Original Radiance, and the True Reward [Bodies] are the power of the Tathāgata’s spiritual efficacy (nirvāṇa-śakti) temporarily manifested through provisional means.

The assembly gathered for the three great assemblies was distinct. When this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra was preached, all those who had come were members of the human and celestial lineages belonging to the three vehicles, with the exception of the great bodhisattva assembly.
All others were mindful of the Tathāgata; their eyes filled with tears as they bore the fragrant firewood, lamenting in bitter sorrow and longing to serve him.
The Buddha-sun. The assembly that has gathered for the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* consists entirely of bodhisattvas within the stage of Buddhahood, all of whom are from the ocean of the nature-wisdom;
they are purely of the One Vehicle, with no other categories.

The multitudes of humans, devas, and gods are of identical root, having entered the flow of the Buddha’s wisdom and being endowed with the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Within this first assembly, there are ten Buddha-worlds.
The multitude of Bodhisattvas, numbering as many as atoms, are all born from the ocean of the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness.
This ocean of roots of goodness is itself produced by the great wisdom of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body wisdom-ocean.
All Buddhas are produced with the fundamental wisdom of the Dharma-body as their root. Were it not so, there would be no gateways of practice whatsoever.

All these belong to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Such a multitude, from their initial generation of the mind of awakening until their entry into the ocean of Buddha-wisdom, are provisionally assigned to the six stages of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, ten grounds, and the stage of Equal Enlightenment.
One should know that this assembly at the Nirvāṇa Sūtra—consisting of bodhisattvas of the three vehicles, śrāvakas, humans, devas, and others—is not the same as that in the *Avataṃsaka*. This is...
Within the stage of the One Vehicle, the assembly of bodhisattvas—beginning from the stage of the initial resolve—are all identical to the stage of the Buddha.
Entering the stream of the Buddha’s wisdom and sharing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, they are true children of the Buddha.
Fourth, regarding the distinction between the principal and the attendant deities of the established Wheel of Dharma:
the primary figures who requested [the teaching] at the beginning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* were Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Siṃhanāda Bodhisattva, Śāriputra, and others.
As for the leaders who requested the establishment of the Dharma’s standards, Māra Pāpīyān was the one who first entreated the Tathāgata to enter parinirvāṇa.
As for the leaders who established the Dharma in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, they were Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, Bodhiśiras,
Dharmamati, Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha, Vajradhvaja, Vajragarbha, and so forth— these ten leaders, representing the ten wisdoms.

The ten forests, ten banners, and ten treasuries—referring to the great bodhisattvas within the stage of Buddhahood—establish the dharma-gate of the formal characteristics of the five stages of Buddhahood.
This is because each stage is itself the Buddha, and the Buddha is himself each stage, clarifying that the fruit of Buddhahood exists within every stage.
Therefore, this is not the same as the case of Kāśyapa Bodhisattva in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The śrāvaka Śāriputra was born into a human family and manifested as one of the ordinary rank to lead those with the seeds of the three vehicles;
seeing the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he was moved by profound grief, his tears flowed until they filled his eyes, and he came to this assembly.

The assembly gathered from the five directions, having heard this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, consists of various śrāvakas, followers of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas of provisional teaching who practice various contemplative exercises (*vipaśyanā*) yet have not yet abandoned their attachments and hindrances.
They take pleasure in and cling to conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), grasping at the characteristics of these formations.
Regarding these characteristics, they are deluded concerning the unconditioned Dharma-body (*asaṃskṛta-dharmakāya*), which is fundamentally self-existent, without realization or cultivation.
This is the essence. For this reason, the Tathāgata, in this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, has taught that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent;
they are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing. Once arising and ceasing have ceased, cessation is bliss.

This is because the wholesome practices one performs and the bodhi one realizes are dharmas of arising, whereas the nirvāṇa realized is a dharma of cessation. Thus, when the mind dwells [in this realization]...
Subject and object arise and perish without ceasing; because they arise and perish without ceasing, one becomes obstructed by the true principle.

Therefore, it is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, and that the Tathāgata’s body is hidden and does not appear. When all subjects and objects of the mind are exhausted, this is called Great Nirvāṇa.
For this reason, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Cunda said to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī: "Do not..."

That is to say, the Tathāgata is identical to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, whether speaking with knowledge or without knowledge, one says that the Tathāgata is identical to all conditioned phenomena.

If one were to say that the Tathāgata is identical to all conditioned phenomena, then one could not say that he is the Sovereign Dharma-King among humans and devas within the triple world. This is so.

Therefore, the Great Parinirvāṇa causes those of the three vehicles to know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), bodhi, that which is capable of realization, and the nirvāṇa to be realized are all impermanent.
That which arises is fundamentally non-existent; one does not realize various cessations. It is called Great Nirvāṇa because it is without conditioned activity and without cultivation.
This is termed "Perfect Quiescence" (*parinirvāṇa*). As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding those who come from other directions:

O Assembly! The humans and devas of this land who have attained their places in this assembly, from the very moment they first resolved to attain enlightenment, have reached mastery over both principle and phenomena, and the non-obstruction between principle and practice.
They have simultaneously and instantaneously impressed the principle of Mañjuśrī and the practice of Samantabhadra, like a seal pressing into clay, without priority, sequence, or interval.
If there were any persistence of beginning and end, or cause and effect in a temporal sequence, these would all be [merely conventional].
All ordinary sentiments are characterized by arising and ceasing; they involve formation and destruction, and merely follow the faculties to break through attachments.
They do not pertain to the orthodox lineage of attaining Buddhahood. This *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is taught directly for those of the supreme, great mind.
It is like bestowing a precious throne directly upon an ordinary person; it is like a dream of a thousand years that vanishes as soon as one awakens; it is like *nirvāṇa*.
As stated in the Sūtra: On the Snowy Mountains there is a grass called "Fatty.
If a cow eats it, she produces only ghee, which has no colors—neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black. It is the same for those sentient beings of the supreme great mind:
they see the Buddha-nature instantaneously and immediately attain perfect enlightenment; they do not arrive gradually through minor stages. This is...
Therefore, the present statement regarding the assembly coming to hear the Dharma separately is based on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which subordinates the particulars to the essence;
it does not yet discuss how wisdom and compassion, as well as the ultimate and conventional truths, are employed together in unimpeded harmony.

The six realms of retributive lands differ according to whether they are pure or defiled. According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha’s retributive land is indicated as being located in the west, beyond Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of thirty-two Ganges Rivers; this is the retributive land of Śākyamuni.

Because those who study through the provisional teachings of the three vehicles have not yet eliminated the distinction between the defiled and the pure, they perceive this Sahā world as defiled, evil, and impure. It is for them that the Tathāgata [manifests] through skillful means.
It is indicated that the reward land (vipākabhūmi) lies to the west. As for the *Avataṃsaka*’s teaching of the ultimate dharma (nitārtha), it is this very Sahā world;
it is pure and stainless because, for the bodhisattvas of the ultimate teaching, defilement and purity have been completely exhausted, and thus their sphere of experience is purely immaculate.
Because Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings perceive impurity within their own stainless and pure realm, the Reward Land (Bhoga-kṣetra) is indicated as being in the West.
Regarding the distinction between the provisional and the real bodies of the Seven Buddhas, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Tathāgata possessing the thirty-two marks is [the provisional body].
Regarding provisional [truth]: the truth of perfect nirvana and quiescence is real, because all retributive marks and immeasurable adornments exist in dependence upon that reality.
As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when Vairocana Buddha’s thirty-two marks enter nirvana, both the Buddha and the marks are real.
Principle and phenomena are non-dual; they do not destroy the dharma-body, yet they follow along with phenomenal appearances.
The ocean is immeasurable and inexhaustible; it is simultaneously appearance, essence, retribution, and principle. Like light and its shadow, it is sovereign and unimpeded.
The eight [aspects] differ in their manifestations of birth, extinction, and nirvāṇa. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* was taught for the sake of all humans, devas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
The Tathāgata perceives that the two vehicles establish the eight phases of enlightenment, such as descending from Tuṣita Heaven to take birth and entering parinirvāṇa;

he likewise speaks for the sake of the Mahāyāna bodhisattvas, teaching that there is no descent from Tuṣita Heaven into the mother’s womb, but rather the eternal, blissful, self, and pure, which is without beginning or end, neither arising nor ceasing. Nevertheless...

Furthermore, he conceals his body and does not appear, yet still designates the land of retribution as being in the West, thereby treating this Sahā world as a transformation land (*nirmāṇakṣetra*) and a defiled realm.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is not like this; it directly reveals the fundamental body and the original dharma, transcending emotional views.
It is without beginning and without end, with the characteristics of the three periods of time severed. It is the single, perfect true retribution, neither arising nor ceasing.
Neither eternal nor annihilated, with nature and characteristics unimpeded, this dharma-gate of the ocean of sovereign fruition is bestowed directly upon those of the highest faculties.
It is not like the provisional teachings, which are accomplished gradually according to a sequence.
It is just as when one has ascended nine fathoms to the peak—one cannot sever one’s tracks; and for one who treads the tenth step of the ladder—one cannot lose its trace.
Traces. One commonly sees those of the first rank in official hierarchy, yet they are regarded merely as ministers.

Suddenly, there is one who ascends to the Nine-Five Throne; the bright pearl shines forth at once, illuminating everywhere without limit. Its bounty drenches the great ocean, every drop filling it to the brim.

Within the empty nature of a single speck of dust, the Dharma-realm is without differentiation. Sentient beings of various classes forcibly create attachments and constraints for themselves; their faculties and capacities are not equal, and thus expedient means are employed.

In truth, they are not the same. Since these teaching gates differ in a thousand ways and ten thousand variations, one must know the provisional and the real, recognize the false to cultivate the true, and must not remain long stuck in provisional schools while remaining deluded regarding the ultimate teaching.

Ninth, the distinction in the modes of instruction and practice: According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, even Bodhisattvas at the stage of the ten abidings (*daśabhūmi*) do not yet clearly perceive or see the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
From the stage of the ten abidings—following the ten levels of faithful mind of ordinary beings—they see it only partially and cultivate it gradually;
it is only within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) that the fruit and practice are finally perfected.

The stage of Perfect Enlightenment is precisely that of the Tathāgata. One should know that this sutra further contains the dharma-gates and spiritual dispositions of five vehicles, six vehicles, seven, eight, nine, and ten vehicles.
Excluding the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, there are three kinds of Bodhisattva vehicles;
when these are combined with those two vehicles, they constitute the five vehicles. Furthermore, including the human and celestial realms, [there are six].

The five precepts and the ten wholesome actions constitute the six vehicles and the seven vehicles. Furthermore, when those of the three vehicles hear [the teaching] together, each attains their own respective dharma;
when these are mutually integrated, there are nine vehicles. What are the three types of Bodhisattva vehicles? First, the vehicle of practicing the dharma-gate of non-self;
second, the vehicle of gradually perceiving the Buddha-nature from the ten abodes through the ten stages; third, [the vehicle of...]
It is like the fat and succulent grass of the Snowy Mountains: if a cow eats it, she produces nothing but *sarpis* (clarified butter).
It does not arise from milk, curd, or *maṇḍa* (fresh butter), but is gradually formed [from them]. As stated in the "Tathāgatagarbha" chapter:
once Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have realized their nature, they all say, "How marvelous, World-Honored One! We..."
They undergo immeasurable cycles of birth and death, constantly deluded and distracted by the notion of non-self.

This refers to what is taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*: that there are bodhisattvas who, throughout immeasurable kalpas, have cultivated the six pāramitās and attained the six supernormal powers;
they have recited and mastered the eighty-four thousand dharma-treasuries, yet they still do not believe this.
The profound sūtras provide examples of this. The supernormal powers they attain do not arise based on their inherent nature;
rather, through the cultivation of various virtues and the contemplation of non-self, they receive retribution as superior devas. They are also like the people of Uttarakuru in the north.
In previous lives, they also practiced the contemplation of non-self. As a result of that retribution, they were born in that land with a lifespan of a thousand years;
food and clothing appeared spontaneously. There was seven-inch *śāli* rice, which was cooked by fire-jewels. Wherever the fragrance reached, all came together to eat it.
Yet, there is no Buddha-dharma, and they do not attain liberation; this is entirely because their past conduct and understanding were erroneous, leading them to this state.
This is a matter of grave consequence. It ensures that what has been attained shall never be lost.

Thus, the dharma-gate of the Buddha-fruit following the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is precisely the point perceived by the initial mind of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
This refers to the grass of the Snowy Mountains called "Fatty. If a cow eats it, she produces only pure *ghṛta* (clarified butter), which possesses no green, yellow, red, white, or black colors.

It is as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: when a Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes first perceives the Way, they suddenly see that both self and others are from beginningless time without end, without past or present, and have been Buddhas from the very outset.
Because the nature and characteristics of body and mind are fundamentally Buddha, one takes this Buddha-gate as liberation.
Riding the Tathāgata-vehicle, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment. This includes the dragon girl, Sudhana, the ten thousand dragons, and the assembly of eight thousand;
as well as the six thousand bhikṣus, five hundred upāsakas, and five hundred upāsikās.
O youth, the five hundred maidens together become eight thousand, suddenly manifesting the five stages and collectively aligning with the gate of the Buddha-fruit’s wisdom and principle.
The first abode (*prathama-bhūmi*) is identical to the ten stages; the first abode is identical to the rank of Buddhahood.

If the first abode were not identical to the rank of Buddhahood, it would be like a minister of state who, from the first of the nine grades up to the attainment of the first grade, has merely attained [a title].
If one acts as a minister, one cannot be called a king.

If one is not called a king, you should know that this is a provisional teaching establishing the sequence of the five stages and the various grounds, ascending them one by one until the completion of the three great kalpas;
yet one remains merely a bodhisattva and is not called the Buddha-vehicle. One does not ride the Tathāgata-vehicle directly to the site of enlightenment; one merely...
Cultivating the contemplation of non-self and possessing compassion superior to that of the Two Vehicles, yet not yet seeing the Buddha-nature, is called being a Bodhisattva.
If one sees even a small portion of this nature, one also attains the Buddha Vehicle. It is like the great ocean:
whether it be a single drop of water or many drops, within each and every drop, the great ocean is present. Thus, within the five stages of the Bodhisattva, there are ten...
Abiding in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), within each and every stage there is the fruit of Buddhahood.

From the very beginning of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*) at the start of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*), one suddenly perceives such a Tathāgata-Dharmakāya—the fruit of non-active Buddha-nature wisdom—and universally practices all the myriad deeds of Samantabhadra.
Following conditions without obstruction, all are entirely non-active nirvāṇa. As the Sūtra says: "The Buddha..."
The nature is not something produced by conditioning; it is merely obscured by adventitious afflictions.
Therefore, from the first stage of the Ten Abodes onward, through the samādhi of non-action, its own essence accords with reality.

Since adventitious afflictions possess no inherent substance whatsoever, there remains only the true essence and function, free from greed, hatred, and delusion. Thus, one spontaneously becomes a Buddha in a single thought-moment.
It is through correspondence. To attain Buddhahood in a single thought-moment, one attains Buddhahood in a single day through correspondence;

why then must one practice gradually over the course of kalpas? Accumulating cultivation over many kalpas and reaching the fruit after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* involves the mind taking the measure of time as its object;
how can such seeing-obstructions ever cease? The Dharma-gates of all Buddhas are fundamentally not encompassed by time. Calculating time to establish kalpas is not the Buddha-vehicle.
Tenth, regarding the distinction between the initial [stage] and that of having a friend as a preceptor:
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is said that a youth from the Snowy Mountains encountered a rākṣasa and resolved his mind on awakening; he valued half a verse more than his own life.

Upon hearing that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing," he spoke of Buddha-nature and nirvāṇa, stating that they cannot be cultivated through practice nor realized by the mind. Not...
It can be practiced through cultivation; yet such practice is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and therefore impermanent.
It cannot be realized by the mind, for it involves the duality of subject and object. Therefore, one cannot cultivate its nature through practice, nor can one realize its principle through the mind.
This is because the mind is itself the nature, and there is no further distinction between subject and object. Thus, Cunda said: "Do not say that the Tathāgata..."
This is consistent with all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), as illustrated by the model established for the youth Sudhana in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
From his initial generation of the bodhicitta under Mañjuśrī until his final encounter with Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, each of the fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) states:
"I previously generated the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"O Mind! Why do you instruct me to study the Bodhisattva path and practice the deeds of a Bodhisattva, rather than teaching such matters as 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent' and so forth?
For what reason? Because this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* elucidates the gateway to the Dharma-realm of dependent origination, wherein principle and phenomena are non-dual;
there is no condition that is not quiescent, and no phenomenon that is not true. The realms of all lands are, in their entirety, of the nature [of the Dharma-realm]."
The ocean is the one true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), for it is not described as being either sentient or insentient according to karma.
Within the *Avataṃsaka*, it is the purely true realm, which is in its entirety wisdom (*jñāna*). Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes take wisdom (*prajñā*) as their realm;
bodhisattvas of the Ten Practices take knowledge (*jñāna*) as their realm; those of the Ten Dedications and the Ten Grounds take the sublime as their realm. It is not so described [here].
The distinction between the two views of the sentient and the insentient is clarified by using the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to manifest the fundamental Dharma.
This differs from the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, which hold that the insentient exist, while the sentient possess birth and extinction.
Therefore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the statement by the Snow Mountain Youth that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" is intended for those of the root-capacities of the Three Vehicles.

Those of inferior disposition and conduct, regarding what has been taught, calculate that their own practice constitutes the ultimate reality; thus they obstruct the nature of non-action and abandon the accord with true principle.
For this reason, it is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent.

This is not like Sudhana’s single thought-moment of generating the bodhicitta, which is suddenly free of subject and object, realizes the nature of the three periods of time, and whose nature transcends past and present, awakening to the fact that one's own mind is fundamentally [enlightened].

This coming is the Buddha. He does not achieve perfect enlightenment, nor does he realize bodhi. Regarding the nature and characteristics of body and mind, there is nothing to be realized or cultivated.
Being neither formed nor destroyed, it is originally thus. Following conditions, it moves or remains still; it does not destroy existence or non-existence.
All practices performed arise solely from wisdom. Therefore, it is not said that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
The *Daśamahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra* contains ten kinds of profound, vast, and incomparable teachings that distinguish it from all other sūtras.
If there are sentient beings of great resolve who generate deep faith in this Dharma-gate, [they shall attain liberation].
One does not read other sutras. At the initial moment of generating the mind of enlightenment, the very first stage of the Ten Abidings, one’s rank is equal to the fruit of Buddhahood.
As it is said in the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter: "Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas..."
One who practices the six pāramitās and cultivates the various factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma),
yet has not heard this Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable great majesty and power— or having heard it at some time, does not believe or understand it,
and neither accords with nor enters into it— is called a "nominal bodhisattva," because they are unable to be born into the family of the Tathāgata. However, if they should hear this...
Having heard this Dharma-gate of the Tathāgata’s immeasurable, inconceivable, unobstructed, and unhindered wisdom, one who believes, understands, accords with,
and enters into it should know that such a person is born into the family of the Tathāgatas and accords with the realm of all Tathāgatas,
just as the great ocean is the dwelling place of beings of immense body. This sutra is likewise supreme.
It is the dwelling place for sentient beings of the Great Mind; the dragons of marshes and ponds do not delight in residing there, just as the great ocean does not harbor corpses.

If there are those who see, hear, believe, and rejoice, they are able to awaken and enter [this state], forever leaving behind the corpses of ordinary people, those of provisional learning, and icchantikas.
They directly become one with the ocean of wisdom of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body. Furthermore, when the Tathāgata appears...
The *Prakaraṇa* (Chapter) says: "O Son of the Buddha, the voice of the Tathāgata is likewise. It is without arising, without activity, and without discrimination;
it neither enters nor exits. Yet, through the power of the Tathāgata’s merit and dharma, five kinds of vast sounds emerge.
What are these five? First: 'You should all know that the various activities (*saṃskāra*) of all sentient beings...'"

All these are suffering: the suffering of hell-beings, the suffering of animals, the suffering of hungry ghosts, the suffering of those lacking merit who are attached to "mine," and the suffering of committing various evil deeds.
Those who wish to be born among humans or devas should cultivate roots of goodness. Being born among humans or devas, they will leave behind all places of hardship.
Having heard this, sentient beings abandon their perversions, cultivate various virtuous practices, and depart from all places of hardship.
They are reborn among gods and humans. Second: "You should all know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are ablaze with manifold sufferings, like glowing iron balls.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are the law of arising and ceasing.

Nirvāṇa is quiescent, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), peaceful, and blissful, far removed from blazing flames and extinguishing all feverish afflictions. Having heard this, sentient beings diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas. Regarding sounds...
Regarding the Śrāvaka Vehicle: one attains the patience that accords with sounds; this is the Śrāvaka Vehicle. Thirdly:

"You should know that those of the Śrāvaka Vehicle understand according to the words of others; their wisdom is narrow and inferior. There is furthermore a superior vehicle called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, which awakens without depending on others;
you should study it. Upon hearing these words, those who delight in the superior path abandon the Śrāvaka Vehicle.

They hear the Way and cultivate the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas. Fourth: "You should know that beyond the stages of the two vehicles, there is a further superior path called the Mahāyāna, which is the practice of the Bodhisattvas;
it accords with the six pāramitās and does not cease the Bodhisattva conduct."
Not abandoning the bodhicitta, one remains amidst immeasurable births and deaths without weariness or fatigue; surpassing the two vehicles, this is called the Mahāyāna.
This is the Mahāyāna of the Bodhisattvas. Fifth: it is the foremost vehicle, the superior vehicle, the most excellent vehicle.
The Supreme Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, the Vehicle that Benefits All Sentient Beings.

If there are sentient beings who possess vast faith and understanding, whose faculties are sharp and keen, who have planted roots of goodness in the past, who are empowered by the spiritual power of all Tathāgatas, and who, possessing superior aspiration and joy, seek the fruit of Buddhahood—upon hearing this sound, they shall give rise to the bodhicitta. This is the Buddha-vehicle. The Buddha...
"O Son of the Buddha, the voice of the Tathāgata does not issue from the body, nor does it issue from the mind, yet it is able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.
O Son of the Buddha, this is the first characteristic of the Tathāgata’s voice; you should know that such is the voice of the Tathāgata."

Because it constantly accords with what the sentient beings of the five vehicles should hear, and because it is like the tide of the great ocean that never misses its time, one should therefore give rise to faith in this Dharma and resolve upon the Great Bodhicitta.

At the very beginning of the first stage of the Ten Abodes, one immediately perceives one's nature and gives rise to the wisdom of the Dharmakāya Buddha, thereby attaining perfect enlightenment; only then does wisdom arise from that nature.
The stage of wisdom involves performing various modes of practice to transform sentient beings; this is the Buddha of Perfectly Awakened Practice.
This differs from the provisional teachings, wherein one first performs the practices of a bodhisattva by studying provisional views such as "false" and "true" *tathatā*.

From the stages prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) through the ten grounds, there still exist obstructions to the ten *tathatās*; thus, what is perceived as *tathatā* according to one's own mental state becomes an obstruction to the practice being performed.
These practices are all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). The bodhicitta thus generated has not yet transcended arising and ceasing.
All discriminative ignorance that can be severed is suppressed through contemplation; only upon reaching the stage of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) can one perceive the nature.

Only after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* does one finally attain Buddhahood, and even then, one must undergo a further hundred kalpas of specialized cultivation to perfect the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*). If one were to take this Great Dharma...
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the fundamental vehicle of the Buddhas.

Those who follow it through its transformation bodies—whether among the superior, middling, or inferior streams of provisional practitioners—yet lack complete faith and understanding, remain far removed from the Buddha. Failing to comprehend the meaning of the sūtra, they will, throughout vast and long kalpas, never reach the time of attaining Buddhahood.
However, if those of the highest capacity believe and understand this sūtra, clearly knowing it to be unerring, then...

One shall mount the Tathāgata-vehicle and proceed directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). At the very moment of mounting it, that is itself the site of enlightenment; there is nothing further to be reached.
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, this is likewise the Buddha-vehicle.

It is the emanation-buddha who leads those of the three vehicles to realize the true Dharma—namely, the three vehicles consisting of the sheep-cart, the deer-cart, and the great ox-cart found before the gate of the burning house of the triple world.
As for the matter at hand: this refers to the three vehicles of superior, middling, and inferior faculties.

Because those of superior faculty possess a degree of compassion that surpasses the other two vehicles, yet because they contemplate only the conventional and have not yet attained the vision of reality, they are termed "untrue bodhisattvas."
These three types of individuals—those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties—all possess the suffering of the three realms.

Those of middling and inferior faculties, as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, loathe [the realms] and seek to escape them. Those of superior faculties, the bodhisattvas, feel weary of them yet do not abandon them;
because their compassion surpasses that of the two vehicles, they possess a mind intent on benefiting others. These three types of people alike do not know the three realms.
The essence and characteristics constitute the single true realm of the Buddha, as explained in detail in the "Appearance" chapter (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*).

Because the Buddha addresses those of provisional learning (*prajñapti-śikṣā*), he teaches that all the marks of retribution (*vipāka-lakṣaṇa*) among a Buddha's merits are produced through cultivation.

This causes those of provisional learning to apply themselves to mental cultivation (*manasikāra*), yet after many *kalpas*, they would ultimately have no prospect of attaining Buddhahood. Therefore, the carriage at the gate is a provisional manifestation (*upāya*) of the Buddha.
Only in the open field does the white ox clearly manifest the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The nature and characteristics of the Dharma-realm are fundamentally nothing but true wisdom;
all conceptual discrimination is merely the activity of that wisdom. Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:

"The various meanings of natures and characteristics—only I and the Buddhas of the ten directions can know these matters; the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the non-regressive bodhisattvas are entirely [unable to do so]."

They are unable to know this; these are precisely the three vehicles before the gate. Because they have not yet clarified that the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding, and that this is the established nature of phenomena (dharmasthiti-dharmatā);
because they all possess within the three vehicles a mind that seeks to weary of suffering and its accumulation while delighting in cultivating cessation and the path;

and because they have not yet clarified that suffering and its accumulation fundamentally arise only from ignorance, nor understood that cessation and the path are fundamentally without cultivation or fabrication.
There is no deliberate effort. To transform all classes of beings, one dwells in the world like an illusion; because one's nature is utterly free from ignorance, this is itself Buddhahood.
One moment of resonance is one moment of Buddha; one day of resonance is one day of Buddha. Why need one laboriously endure for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*?
Simply by realizing for oneself that the karma of the triple world can be emptied at its source, one spontaneously receives and brings forth sentient beings—this is itself Buddhahood.
Indeed, "Buddha" means "Awakened. One awakens to the true nature of karma; karma is without arising or ceasing, without attainment or realization, neither emerging nor submerging.

Its nature is without change; it has been thus from the beginning. Because this is itself the Buddha, one follows conditions within the six realms to practice the bodhisattva path, employing transformative supernatural powers to guide the stream of deluded beings. The Buddha is not a mere transformation. (From the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*)
It is said: Although he has attained perfect enlightenment and turned the wheel of Dharma, he does not abandon the path of the bodhisattva; for this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Thus, with this initial mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), Sudhana [sought instruction] at the foot of Mount Megha on Mount Sumeru from the bhikṣu Meghashiri.
One attains the Dharma-door of the Wisdom-Light of Universal Vision, which encompasses the spheres of all Buddhas, and thereby immediately achieves perfect enlightenment.
Only thereafter does one go to one's companions to seek the Bodhisattva path and practice the Bodhisattva deeds.

One should know that at the very moment the essence and function of perfect enlightenment are realized, the mind is in a state of non-action; since this is itself the Buddha, there is no need for further cultivation.
Even if his practice were to reach fulfillment, it would not differ from the present state.

This is like when a transformation Buddha displays the signs of attaining enlightenment—such as practicing austerities on hemp and wheat, shaving his hair, donning robes, and discarding all ornaments to sit upon grass—these acts are performed to transform non-Buddhists who delight in asceticism and those among the three vehicles whose faculties are lax.
The Buddha has already reconciled this within the sutras.
The Buddha does not require such practices as these for himself; for one who is free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*), why would such things be necessary?

When the Buddha of the nature of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) is entrusted to a single thought-moment and wisdom manifests before one, being without attainment or realization—that itself is Buddhahood.
For example, it was only after Sudhana had realized awakening that he sought the Bodhisattva path and practiced the Bodhisattva deeds. Why was this so? It was because...

Only after awakening to the Way is one fit to enter the bonds of the world; dwelling within those bonds without being fettered, one is then able to preach the Dharma for sentient beings to untie their bonds.
If one were oneself bound, it would be impossible to untie the bonds of others. Although there is a sequence of before and after in preaching, the Dharma itself is timeless.
Therefore, you should know that if you wish to practice the bodhisattva path, you must first achieve perfect enlightenment. Question:
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). The three vehicles before the gate are the great ox-carts; [this sūtra] provides the white ox-cart in the open air.
Since both are oxen, what difference is there between them? The answer is: the three vehicles before the gate are presented in contrast to the suffering of the triple world.

Furthermore, they cause [beings] to leave the burning of the fire-house, temporarily escaping the calamity of fire. Bodhisattvas of the provisional Mahāyāna teachings delight in practicing compassion and possess the will to benefit others;
though they have escaped the calamity of fire themselves, they do not leave the triple world.

Possessing even a partial resolve to deliver sentient beings, they surpass the two vehicles which seek only their own liberation. Because they attain even this one portion of the mind that carries [others across], it is so named.
It is called the "Great Ox" because it is vast in comparison to the two vehicles. One attains Buddhahood only upon seeing the nature at the tenth stage;

even after passing through many kalpas, one can finally become truly [enlightened]. Therefore, in comparison to those two vehicles, this is merely called the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna, not the Buddha-yāna.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The Buddha-vehicle is only one; there is no second, nor is there a third. This means that those of the three vehicles are all led back to the single vehicle.
Although followers of the Small Vehicle possess the faith and permission to attain Buddhahood, it is somewhat difficult for them to transform their habitual tendencies;

therefore, [the sūtra] designates a period of distant kalpas. Yet, the Dragon Girl attained the Buddha-vehicle in the mere twinkling of an eye, which clearly demonstrates true realization—realizing that suffering itself is the truth.
Because there is nothing to be weary of. For this reason, the vehicle at the gate is established in contrast to the Three Vehicles;

the white ox in the open space clearly illustrates reaching the place of non-reliance. "Open space" (lùdì) is precisely the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*), because the Buddha-wisdom has no point of support.
Therefore, it is said that the white ox in the open space is the Dharmakāya, which is [the union of] compassion and wisdom. Since the Dharmakāya is without...
The mark is called "white. Wisdom that observes the capacities of beings and compassion that rescues all things is called the "ox," because it is like an ox capable of carrying a load.
It is metaphorically likened to an ox because the Dharma-body of non-conditioned activity uses both compassion and wisdom to rescue all things.

The ox at the gate represents one who contemplates emptiness with increasing excellence; yet, as the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are not yet complete, they have not seen the Buddha-nature and have not attained realization.
The fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya is not described as "white," nor is it described as being "in the open air.

This is because, while relying on provisional *tathatā* (suchness) and the contemplation of emptiness, the mind still has something upon which it depends; thus, it is not called white. Because there is still something upon which it depends, it is not said to be in the open air.
Although one may turn the mind to believe in this One Vehicle, even upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, one has still not yet fully attained it. However—
They followed the Buddha’s words and believed them accordingly; however, because their minds had not yet established firm faith, they returned to seek the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
As they did not yet dare to rejoice in the Great [Vehicle], the Buddha then enticed and guided them to establish the power of faith, giving them great chariots equally.

Thus it is said: "These were not what I expected, yet now they are all given to me. This clarifies that those who turn their minds from the three vehicles are like the ox-carts at the gate. It is not...
It says it is white in color, but does not say it is adorned because it is subject to outflows (*sāsrava*).

This is not like the vehicle of the white ox in the open air, which is described in full detail regarding its height, breadth, adornments, and so forth; this [vehicle] is entirely distinct and different from the vehicle in the open air at the entrance.
Second, clarifying the distinctions according to the teachings of the religious schools: When the Great Awakened One appeared in the world, he exercised mastery through true wisdom;
his Dharma-body was boundless, and he shared the same essence as all classes of beings. He manifested forms according to their capacities and bestowed teachings in accordance with their faculties.
Like an echo in a valley, sound is produced by striking; yet the echo has no mind and no location. The Tathāgata’s establishment of the teachings is likewise so.

It is so. For instance, the teaching of Vairocana is without beginning and without end; it accords with the nature of reality (dharmatā) and is without fixed direction; it is uninterrupted and unceasing.

According to the various capacities of sentient beings, they perceive for themselves the beginning and end of the Buddha’s life—his entry into the womb, his renunciation, his preaching of the Dharma, and his entry into final nirvana.

In reality, however, the Tathāgata is fundamentally not like this; it is merely that, within a single kalpa, he appears both in commonality and in difference, established according to these provisional distinctions.
The ten teachings of Master De: First, Bodhiruci of the Later Wei established the teaching of the single sound (*ekasvara*).
Second, Paramārtha Tripiṭaka Master of the Chen dynasty established the two teachings as being simultaneous. Third, the Vinaya Master Guangtong of the Later Wei established three types of teachings.
Fourth, Dharma Master Dayan of the Qi dynasty established four types of teachings. Fifth, Dharma Master Hushen...
First, the establishment of five types of teaching. Second, the simultaneous establishment of four teachings by Master Tanyue (Zhizhe) of Nan Yue during the Chen dynasty.
Third, the establishment of four teachings by Dharma Master Wonhyo of Silla (Haidong) in the Tang dynasty, who also composed commentaries on this sutra.
Fourth, the establishment of three types of teaching by Dharma Master Jizang in the Tang dynasty. Fifth, [the system of] Guangzhai during the Liang dynasty.
The Dharma Master Sīyún established four teachings. The tenth, the Dharma Master Yìn of the Jānān region during the Táng dynasty, established two teachings.
The above ten schools of interpretation were all compiled by the Dharma Master Jízàng of the present Táng dynasty. Each of these differing views constitutes a distinct school;
they were all men of extraordinary talent of their time, whose wisdom surpassed that of their peers, and who all served as generals of the Dharma for the worthy and the spiritually gifted.
He opened the bright lamp of the Buddha-sun; it is impossible to add or subtract from his name.
It was just as when the Buddha spoke the words "internal, external, and intermediate," and immediately entered meditative concentration. Later, five hundred arhats each interpreted these words.

After the Buddha emerged from concentration, they all asked the World-Honored One which interpretation accorded with his intention. The Buddha said, "None of them accord with my intention. The people asked: [Why so?]

"Buddha, since these do not accord with the Buddha’s intent, will they not incur sin? The Buddha said: "Although they are not my own intent, each follows correct principle and is fit to serve as holy teaching;
there is merit in them and no sin. Furthermore, what these virtuous ones have expounded each has its scriptural basis and authority.

I respectfully consider their lofty insights and cannot judge them all at once. However, having personally investigated the profound mysteries within the holy teachings, I shall now describe my thoughts according to my own limited perspective."
I respectfully present this to later sages. Based upon its doctrinal principles, I have briefly established ten categories. What are these ten?

First, the teaching of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) which asserts pure existence, taught during the first period. Second, the teaching that refutes existence and clarifies emptiness (*śūnyatā*), as taught during the second period.
Third, the teaching that reconciles emptiness and existence and clarifies that which is neither empty nor existent, as taught during the third period through the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
In the fourth period, he preached the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, clarifying the teaching that what is provisionally established is identical to the ultimate truth.

In the fifth period, he preached the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, clarifying the teaching that the conventional is eternally true. In the sixth period, he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, clarifying the teaching of leading provisional means back to the ultimate reality.
In the seventh period, he preached the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, causing those of the three vehicles to abandon the provisional and turn toward the ultimate. Eighth...

At that time, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was preached. Within a single kṣaṇa, it comprehensively encompasses the ten periods of time in a perfect fusion, devoid of beginning or end, priority or posteriority, and universally subsuming the teachings:
the ninth, the teaching of both the common and the uncommon; and the tenth, the teaching of the uncommon and the common.

As for the first period, the teaching of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) as purely existent, it was taught for the sake of ordinary beings who are bound by and attached to worldly phenomena, regarding them as real.
There is. Following after the objects of form, one performs various unwholesome deeds; because of these unwholesome acts, one falls into the realms of suffering.
One then takes the bridle of the dharma to restrain that mind, using the precepts to guard against and subdue all unwholesomeness; therefore, it is called the "teaching of pure existence."

Within the Hīnayāna, it is likewise taught that the nature of non-manifest precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*) and so forth generally apply to the whole, though their practical application differs according to the faculties and dispositions of individuals;

the Bodhisattva precepts are also like this. As a sutra states: "If a person receives the Buddha's precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas"—this is also discussed in terms of the nature of the precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*).
Furthermore, it says: "In this way, thousands of billions [of beings] each receive [the transmission]..."
As for the multitude of beings who all come to my presence: first, they are guided and received through the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) which transforms their retributive bodies;

subsequently, they are led to return to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and its true retribution. For those of superior faculties, the phenomena and principle of the Dharma-body serve as a simultaneous basis, because they are the fundamental source.

Regarding the teaching of the second period, which explains the *Prajñāpāramitā* to refute existence and clarify emptiness: having established the provisional reality of the Hīnayāna as a formal standard,

and having regulated the body, speech, and mind so that they abide in wholesome dharmas, one then teaches the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and subsequently the teaching of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) to shatter attachments to those [provisional realities] and gradually lead toward the Dharmakāya.
The third period was the teaching of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*. It was intended to harmonize the teachings on emptiness and existence;

to reconcile the two preceding doctrines of emptiness and existence so that those with extremist views would not remain stuck in the gates of either emptiness or existence; and to provide a teaching of neither non-emptiness nor non-existence.

For the sake of those of the two vehicles who, having extinguished consciousness, realize quiescence and abide in a state of silent ignorance, it was taught by means of skillful expedients in order to turn them away from that state.
The ninth *ālayavijñāna* is said to be the purely immaculate consciousness. The fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses always rely upon that ninth consciousness as their support.
Ordinary, ignorant people do not understand this and falsely grasp it as a self (*ātman*).

Just as a torrential waterfall does not exist apart from the substance of water, and all waves depend upon water as their basis, so too the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses always [rely upon it].

Because they take pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) as their support, those of the two vehicles gradually turn their minds away from [the mundane] and realize that consciousness is transformed into wisdom.

Why are nine consciousnesses established as pure consciousness? It is because those of the two vehicles have long harbored fear toward the seeds of karma within the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses throughout saṃsāra.
Fearing that they might find it difficult to believe, [the Buddha] employs skillful means to establish "purity" separately, outside of the seeds of saṃsāra.
Consciousness gradually leads [the practitioner] forward, with the intention of causing them to retain their afflictions without extinguishing them, so that compassion and wisdom may gradually arise.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "In this way, although the bodhisattva abides by the stage of the Dharma, they take wisdom as their reliance."
Gradually causing the view of emptiness to reach the stage of discernment and become wisdom, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* was taught during the fourth period.

Regarding what is called "teaching that the provisional is itself the real," as in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, it directly addresses those with Mahāyāna faculties by suddenly teaching the eighth consciousness of karmic seeds, naming it the Tathāgatagarbha-consciousness. Furthermore,

It is said: that which attains characteristics is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which does not attain characteristics is called wisdom (*jñāna*). The *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*) also speaks in this same way.
Although this teaching states that the seeds of ignorance and karma become wisdom, it still aspires to transcend the mundane and has not yet manifested [wisdom] while remaining within the fetters.
The fifth period is the teaching of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which clarifies that the conventional is eternally true.
This is because within the *Vimalakīrti*, those of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles, as well as bodhisattvas of the three vehicles, are not regarded as knowers of the Dharma.
Consequently, the ten great disciples remained silent at Vaiśālī, and Maitreya, Prabhāvyūha, and Sugandhakūṭa ceased their eloquent discourse at the Dharma assembly. This...
The Sūtra refutes the four preceding types of teachings in which Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas have not yet integrated defilement and purity, and thus constantly delight in transcending the mundane.

By having Vimalakīrti dwell in the body of a layman, it clarifies that the mundane is eternally true. It destroys those pure appearances and shows that one should always harbor [the realization that] defilement and purity are one;
therefore, it says that the physical body is the seed of the Tathāgata, and that ignorance and craving are the seeds, and so forth, in order to cause [beings to realize this].

For the assembly of the Three Vehicles, pure marks and conceptual minds have vanished; whether emerging from the mundane or entering into worldly entanglements, they are equal and unimpeded—only then can their true virtue be clarified.

In the sixth period, he preached the Lotus Sūtra to lead those of provisional teachings back to the ultimate teaching; this was for the sake of the Arhats who had gathered at the assembly of emptiness.
Śānta. The Pratyekabuddha assembly [realizes] that the twelve links of dependent origination all lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

By clarifying that the six sense organs, consciousness, and the three factors of name-and-form, mind, and object are by their very nature unarisen, these two types of persons both bring about the cessation of mental consciousness and the cessation of karma within the triple world.
Wisdom and compassion do not arise; furthermore, they analyze phenomena to clarify emptiness, using emptiness to destroy delusions, and thus take delight in birth.
Those who dwell in the Pure Land, as well as Bodhisattvas who retain afflictions to moisten their rebirth,

do not fully realize that the ignorance and various delusions of all sentient beings are all produced from the fundamental nature-purity, universal radiance, and centerless and boundless wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
They all harbor various false views, such as regarding pure lands and defiled lands, or one’s own Buddha and other Buddhas, with feelings of delight and aversion.
This does not accord with ultimate truth. It is by drawing forth these three faculties that they are led back to fundamental wisdom.

Thus, through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the Wonderful Dharma), one is made to know that the nature of ignorance and birth-and-death is fundamentally nothing but the essence of wisdom, inherently free from defilement;

it is only that delusion and awakening differ, yet there are no two natures. This is illustrated by the metaphor of the lotus flower, which draws those three faculties back to their source. This is...
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies that the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.
When the seventh [sūtra], the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, was preached, it caused those of the three vehicles who were following provisional teachings to turn toward the true teaching.
Within this sūtra, it is clarified that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, which is no different from that of a Buddha; they are merely covered by ignorance.

Therefore, it is not seen. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* represents the relinquishing of the provisional and the embracing of the true aspect (*lakṣaṇa*) among the three vehicles, whereas the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*) represents the relinquishing of the provisional and the embracing of the true wisdom (*jñāna*).
Both sūtras belong to the sixth period of teaching within the three vehicles;

however, because they are explained as preceding or succeeding one another in terms of the sequential order of the teachings for the sake of conversion, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* is categorized as the seventh period of teaching. Nevertheless, its...
The realm of wisdom has no sequence of past, present, or future.

When the eighth [Buddha] preached the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), he universally encompassed the three periods of time and the ten periods of time in a perfectly integrated teaching.
As the sūtra says: "Entering the samādhi of the momentary limit, he descended from the Tuṣita heaven, took birth, and manifested the eight phases [of a Buddha's life]."

The attainment of enlightenment and the entry into nirvana do not take even a moment; this is because one relies on the fundamental nature of principle and wisdom (*dharmatā-jñāna*), which is inherently timeless.

It is not that [the Buddha] relies on provisional means based on the fundamental [nature]. Therefore, it is called "entering. It is not that within the fundamental dharma-nature there is the entering or emerging from samādhi.
These are merely skillful words employed according to the ritual conventions of transformation. For this reason, wise people should not follow them [as literal reality].
It is said: "The Buddha, the World-Honored One alone, enters the Samādhi of the Limit of a Single Kṣaṇa. This teaching of the sūtra is without beginning and without end;
it is the Buddha’s true fruition of retribution and merit, its nature and characteristics being perfectly complete. If one seeks its beginning or end, its length or brevity,"
From beginning to end, the path is cut off; to depart from this Dharma and give rise to separate conceptual calculations is entirely a provisional gate, not the ultimate teaching.
In such a Dharma-gate, even if a Buddha does not appear in the world, there is likewise no nirvana. All natures are one nature; all wisdoms are one wisdom; all marks are one mark;
all practices are one practice; the three periods of time are one thought-moment, and one thought-moment is the three periods of time. Thus...
Up to the tenth stage, such dharmas as these are without beginning and without end; this is called the eternally turning wheel of Dharma. It is like a perfect sphere that has no fixed direction;
like a bright mirror that reflects instantaneously; like empty space that is without obstruction; like an echo that has no basis; like a shadow that is not hindered;
like the birth of a magically conjured person. If a person can thoroughly realize this dharma-gate, the Buddha-wisdom will manifest spontaneously.

The wisdom of no-teacher is that which manifests through wisdom; because this Dharma has neither arising nor ceasing, one naturally attains it by means of the wisdom of natural non-arising and non-ceasing.
It is not something that can be attained through the conceptual deliberations of the mind.
All provisional teaching methods are entirely contained within this and expounded simultaneously; for all provisional teachings do not transcend the Dharma-realm, which has no three periods of time.
Each, according to its own views, presents infinite differences.

The ninth [category], the shared and unshared teachings, refers to the preaching of various Mahāyāna sūtras. While humans, devas, and those of the three vehicles hear them together, the benefits they derive are each distinct.
As a sūtra states: "A bodhisattva attains equal and perfect enlightenment within the body of a single small sentient being."
He turns the wheel of Dharma and delivers immeasurable sentient beings, yet these small sentient beings do not know it and are not aware of it.
This is because he is constantly with sentient beings; both those of the Great and Small Vehicles are together within the ocean of the Buddha.

Body and mind are fundamentally without distinction. Nevertheless, there are those who see the Buddha and those who do not see the Buddha; those who hear the Dharma and those who do not hear the Dharma; and [the differences in] the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Because [beings] differ in their size, as well as in their respective experiences of suffering and pleasure, these are called the "shared" and "unshared" teachings. Furthermore, a sutra states:

"Entering the samādhi of the limit of the moment (*kṣaṇakoṭi*), he manifests descending from Tuṣita Heaven, entering the mother’s womb, appearing in the world, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering nirvana.
This occurs within the "timeless" state, such that all sentient beings perceive it for themselves.

Regarding time, one perceives its beginning, middle, and end. Within a single sound of the Dharma, beings spontaneously attain the fruits of the Way—whether as devas or humans, or through the vehicles of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Buddhas—each being distinct from the others.
One likewise perceives the differences in the Buddha’s dwelling in the kalpas and the length of his lifespan, each varying according to circumstances.
Yet, in reality, the nature of the Tathāgata is without fabrication, without arising, and without cessation; it is simply because of this non-action [that these distinctions appear].
The wisdom of the stainless, pure, and white nature of phenomena is inherently pure; it can accord with their thoughts and ensure that no opportunity is lost.
Thus, they share the same Dharma, the same wisdom, the same time, the same body, the same mind, and the same vehicle as the Buddha.
Because their knowledge, vision, and liberation are each unique and not shared [with others], it is called the "shared and unshared teaching," just as in the case of the five hundred śrāvakas.
To be present together at the Avataṃsaka assembly yet to be as if deaf or blind—this is precisely what that refers to.

Tenth, regarding the "unshared shared teaching": as in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, the bodhisattvas who have gathered from the ten directions and the Buddha-lands from which they come each differ in their respective origins, yet they preach the Dharma with a single, common voice.
In general, they hear the Dharma together; their attainment of benefit may be both collective and individual.

Furthermore, among those in the assembly—devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, humans, non-humans, and so forth—each is distinct, yet they equally attain the dharma-gate of the fruit-virtue of Vairocana, possessing mastery over both the collective and the individual.

Part Three: Clarifying the Distinctions Between Teachings and Meanings Now, the Great Hero of the Triple Realm, the Arhat, dwells in silent stillness; his body, mind, and nature—

In their essential nature, they have no purposeful activity whatsoever. Nevertheless, through the spontaneous arising of great compassion, they accord with the Dharma as being of one substance. From non-conceptual wisdom (*nirnimitta-jñāna*), they give rise to teachings that follow conditions.

Like a single rain universally nourishing all things, each grows according to its own nature. Thus, there are cases where the names are identical but the meanings differ (such as the ten stages of the gradual teaching versus the ten stages of the perfect teaching);

or where the words differ but the meaning is the same (as when the Dharma-gates of the worlds in the ten directions are all, in essence, the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths); or there are the two vehicles of principle and phenomenon; or...
The essence and its function penetrate one another; whether sudden or gradual, abrupt or perfect, the Dharma does not bestow itself but is established in reliance upon faculties and teachings.

When the faculties are weak, the Dharma appears inferior; when the vessel is vast, the Way is perfected. This accords with what is appropriate for each being, and the great or small [teachings] follow their respective perceptions.

Some may delight in the carriage at the gate and abandon the journey on the open-air vehicle; this is merely a provisional arrangement for those of the highest caliber and those who progress gradually.
O Assembly, I have briefly set forth these ten dharmas so that those who are beginners shall not be hindered by provisional means and thereby obstruct the ultimate reality.
First, regarding the distinct identity of the Teacher when a Buddha appears in the world: this teaching takes Vairocana as its Teacher.
In Sanskrit, *vi* means "various" and *rūpa* means "light. Thus, *Vairocana* means "Universal Illumination.
Furthermore, *vi* signifies "pervasive," indicating that he illuminates the faculties and capacities of all sentient beings with the various lights of great wisdom.
This name is derived from his Dharma-body’s compassion and wisdom; it is not like the provisional teachings which use a clan name as a title. *Muni* means "silent sage" (*jīmò*). However—
Furthermore, the essence of the Dharma is praised as being beyond verbal expression; it does not speak of wisdom and compassion.
These two radiances represent the distinct manifestations of the Dharma.

This excludes the light emitted from the ninety-seven kinds of marks within the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Tathāgata’s Ten Bodies," as well as the light emitted by the gods of the Yāma Heaven and others; it refers only to—
Furthermore, to discuss directly the manifestations of the light of the Dharma, there are ten from beginning to end, each of which represents the sequential order of cause and effect.
This differs from the other teachings of the Buddhas who emit light— whether they emit many rays, or a single ray, or emit them from their entire bodies without sequence—
or who emit the light of the fruit without the cause, or emit the light of the cause without the fruit.
As in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the fruit-light from the tuft of hair between the eyebrows is emitted directly, without the causal light of the stage of faith beneath the wheel of the feet.

As in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Buddha emits light from beneath the wheel of his feet that radiates directly upward from below, thereby establishing a gradual progression from the ordinary person toward sainthood;
it is only after the accumulation of practice over many eons has reached fulfillment that [the fruit] is finally accomplished.

Regarding the fruition and its virtues: unlike this sutra’s emission of light, which proceeds from fruit to cause and achieves the fruit through the cause, here cause and fruit are of one essence, so that the diligent cultivation of practice remains undiminished.
First, ten kinds of light are emitted from between his teeth.
Adorning all dharma-assembly sites throughout the dharma-realm as he first attains perfect enlightenment, he proclaims to the multitudes of the ten directions, causing them all to assemble.
This is the "Light of Proclaiming to the Multitudes and Gathering the Clouds."

Second, light from the fruit [of enlightenment] is emitted from between the eyebrows and enters into the wheels of the feet; by means of the fruit, the cause is established, marking the beginning of the arising of faith.
Third, the light of the fruit that had entered returns from the wheels of the feet and is emitted outward to illuminate the Golden World-Honored One.
The Buddha Akṣobhyajñāna of the realm [takes] that fruit-light from between his eyebrows and causes it to enter into the wheels of [his own] feet;

this is the process of using the fruit to establish the cause. Then, taking that very fruit-light which had entered the wheels of the feet, he emits it again to illuminate the Buddha Akṣobhyajñāna of the Golden World;
this is the process of using the cause to establish the fruit. Thus, cause and fruit are shown simultaneously, employing them to bring about completion.
The gateway of initial faith is established by means of the ten bodhisattvas, beginning with Jñānaśrī, to constitute the stage of faith.
Furthermore, when the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes" was taught in the fourth [assembly], they ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru;
there, the Tathāgata emitted light from the tip of his toe to illuminate the commencement of setting forth and the initial vision of the Path, abiding therein through the power of samādhi.
The Pinnacle of the Dharma. From the preceding stage of faith, one enters into the realization of reality; therefore, Bodhisattvas of the ten stages of abiding are all designated as "Wisdom.
Fifth, when the Tathāgata ascended to the Yāma Heaven, he emitted light from his upturned feet, thereby accomplishing it through the function of illumination.

Regarding the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*): because this heaven is detached from the terrestrial realm, it is described as having ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*), signifying that its functional activity arises based upon space.
This clarifies that one first realizes the fundamental wisdom of the *dharmakāya* and only then initiates the myriad practices.
In the sixth chapter, "Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace," light is emitted from the Tathāgata’s knees as he expounds the Ten Dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).
This indicates that within this celestial realm of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena; therefore, it is called dedication.
At the stage of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), principle and phenomena are likewise unobstructed; it is not only in this specific place that dedication exists, but rather—
The sequence of conventional designations must be established; however, within the actual substance, each and every stage is fully present.
"Knee" (*jānu*) clarifies the mastery of bending, extending, and revolving; thus, it expresses the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmana*).
Because it symbolizes mastery over the ultimate and the conventional, and because it signifies the spontaneous accomplishment of wisdom and compassion through mastery over saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

In the seventh [heaven], the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), he emits from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows the light of the fruit-virtues of the causal and resultant stages of the tenth-stage bodhisattvas.
This returns to resemble this heaven because, while relying on the emanations of others, they lack the power to emanate by their own mind.
This signifies that the tenth-stage bodhisattvas merely act for the sake of what sentient beings require for their transformation, having no [self-directed] activity of their own.

It is a transformation through karma. Furthermore, because there is no desire at the very limit of the desire realm, it is identical to the dharma-gate of the four dhyānas and the transcendence of the three realms.
It differs from the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which cultivates birth-and-death to attain nirvāṇa by exiting the delusions of the three realms.
It also differs from the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings, who accomplish the ten stages within the fourth dhyāna. Moreover, [it proceeds] from Tuṣita...
Regarding the heavens from those exceeding the Nirmāṇarati Heaven up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven: this signifies that the dharmas of the ten stages pervade the entire Dharma-realm;
thus, there is no need for sequential progression. The four dhyānas of the upper realms are likewise present within this assembly;
they arrive without coming and are seen without moving. All the heavens, both above and below, abide therein throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

They all reside within the pores [of the Buddha], yet the manifestation of the Dharma follows such a sequence of stages. In reality, there is no coming or going, nor any distinction of above, below, self, or other.
The Assembly of Samantabhadra’s Buddha-Flower Samādhi of the Eleventh Bhūmi was preached in the Heaven of the Third Dhyāna.
The preceding text is incomplete.
Eighth, in the Universal Radiance Hall (*Samantaprabhā-kuṭāgāra*), the Tathāgata preached the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata" (*Tathāgatotpattisambhava-parivarta*).

He emitted a ray of light from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows to anoint the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head, clarifying that the fruit of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*)—the culmination of the third dhyāna—has been reached.
The stage of middling awakening concludes. Even if the Dharma has already been established, it is presented as the original teaching of the manifestation;

it is only thereafter that the manifestation appears. If the Dharma-gate had not yet been taught, how could it be called a "manifestation"? Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of Worldly Lords," the manifestation occurs at the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment;
subsequently, in the "Chapter on Manifestation," the manifestation is described as occurring through one's own realization of what is seen according to the Dharma. This clarifies [the distinction].
From beginning to end, upon the essence of the Buddha-dharma realm, the gateway of the successive stages of the grounds is established from start to finish, perpetually manifesting.
Originally of one single limit, it is without before or after. Light is emitted to consecrate the crown of Mañjuśrī;
with the light of the fruit, the fruit-dharma is consecrated, for Mañjuśrī is the Dharma-body of the Buddhas.
Regarding the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), [the scripture] intends for the Bodhisattvas Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra to engage in mutual dialogue.
Knowing [the answer], Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asks intentionally. As the Sūtra says: "Who is the eldest son of the Buddha? Whom shall I now question?
Thereupon, the Tathāgata emits light from his mouth, which灌 (pours) into the mouth of Samantabhadra.
In the ninth [scene], light is emitted from the mouth of the Tathāgata and poured into the mouth of Samantabhadra. This light from the mouth is the light of the Buddha’s teaching;
it is intended to cause Samantabhadra to expound, by means of his discriminative wisdom, the dharma-gate of the fruit and virtue of the Buddha’s appearance in the world.
Because Mañjuśrī was illuminated by the Buddha’s emission of light, he finally came to know the place where the Dharma was being asked about. Indeed, sacred wisdom fundamentally knows itself;
now, it is perfected by the seal of the Buddha-dharma (dharmamudrā) to establish the principles for future generations.

This constitutes the ninth time the light was emitted, thereby perfecting the rules governing the beginning and end of this entire scripture and consolidating the essence of the causes and effects of the five preceding stages.

The Gate of Application. Because these three persons are never separated from one another from beginning to end, it is clarified that the Tathāgata is the fruition of the two, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra.
In the tenth [chapter], once again within the Jeta Grove, he further emitted the light of fruition from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows. Thus it was concluded.
The causes and effects of the five higher stages have already been perfected. Now, by employing these resultant dharmas to benefit sentient beings,
he enters the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" chapter, causing ordinary beings among gods and humans, six thousand bhikṣus, five hundred upāsakas,
five hundred upāsikās, and five hundred youths and maidens, all to attain the Way within this Dharma-gate.
He attained Buddhahood. From this point upward, he emitted light ten times to symbolize the perfection of his virtues, fully possessing these ten.
This differs from the light emitted by transformation-buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya*), who may emit light only once when preaching a single sutra.
