Or rather, it refers to the entire body. Never before has there been a sūtra such as this, in which every aspect from beginning to end is perfectly complete, and its virtues are fully endowed with the number ten.
It merely speaks of "ten," yet the perfected virtues are inexhaustible; the number ten is used because it represents a perfect, circular number.

Regarding the threefold distinction between the primary and the attendant in the subject matter of the questions and answers: the questions and answers of this single section of the sutra possess three general characteristics of excellence.
First, the Buddha; second, Mañjuśrī; and third, Samantabhadra. The Buddha represents the fruit of virtue (*phala-guṇa*), which is ineffable—unspeakable, uncultivable, unattainable, and unrealizable.
Mañjuśrī accomplishes the praise of the *dharmakāya* and fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Samantabhadra... [text fragment ends]
The Worthy One (Bhadra) perfected the virtuous conduct of the wisdom of differentiation (*vibhāga-jñāna*).
All Buddhas rely upon these two Honored Ones as their teachers and models, thereby being able to achieve the ultimate fruit of Great Bodhi.
Some say that Samantabhadra is the eldest son, while others say that Mañjuśrī is the youngest son; they are the first to realize the Buddha-nature of the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya.

Because he is the one who brings forth the noble nature and wisdom of all newly born Buddhas, and because he is the foremost in initiating enlightenment and illuminating the mind, he is the "Youngest Son.
He presides over the northeast and corresponds to the hexagram Gen. Gen represents the Youngest Son; furthermore, it represents the mountain and the stone.
Between the hours of Chou and Yin, it represents the first light of dawn when darkness has already vanished but the sunlight has not yet fully appeared;
this signifies the beginning of enlightenment. Therefore, Mañjuśrī is pointed out as being on Mount Qingliang in the northeast.
Furthermore, by taking the geographical location of this Jambudvīpa continent as a basis, the Dharma is entrusted to the mundane world so that it may be easily understood. Universally...
O Worthy Eldest Son, your position is in the East, at the hour of the Rabbit (Mao). You are the Trigram Zhen. Zhen represents the eldest son;
it is the head, the crown, the Azure Dragon, auspiciousness and celebration, the springtime birth, and the beginning of establishing laws and regulations.

It symbolizes the rising sun that shines universally upon all things, making them all clearly manifest. It is fit for undertaking tasks and applying oneself according to conditions. Therefore, it is universal.
The Worthy One (Bhadra) is the foremost of those who practice; he is the eldest son. Avalokiteśvara is the foremost of those who manifest compassion; his station is in the West.
He dwells on the western slope of Vajra Mountain and preaches the *Maitrī-karuṇā-sūtra*. The hour of You (the Western direction) corresponds to the position of You. You is the trigram Dui.
Dui represents metal, the White Tiger, misfortune and peril, and the autumnal killing force. Therefore, the compassionate Avalokiteśvara presides over it. Thus says the Buddha.
The Dharma is wordless; it is through worldly phenomena that it is expressed by means of things. Whatever involves verbal expression is entirely a worldly phenomenon.
If there were no words, how could those who are unenlightened attain understanding?

For this reason, the three virtues of the Buddhas—Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Avalokiteśvara—are employed as mutual primary and secondary factors to establish the Dharma-principle. The Buddha encompasses all fruition; Mañjuśrī... [text truncated]
Mañjuśrī gathers the fundamental wisdom of the *dharmakāya*, which is the cause and fruit of all practices;

Samantabhadra gathers the differentiated wisdom of the bodies of all causal and fruitional practices. For this reason, it is sometimes said that Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are the teachers of all Buddhas.
Mañjuśrī is the gateway to the fundamental wisdom of the *dharmakāya* at the initial moment of seeing the Path; Samantabhadra is...
This serves as the gateway for the practice undertaken after first seeing the Path. The Buddha is the unconditioned essence (*anabhisaṃskāra-svabhāva*) within these two matters.
This which is signified does not exist within the teachings of the Transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*). In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha conceals his body and does not appear.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita seeks the gateway of the *prajñāpāramitā* and fulfills the six perfections.
Regarding the *pāramitās*: the *upāya-pāramitā* and the other ten *pāramitās*, such as those of aspiration, power, and wisdom, do not yet exist [in this context].

This is solely because they are intended to lead in those of small capacity—such as *śrāvakas*, humans, and devas—who are not yet able to hear of the *pāramitās* of skillful means, aspiration, power, wisdom, and so forth.
The reason that the *upāya-pāramitā* is not included among the six *pāramitās* is for the sake of the *upāya-pāramitā*.
They walk upon unwholesome paths; those of small capacity are unable to hear it. Why is this so? Because they possess fear and attachment.
Furthermore, in that sutra, there are many śrāvakas who engage in dialogue with the Buddha, rather than great bodhisattvas.
Even if there are bodhisattvas present, they are not Mañjuśrī or Samantabhadra; even if Mañjuśrī is present, he is without Samantabhadra.

This is because their outward manifestations have not yet fully realized the practice. Even if Samantabhadra were present without Mañjuśrī, it clarifies that they do not perceive the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya.
Even if both Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra were present, if they did not engage in mutual dialogue, it would clarify that the principle and its phenomena have not been thoroughly penetrated.
The fourth section distinguishes between the perfection of causes and the fulfillment of results, revealing three distinct aspects of the Buddha-fruit:

first, the fruit of the unconditioned *dharmakāya*, which transcends words and ceases all practice; second, the fruit resulting from the accumulation of cultivation through practice, wherein the path is perfected and merit is accomplished.

The fruit is first attained only after many kalpas. Regarding the three occasions of first generating the bodhicitta: at the initial stage of the ten abidings (*daśabhūmi*), the essence and function manifest according to conditions to produce the fruit.

This fruit is clarified only after the practice has been accumulated through cultivation for many kalpas until the practice is perfected; this refers specifically to the provisional teachings (*upāya-deśanā*).
The twelve links of existence, which are ignorance and non-comprehension, are fundamentally the wisdom of the Dharma-body.

One becomes weary of them and uses the contemplation of emptiness to subdue the active afflictions, while taking delight in other gates of purity. All such Buddha-qualities are entirely produced through cultivation.
For one hundred kalpas, one cultivates the karma for the primary and secondary marks; by making offerings to Dīpaṃkara, one attains radiance; by not killing, one attains longevity;

by practicing generosity, one attains wealth and resources; and by practicing patience, one attains physical perfection. Each cause and its corresponding result are perfectly matched in their similarity.

Furthermore, by means of various gates of practice that serve as antidotes, one finally realizes the nature and becomes a Buddha. This is not the case in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where [the realization occurs] in a single [moment].
Contemplate the Dharma-gate of the sudden realization of the *dharmadhātu*. The nature and characteristics of body and mind are fundamentally nothing but the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Whether in active application or stillness, by relying on non-active wisdom (*anabhisamskāra-jñāna*), one is precisely the Buddha. Within the universal gate of the *dharmadhātu*, the various obstacles of principle and wisdom are naturally absent;
there is no need for separate remedies, nor for separate cultivation or severance. One does not perceive transformation, for that which changes and that which does not change are without distinction.
Because of the nature and characteristics [of phenomena], one should universally contemplate that there is nothing that is not a Dharma-gate and nothing that is not liberation.
However, because one’s own mind forcibly gives rise to attachments due to manifold concerns, one sinks into the current of suffering;

for this reason, the Sage laboriously taught various distinctions. Yet, regarding those teachings, one again gives rise to attachment. For this reason, the Sage’s teachings differ, sometimes being gradual...

It may be circular, corresponding to the capacities of various faculties. Therefore, other teachings present cause before effect, which differs from this teaching where cause and effect are simultaneous.
This is because within the ocean of the wisdom of *dharmatā*, cause and effect cannot be apprehended as distinct entities.

Where cause and effect can be apprehended, they necessarily possess a sequence of before and after; whatever is thus apprehended is impermanent and is not the ultimate teaching. If [one were to claim] that first...

If the cause follows after the effect, the cause itself cannot be established; therefore, the effect is also destroyed. Because phenomena produced by conditions do not continue in succession, they would be subject to annihilation.
Since neither self nor other can be established, it is like counting one coin without counting the subsequent coins.
If the latter two do not exist, the former one also cannot be established, because moments would not be continuous. If moments are not established, the fruit is also destroyed.
If many eons were not continuous, the cause and fruit across those many eons would be destroyed; it must depend upon the subsequent time of counting coins.
The prior and the subsequent are established as such; cause and effect are likewise. It is only when they are simultaneous and uninterrupted that cause and effect are established.
If this were so, it would be like counting two coins at the same time: being without priority or posteriority, which would be "one" and which "two"?

It would be like holding up two fingers: which would be the cause and which the effect? Just as with the two fingers, depending on the point where the mind counts, the preceding becomes the cause and the subsequent the effect.
Regarding the fruit: if there were a prior and a subsequent, there would necessarily be an interval between them; yet that which has an interval cannot constitute cause and effect.
If they were simultaneous, like two fingers held upright, with neither prior nor subsequent, who could be the cause and who the effect?
Thus, it is also not established. This is as stated in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra regarding cause and effect being simultaneous.

In both cases, there is no such thing as cause and effect in sequence or simultaneity, nor are there the deluded attachments of mental constructs regarding existence, non-existence, both, or neither, permanence, impermanence, and so forth—attachments to cause and effect.
One simply realizes that the essence of phenomena is not something that can be conceptually constructed.
That which is not bound by cause and effect is called "cause and effect"; it is a delusion regarding simultaneity and sequence established by those who are not sentient beings.

The characteristics of the practices performed in the various stages of the five sciences differ; those who give rise to the Mahāyāna mind should rely upon their own respective faculties and dispositions.
There are six kinds of vehicles (*yāna*), distinguished by three types, five stages, and ten levels, with differing modes of practice (*ākāra*).

What are these six? First, the gate of recollecting the Buddha and aspiring to be born in the Pure Land; second, the gate of the Pure Land produced through the cultivation of pure land contemplation (*vipaśyanā*);
third, the vehicle of cultivating emptiness and non-self; fourth, the gate of the wisdom that contemplates the synthesis of existence and non-existence; fifth...
The gate of gradual cultivation for perceiving the Buddha-nature; and the gate of sudden realization for the perfect interfusion of the Buddha-nature.

What are these three types of five stages and ten grounds? First, by cultivating provisional designations, provisional wisdom, and provisional *tathatā* (suchness), one establishes the five stages and ten grounds.
Second, by cultivating partial truth and partial realization of a portion of true *tathatā*, one establishes the five stages and ten grounds. Third, [the gate of] sudden...

Cultivating sudden realization, sudden truth, and the sudden teaching of the Buddha’s realm—the perfect *tathatā*—one establishes the characteristics of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the five positions (*pañca-sthāna*).
Within this Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), there are no provisional teachings, words, names, or signs; it is entirely the ultimate truth.

These three types of characteristics for the ten stages and five positions—whether directed toward Bodhi, practicing as a bodhisattva, or fulfilling the fruit of Buddhahood—are all encompassed therein.
Among these, first, by relying on the power of mindfulness of the Buddha, cultivating the precepts, and generating the power of aspiration, one is born in a Pure Land.

This is the Pure Land of an Emanation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*), not a True Pure Land (*sambhogakāya*). This is because such a person has neither seen their own nature nor fully understood that ignorance is the essence of all Tathāgatas.
Because it is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), yet it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); such is the case with the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Second, the pure land produced through the practice of visualization of the pure land is a transformation pure land (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*). Because it arises from mental conceptions, it is conditioned;
because one has not yet perceived the Buddha-nature’s original wisdom, this refers to the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*.
This refers to the Sūtras.

Regarding the gateway of the threefold cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness and non-self: it is for the sake of first teaching Prajñāpāramitā, so as to shatter the ordinary person’s attachment to substantial reality and the two vehicles’ attachment to a self within the emptiness of persons;
thus, one extensively cultivates the dharma of emptiness, wherein both emptiness and existence are equally empty.

Emptiness is superior. Although one practices the six pāramitās, cultivates various factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), and attains the six supernormal powers (abhijñā), thereby excelling in the merit of the bodhisattva path over humans and devas, such a person is not born into the family of the Buddhas and does not perceive the Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu).

In order to analyze phenomena and clarify emptiness, yet failing to realize that ignorance is itself the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata, within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, declared that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature—characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
There are some bodhisattvas who, repenting their own transgressions, say: "For immeasurable kalpas, I have wandered through birth and death."
It is solely because one is deluded by the notion of "no-self" that such faults arise; only by turning the mind away from this can one realize the nature.
To penetrate the self is wisdom.
This is the gateway of the contemplative wisdom regarding the existence and non-existence of the fourfold combination. As a verse in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* says: "All dharmas..."
All are without intrinsic nature; they are without arising and without cessation, quiescent from the beginning. The self-nature of all phenomena is eternally nirvāṇa.

What wise person would [interpret this] without a hidden intent? This sūtra, in order to refute those who cultivate emptiness through the perfection of wisdom with excessive zeal, speaks of both emptiness and existence, mutually refuting one another, so as not to allow for the conceptualization of existence nor the conceptualization of non-existence. Furthermore, this sūtra...
Although ten stages (*bhūmi*) are established, within those ten stages it is further taught that there are eleven kinds of *dausthulya* (coarseness) and twenty-two kinds of ignorance (*moha*).
For this reason, this sutra does not establish the preparatory practices—namely the three stages of worthiness (*kṣānti*) and the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*)—prior to the [ten] stages.
This is because the stage prior to the [ten] stages in this sutra is not the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Furthermore, for the sake of the second...
In the interim teachings of the three periods, there is merely a reconciliation of existence and non-existence;
yet this is not yet the stage where the principles and phenomena of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra mutually encompass one another through the perfection of practice. Why is this so?

Because these eleven stages constitute the rank of Buddhahood, and within the rank of Buddhahood, there still remain obstacles. This clarifies that prior to the eleventh stage, the fundamental reality has not yet been attained.
Because of wisdom. If the true reality-wisdom were complete [in all stages], how could there be eleven kinds of grossness (*dauṣṭhulya*) across the eleven stages?

Since such grossness exists, it follows that Buddha-wisdom does not exist within each stage. Such teachings as these are all provisionally established in accordance with those of provisional faculties;
they are spoken by the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha solely to lead those of middling and inferior faculties who have not yet [attained realization].

This is spoken according to reality. As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, within the initial stage of the "Abiding in the First Resolve" among the Three Grades of Worthies prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*), one is able to suddenly realize the dharma-gate of the Buddha-fruit.

This universally seals all positions—the ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, the ten stages, and the stage of Equal Enlightenment—just as when a seal is pressed, the patterns and characteristics are fully complete without any deficiency.
Regarding the future limit: at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta, one suddenly seals the ignorance of the triple world, thereby making it the ocean of Buddha-wisdom.

By means of the seal of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, Wisdom-body, and Great Compassion, one suddenly seals the entire world with a single stroke, establishing it as the great function of the Dharmadhātu.
The fifth is the gate of progressive cultivation for gradually perceiving the Buddha-nature. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas of the ten abodes perceive the nature to a small degree;
even those in the ten stages have not yet attained complete clarity. The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Bodhisattvas of the ten abodes..."

One attains a partial vision of the Dharma-body because it manifests through the transformation of the eight phases of enlightenment. As that treatise explains, this is brought about by the power of vows;
since it is produced by the power of vows, it is not a fruition of actual retribution. In general, this serves to gradually perceive the Buddha-nature.

From the moment one first abides in the stage of generating the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta), the realization of the fruit of Buddhahood is not restricted to a fixed number of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Why is this? As recorded in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the butcher Pūraṇa (Guǎngè) was prophesied to attain Buddhahood within the present Bhadrakalpa;

even an icchantika who has only recently generated the aspiration for enlightenment possesses the merit to transcend such kalpas, let alone one who is fully endowed with the faculty of faith and can further practice even a small portion [of the path].
For one who has realized their nature (jìng xìng), how could there be such a thing as the *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas?
There are those of virtue in the world who claim that the butcher Guang'e was a manifested transformation; this is merely to conform to human sentiments and fails to grasp the Buddha’s intent.

How could the gradual guidance from the provisional toward the real ever allow the perception of kalpas to persist in one's emotions, thereby causing a deviation from the fundamental? [The Buddha] gradually guides...
As for the Dragon Girl and Sudhana attaining Buddhahood within a single thought-moment, this is finally the true teaching.

Those with the limited views of the Three Vehicles merely contemplate over long periods of time; yet the essence of time is fundamentally non-existent. To sigh in admiration and yearning is but to bind oneself without a rope—when will there ever be a time of rest?
Previously, three types of ten stages were briefly explained, and now they are further evaluated according to the meaning of the sutras.
There are six kinds of ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Within the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, there are three kinds of ten stages;
within the definitive teachings, there are likewise three kinds of ten stages, as found in the *Renwang jing*, the *Jieshenmijie daping jing*, and other such scriptures.
The ten stages taught in these three classes of sutras mostly establish the gate of provisional *tathatā* (suchness) to accomplish the practices of the ten stages.

Aspect. These are the three types of ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) within the provisional teachings. As stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, a Bodhisattva at the stage of the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*) perceives the nature (*dharmatā*) only partially;
a Bodhisattva at the stage of the Ten Stages perceives the nature but not yet with complete clarity.

This clarifies that one takes Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) as the gateway for the vehicle, and thus practices and realizes the ten stages in a partial manner. Furthermore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the [analogy of the] ox...
"Eating the fatty grasses of the Snowy Mountains and obtaining only the *sarpis* (clarified butter)" and so forth, clarifies the realization of the Buddha-stage.
This constitutes the fivefold *daśabhūmi*. As taught in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the gates of the *dharmadhātu*—the profound and inexhaustible Dharma—constitute the ten stages;
this is the sixfold *daśabhūmi*. As in the *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra*, there are the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*).
A Bodhisattva perceives only a small portion of the nature [of reality]. Nevertheless, by the power of their vow, they are able to manifest the attainment of Buddhahood through the eight phases.
Although this is not yet complete, because they perceive even this small portion of the power of that nature, their capacity is such.

It is like a crown prince who, due to specific causes and conditions, is ordered by his father, the King, to preside over and succeed to the administration of state affairs; because he is truly the King’s son, he possesses the requisite strength.
For this reason, it is because they have seen a portion of the Buddha-nature; it is because they are true sons of the Tathāgata born into the family of the Buddha.
This differs from other teachings, which rely on provisional *tathatā* (suchness) and provisional wisdom, waiting until the first stage (*bhūmi*) before one is born into the family of the Buddha.
The power of clearly seeing the nature [of reality] is truly superior to other schools, even in its partial manifestation; how much more so when it is fully attained?
Sixth, the Gate of the Perfect Integration of Buddha-nature, Principle-Wisdom, and Myriad Practices through Sudden Realization.

As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the bodhisattvas within the stage of the ten faiths all come from the presence of the Buddhas of the ten wisdoms. This is because, within the stage of the ten faiths, one establishes faith by means of the fruit;
it clarifies that they come from the fruit, taking the fruit as the cause. If this were not so...
Taking the fruit as faith means there is nothing to be believed; therefore, faith has no basis. Why is Mañjuśrī the leader?
Because Mañjuśrī represents the faith that precedes the fruit, while Samantabhadra clarifies the differentiated wisdom that constitutes the practice following the fruit.
Mañjuśrī is called the "youngest son" because he is the first-born, having been the first to realize [the truth].
Because the Dharmakāya of Original Wisdom (mūla-jñāna) is able to give birth to the Buddha-family, Samantabhadra is the eldest son;

this is because he relies on fundamental wisdom to give rise to the various wisdoms of practice, thereby governing the Dharma of the Buddha-family and attaining mastery over the activities of the various pāramitās.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī rides upon a lion to clarify that he is the root of the Buddha-nature through which the Dharmakāya is first realized.
Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is the steed that severs delusions. Thus, Samantabhadra riding the fragrant elephant-king symbolizes that his conduct is orderly and majestic.

Furthermore, the reason Mañjuśrī constantly resides in the Eastern World of Golden Color at the abode of Akṣobhya Buddha is to clarify that gold is white in color and capable of being free from defilement. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva always...
Those who dwell in the presence of the Buddha Jewel Majestic Virtue Supreme King (Ratna-tejo-vikrāmin) understand that the myriad practices constitute "jewels.
It is through these practices that one achieves majestic virtue (*tejas*). If one fully possesses these practices, one attains sovereign mastery over the body of the Dharma-jewel;
with majestic virtue, fearlessness, and sovereignty, one becomes a king. If one does not fully possess these practices, one will have things to fear, even if one dwells [in that realm].
The position of high rank. One must not act as a king, for there would be cause for fear. Therefore, Zi (the seventh branch) represents the stage of Buddhahood;

Chou (the eighth) represents the stage of faith; Yin (the ninth) represents the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*); Mao (the tenth) represents the ten practices (*daśacaryā*); Chen (the eleventh) represents the ten dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*); Si (the twelfth) represents the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*);

Wu (the thirteenth) represents the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); Wei (the fourteenth) represents the period of darkness. Entering into the secular world during the period of brightness, one transforms the deluded by conforming to worldly ways. Shen (the fifteenth) and You (the sixteenth)...
The *xu* and *hai* positions are established for the sake of those to be transformed. Such is the manner in which the laws of Dharma are ordained; it is because the Dharma is inherently thus.
Therefore, the Tathāgata governs the *kan* position to manifest illumination. Samantabhadra is the embodiment of wisdom and presides over the myriad practices (*sarva-caryā*).
Avalokiteśvara is the foremost of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), acting as the supreme general who subdues calamity and peril. Mañjuśrī is the foremost of those who awaken the ignorant.
They constantly act as teachers who receive the teachings, with their mutual natures interpenetrating, so as to uphold the Dharma of the Buddha’s house.
They cause all sentient beings to abide in the Middle Way and dwell in a nature of tranquility and harmony. Through wisdom and compassion they benefit all things;
for this reason, their bodies are entirely golden, their eyes and hair are deep blue-black, and while their skin is white, their features are yellow—this is the harmonious vital energy of the Arhats.
All are forms without form and colors without color. As the sutra says: "In every place is Samantabhadra Bodhisattva;
in every place is the Golden World; in every place is Mañjuśrī; in every place is Acalajñāna Buddha. The sutra further states:
"The Buddha-body pervades the entire Dharma-realm, universally manifesting before all sentient beings."
Before his passing, he had completely filled all those who were ready to be transformed. Therefore, the Buddha remains here at this Bodhi tree.
Within as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms of dust, Buddhas sit within a single pore;

each is surrounded by immeasurable assemblies of bodhisattvas, who are each fully instructed in the practices of Samantabhadra. Furthermore, he questioned the Bodhisattva Daśaśīrṣa and others, yet they could not know their karma.

Regarding the mind: the ten questions, such as "the mind does not know karma," cause those who have given rise to faith to observe and reflect within themselves, thereby making their realization increasingly profound and firm.
As the Sūtra says: "All phenomena lack functional activity and possess no intrinsic nature;
therefore, they are all mutually unaware of one another. Furthermore, it describes how they arise from the earth, like the flow of water, the flame of fire, and the rising of wind.

The analogy of mutual unknowing. Furthermore, the subsequent verse says: "Discerningly observing the internal body, who herein is the 'self'? If one can understand in this way, they will realize the existence or non-existence of the self.

Moreover, in the *Bhadramukha-parivarta*, it is stated that from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), taking faith as the foremost, one resolutely takes up the fruit of the Great Bodhi of the Buddha; thus, from the ground of an ordinary person...
It is because one believes that the Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) of the Buddhas of the ten directions is no different from the wisdom of one's own mind.
It is simply due to being deluded by ignorance (*avidyā*). For ignorance and the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions have been fundamentally non-dual from the very beginning.
From the stage of ordinary beings, one has faith that the fundamental wisdom of the bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions is no different from one's own body.
Why is this? Because they are all the same Dharma-nature body and the same fundamental wisdom, just like the branches of a tree.
From a single root arise many branches, leaves, and so forth; because of causes and conditions, growth and decay differ upon each branch of a single tree.
Thus, from the stage of an ordinary person, one comes to believe in the Tathāgata’s ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten stages.

I am fully capable of practicing all of them. Why is this? Reflecting back upon myself since beginningless time, I have performed even those things that were useless while drifting in the ocean of suffering;
how much more so, then, can I now perform these beneficial deeds?
How could a Bodhisattva not be able to carry out the myriad practices for the sake of saving sentient beings? Therefore, from the stage of an ordinary person, one must have faith.
I, too, shall attain the wisdom of the Buddhas. Why is this? Because all Buddhas come from the state of ordinary beings;
the Tathāgatagarbha-body is itself the Dharmakāya, and within it there is no ocean of merit and wisdom that does not abide.
Therefore, it is called a "Treasury" (piṭaka). If one does not perceive the Dharmakāya, all merit, wisdom, great kindness, and great compassion will fail to be accomplished;
they will all belong to the realm of arising and ceasing.

Samantabhadra’s conduct and Mañjuśrī’s fundamental signless wisdom of the Dharmakāya—these two are of a single essence, acting as both principal and attendant to one another. The intermediate non-active wisdom is precisely...
The fruit of Buddhahood: the substance of these three persons is one, provisionally established across five stages to guide ordinary, deluded beings.

If there is an ordinary person whose faith is fulfilled and who resolves to attain enlightenment, they simultaneously realize the three bodies at the beginning of the ten abodes. Mañjuśrī is the Buddha’s Dharma-body.
Samantabhadra is the Buddha’s body of practice (*caryā-kāya*). The fruit of non-active wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*) is the Buddha’s reward body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).

At all times, Mañjuśrī’s Dharma-body and wondrous wisdom of signlessness serve as the precursor; while there is a sequence in the order of their exposition, in realization, the three bodies are simultaneous.
Such is the correspondence of the Dharma; it is impossible to omit any one of them. If one were to omit Mañjuśrī and retain only Samantabhadra, [the principle would be violated].

All practices belonging to the gates of conduct (*caryāmukha*) are subject to outflows (*sāsrava*). If one discards Samantabhadra while retaining only the textual fragments, that which is realized as tranquil concentration belongs to the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*).
If one discards the Buddha while retaining only Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, [this is untenable], for "Buddha" has the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*), and there would be no one who awakens.
For this reason, one cannot discard any one of these three persons; if one were discarded, the triad would not be established.
Therefore, within the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles, these three types of persons do not depart from one another from beginning to end.

Because the gates of those teachings are not yet ultimate, they are all collectively transformation bodies (nirmāṇakāya). To provisionally follow those of lesser faculties, the teaching is briefly and expediently bestowed;
only when they have reached maturity is it then shifted toward the ultimate reality. Thus, the initial stage of the Ten Abodes in this sutra is identical to the Ten Practices.

The ten dedications lead to the ten stages and the state of Equal Enlightenment. Within each stage, one attains fifty dharma-gates because they mutually penetrate one another, extending even to the inexhaustible sequence of all stages.

The progressive levels of the characteristics of practice do not abandon gradualness while being simultaneous, nor do they abandon gradualness within the simultaneous; within these stages, there are thirty [aspects].
Regarding the seven bodhisattvas who share the same name, "Treasury" (Zàng): this is to clarify that the fruit of this dharma-gate of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) has reached its conclusion.
With the intention of discerning and knowing the primary path and the auxiliary paths, thirty-seven bodhisattvas are established to constitute the thirty-seven auxiliary dharma-gates.
This clarifies that all practices of the bodhisattvas from the ten abodes (daśavihāra) onward are auxiliary.
The Way is not merely the non-abiding and non-practicing of the five stages; it is the spontaneous, true essence itself, which is designated as the "correct fruition.

Thus, from the very first stage of the Initial Resolve, by means of the fundamental wisdom of the signless nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one performs all myriad practices without departing from the essence that is devoid of functional activity.
In this way, the Bodhisattva and the Buddha are fundamentally equal in essence regarding cause and fruit.
If one excludes the fruit of Buddhahood, then from the point when the Bodhisattva’s correct application begins until that state is reached, it is collectively termed "auxiliary to the path.
Because movement and stillness are non-obstructive, the primary and auxiliary practices have from the outset been no different; they are a single dharma-gate.
The six stages cause Sudhana to realize the distinctiveness of the Dharma.

Since the sutra contains only the Dharma-gates but no one yet to seek and study them, it causes Sudhana to inquire of his friends and practice each one through conduct, exactly according to the rules of the preceding sutras, so that future students may proceed without obstruction.
Maitreya causes Sudhana to see Mañjuśrī again, clarifying that [the path] proceeds from the Dharma.

The fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the body’s principle and essence serves as the cause; seeing Maitreya Bodhisattva is the result of the wisdom of the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*) upon which Sudhana mounts.
Furthermore, by practicing the conduct of Samantabhadra under the guidance of the various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), one brings about one's own fruition of Buddhahood.
After seeing Maitreya, one enters the universal gate (*samanta-mukha*) of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and perceives one’s own body entering the body of Samantabhadra.
Although he has attained perfect enlightenment, he constantly benefits sentient beings through the practices of Samantabhadra;

this clearly shows that Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya—the three Buddhas of fruition—share one and the same locus from beginning to end, signifying the thorough penetration from cause to fruit.
The path of these three is the great capital of the ancient Buddhas and the ultimate limit of the source of the Dharma. For those who are deluded or awakened, it is the very foundation.

Those who come to fully attain it are those dwelling in delusion who have submerged themselves in saṃsāra; yet for the Way and Dharma of the ancient Buddhas, this has always been thus from the beginning.
It is not a phenomenon of arising and ceasing, for it is without action and without conditioning.
Seventh, clarifying the distinction between the bodhisattvas who have come from the six stages.

As explained within the provisional teachings regarding the sequence of the bodhisattva stages, it is taught that only the conventional *tathatā* (suchness) serves as cause and fruit. Furthermore, during the three stages of worthiness prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*), one has not yet attained direct realization.
Within the first ground, one realizes one *tathatā*; within the tenth ground, one realizes ten *tathatās*. Thus, one realizes ten...

Only after realizing *tathatā* (suchness) can one first perceive the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Yet, regarding the prior realization of *tathatā*, it is further stated that there are ten obstacles to *tathatā*.

Since *tathatā* itself can constitute an obstacle, it is clear that within the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*), what is established is a conventional, nominal *tathatā*, not the fundamental reality.
The stages and ranks thus established are heard by those of the three vehicles alike, and are attended by both *śrāvakas* and those among the devas and humans.

This sutra is not like that; it concerns bodhisattvas who are entirely at the stage of fruition. Mañjuśrī is the causal factor capable of realization, while Akṣobhyajñāna Buddha is the fruit to be realized.
Now, by citing this identity of cause and fruit as non-dual, it serves to establish the initial gateway of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
It further causes those who possess faith to believe that the cause is established through the fruit, and thus they return to practice.
The fruit-dharma takes the causal stage as its basis; upon the initial mind of the ten abodes, one immediately attains perfect enlightenment.

This is because the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realized from the attainment of the fruit serves as the cause. Therefore, this sutra states below: "By means of slight expedient means, one swiftly attains Bodhi.

This is not like the Bodhi of the provisional teachings, for that is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and thus establishes a distinction between the realizing subject and the realized object. [This occurs] in a single thought-moment.
Between these, there is neither subject nor object. The exhaustion of subject and object is called perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).
This is not the same as the extinction of subject and object in the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), for it realizes that subject and object are fundamentally unmoving.

All the assemblies of the ocean-like multitudes of Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and various spirits are indeed the ocean-like assembly of Bodhisattvas at the stage of Buddhahood; they are not ordinary beings.
Because those who wish to enter [the path] are identical to the Sages, it is clarified that the realm of Vairocana’s transformative guidance pervades all sentient beings.
Therefore, at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta, one immediately attains perfect enlightenment; within a single kṣaṇa, one fully realizes this Dharma.
It is not permitted that there be a separate time for attainment outside of this kṣaṇa, for such would not be the fundamental Dharma.
If there is someone who, within the Buddha’s Dharma, perceives the Buddha attaining enlightenment and forms views regarding the duration of eons,
their extent, or the location, then their faith is not yet established.
Eighth, it clarifies that within the Dharma-gates of provisional teachings, such as those of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha, there is a distinction between principle and phenomena;
for instance, it is taught that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature while insentient things lack Buddha-nature, and that all grasses and trees cannot attain the Way or turn the wheel of Dharma.
As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, this is the teaching that transcends conceptual emotion and reveals reality.

For instance, regarding the lands from which the ten Forest Bodhisattvas, such as Guṇakāśa (Virtue Forest), have come: those lands are also named "Wisdom. All objective realms are collectively termed the "essence of wisdom.
Why is this so? Because there is neither the sentient nor the insentient. And why is this so? Because there is no dualistic view. For...
The realm of the single true wisdom is such that there is neither one who attains Buddhahood nor one who does not.

This is because the categories of "sentient" and "insentient" are spoken of in dependence upon karma; however, that which is discussed as attaining Buddhahood does not belong to the domain of karma, as stated in the sutras.
These dharmas have the characteristic of emptiness: they are neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure;
the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. This is the dharma abiding in its own place. Is such a path for sentient beings or for non-sentient things?

If one harbors conceptual attachments, one sees sentient beings attaining Buddhahood while seeing non-sentient things as not attaining Buddhahood. This is the karmic clinging of one's own self. As it is said:

Such an interpreter will ultimately fail to attain Buddhahood. This is because they have not yet seen the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), do not rely on true wisdom, and have not realized that all worldly characteristics are primordially and eternally abiding;
instead, they perceive only the characteristics of arising and ceasing produced by the transformations of deluded consciousness.
Ninth, it clarifies the distinctions in the fruits attained by those of the three vehicles, as taught in the sutras:

for śrāvakas, the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths concerning birth, aging, sickness, and death is taught; for pratyekabuddhas, the twelve links of dependent origination are taught; and for bodhisattvas, [the Dharma of the six perfections is taught].
It is taught that [the path] corresponds to the six pāramitās. Now, this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* also teaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths;

however, it differs from the Four Noble Truths of the Śrāvakas. As clarified in the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths," the fundamental reality of suffering and its origin is originally none other than the Fundamental Wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

This is because it does not involve the acceptance or rejection characteristic of the three vehicles. When Śrāvakas contemplate the two truths of suffering and its origin, they [view them with deep...]* *(Note: The source text appears to be truncated. The translation reflects the provided fragment.)*
One gives rise to weary detachment and practices contemplations such as impermanence, impurity, white bones, and fine dust, knowing that the body is empty and quiescent.

Following this dharma of emptiness and quiescence, wisdom ceases and the body perishes, such that neither compassion nor wisdom arises; this is called "extinction. By means of this state of extinction, [one attains liberation].

That which is called *nirvāṇa* is the extinguishing and subduing of all sufferings; it is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). By means of this Truth of Cessation, it is also called the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
Those of the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhas understand that the dharma of the twelvefold dependent origination has no real substance from the beginning and is entirely empty.
They know that both body and mind are inherently without a master; since body and mind have no master, their nature is eternally without self (*anātman*). Because there is no...
Thus, my ignorance is extinguished, and with the extinction of ignorance, the twelve links of dependent origination are extinguished.

I dwell in leisure, following my own nature, abiding alone as a Pratyekabuddha. Because I differ from the Śrāvakas, I do not hasten toward [their] quiescence; because I differ from the Bodhisattvas, I lack [their] compassion and wisdom.
Because I do not hasten toward quiescence, I am superior to the Śrāvakas; because I am able to uphold the Dharma, I am not inferior to the Śrāvakas. For...
Śrāvakas, upon hearing the Mahāyāna sūtras spoken by the Buddha, are also able to propagate them; however, they have not yet personally realized them.
Expediently taught Bodhisattvas who have recently turned away from the two vehicles, as well as lesser bodhisattvas, have not yet fully possessed the wisdom of great compassion;
they merely teach the six pāramitās to inspire those of inferior faculties and cause them to develop wisdom, because they practice in a partial manner.
Fixed karma causes one to stagnate in ignorance; thus, one still fears birth and death.

The seven, eight, nine, and ten *pāramitās* have not yet been taught, and from the first through the ninth stages (*bhūmi*), the Buddha-nature has not yet been clarified, because practicing that provisional wisdom constitutes an obstruction.
This sutra, however, suddenly reveals fundamental wisdom to those of the highest faculties. When the initial mind first arises, it is at the level of the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*).
This is identical to the Buddha, for by relying on the dharma of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), there is nothing further to be cultivated;

since it is fundamentally unobstructed, compassion and wisdom are spontaneously accomplished without effort. Following conditions within the six realms, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

One realizes that the self-nature of dependently arisen phenomena is eternally true, such that there is no further cultivation or action required. All thoughts and reflections arise from wisdom; one simply knows how to let things be.
The Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya) manifests physical forms and preaches the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of beings, like echoes responding to one another.

It constantly dwells within the stream of birth and death, yet its Dharmakāya remains eternally quiescent; though many kalpas pass, its essence does not shift for even a moment. Entering death and being born again is not a matter of perishing and being reborn.

Entrusting oneself to the wisdom of great compassion, one does not abide in the realization or cultivation [of stages], for such is the nature of the Dharma. This is clearly illustrated by the cases of the Dragon Girl and Sudhana.
This Dharma is difficult to believe; those of the Three Vehicles fold their hands in submission, distantly claiming that this is a transformation-body and not the result of human cultivation.

To speak directly, the *saṃkhyeya* kalpas are established merely to follow worldly sentiments. How could one believe this gate of timeless wisdom? Even if one were to exert effort through many kalpas...
Practicing with toil involves seeking attainment and striving for results; it involves making things long or short, right or wrong, and creating or destroying.
It requires sacrificing the body and forfeiting one's life. How could there ever be a time of attaining Buddhahood through such means?
How much more effortless it would be to enter the realm of Buddha-wisdom from the very first thought! For this reason, the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings—

The lack of true understanding regarding the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the realm of true wisdom—the *dharmakāya* and *tathatā*—is entirely due to the skillful means (*upāya*) of Vairocana, who leads practitioners toward this ocean of the *Avataṃsaka*’s ultimate reality.

This causes them to return to the fundamental Dharma and act according to their wisdom. The various stages (*bhūmi*) thus cultivated are performed in accordance with that wisdom; without giving rise to a sense of agency, they all [proceed].
This brings about the fulfillment of all-aspect omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*). Unlike other teachings, it does not require separate remedies for those on the stages (*bhūmi*).
The distinct transmission of the Dharma-treasury entrusted by the Ten Illuminations is explained in the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata":
"O Son of the Buddha, this Dharma-gate was not taught by the Tathāgata for other sentient beings; it was taught solely for those bodhisattvas who are intent upon the Mahāyāna."
It is said: "This Dharma-gate of the sutra is taught solely for the sake of Bodhisattvas who ride the inconceivable vehicle.
It does not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings. Son of the Buddha, it is like the seven treasures possessed by a wheel-turning sage king;
because of these treasures, he is manifested as a wheel-turning king. These treasures do not fall into the hands of other sentient beings, except for the first queen."
O Son of the Buddha, just as the crown prince born with the full endowment of the marks of a noble wheel-turning monarch does not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings—
except for those true sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King,

who are born into the family of the Tathāgata and have planted the roots of goodness that produce the marks of a Tathāgata— so too is this jewel of a sutra; it is not entrusted to others as is done in the provisional teachings.
It is transmitted for the common practice of both Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, while the teachings of the Three Vehicles are mostly entrusted to the various sages and to ordinary beings who have not yet been born into the Buddha-family, this sutra is entrusted to those of the most supreme great mind—ordinary beings who seek only the Tathāgata’s inconceivable vehicle and are born into the Buddha-family. Why is it that the teachings of the Three Vehicles are mostly entrusted [to others]?
I entrust this to all the holy ones to ensure its circulation, and I charge it upon all ordinary beings who have not yet been born into the Buddha-family.
Because the Dharma of the Three Vehicles has not yet emerged from the defilements of the mind, and because the clarity of the Dharma is not yet realized and is thus easily misinterpreted,

I shall first cause both ordinary beings and sages to praise it together, so that the teaching may spread and the roots of goodness remain unbroken— unlike the conclusion of these ten stages of faith.
One is a Buddha in a single kṣaṇa. For this reason, the teachings of the Three Vehicles were provisionally established to gradually lead beings forward;

as long as one has not transcended the sensory dusts of the mind, it takes three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas to attain Buddhahood. Because these teachings that accord with worldly sentiments are easy for those of various capacities to believe, they are praised by both ordinary people and sages, and thus all may receive and transmit them.
This is not the same as the fundamental wisdom-dharma of the Buddhas of the ten directions in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, nor...
The wisdom of discernment, great kindness, and great compassion—this Dharma transcends the sensory dusts and its teaching is so profound it is difficult to believe.
It must await the attainment of realization at the stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), being born into the Buddha-family and becoming a true son of the Buddha, for it to truly circulate.

If there are only the words of the sages but no one who attains realization, it cannot be called circulation. If there are only the teachings spoken by ordinary beings with no one who attains realization, it likewise does not constitute circulation.
Nor can it be called "circulation," because one's own Dharma is not yet clear and doubts still remain;

for this reason, since one has not yet definitively understood the Buddha’s intent and has not dispelled the darkness within oneself or others, the entrustment is made to ordinary beings of great resolve who have entered into realization.
IV. Clarifying the Identity and Distinction of Attaining Buddhahood The wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) is vast and boundless; it encompasses all phenomena (*dharmas*) to form its physical frame.

Since all phenomena are formless, they share the same substance as the wisdom-body. When one deviates from the true nature, they are separated by a gulf; when one realizes the fundamental source, their forms become identical.

It is solely because of the divergence from the source and the distinctness of appearances that the modes of transformation (*nirmāṇa*) differ. I shall briefly establish ten gates concerning the differences in the realization of the Way (*bodhi*), so that those who are still in the stage of childhood may [understand].

Arousing faith, generating liberation, and dispelling doubts; recognizing that the fundamental nature is free from expedient means, and aspiring with one’s whole being for supreme virtues. Regarding the ten gates:

first, the distinction of the Buddha-body. This refers to the body of Vairocana Buddha as described in the sutra, which possesses ninety-seven kinds of marks as well as an inexhaustible body of marks;
it is not the body of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics.

Second, there is a difference regarding the time of attaining Buddhahood. In the provisional teachings, the time is defined as the period following the Buddha’s birth, when he left the city to renounce the world and attained equal and perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree—as was the case with Śākyamuni Buddha. However, it is not so for Vairocana Buddha.
Furthermore, it is said: "The Tathāgata establishes manifested forms (*nirmāṇa-rūpa*) in order to deliver sentient beings of the three vehicles;
they should see him thus as one who has left home and attained Buddhahood. However, this is not the case regarding the true Dharma-realm ocean (*dharmadhātu-samudra*) within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: 'Since my attainment of Buddhahood, an immeasurable number of asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed. This is precisely the turning back of that [former teaching]."

Regarding the persons of the three vehicles, speaking from the perspective of ultimate reality: this Vairocana Buddha attained great enlightenment by relying upon the fundamental dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and he likewise relies upon that same fundamental dharma-realm without any temporal division.
As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, nor is there any parinirvāṇa.
This is the definitive teaching. Furthermore, wearing a flower crown is inherently not the way of one who has left the household life; it is entirely [without such distinctions].

Regarding the matters of the eight phases: if there is anyone who can know that the Tathāgata neither emerges nor disappears, neither comes into being nor perishes, they will immediately know that the Tathāgata dwells eternally in the world and constantly turns the wheel of Dharma; this is precisely Vairocana appearing in the world.
Furthermore, from the Tuṣita Heaven, he descends to enter the mother’s womb, turns the wheel of Dharma, and enters nirvāṇa.
Within a single kṣaṇa, before that deva had yet descended and before he had yet emerged from the mother’s womb, he has already entered parinirvāṇa;
all matters concerning the dharmas are hereby fully concluded.

Third, there is a distinction regarding the Bodhi tree. Among the three vehicles, the Bodhi tree seen by those on the Buddha-vehicle is a wooden tree, its height and proportions corresponding to those of the human world.
However, in the context of the One Vehicle, the tree under which the Tathāgata attains enlightenment is a jewel-tree, lofty, radiant, and extraordinary.

Fourth, the distinction regarding the seat upon which one sits. Within the Three Vehicles, when a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) attains enlightenment, it renounces honor and nobility to rest upon a mat of grass.
Within this One Vehicle, however, the original body (mūlakāya) attains enlightenment, sitting upon a lion throne of precious lotus flowers, adorned with exquisite jewels.
Possessing all manner of adornments, the five great assemblies are distinguished. At the place of Vairocana Buddha, there is a great assembly surrounding him;
these are all such as Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, as well as those who have newly resolved their minds. All are members of the Dharma-realm assembly who aspire to seek the fruit of Buddhahood.
In all cases, wisdom is perfected such that many kalpas are a single limit; there is no multitude of times distinguished by before or after.

Sixth, the distinctions in manifested signs are as in the provisional teachings: namely, taking birth in Tuṣita Heaven, descending with the spirit to enter the womb, the eight phases of attaining enlightenment, and so forth;
or [manifesting] in the heaven of Maheśvara, sitting upon the precious throne of the Flower King; or...

Taking the three-thousandfold great thousand-world system as the objective field for retribution, such an arrangement of dimensions and limits serves as a transformative device to gradually broaden the minds of sentient beings;
yet this is not yet the ultimate reality of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Thus, the wondrous gate of the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm is divided into ten sections, encompassing Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms within a lotus treasury ocean of worlds.
Reflecting one another in layers, they illuminate the inexhaustible Buddha-lands, mutually penetrating so that each and every Buddha-field fills the ten directions.

Within Buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms of ten Buddha-worlds, there is no limitation or obstruction; body and land correspond perfectly, such that there is no appearance of coming or going between this and that.
Thus, within this ocean of Vairocana’s marks, not even a single atom separates them from the ten directions, nor does a single hair—
How could Kongju fail to encompass the ocean of lands? The manifestations of the Three Vehicles cannot be compared to the illumination of the sun and moon by the light of a firefly;
lapis lazuli cannot be likened to the purity of a maṇi jewel. This is not due to the Buddha himself, but simply because their capacities are inferior.
The seventh is the distinction regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma. Transformation Buddhas turn the wheel of the Three Vehicles, whereas Vairocana turns the wheel of the One Vehicle.
To claim that the teaching of the Three Vehicles states that a dragon girl attains Buddhahood in an instant is merely a transformation; to say otherwise would constitute a slander of the teachings.
This does not accord with the Buddha’s mind or the Buddha’s original intent. To cause the dragon girl to attain Buddhahood in a single instant is the fundamental teaching;
since the Dharma itself is timeless, the moment one realizes the exhaustion of time and place is itself the true Dharma. To claim instead that this is merely a transformation is truly lamentable.
What shall we do now? We did not expect that the nectar of immortality would instead become a poisonous drug, nor that precious jewels would be mistaken for mere dust.
Taking the real for the unreal and the unreal for the real—may future sages refrain from following the footsteps of former worthies.

This must be contemplated deeply by those who possess a thorough understanding of the Buddha’s intent, so that they may transmit the teachings according to the school, bringing benefit and merit to humans and devas, and causing the gold and jade [of the Dharma] to shine resplendently.
Nevertheless, each does not sink; for this reason, the emanation-buddhas teach the three vehicles.
This is like the parable of the fat grass on the Snowy Mountains: if a cow eats it, she obtains pure *sarpis* (clarified butter) and so forth—all of which are possessed in part.
It has not been fully revealed; the gate of the complete and individual characteristics of cause, condition, retribution, and appearance is found only in this *Avataṃsaka*.
Therefore, it is said here that the turning of the wheel of Dharma is distinct.
Eighth, the distinction of the locations where the wheel of Dharma is turned. In the provisional teachings, the transformation Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma;
some say it is at the Deer Park, while others say it is at the Givaka-kuṭāgāra Garden, and so forth. In all these cases, there are specific locations where [the Buddha] comes and goes.
This sutra, however, consists of ten locations and ten assemblies, as well as within all atoms, wherein the Buddha lands and Buddha bodies are layered upon layer, infinitely and inexhaustibly.
Inexhaustible, inexhaustible. Constantly turning the wheel of Dharma. Neither going nor coming; neither emerging nor submerging.
It is said that without leaving the site of enlightenment, one ascends to all places.

The ninth section concerns the distinctions of the grand assemblies’ adornments. When this sutra was being preached, the ten assemblies gathered simultaneously from ten locations among devas and humans.
The noble multitudes of the ten directions and sentient beings of great resolve likewise came from the ten directions;
for each of these ten assemblies, it is said that there were as many beings as atoms in ten buddha-fields who had come to the gathering from their respective directions.
In each position and on each stage, the assembly increases tenfold, hundredfold, and thousandfold in succession to clarify its inexhaustibility.

Furthermore, the assemblies in each and every gathering pervade the entire Dharma-realm, layer upon layer, like reflections of light. Within even a single mote of dust, there are likewise layers of assemblies;
within each and every mote of dust, these assemblies are equal in extent to the empty space of the Dharma-realm. Such are the assemblies.
Indeed, these assemblies consist entirely of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose nature pervades all places;

because their bodies, lands, and assemblies all pervade every location, they do not resemble the assemblies of transformation-buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) within the Three Vehicles, which possess specific locations, limitations, and boundaries for their coming and going.
This is because the faculties of those beings are inferior; it is not so for the Buddhas.
Tenth, the distinction between the Dharma-gates bestowed [upon beings]. As in the provisional teachings, some may begin from the Hīnayāna by practicing the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths.

Within these, the two truths of Suffering and Accumulation are regarded as conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), while the two truths of Cessation and the Path are regarded as ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).

By contemplating that Suffering and Accumulation are truly suffering, they develop a profound sense of weary detachment and seek to attain cessation; therefore, Suffering and Accumulation are fundamentally non-existent.
When consciousness ceases and knowledge perishes, one takes emptiness as the realization, thereby bringing suffering to an end.

Only then does one preach the Mahāyāna Dharma for them, causing them to turn their minds toward practicing the contemplation of dharma-emptiness and the six pāramitās, gradually giving rise to compassion and wisdom.

Alternatively, there may be those with the lineage of a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva who, through the practice of contemplation, counteract that Hīnayāna [tendency]; such individuals possess the nature of compassion.

They joyfully practice the various perfections (*pāramitās*) without realizing emptiness prematurely; they retain their afflictions to benefit sentient beings and accomplish the contemplations on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and so forth.
Alternatively, there are those of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva lineage who, from the very beginning, suddenly cultivate the contemplations on the provisional and the True Suchness (*tathatā*).

By means of the gate of provisional True Suchness, they apply preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for subjugation; after three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they perceive the nature [of reality] in the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and only then attain Buddhahood. As it is said:
This *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is not like that; it is intended solely for those of the highest faculties.
From the very beginning, it directly imparts the Dharma-realm itself—the fundamental Dharmakāya, the ocean of wisdom of the ancient Buddhas—which has been obscured by ignorance.

It causes this to manifest suddenly through the samādhi of skillful means, bestowing the entirety of the Buddha-fruit all at once upon the initial mind of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*). In a single thought-moment...
At that time, the single limit and the single Dharma-realm gate are suddenly encompassed.
○ Fifth, clarifying the differences in seeing the Buddha: Now, the nature and characteristics of the Buddha’s body are one essence without distinction.

Yet, the vessels [of sentient beings] have ten thousand variations, differing according to their faculties. Sentiments harbor the barriers of conceptualization; thus, while the vision is severed, the essence remains uniform. As the body stands, reflections arise; as sentiments linger, the Buddha appears.

They differ. The Buddha responds according to sentient beings' dispositions; thus, these [conventional views] deviate from the truth. When the mind is exhausted and emotions have vanished, the Wisdom Body manifests spontaneously.
Following conditions without artifice, movement and stillness are both true. To be in such resonance is what is called Vairocana Buddha.

These ten gates are briefly established to show the distinctions in perceiving the Buddha, so that those who have newly set their minds on faith may turn away from the derivative and return to the source.
1. When humans see the Buddha, they see only the thirty-two marks.
2. When the devas see the Buddha, they see only the eighty secondary characteristics.
3. When the nāgas see the Buddha, they may see him as a human, or they may see him simply as a great nāga king; as for the other animals...
4. In another way, when the various ṛṣis see the Buddha, they see only an ṛṣi.
5. When the other non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika) see the Buddha, they see him as being of their own kind.
Sixth, the eight classes of spirits and deities see the Buddha as their own king.
Seventh, those of the Hīnayāna see the Buddha as a great śrāvaka.
Eighth, those who are pratyekabuddhas see the Buddha and perceive him as a pratyekabuddha.
In the nine provisional teachings, when bodhisattvas behold the Buddha, they see him merely as the lord of a trichiliocosm,
with his merit and wisdom filling and pervading that trichiliocosm.

Within the eleven vehicles of the teaching, bodhisattvas perceive the Buddha as the sovereign of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), presiding over ten buddha-fields as numerous as the atoms of a lotus-treasury world-ocean.

These ten distinct modes of perceiving the Buddha all arise from the differences in faith and aspiration at the time of generating the resolve for enlightenment; it is through this faith and aspiration that [these distinctions occur].

Because of these powers, one’s vision of the Buddha differs. Therefore, you should know that those who resolve their minds to practice must give rise to a vast mind, believe in the vast gateways of the teachings, make vast vows, perform vast practices, and enter into vast wisdom.

By benefiting and bringing to fulfillment inexhaustible sentient beings, they will swiftly accomplish the bodhisattva practices, vows, merit, and wisdom, such that all are completely perfected. If it were not so...
This is so. Ultimately, it does not constitute the final attainment of Great Bodhi.
Sixth, clarifying the timing of the teaching: When one first awakens the mind of Right Enlightenment, the source of the Way is empty and still.

Wisdom is perfected throughout the three periods of time; beginning and end are both exhausted. It encompasses all phenomena, unifies existence and non-existence, blends the past and future, and seals the ancient and modern. It is vast and open, only...

The Divine is tranquil and detached, a true sage (*arhat*). Sentimentality has perished and wisdom is established; conceptualization is severed and compassion remains. The perfect sound spreads afar, and beings receive benefit according to their faculties.

As a single rain universally nourishes all things, the hundred plants each attain growth in equal measure. Like an echo in a valley, the sound accords with the striking to form a melody; so do all capacities receive benefit, functioning through wisdom without artifice.

Briefly relying on the provisional and the ultimate, ten types [of teachings] are established. As for the temporal sequence of when these teachings arose: [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be a fragment from a Buddhist treatise concerning the nature of the Buddha’s teaching and its pedagogical manifestations.*
The same. First, as stated in the *Malla-sūtra*: after the Buddha had first attained enlightenment and reflected for one week, he immediately preached the Dharma at the Deer Park.

Second, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: at the Deer Park, the Buddha turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths, whereby immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the mind of a śrāvaka, up to the mind of a pratyekabuddha and the mind of great bodhi, and so forth. Third, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

1. The Sūtra states that he went to the Deer Park to preach the Dharma after twenty-one days. 2. According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra*, he preached the Dharma on the sixth day.
3. According to the *Udānavarga* and the *Sūtra on the Arising of Practice*, he preached the Dharma on the seventh day.

4. According to the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, he preached the Dharma on the eighth day. 5. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, he preached the Dharma on the fifth day. 6. [The text mentions] five weeks.
1. The Japanese school asserts that the Dharma was preached [immediately]. 2. This is as stated in the *Dvādaśavyākaraṇa-sūtra*. 3. One school holds that no Dharma was preached for one year. 4.
Following the Tang dynasty’s Master Zang, it is judged that after the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, he waited for a fixed period of twenty-one days before preaching the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
5. The School of Profound Mystery (Tongxuan). 6. Now, following this Dharma-gate of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, we do not rely at all on what has been stated above. Thus it is.

The Sūtra takes as its primary tenet the fundamental reality of the Great Compassion of Principle and Phenomena, which is the intrinsic nature and function of the primordial wisdom of the Dharma-realm.
It does not rely on explanations based on emotional measures or temporal divisions; it exhausts all views of past and present, constantly turning the Wheel of Dharma without beginning or end.

Such is the fundamental nature of the Dharma, as described above. All of this relies upon the individual faculties and the temporal perceptions of those who see; it is not that the Tathāgata possesses such [limitations].

It is the same. The essence of the Tathāgata’s fundamental dharma-wisdom cannot be established as having temporal divisions; rather, simply causing the mind to believe and resolve that the dharma-realm is timeless is itself the time when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma.
When emotions vanish and the mind is exhausted, such that one acts according to innate wisdom, this is the time when the Tathāgata attains Buddhahood and turns the wheel of Dharma.
If, however, emotions persist and views are established, to say "the Tathāgata is thus" [is merely a conceptual construction].

The times when [the Buddha] appears in the world, and likewise the times when he preaches the Dharma, do not rely on the perception of a Buddha; they are entirely matters of one's own subjective sentiment.
This sutra, however, is the time that is timeless, preached at all times. As the Lotus Sutra says:
"Since my attainment of Buddhahood, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed. Since measure is fundamentally non-existent, how could one know what constitutes the time for preaching the Dharma?
All of these are the functioning of the Tathāgata’s single wisdom, his single perfect sound, at a single moment—
using that which is timeless as the time for preaching the Dharma.
○ Seventh, clarifying the provisional and the real regarding the Pure Land: As for the surging ocean of wisdom, its vastness makes its shores impossible to fathom;

as for the distant source of truth, its boundlessness makes its limits rarely found. Within the Dharma-realm of Vairocana, its essence and manifestations encompass as many phenomena as there are grains of sand.
The vast and wondrous gateway of the Dharma is such that purity and defilement intermingle infinitely.

It is simply according to the karmic applications of one's own cultivation that perceived realms differ, causing the sacred teachings to appear contradictory as they are not fixed according to the faculties [of beings]. Sometimes, the Pure Land is provisionally divided into other lands, while the defiled realm is pointed out as Sahā;
sometimes, this place is shown as a provisional means of transformation, while the lower direction is indicated as the land of true retribution. Thus Mañjuśrī dwells...
Avalokiteśvara comes from the Golden World in the eastern land, while Guanyin arrives from the wondrous land of peace and bliss in the western direction.

Thus, their provisional manifestations differ. For those beginning their studies who lack a point of reliance, I shall now briefly synthesize these various approaches into ten categories to provide a definitive guide.
First is the Pure Land of Amitābha. This is for those ordinary beings who grasp at signs and have not yet believed in the true principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

By focusing their mindfulness exclusively, the aspect of that recollection does not shift; because of this single-minded sincerity, their minds become partially purified, and they attain birth in the Pure Land.
This is provisional and not ultimate.

The Pure Land described in the *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* is intended for those sentient beings who have not yet gained faith in the true principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) and who delight in sublime forms and appearances;
it enables them to bring those forms and images to mind through mental visualization, so that through the perfection of such visualization, [liberation may be attained].
And thus one is born in the Buddha-land. This provisional [manifestation] is not the ultimate reality.

Third, regarding the Pure Land in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra: the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe and, through the application of his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), briefly manifested it before it vanished again.
This is the land of true retribution (*vipākabhūmi*). Its full extent—whether broad or narrow—has not yet been fully described; thus, while it is real, it is not yet fully extensive.
In the *Four Brahma-Net Sūtras* regarding the Pure Land, although it is said that there is one great Flower-King with a thousand petals,
and upon each petal there are ten billion transformation Buddhas who convert ten billion sentient beings throughout the four continents,

the thousand petals and that Flower-King are presented as a realm of retribution for the sake of the bodhisattvas of the three vehicles whose vision is not yet expansive; thus, they have not yet been fully established.
This is complete, yet it is provisional and not yet ultimate.
In the pure land of the five Maheśvara heavens, the Tathāgata sits upon a precious lotus throne and attains equal and perfect enlightenment;
this constitutes the true retribution. Here in Jambudvīpa, within the Bodhimaṇḍa of the kingdom of Magadha, he attains [enlightenment].

The Perfectly Awakened One is a transformation [body]. This is taught as a provisional teaching among the Three Vehicles for those bodhisattvas whose defilement and purity have not yet been extinguished.

It is said that this Jambudvīpa and the six heavens are the contaminated (*sāsrava*) realm of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while that Maheśvara heaven of the higher realms is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Thus, their minds still harbor defilement and purity; since they have not yet transcended these dualities, this is a provisional [teaching].
This teaching is not yet the definitive exposition.

Regarding the Pure Land indicated in the *Ṣaṇ-nirvāṇa-sūtra*, which states that there is a "True Reward" (*sambhoga*) Pure Land of the Tathāgata located to the west beyond thirty-two *gaṅgā*-sands of Buddha-lands,
this refers to a portion of the provisional teachings for the three vehicles concerning the defiled [realms].

To purify those who have not yet passed away, it is said that this trichiliocosm is entirely a land of defilement, and that the Tathāgata’s retributive pure land is provisionally situated in the west.
This provisional teaching is not the ultimate reality.

Regarding the sevenfold transformation of the Pure Land in the *Lotus Sūtra*: this refers to those bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles for whom defilement and purity have not yet been extinguished;
it speaks of moving various humans and devas and placing them in other lands. This is a provisional teaching, not the ultimate reality.

The Pure Land indicated by the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is intended for those bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings within the Three Vehicles whose notions of defilement and purity have not yet been extinguished;
it causes them to know that this very land is eternally pure despite its apparent impurity. While the multitude may believe this, they are as yet unable to perceive it for themselves.
This is the reality, not the provisional. One may have faith yet not yet see it. Ninth, the Pure Land of Mind-Only:
when one realizes one’s own mind, its very substance is non-mind; its nature is solely true wisdom. This is the truly pure land.
