Therefore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "According as the mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure. If one wishes to attain purity...
The earth should purify the mind.
The pure land where Vairocana dwells is precisely the lotus buddha-fields within the dust motes of ten buddha-lands;
it encompasses both the pure and the defiled. It is neither defiled nor pure, and is devoid of the characteristics of high and low, this and that, or self and other.
Each and every Buddha-land fills the entire Dharma-realm without any mutual obstruction or partition. To speak briefly, there are lands as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields;
yet one should know that these inexhaustible Buddha-lands do not emerge from outside a single atom, for they have neither small nor large dimensions, nor are they established with fixed limits.
Taking the Dharma itself as their boundary, they are not restricted by perimeters. Their oceans of marks are both pure and mixed, and their forms and images are layered upon one another. This...
This constitutes the true fruition; it is not a provisional gathering.
Eighth, clarifying the realm of transformative guidance: The Buddha’s realm is boundless, yet it varies according to the capacities of beings.

Depending on the breadth or narrowness of their dispositions, there appear differences in what they perceive; this is not because the Tathāgata has partitioned its dimensions. When one's disposition is subtle, the realm appears narrow; when one's capacity is vast, [the realm appears vast].

Thus, the scope of the objective realm is vast. If wisdom accords with the true source, the Buddha-realm pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*. At times, one perceives Jambudvīpa as the field of transformation;

at times, one perceives the four continents for the sake of saving sentient beings; at times, one perceives a form that fills the great trichiliocosm; and at times, one perceives the reward body within the ten oceans.
Since such various methods of establishing the teachings differ, upon what should those who are beginning their studies rely? Briefly, five [points] are indicated.
Entering this gate, one recognizes its provisional and ultimate aspects, enabling one to abandon the branches and follow the root to swiftly realize Bodhi.
Within a single person, one perceives the realm of the Buddha; one sees only the transformation of sentient beings throughout a single Jambudvīpa.
Second, when the various devas see the Buddha, they see only their own respective realms. For instance, Śakra is at the stage of a Bodhisattva of the second bhūmi;
as they gradually ascend to the rank of Brahmā, this is the stage of a Bodhisattva of the tenth bhūmi.

Alternatively, for a temporary period, through the accomplishment of sentient beings by the Buddha’s supernormal powers, he causes ordinary beings among gods and humans, as well as those of the two vehicles, and...
Junior bodhisattvas are all able to perceive the realm of the Buddha’s land of recompense;

this is just as in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, where the pure land manifested when the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe. Or, at times, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, he enables humans and devas to see one another;
this is as described in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* regarding the Jewel Mansion situated above the desire realm.
Below the realm of form (rūpadhātu), the great assembly of devas and humans is gathered therein.
Among the three vehicles, the Arhats perceive the Buddha’s sphere of gathering and transforming beings;

just as a great Arhat, through the power of the divine eye (divyacakṣus), can see the Buddha’s sphere of gathering and transforming beings throughout the trichiliocosm, so it was said of Aniruddha: "I..."
With the divine eye, he sees the trichiliocosm of Śākyamuni Buddha’s land as clearly as looking at an *āmala* fruit in the palm of his hand.
This is unlike a lesser arhat, whose vision is not fixed;

for while he may see the Buddha gathering and transforming beings in a single Jambudvīpa, this is achieved through the power of long-subdued patience (*kṣānti*) that can sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*), yet he has not yet attained the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), nor has he yet...
There are matters such as supernatural powers, spiritual penetrations, and transformations.

Regarding the realm of the Buddha’s skillful means in gathering and transforming beings according to the four provisional teachings: at the first stage (bhūmi), one sees a hundred Buddhas; at the second stage, a thousand Buddhas.
At the third stage, there are ten thousand Buddhas; from this point on, they increase progressively as described in the teachings of the Three Vehicles and the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the realm of the Buddhas who gather and transform beings as perceived by Bodhisattvas of the Five Real Teachings:
a Bodhisattva at the first stage sees many hundreds of Buddhas—meaning an inexhaustible hundred, not merely a numerical hundred. A Bodhisattva at the second stage sees...
"Many thousands of Buddhas" refers to an inexhaustible thousand. "Bodhisattvas of the third stage" refers to many tens of millions and so forth.
To speak according to reality, the Bodhisattvas of all stages see [the Buddhas] equally, like a net of Indra; the same is true for the Bodhisattvas of the three levels of worthiness (trīṇi kṣānti).
It is not only the Lotus Treasury World (*padmagarbha-lokadhātu*), with its dust-motes of ten Buddha-lands, that serves as their retributive realm; rather, it is the entire *dharmadhātu*.

Space is entirely equal throughout. This is because at the very first moment of the initial mind of the Ten Abodes, when one first perceives the Path, there is already no perception of "great" or "small";
thus, one perceives the Buddha’s transformed realm in its entirety as being identical to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

The vision of many hundreds of Buddhas' realms in the First Ground clarifies the meaning of "fulfillment. This is not like the mere "hundred" of the Three Vehicles; these "many hundreds" are equivalent to the inexhaustible.
...for this reason.
○ Ninth, clarifying the extension and brevity of cause and effect: Now, the Dharmadhātu is perfectly quiescent, without beginning and without end.

Its principle and wisdom are like empty space; it is neither cause nor effect. It is only for the sake of the habitual measures of sentient beings that names are provisionally attached. When these mental afflictions cease and such measures are exhausted, what [remains]?

What is called "the means of establishment" (sādhana) does not establish itself; it originally arises from valid cognition (pramāṇa). When valid cognition ceases and mental afflictions are exhausted, the name itself becomes true.
Now, by means of this true name that is nameless, we discuss the true fruit that is fruitless; by means of this true discourse that is unspeakable, we discuss the true cause that is causeless.
Those who are beginners must not become stuck on the name; those who are at the stage of initial study [must likewise not be so hindered].
By abandoning their doctrines, names become fixed; by abandoning doctrines, words vanish. One should simply follow one's nature and accord with conditions:
when arising, it arises as the Dharma; if there are no conditions, its cessation is merely the cessation of the Dharma. As for that which possesses this Dharma, its nature does not know itself.
Now, discussing the extension or brevity of cause and effect is like bird tracks in the sky or the son of a barren woman.

It is only because sentient beings possess minds of varying degrees of delusion and wisdom that their perceptions of confusion differ according to their own minds, resulting in different speeds of realization. Like splitting bamboo or climbing a ladder, these are each distinct according to individual capacity.
The categories based on compassion differ in their duration and brevity; it is not that the sun and moon act as the temporal divisions for them.

The teaching is not bestowed arbitrarily, but arises because of sentient beings' capacities. The teaching accords with their faculties; when there are faculties, the teaching arises. Now, based upon these faculties, ten gates are established.
First, those who attain the fruit of arhatship through the "Come hither" (ehibhikṣu) ordination of the Hīnayāna;
second, those who attain the fruit of arhatship after one more birth in the Hīnayāna;
third, those who attain the fruit of arhatship after three births in the Hīnayāna.
1. Those of the Hīnayāna attain the fruit of Arhatship after sixty kalpas.
2. Pratyekabuddhas attain the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood after four births. 3.
There are also Pratyekabuddhas who, being slow, attain the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood after passing through a hundred kalpas.
Seventh, according to the provisional teachings, Bodhisattvas attain Buddhahood only after a fixed period of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Eighth, according to the *Lotus Sūtra* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra), which teaches the convergence of the three vehicles into one through the ultimate truth, even a dragon girl can attain Buddhahood in a single kṣaṇa.
The *Pobijing* (Sutra on Destroying the Three Vehicles) states that one only attains Buddhahood after many kalpas;
the *Jiuhua jing* (Ninefold Avataṃsaka Sutra) says that a devaputra of Tuṣita attains the fruit of the tenth bhūmi in three lifetimes;
and the *Shancai tongzi* (Sudhana Kumāra) attains Buddhahood in a single lifetime.
As stated above, all of these are the holy teachings of the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle, taught according to the faculties and capacities of beings.
For example, the dragon girl shattered the fixed kalpa of the Three Vehicles to establish the actual gateway of the *kṣaṇa*;

the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* granted the prophecy of future Buddhahood within the Bhadrakalpa to the butcher Viśālakṣa, thereby shattering the notion that icchantikas lack the Buddha-nature; and the devaputra of Tuṣita [revealed...]
Through the extraordinary power of the One Vehicle teaching, one may hear it and give rise to faith; even if one does not practice, this can still serve as the seed [for enlightenment].
By being touched by the light and coming to be born in the Tuṣita Heaven, one ascends to the stages of the ten bhūmis.

Taking this single instance as an example, the intent is that those who believe in what the Buddhas have mounted as their vehicle—because it is difficult to believe—will, upon believing, certainly establish the seed. This is for the sake of...
When faith and understanding internally permeate, one will inevitably attain Buddhahood.

As in the case of the youth Sudhana, who attained Buddhahood in a single lifetime, this clarifies that at the initial mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), within a single kṣaṇa, emotions vanish and conceptualizations are exhausted; the three periods of time become a single thought-moment, and nothing further arises.

This is called "one birth. It does not mean taking up emotional attachments to establish the divisions of time and kalpas within a birth; rather, such non-arising immediately brings about the fruit of Buddhahood.
Because it accords with the original nature of birth, it is called "one birth. This is identical to the case of the dragon girl in a single kṣaṇa:
when emotions are exhausted and time has ceased, one is named a Buddha.
X. Clarifying the Beginning and End of the Teachings of the Assembly The World-Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom, shines universally throughout the Dharma-realm.
His wisdom encompasses all things, and he shares the same reality as both ordinary beings and sages. Principle and phenomena are mutually integrated; essence and function penetrate one another.
Thus, the sublime scriptures of forty chapters interweave from beginning to end, and the wondrous words of one million stanzas reflect one another from first to last across the ten locations.
The ten assemblies are as layered as a celestial net; the ten lands and ten bodies are like reflections in a mirror, mutually entering one another.

When one gate is opened, all gates are simultaneously activated; when one chapter is discussed, all chapters are collectively revealed. As the Way-tree was first perfected, the nine heavens arrived together.
The Universal Radiance is gathered as one; all ten stages are ascended simultaneously. There is no difference between past and present; the old and the new are but a single thought-moment.

Without departing from this single station, one distinguishes the gates of the five stages. Within a single practice, an ocean of practices as vast as the sands of the Ganges is established upon the essence of the Dharma-realm.

The terminology established for instructing the laity is uniform in its fruition and virtue; the teachings devised to lead beings toward birth [in the path] have Mañjuśrī extolling and elucidating the essence of the Dharma, while Samantabhadra brings the cultivation of practice to completion.
The light of these two—compassion and wisdom—intermingles, causing the clouds of the Dharma to nourish the precious moisture [of sentient beings].
Within the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," it further enjoins Sudhana to cultivate anew. Following this model throughout this entire scripture, each and every...

The aspects of their practice and the bodhisattvas’ methods for receiving and delivering sentient beings are each clearly delineated in successive order. Now, they are categorized into ten dharmas to summarize the essential framework.
First is the clarification of Vairocana’s initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, which corresponds to the first chapter of the sutra, "The Sublime Array of the World Ruler."

Regarding the phrase "initially attaining perfect enlightenment": by means of one's own body and mind, one realizes all phenomena of the three periods of time—past, present, and future—as being equal within a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*), wherein there is no distinction between long and short durations.

Yet, within that single thought-moment, one does not destroy the wisdom regarding the long and short kalpas of the three periods of time for sentient beings, nor the wisdom of various distinct cognitions and views of sentient beings. Thus, [the wisdom] of above and below, before and...
The final forty chapters of this sutra were, in their entirety, instantaneously sealed at the single moment when [the Buddha] first attained perfect enlightenment.
By means of the Dharma-realm oceanic wisdom-seal samādhi-gate, he simultaneously and suddenly sealed them;

through his physical form, color, and vocal sounds, he proclaimed all Buddha-dharmas, universally disseminating them throughout the oceans of lands within every atom. This continued until his entry into nirvana, without shifting even for a single moment.
At that time, the single limit and single nature mean that the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future are all in one and the same time.

Manifesting differentiated teachings according to the various sentient beings, with the ancient and the present penetrating one another, is called "Beginning" (Śā). To accord with the Dharma in this way is called "Establishment" (Sam).
To rely on the Dharma in this way, not being a mental fabrication, is called "Rightness" (Mmyaṅ). To have wisdom reach this principle is called "Awakening" (Dra).

Regarding the manifestation of the three periods of time within a single thought-moment: this is for the sake of sentient beings; it is not that the three periods of time exist within the fundamental dharma itself.

Second, the explicit indication of the fruit and the exhortation to practice consists of the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Manifestation of Signs," the "Chapter on Samādhi of Samantabhadra," and the "Chapter on the World."
These are the five chapters of the sutra: the Chapter on Accomplishment, the Chapter on the Flower Treasury World, and the Chapter on Vairocana.

In the Chapter on Manifesting Signs, light is emitted from between the Tathāgata’s many teeth, and through the sound within that light, he announces to the assembly in the ten directions, causing them all to gather.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is the Buddha’s eldest son; he governs the Buddha’s...
The Family Dharma: Entering the Buddha’s Samādhi and extolling the virtues of the Buddha-fruit, so as to cause the assembly to feel reverence and affection, giving rise to faith, joy, and practice.
When the three types of faith and understanding are fully perfected, there are these six chapters from the second assembly:

the "Tathāgata Name" Chapter, the "Four Noble Truths" Chapter, the "Light and Enlightenment" Chapter, the "Bodhisattva Inquiry on Wisdom" Chapter, the "Pure Conduct" Chapter, and the "Worthy Leader" Chapter.
The Sūtra was preached within the Hall of Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā-maṇḍala).

Since the Hall of Universal Radiance is the fundamental abode where the fruition of the Buddha’s wisdom-activity reaches full maturity, it is from within this very place that the Dharma-gate of the stage of faith (śraddhā-bhūmi) is taught; this is to clarify that the realization of the fruit serves to perfect faith.

Having already established faith in the merit of the fruition, from this point onward— extending from the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) and the eleventh stage up to the "Chapter on the Flower of the Buddha" (*buddhapuṣpavarga*)—
one clearly elucidates the entry into the Way and the progressive cultivation until the five stages are fully perfected. Because there is no temporal interval between the cause and the fruition,
all ten Buddhas, beginning with the Fundamental Immovable Wisdom (*mūlācalajñāna*), serve as the gates of that which is to be believed.

The fourth section clarifies the entry into the realization of reality. From the third assembly, [the Buddha] ascends to the summit of Mount Sumeru and emits light from the tips of his two great toes;
therein he speaks six chapters of the sutra: first, the Chapter on Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru;
second, the Chapter on Verses of Praise on the Summit of Mount Sumeru; third, the Chapter on the Ten Abodes; fourth, the Chapter on Holy Conduct; fifth...
The Chapter on the Merit of First Resolving Mind; the Sixth, the Chapter Clarifying the Dharma.

These six chapters of the sutra clarify the initial realization of the dharma-gate, dwelling where the Buddhas dwell, being born into the family of the Buddhas, and sharing the same nature of Buddha-wisdom. Their merit, understanding, practice, principle, and wisdom are like those of the Buddhas;
at the very moment of first resolving mind, they achieve perfect enlightenment. As for "ascending to the summit of Mount Sumeru," this clarifies [the stage] following from prior faith.
The mind now ascends to the summit of the mountain of the Dharma King of the Ten Abodes. Upon reaching the limit of the Dharma, wisdom shines forth without obstruction;

like ascending a high mountain, one reaches the point where all characteristics are exhausted. From this point onward, one acts in accordance with the Dharma without effort; from beginning to end, one is entirely Buddha.
One does not attain perfection through the eight stages; it is effortless. The *Sūtra of the Adornment of the Tathāgata* states:

"The Bodhisattvas of the Three Sages, within the stream of the Dharma, spontaneously reach Buddhahood. The initial water and the subsequent water are of one nature, because the Buddha as cause and the Buddha as fruit are of one nature.
Within this, there is no beginning, middle, or end, for there is no separation between moments, and it relies upon the fundamental Dharma. Thus, there is none.
Thoughts may be interrupted, and thus cause and effect would come to an end; for it is said that "with each thought-moment in accord, there is a Buddha.

One does not concern oneself with the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) or with supernatural powers (abhijñā). These marks and powers are obtained from within this true awakening (samyak-saṃbodhi). If one realizes true awakening, one immediately ceases to cling to any signs.

Fifth is the practice of setting forth [the path]. From the fourth assembly, he ascends to the Yāma Heaven and emits light from between the Tathāgata’s two feet, wherein he expounds four chapters of the sūtra: first, the "Chapter on Ascending to the Yāma Heaven Palace";

second, the "Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Yāma Heaven Palace"; third, the "Chapter on the Ten Practices"; and fourth, the "Chapter on the Inexhaustible Treasury. This stage proceeds from the Tathāgata...

The emission of light from between his two feet and the ascent to the Yāma Heaven to preach are intended to clarify that, from the summit of Mount Sumeru to the limit of the phenomenal realm, he realizes the Buddha’s Wisdom Body;
then, descending to the Yāma Heaven, he acts in accordance with the fundamental wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena.
The myriad practices of Samantabhadra are initiated; these locations are used to symbolize the dharmas so that they may be easily understood.

Just as those various devas are detached from the surface of the earth, this deva-dwelling abides in space to clarify the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), because one proceeds by relying on the dharma of fundamental wisdom and emptiness.

Sixth, the mutual interpenetration of phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*). From the fifth assembly, [the Bodhisattva] ascends to the Tuṣita Heaven palace and emits light from atop the Tathāgata’s knee to expound the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
"Dedication" means causing all phenomenal dharmas to enter into the principle;

by means of the ten phenomenal dharmas of practice, they enter into the preceding ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*). Because phenomenon and principle are without obstruction, it is called dedication. The preceding ten...
"Abiding" refers to the fundamental wisdom of Mañjuśrī’s Dharma-body. The subsequent ten practices refer to the myriad deeds of Samantabhadra.
This clarifies that the essence and function of these two figures penetrate one another; this is termed "dedication.

As for the light emitted from the knees, it clarifies the sovereign mastery over the unfolding and rolling up of principle and phenomena, just as a person's bending, extending, and turning all depend upon the knees.
Seventh, the explanation of the virtues accomplished through the cultivation of the aggregates. From the sixth assembly, [the Tathāgata] ascended to the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
The Tathāgata emitted a ray of light from between his eyebrows; this light was identical to the ray of light emitted from between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows during the first assembly.
Because one returns to the original place after completing the cycle, it is said that the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* constitutes a single chapter.
Why is there no "Chapter on Ascending to the Palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven" and no "Chapter of Verses of Praise"? It is to clarify that the fruit of the ten stages is complete;

abiding in the palace of the fundamental Dharma, one is eternally and universally present in all things. With merit completed and practice perfected, there is no further ascent or progress. The wisdom of the ten stages is full, and there is no further advancement.
Because of cultivation; because one constantly faces all Buddhas as if they were present before one; and because it is not something newly arrived, for which there would be no praise.
This gate of the ten stages merely involves the accumulation of merit within the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications until it is perfected and brought to full maturity.
Thereafter, there is no further dwelling; it is accomplished spontaneously, naturally bringing about the fulfillment of all dharmas.

Eighth, the unimpededness of following conditions. In the seventh assembly, at the Third Dhyāna Heaven, he gathered the assembly of the eight dhyānas and spoke of the Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood (Ekajātipratibaddha).
He entered the Buddha-flower Samādhi and explained the practice of the Universal Worthy (Samantabhadra) within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi) across the eleven stages.
This universally clarifies the entry into the mundane world and the pervasive pervasion of the Dharma-realm; it is called "Universal" within the stage of Equal Enlightenment.

This refers to the conduct of the worthy ones. Regarding the term "Buddha-flower Samādhi": "Buddha" means awakening. This signifies that one has already completed the realization of Buddhahood through the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Subsequently, in the eleventh stage, the practice of awakening is perfected.
The ninth [section] clarifies the conclusion of the stages of cause and effect. From the Chapter on the Ten Samādhis, the Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers, the Chapter on the Ten Patiences,
the Chapter on the Incalculable [Aśaṃkhyeya], the Chapter on the Lifespan, the Chapter on the Abodes of All Bodhisattvas, the Chapter on the Inconceivable Dharmas,

the Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata, the Chapter on the Merit of the Radiance of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks, the Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra, and the Chapter on the Emergence of the Tathāgata.
These are the chapters from "The Chapter on Manifestation" to "The Chapter on Transcending the World. Why is this so?

Because the chapters from "The Ten Samādhis" to "Transcending the World" comprehensively encompass the five stages, the ten bhūmis, and the stage of Buddhahood, as well as the ten thousand practices of Samantabhadra;
thus, they penetrate the gates of cause and effect from beginning to end.
The tenth [chapter] clarifies that ordinary beings may realize the truth. From the eighth assembly, within the Jeta Grove, the Tathāgata entered the samādhi-gate of the Lion’s Stretch;
he again raised up the fruit-virtues of the Dharma-realm and manifested them to all worlds, causing sentient beings to give rise to faith and joy and to penetrate the true reality of the Buddha.
Five hundred śrāvakas, including Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra, appeared as if they did not hear, acting as a foil for the same purpose.

The followers of the Two Vehicles have both faith and lack of faith. Among those in the assembly, six thousand bhikṣus—clearly ordinary persons—suddenly attained clarity regarding the ten ears and ten eyes in the presence of Mañjuśrī.

Furthermore, in the ninth assembly at the eastern side of the city of Vārāṇasī, there were ten thousand nāgas, five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, five hundred youths, and five hundred maidens.
The women were all ordinary beings who attained the rank of Buddhahood together; immeasurable nāgas were reborn in the human realm; ten thousand nāgas gave rise to the bodhicitta;
and the five assemblies of Vārāṇasī all ascended to the fruit of Buddhahood. The five hundred represent the five stages; the six thousand represent the six stages;
and the ten thousand nāgas represent the gateway of the ten thousand practices. There was not one...
Because it is a provisional designation for the sake of the matter, the great stūpas of the past Buddhas serve as the assembly hall for its practitioners.
This clarifies that the traces of the path of ancient Buddhas and present Buddhas are not different; they are identical to being within the assembly of a Tathāgata.

Thus, for those who possess faith and understanding, as well as those who have newly resolved to attain awakening and enter [the path], this Dharma-gate of the Buddha-fruit within the Dharma-realm is like a lion king.

When this child was first born, although he was not yet able to match the sovereign power and strength of the lion king, his lion-like characteristics were entirely without difference, and all beasts were naturally afraid of him.
Likewise, those who have first entered and realized the fruit-stage dharma-gate of this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* are also like this; they are able to believe in themselves.
The nature and characteristics of body and mind are, in their entirety, the self-substance of the Buddha-fruit, eternally true and fundamentally without cultivation or construction.
By means of this gate of truth, one perfects and prepares for the progressive cultivation of the myriad distinct practices.

Although one has not yet attained the power and function equal to that of a Buddha, this is called "planting the seeds of Buddhahood" and is called "being born into the family of the Buddhas. To act as...
The true sons of the Buddha immediately transcend those three vehicles. They perceive that all persons of the three vehicles, devas, humans, and non-Buddhists cannot fathom this with their wisdom.

the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World-Ruling Lord," which was held at the Bodhimanda and expounds upon the fruit-dharma of the ancient Buddhas.
Now, in elucidating the teachings and propagating the sutras, one must distinguish four points:
first, the extended analysis of the sutra’s meaning; second, the clarification of the sutra’s central tenet;
third, the identification of its doctrinal essence; and fourth, the general enumeration of the assemblies.
Regarding the general outline of the meaning of this scripture, it is briefly divided into ten sections: first, elucidating the Tathāgata’s initial attainment of perfect enlightenment;

second, elucidating the exhortation to practice by citing the fruit; third, elucidating the establishment of faith through the fruit; fourth, elucidating entry into the realization of reality; fifth, elucidating the initiation of practice and cultivation;

sixth, elucidating the mutual integration of wisdom and compassion; seventh, elucidating the perfection of virtues through accumulated cultivation; eighth, elucidating the benefiting of sentient beings. [The remaining two sections are: ninth, elucidating the manifestation of the great function; tenth, elucidating the ultimate consummation.
1. Sovereignty; 2. Ninefold clarification of the stations where the worthy ones reside; 3. Tenfold clarification of causing ordinary beings to realize the truth;
4. Clarification of those who have first attained perfect enlightenment—this is the "Chapter on the Wondrous Adornment of the World Ruler."
Second, as for the exhortation to practice by citing the fruits [of the path],

this consists of the five chapters from the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs" (*Prakṛty-abhisaṃbodhi*) down to the "Chapter on Vairocana," as well as the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World-Ruling Lord" (*Lokendra-vyuha*). These cite the fruits accomplished by the Buddha to inspire others to practice.

Regarding the "Three Clarities (Tri-vidyā) that Establish Faith through the Fruit": this refers to the six chapters of the sutra from the "Chapter on the Names of the Buddhas" down to the "Chapter on Worthy Leader.
It may also be understood as encompassing everything from the preceding "Chapter on the Sublime Adornments of the World-Ruler" onwards.
Thus, one takes the ten Wisdom Buddhas as the fruit of one's own mind, with Wisdom Buddha Immovable (Aksobhya-jñāna-buddha) as the foremost, thereby clarifying the self.
Because the mental faculty remains unmoved by the nature of conceptual discrimination.
As for the fourth, the realization of the true reality, it consists of the six chapters of the sutra beginning from the "Chapter on Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru."
It takes the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*) as its essence, because it abides in the house of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Fifth, the "Practice of Undertaking" refers to the four chapters of the sutra from the Suyama Heaven Palace downward;
it takes the ten practices (*daśacaryā*) as its essence, because it practices the conduct of the Buddha.
Regarding the sixth, the mutual entry of wisdom and compassion: this consists of the three chapters beginning from the "Chapter on Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace.
Its essence is the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*). Because its essence perfectly integrates the ultimate and conventional truths, it accomplishes great compassion.

Seventh, regarding the virtues accomplished through the cultivation of the aggregates (*skandha-bhāvanā-sampanna-guṇa*): this refers to the single stage of the tenth bhūmi within the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
This is because the first three dharmas of the cultivation of the aggregates have been brought to mastery through habitual practice.
Regarding the eighth, mastery in benefiting sentient beings: this comprises all twelve chapters from the "Ten Samādhis" chapter onwards, up to the "Universal Worthy’s Conduct" chapter.

Because one has accumulated virtues and perfected accomplishments within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and because the conduct for benefiting sentient beings is fulfilled in the eleventh stage, one is then designated a Buddha whose Dharma-practice is complete.
Ninth, regarding those who dwell in the state of entrustment: this refers to the bodhisattvas of the six aforementioned stages, as well as the "Chapter on the Appearance of Buddhas in the World.
All of these manifest their bodies through skillful means from within the realm of the great wisdom of the ocean of nature.
By means of the dharma-gate of the eleven stages— consisting of the provisional positions of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten grounds,
as well as the stage of Equal Enlightenment— it causes ordinary beings to believe and enter.

The tenth [chapter] clarifies that those who have realized the reality for themselves establish the six stages, beginning with the ten faiths, as skillful means for progressive cultivation within the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.

In these practices, the activity is inseparable from the function, and the skillful means remain unimpaired; thus, while their wisdom becomes ever more sublime, their conduct remains ever more humble.
Because they fulfill their practice in accordance with their faculties, it is called "progressive cultivation. One establishes the various stages according to one's capacity and capability.
The above ten sections conclude the extended analysis of the meaning of the scripture.

As for the "Dharma-realm" chapter (*dharmadhātu-paṭala*), it comprehensively encompasses the preceding forty chapters of the sutra because it is the totality of the Dharma-realm. This "Dharma-realm" chapter is the fruition of all Buddhas and all sentient beings.
If, within the gateway of the fundamental Dharma-realm, one gives rise to views of extension or contraction, these are all [the delusions of] oneself.
Those with deluded views do not establish the seeds of faith within the Buddha’s True Dharma;

it should be known that such persons, even if they practice and attain the fruit of transcending the triple world, lack the seed for attaining Buddhahood. These are precisely the bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings who possess the six supernormal powers, as well as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Even the non-retrogressive bodhisattvas mentioned in the *Lotus Sūtra* cannot understand this. This clarifies their transcendence.
Regarding "non-retrogression from birth and death": this refers to not retreating while still within the realm of birth and death prior to full realization.

Furthermore, it merely means that by using the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to subdue active afflictions (*kleśa*), one enters the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) at the first ground (*bhūmi*); it does not mean that one has already reached fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).

Having attained fundamental wisdom, one does not regress from the vision [of reality]. Such is the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) of the three vehicles; these are all Bodhisattvas of the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*).

None of them possess the non-regression of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*) in the stage of "Abiding" (*vihāra*), such as attaining Buddhahood throughout the ten directions within the fundamental great perfect mirror-like wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*.
Regarding the three types of mind-made bodies: the first, second, and third stages are called *samāpatti*.

The "body born of the mind that delights in mastery" belongs to the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages. The "body born of the mind that realizes the self-nature of dharmas" belongs to the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages.
The "body born of the mind that is spontaneously produced according to its kind and is free from effort" belongs to the [same] seventh through tenth stages.

These three types of mind-born bodies of Bodhisattvas are all the great ocean of wisdom of the perfectly round luminosity of the Dharma-realm; they are merely provisional shelters in grass huts outside the main gate of the Great Mansion.
He then established them securely, causing his sons and others to temporarily escape the calamity of fire. As stated in the latter part of this sutra:
the śrāvakas in the assembly are like the deaf or the blind; even if bodhisattvas possessing the six supernatural powers hear this sutra, they are unable to give rise to faith.

Even if they can give rise to faith in the Buddha-dharma, it is merely a faith born of their own subjective sentiments, because they are deluded regarding the realm of their own wisdom. Thus, there is no realization of true wisdom through their own accord.
Because they practice through faith alone, if they do not turn their minds [toward the Great Vehicle], they will ultimately fail to attain Buddhahood.
Even if they were to teach and transform sentient beings, they could only bring about the seeds of the Three Vehicles or of humans and devas;
they would merely dwell in a pure land of a single direction, lacking the great vision of universal wisdom that is equal in measure to the vast Dharma-realm and as boundless as space.

Second, regarding the elucidation of the sūtra’s essential purport (*piṇḍārtha*), there are six points: first, clarifying the sūtra’s essential purport; second, identifying which collection (*piṭaka*) this sūtra is subsumed under;
third, distinguishing its introductory section (*nidāna*); fourth, determining its main body (*samyag-deśanā*); and fifth, clarifying to whom this sūtra was entrusted.
Sixth, clarifying where this sutra circulates. First, clarifying the essential purport of the sutra:
This sutra is named the Great Wisdom Dharma-realm of Vairocana. Its fundamental true essence is the perfection of both quiescence and function;
its resultant virtues consist of the Dharma-body and the Reward-body, wherein nature and characteristics are non-obstructive. It is that which the Buddha himself rides upon.

The core tenet [of this school] is as stated in the Sūtra: "For those who joyfully seek the fruit of Buddhahood, one speaks of the Most Victorious Vehicle, the Supreme Vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle, the Inconceivable Vehicle, and so forth.
This is intended to cause those who have first resolved their minds toward awakening to aspire to the vast and great;
thus they shall attain the fruit of such Tathāgata-great-wisdom, becoming one with their own wisdom in a state of non-duality. This is the essential purport of this Sūtra.

It is profoundly deep and difficult to believe. If there are those who have faith, their merit would surpass that of one who serves Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields for the duration of an entire kalpa;

the merit they obtain is not equal to what one naturally possesses by believing in this gateway to the dharma-realm of the Buddha-fruit and the Tathāgata’s great wisdom within this sutra. As stated in the latter part of the sutra: "Suppose there were..."
A bodhisattva who has practiced the six pāramitās for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kalpas and attained the six supernormal powers is still called a "provisional" bodhisattva.
Even if such a person hears this sutra, they will not believe it and will not enter into it, as described in the Lotus Sutra.
This is also for the purpose of turning those of the three vehicles back toward the One Vehicle.
It shatters the various bases upon which they rely, so that they may attain the Tathāgata’s wisdom of non-reliance and fundamental sovereignty.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was taught immediately upon the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, specifically for those of superior faculties. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, however, was taught forty years after the Buddha appeared in the world.
Throughout the year, [the Buddha] speaks for the sake of those who would turn toward the three vehicles. Furthermore, the Buddha-vehicle and the three vehicles are taught collectively at once;

yet, according to their respective faculties, they naturally correspond, and within this single-sound dharma-gate there are distinct differences. While the meanings of the general and the specific arise, the true essence is timeless.

Because there is nothing that can be established as preceding or following. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma;
there is neither a second nor a third. It is only by means of provisional names that sentient beings are guided. It further says:
"This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. Regarding "the other two":

it is because the gateway mounted by all Buddhas of the ten directions is taken as the reality, while the three vehicles are the "other two. That which is merely provisionally established and not real is called "the other two.
When the single reality is contrasted with all provisional teachings, they are all "the other two. This is for the purpose of reproaching the śrāvakas in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Because those who hear of the Pratyekabuddhas and non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas—the three vehicles and so forth—are all unable to believe in the Dharma of the One Vehicle;
thus, they are considered Bodhisattvas of provisional teaching. Although they possess a partial aspiration for Bodhi, they still harbor fear toward birth and death.
One attains non-retrogression by being free from defilement; one attains non-retrogression through the equality of defilement and purity that accords with reality when it has not yet been attained.
This is like a bodhisattva practicing the contemplation of emptiness whose delight in emptiness increases and prevails, as well as various bodhisattvas who delight in being born in pure lands;

all such beings are able to leave birth-and-death and transcend the entanglements without retrogressing, because they have not yet entered the ocean of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, the single truth that is free from the gates of longing and aversion. In comparison to this...
Regarding this Buddha-vehicle: for those who delight in birth and death, as well as those who loathe birth and death, both are subject to regression.

Even if one contemplates emptiness with increasing excellence, cultivates the gate of conventional *tathatā*, practices the six *pāramitās*, and attains the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), this constitutes non-regression from birth and death;
it is not, however, non-regression within the single nature of birth and death and *nirvāṇa*. For this reason:
The *Avataṃsaka* and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sūtras state that even bodhisattvas who have attained the six supernormal powers do not hear or believe in these scriptures.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* says: "Suppose there were a bodhisattva who recited and studied the eighty-four thousand dharma-treasuries."
To explain this for others and attain the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) is not yet considered difficult; however, to read this sutra even for a moment is what is truly difficult.

This realm of wisdom alone contradicts what the mind habitually understands, and is therefore extremely difficult to believe. The faith and understanding of the Three Vehicles accord with what the mind delights in.
Why is this? Because they teach that the fruit of Buddhahood occurs only after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, whereas [this sutra] teaches the Buddha...
The Pure Land lies in another direction; this Sahā world is a defiled land. Those who cultivate bodhi loathe defilement and rejoice in the true, delighting in being born in a pure realm.

Even if there are bodhisattvas dwelling in this world who claim to "retain delusions to moisten their births" for the sake of saving sentient beings, this is not because it is so by the inherent power of fundamental wisdom (*dharmatā-jñāna*), but rather through the power of mastery (*vaśitā*). Thus it is.

The teachings for bodhisattvas all accord with worldly sentiments; because such dharmas are easy to believe, they do not speak as this sutra does—that entry into the fruit of Buddhahood occurs in no more than a single kṣaṇa.
Rather, it speaks of immeasurable kalpas by distinguishing between delusion and awakening, yet in total, not even a moment is ever displaced.
It is taught that when one first perceives the Path from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), cause and effect are simultaneous, lacking any temporal sequence.

One does not perceive a time before becoming a Buddha, nor does one perceive a time when perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is attained. One does not perceive the severance of afflictions (*kleśa*), nor the realization of Bodhi.

Ultimately, there is not even the movement of a hair’s breadth or a single thought. Having fulfilled the cultivation of the fifty stages, all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) is entirely [perfected].
Accomplishment—whether total or partial, identical or distinct, formed or disintegrated—is all simultaneously sovereign and entirely beyond what is perceived by worldly minds;
therefore, it is difficult to believe. That which one should believe is that one’s own mind is of a nature that has no dependence or abiding;
this liberation through wondrous wisdom is Mañjuśrī himself. Within this non-abiding of the mind, there exists a portion of sovereignty within the wondrous principle of essencelessness.
Distinct. Being devoid of a nature that can be moved, he is named the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom (*Acalajñāna*).
Since wisdom and principle are non-dual and his wondrous function is sovereign, he is titled the Bodhisattva Wondrous Virtue (*Mañjuśrī*). Therefore, all Buddhas arise from this faith;
thus Mañjuśrī is called the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions, and is also called the Youthful Bodhisattva (*Kumārabhūta*). For...
Because faith is the primary birth [of the path], when the mind of faith is perfected, the initial mind of the ten abodes (daśabhūmi) immediately achieves perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
One who is capable of practicing the stages of conduct is designated as Samantabhadra. To be in accord with one's own realization is called "perfect enlightenment";
to be in accord with one's own realization is called "abiding mind. Because this is to abide where the Buddhas abide, the essential purport of this sutra is the Great [Vehicle].
If the mind of sentient beings were established according to this Dharma, it would cause Sudhana to attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime (*ekajāti*). To explain:

"a single lifetime" refers to the period from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) after the arousal of faith; from that point onward, one is born by the power of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, not by means of karmic birth.
Second, as for which treasury (*piṭaka*) this sutra is subsumed under: this sutra elucidates the *dharmadhātu-garbha* of Vairocana.
It is so named because it universally illumines the ocean of the *dharmadhātu*, as all dharma-gates are entirely contained within it.
Therefore, in the "Dharmadhātu" chapter that follows, the pavilion where Maitreya resides is called the "Vairocana-alaṃkāra-garbha.
Once Sudhana has entered it, he perceives only the infinite dharma-treasuries, the gates of practice, and the adornments of the marks of fruition of all Buddhas.
The marks of inexhaustible merit are all incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*). Therefore, this sutra always takes the fruit of Buddhahood as the path of progress and cultivation.
It is the ancient site of the Buddha’s fundamental great wisdom;

because it cultivates the wisdom of distinctions, if one were to practice progress and cultivation apart from the ancient site of the Buddha, there would be no principle of attaining Buddhahood—just like the three vehicles, which at best merely avoid a portion of coarse birth and death.
It is suffering; it is not that one relies on the ancient traces of the essence of the Buddha’s wisdom to practice the Buddha Vehicle.
Therefore, this sutra is contained within the treasury of Vairocana, and is not subsumed under the Bodhisattva-piṭaka of the Three Vehicles.
The introductory section (*nidāna*) of the *Tri-vidyā-vibhāga-sūtra* is divided into two categories: first, that which encompasses the entire work;

second, the introductory sections belonging to each individual chapter. Regarding the first, that which encompasses the entire work, this refers to the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World-Ruler" (*Lokendra-vyuha*).

Regarding the second, the introductory sections belonging to each individual chapter, as found within each chapter and each assembly (*parṣad*) of the sūtra, there is always the phrase: "At that time... (*tena khalu samayena*).
Thus it is. To speak of it in general terms: all Buddhas of the past, present, and future attain Buddhahood entirely at one and the same time;
likewise, the birth and death of sentient beings does not shift by even a single kṣaṇa. It is only because sentient beings falsely calculate that there are long and short durations of years and ages.
As the Buddha has taught, birth and death occur simultaneously without shifting in time. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "One..."
Recalling and universally observing immeasurable kalpas—without going, without coming, and without abiding—one thus fully knows the matters of the three periods of time.

Transcending all provisional skillful means, one accomplishes the ten powers (*daśabala*). It is clear that from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), by giving rise to the thought of enlightenment in a single moment, one suddenly perceives the Way.
Thereafter, one advances through the five stages: the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh ground.
The Dharma—from attaining Buddhahood, turning the wheel of the Dharma, to entering nirvana—does not shift for even a single kṣaṇa.

This is because the gateway of the Dharmadhātu is used as the means for revealing, awakening to, and entering [the truth]. Therefore, it is called the gateway of the Dharmadhātu of the One Vehicle of the Real Teaching; such is the nature of the Dharma.

This is elucidated by means of the names of samādhis. This chapter as a whole presents this fundamental *dharmadhātu* of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), clarifying that time does not shift and that there is no shifting of location, because the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) has neither center nor periphery.

Thus, all practices cultivated are always equal to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), for throughout the three periods of time they are without increase or decrease and without coming or going. Next, one enters the Dharma...

The Chapter on the Realms (*Dhātu-varga*). This chapter encompasses all of heaven, the human world, and the worlds of the ten directions, constituting the entirety of the inconceivable essence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Because its quiescence and function are sovereign, it causes sentient beings to awaken to and enter it.

Therefore, this single chapter was spoken by the Tathāgata solely through inconceivable supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*), without relying on verbal discourse, thereby clarifying that the mundane world is universally true and universally divine.
Because there is no arising or ceasing.

Regarding the fourfold determination of the primary teaching (zhengzong), there are three kinds of primary teachings: first, the primary teaching according to stages; second, the primary teaching according to chapters;
and third, the primary teaching of the great essence. If one follows the primary teaching according to stages, there are the ten faiths, the ten abidings, and the ten practices.

The ten dedications, the ten stages, and the eleventh stage each have their own primary doctrine (*zhengzong*). The ten faiths take the Buddha’s fundamental immovable wisdom as their primary doctrine.
The ten abidings take the wondrous wisdom of the principle-body and the realized merit of the Tathāgata—the wisdom that enters and realizes the Dharma-realm—as their primary doctrine.
The ten practices take the arousal of the conduct of Samantabhadra from the Buddha’s fundamental wisdom as their primary doctrine.

The Ten Dedications take the harmonious integration of principle and wisdom (*prajñā*) with the ultimate and conventional truths as their basis for arising, and the fulfillment of great vows through the perfection of compassion and wisdom as their primary doctrine.
The Ten Grounds take the cultivation of compassion and wisdom through accumulated practice, reaching mastery and functional efficacy, as their primary doctrine.

The Eleventh Ground takes the conduct of Samantabhadra, which flows equally with the mental states of all sentient beings and fills the ocean of the Dharma-realm, acting at will to benefit living beings, as its primary doctrine.

I. The primary thesis (*zong*). This constitutes the primary thesis according to the stages [of the teaching]. II. Within each of the forty chapters of the doctrinal gate of this single division, there is its own respective primary thesis.
III. The primary thesis regarding the general essence of the teachings of this single division:

taking the fruit of Buddhahood of the One Vehicle—wherein the nature of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom and the *dharmadhātu* transcends past and present and is perfected in both essence and function—as the primary thesis. Always take this Buddha...
This is the section on the Fruit and the True Teaching. It is intended to provide instruction, realization, and entry for further cultivation, so that habitual practice may reach fulfillment.
Fifth, as for to whom this Dharma-gate of the sutra is entrusted: this sutra’s Dharma is entrusted to ordinary beings of great resolve.
The Sūtra says: "The Dharma of this sūtra shall not fall into the hands of other sentient beings. The commentary explains:

"Other sentient beings" refers to those of the three vehicles, as well as non-Buddhists who are attached to the pleasures of humans and devas, and those who seek the bliss of transcendence from the world. Why is this?

Even Bodhisattvas of the three vehicles, though they possess the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), are still unable to hear this sūtra and give rise to faith; how much less so can those of the two vehicles, humans, or devas?

O outsider, the Sūtra says: "Except for those born into the family of the Tathāgata, the true sons of the Dharma King"—that is, the ordinary beings with great resolve who are able to give rise to faith, realize it, and enter [the path].
They are said to be "born into the Buddha-family," but this does not refer to the great Bodhisattvas who have already been born into the Buddha-family.
These great Bodhisattvas constantly preach the Dharma for sentient beings; there is no need for ordinary beings with great resolve to provide them with faith and realization.
This is called an entrustment (*parindanā*), not a circulation (*pravartana*), because there is no one who believes and no one who enters into realization.
Sixth, as for clarifying the locations where this sutra circulates, the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava-parivarta* (Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata) demonstrates the underlying principle.

Because the causes and effects of the five stages from beginning to end are fulfilled, the light from between [the Buddha’s] eyebrows is poured onto the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head, and the light from his mouth is poured into Samantabhadra’s mouth, causing these two persons to engage in mutual dialogue regarding essence and function, cause and effect.
Mañjuśrī is taken as the essence (*tattva*) of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and Samantabhadra as its function (*vṛtti*); thus, the two serve as each other's essence and function. Alternatively,
Mañjuśrī is the cause; Samantabhadra is the fruit. Alternatively, these two persons serve as cause and fruit for one another.

Throughout this entire section of the sutra, these two figures are constantly used to symbolize essence and function, as well as cause and fruit. Buddhas of the past and present alike rely upon these traces to clarify the benefits of practicing the cultivation of cause and fruit.
"Light from the mouth" signifies the meaning of entrustment and the meaning of circulation. "The hair-tuft between the eyebrows" [signifies...]
The "Light" signifies the meaning of the fruit (*phala*). By emitting the light of the fruit and entrusting it to Mañjuśrī, he causes Mañjuśrī to pose questions regarding the dharma of the fruit.
Samantabhadra’s exposition on the appearance of the Buddha constitutes the propagation (*pravartana*).

Regarding the essence of the teaching of the Threefold Clarification (Sanming), according to the explanation of Master Sheli (Shelifa Shi), there are six aspects of the essence of the scriptural teachings that emerge from the sutras.
Now, Tongxuan, relying on this *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, establishes ten dharmas as the essence of the teaching.

The Buddha’s single perfect voice accords with the capacities of all sentient beings; in a single thought-moment, it revolves the wheel of Dharma throughout the three periods of time—without beginning or end—as the very essence of the teaching.
Second, the adornment of the spheres of all noble ones and ordinary beings as the fruit of retribution serves as the essence of the teaching.
This is because the mind is awakened upon seeing the sphere [of reality], without depending on verbal instruction; furthermore, because there is not a single phenomenon that is not a Buddha-activity.
Third, the intrinsic purity of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-prakṛti-viśuddhi*) serves as the essence of the teaching. By the power of contemplation, the mind accords with its own nature;
because it does not depend on verbal expression, [it is realized].

Fourth, the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—are taken as the essence of the teaching, because seeing [the Buddha] and generating the aspiration for enlightenment do not depend upon speech.
Fifth, the appearance and parinirvāṇa of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are taken as the essence of the teaching; by means of these dharmic events, all sentient beings are...
Sixth, the Buddha and Bodhisattvas take the power of their supernormal knowledges as the essence of their teaching;
they manifest various sovereign powers so that those who see them resolve their minds [on enlightenment],
without depending on words and phrases.
Seventh, taking impermanence, suffering, and emptiness as the essence of the teaching, because the practitioner generates the aspiration for enlightenment without depending on words.
Eighth, taking wordless silence as the essence of the teaching, as exemplified by the layman Vimalakīrti’s silent response,
which does not depend upon names, phrases, syllables, or speech.

Ninth, the teaching-body (*deśanā-kāya*) consists of the collections of names, phrases, and phonemes, as well as speech and the faculties of sentient beings, because it manifests only by means of words.

Tenth, the teaching-body consists of the fundamental reality of all phenomena within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), because it enables sentient beings to purify their defilements through the Dharma.
To state the essential point: for all sentient beings, the ocean of afflictions and all that pertains to sentient beings [is purified] according to their respective capacities.
Roots of goodness; the fruits of happiness for humans and devas; the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas; liberation and nirvāṇa;
the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables, as well as vocal karma and so forth; and all karmic retributions, whether good or evil; empty space and the dharma-realm;
speech and the ineffable—all phenomena without exception constitute the essence of the teaching. Whether by means of one’s own wisdom of contemplation, or through hearing the Dharma, or by oneself...
Through contemplation, internally perfumed wisdom manifests, enabling one to abandon all evils and attain nirvana. Whether taught or not taught, both constitute the essence of the teaching.
If there were no afflictions, there would be no essence of the teaching.

Fourth, a general presentation of the assemblies. Within this, there are three main points: first, a general enumeration of the number of assemblies; second, an exposition of the purpose of the assemblies;

and third, an explanation of the reasons for the Buddha’s appearance in the world. First, the general enumeration of the number of assemblies: there are ten such assemblies. Second, the exposition of the purpose of the assemblies.
The first assembly was held at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), where he clearly manifested his initial attainment of perfect awakening for the sake of transforming sentient beings.

The second assembly was held in the Hall of Universal Radiance (Samantāloka-prabhāsa-maṇḍala), where the phrase "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam) was repeated to indicate the commencement of the first assembly.
Originally, the essence of the bodhimanda in the araṇya is not separate from this very essence for attaining the Way.
This is because it is the dwelling place where the retribution-body resides, just as worldly people attain the Way in a pure place and only then return home.
He manifests this dharma, which is fundamentally without coming or going, by shifting its temporal manifestation.
In the third assembly, [the Buddha] ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru to the palace of Śakra, where he expounded the gates of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*).

He clarified the stages of the Ten Abodes, wherein those who have newly attained the state of a *arhat* find their minds in union with emptiness; having spontaneously realized the function of wisdom, they are as sovereign as the gods.
As stated above, "the body merges with space atop a high mountain.
Regarding the fourth assembly being held in the palace of the Yāma Heaven: this clarifies that the Yāma Heaven dwells at the limit of space and is not connected to the earth.
This clarifies its ten practices: practicing by relying on space, remaining constantly empty within practice because there is nothing upon which to rely.
Regarding the fifth assembly held in the Tuṣita Heaven palace: it clarifies that this celestial realm is one of joy and contentment;
therefore, the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) are taught to symbolize the stage of dedication wherein principle and phenomena are harmoniously integrated.

It ensures that one does not crave *nirvāṇa*, nor cling to great compassion, nor cling to great vows, so that one may dwell in the world like a lotus flower—remaining amidst the dust yet unstained by it. Furthermore, [it serves to manifest...]

This indicates that this heaven is situated in the middle of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): below it are the Trāyastriṃśa and Yāma heavens; above it are the Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens.
This heaven is located in the midst of the desire realm, yet it still expounds the ten gates of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

This is so as not to allow the mind for supramundane cultivation to increase—as occurs with those of the three vehicles who delight in such practice—nor to allow the two vehicles to hasten toward quiescence (*śama*), nor to cause Bodhisattvas to cease their rebirths or abandon the pure lands.

[This is] a mistake. The principle of the Dharma is thus: it does not necessarily mean that one must be born in that heaven. This clarifies the turning back from the ultimate to enter the conventional, ensuring that compassion and wisdom are balanced.

The sixth assembly was held in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*); for the sake of this heaven, he expounded its ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). For this reason...
The Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*) achieves its own bliss through the transformations of others.

This clarifies that the great compassion and great wisdom of the tenth stage merely transform sentient beings, taking this as one's own bliss of nirvāṇa, because there is no personal pleasure [inherent therein]. Question:

Why does it transcend the Heaven of Joyful Transformation (*Nirmāṇarati*) and explain the practice of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) specifically regarding the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations? Answer: It is to clarify that from the ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-praṇidhāna*), they are equalized...
Fusing wisdom and principle, their great compassion and great vows reach fulfillment and increase in excellence;

they transcend the Joyful and Purity stages without following the sequential order, unlike those of lower stages who practice step-by-step. Furthermore, this clarifies the characteristics of a Bodhisattva’s progressive cultivation:

while it is natural for the levels of the ten stages to follow a gradual progression of spiritual power and meritorious practice, because the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) has not yet been fully matured, [the higher stages cannot be attained].

Because it is luminously pure, the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) only reaches its ultimate end at the final stage. Even upon reaching the eleventh stage (*bhūmi*), two types of delusion still remain.

Therefore, regarding the two sections of this sutra—the "Chapter on the Incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*) and the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks and Merits"—the practices of Samantabhadra, though fulfilled throughout the eleven stages prior to the fruit of Buddhahood, have not yet reached their ultimate consummation. At the very least...

The "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter is expounded through the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata. It represents that within the Dharma Realm, all phenomena are collectively divine, collectively true, and collectively inconceivable.
It is only through these two forms of ignorance that the state of Buddhahood is finally attained.

Therefore, at the stage of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*), according to what one’s capacity can bear, one is able to reach this celestial realm; thus, although there are distinct differences between each successive stage as one progresses through cultivation, [the ultimate goal remains the same].
However, regarding the essence of the Dharma-realm, in a single moment and at a single instant, one attains all by attaining one;
one must not immediately give rise to views that contradict principle through sentimental thoughts concerning beginnings and ends, or long and short.
The seventh assembly was preached in the third dhyāna. This single assembly consists of one hundred trillion verses.

It clarifies that within the three dhyānas, the first dhyāna eliminates sorrow (*daurmanasya*), and the second dhyāna extinguishes suffering (*duḥkha*). Since sorrow and suffering are absent, the third dhyāna consists solely of the joy and bliss of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti-sukha*).
Because of this Dharma-bliss, the movement of joy (*prīti-īraṇā*) still persists; because of the movement of joy, the form and mind (*rūpa-citta*) still remain present.
This form and mind delight in the joy of dhyāna; they delight in form without volition, for it is not like the form of the desire realm.
Thus, the mind possesses the form of dhyāna-joy without volition. While the inhalation and exhalation of breath still persist, the body obtained as karmic retribution is pure;
the body is like white snow, and the clothing is golden, measuring one body-length in width. When walking, one travels through space without the feet touching the ground.
The bodies of those in the first dhyāna are two and a half *li* tall; in the second dhyāna, five *li*; and in the third dhyāna, ten *li*. Their garments are twice the size of their bodies.

This explains that the Dharma-gate of the eleven stages (*ekādaśa-bhūmi*) is taught for this heaven, signifying that within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one accords with the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), performs the myriad practices (*sāhasra-pratipatti*), and transforms sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), because of the constant presence of the joy of the Dharma. Upon reaching the [fourth... (Note: The source text appears to be truncated at "至第" [reaching the...]).

Based on the context of Buddhist cosmology and the progression of the *Ekādaśabhūmika-sūtra*, the passage describes the physical dimensions of the deities in the lower three heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and introduces the significance of the "Eleven Stages" as a teaching for these realms, emphasizing the realization of the *dharmakāya* and the universal activity of a Bodhisattva. The final phrase likely refers to the transition toward the higher stages of the path.)
The fourth dhyāna. Because it is entrusted to the same Buddha-stage, it is called the true *dharmatā*. It is without inhalation or exhalation;
it universally pervades according to principle and accords with the perceptions of sentient beings. The delusions of habitual tendencies regarding phenomena are entirely exhausted.
There is no phenomenon, mundane or supramundane, that it does not penetrate. This is designated as the meaning of "various lights shining everywhere. This is because wisdom is fulfilled.

Therefore, the manifestation of the Dharma is thus. This single assembly transcends the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and surpasses the two heavens of the first and second *dhyāna*, because it clarifies that the wisdom of these eleven stages increases manifold.

The eighth assembly was held in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsakūṭa*). Therein, the Dharma-gate of the Ten Samādhis was taught. The name of that samādhi is "Entering the Limit of a Kṣaṇa.
Because a *kṣaṇa* is extremely brief and beyond the reach of discursive thought, it is ultimately not discussed as having distinct arising and ceasing.
This clarifies that from beginning to end, the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world does not depart from the limit of a *kṣaṇa*; for this reason, it is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Taking intrinsic nature as the fixed essence, there is no further distinction of long or short, beginning or end, nor the three periods of time.
Rather, the Buddha takes his own non-active great compassion as the mother; he takes all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) as the Buddha;

he takes the absence of self-nature and the lack of dependence in phenomena as the seasons, days, months, and years; and he takes the faculties of all sentient beings as a clear mirror. Thus, regarding a single [moment] by the Buddha...

The ocean of dharmas for all sentient beings allows each being to see according to their own capacity and to attain their own respective dharma, causing them all to turn toward goodness and attain Bodhi.
This is not because the Tathāgata possesses the marks of coming and going repeatedly;

rather, it is to clarify that this Hall of Universal Radiance is the Tathāgata’s own nature, the sovereign essence of all-knowledge and the knowledge of all modes. It serves as the basis for the environment.
He dwells in this samādhi of the limit of the present moment (*kṣaṇāntika-samādhi*), because it is the dharma-nature of the Buddha’s omniscience and knowledge of all modes.
His intention is to encompass the totality of the ocean-like assemblies of all realms of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), so as not to allow students to perceive any distinction between coming and going,
or self and other.

Regarding the ninth assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsā-maṇḍala*): this clarifies that from this point one gives rise to faith and initiates practice to cultivate the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the ten concentrations (*samādhi*), the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the ten patiences (*kṣānti*).

This continues up to the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter (*Tathāgatotpattisambhava-parivarta*), concluding with the stage of Buddhahood. Throughout all of these, one never departs from the original practices of Samantabhadra; this clarifies that it is by means of the *dharmakāya*.
The essence of meditative concentration is perfect penetration from beginning to end; it is a single boundary and a single location where the three dharmas are identical.

Without leaving the abode of the retribution-body in the Hall of Universal Radiance, they simultaneously and universally seal all things, such that there is no need for a third assembly after having departed and returned.
Because the gateway of the *dharmadhātu* cannot be understood through worldly conceptualization, it is like Sudhana, who,

having first conceived the mind of faith at the Great Stūpa to the east of the City of Enlightenment where Samantabhadra was born, passed through fifty stages and gateways before seeing the Tathāgata Maitreya,
who then directed him back to see Mañjuśrī; this clarifies that the present attainment of the fruit is not separate from the beginning.
The gateway of faith: through the wisdom of bodhi, one hears the name of Samantabhadra and beholds his body as equal to that of Samantabhadra.
As the sutra says, "further entering immeasurable samādhis" is for the purpose of clearly realizing and transcending the two kinds of ignorance within the stage of the fruition of Buddhahood.
These two ignorances are: first, ignorance regarding the vast number of asaṃkhyeya; second, [ignorance regarding] the state of Buddhahood—
The vast ignorance regarding the internal secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) and their merits—these two dharmas are realized only by the Buddha to the ultimate degree.

For this reason, these two chapters of the sutra were spoken by the Tathāgata himself, as was the Dharmadhātu chapter, which was spoken through the inconceivable supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*) of the Tathāgata.
This was done to clarify that the Dharmadhātu is the common, ultimate fruit realized by all Buddhas. Thus, by means of...
This chapter reveals and awakens sentient beings; the remaining thirty-seven chapters are spoken by Bodhisattvas at their respective stages. The *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states:
"The ground of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) is eliminated only upon the stage of Buddhahood."

The tenth assembly expounds the "Chapter on the Dharma Realm. This single assembly is clearly shown to universally encompass all other assemblies, as well as the oceans of lands in the ten directions, the Dharma Realm, and the realm of empty space;
in sum, it constitutes a single assembly that is infinitely layered and inexhaustible, and which is both inexhaustible and infinitely layered.
All the ocean-assemblies of all Buddhas and the ocean of all sentient beings are, in their entirety, contained within this single chapter on the Dharma Realm.

All are of one essence. If one perceives the Tathāgata as having only recently attained perfect enlightenment, or views him through the teachings of the three periods—Right, Semblance, and Final—it is not the vision of perfect enlightenment, nor is it seeing the Buddha’s manifestation in the world. This is merely the view of sentient beings with inferior understanding;
those who seek perfect enlightenment should not see him in such a way. Question: How should one perceive the Buddha’s manifestation in the world? Answer:
One should perceive one's own self as being without body and without mind, with no place of abiding in either the mundane or the supramundane.

There are no mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), nor is there any dharma or mind; the mind and its factors have no support. By means of the wisdom that dwells in non-abiding, one preaches such a Dharma to teach and transform sentient beings, causing them all to awaken and enter [the path].
This is called seeing the appearance of a Buddha; it does not cause sentient beings to grasp at a Buddha.

The characteristics of arising and ceasing appear; one perceives the beginning and the end, seeing only the body of oneself and the bodies of sentient beings, yet the mind is without arising or ceasing, its essence being supramundane.
"Thus have I heard at one time.
Because the Buddha is suchness (*tathatā*), for all phenomena are suchness; he is therefore the Buddha. Thus it is said, "Thus" (*evam*).

By means of the true self of the great wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, one hears the true scripture of the great wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* as taught by the Buddha. Therefore, it is said, "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*). This clarifies the Teacher.

The essence of the Dharma is one. Furthermore, all dharmas are suchness (*tathatā*). Because the essence of the Dharma is suchness as that which is taught, and because the Dharma itself is also suchness;
and because the wisdom of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-jñāna*) is the wisdom by which it is heard, and that wisdom is also suchness—therefore, it is called "thus" (*evam*).
Only when mind and object are non-dual can one hear the sutras spoken by the Buddha. If there were a discrepancy between mind and object, one could not hear what the Buddha has spoken. Nor...
Furthermore, they are unable to believe in, accord with, or receive [the teaching], saying: "What I have heard is the true self of the wisdom of the dharma-realm;

it is the seeing of the true Buddha of the wisdom of the dharma-realm; it is the hearing of the true sutra of the wisdom of the dharma-realm; it is the true person of the totality of the wisdom of the dharma-realm."
They act as mutual principal and attendant, transforming back the true sentient beings of the *dharmadhātu* and causing them to awaken to and enter the true nature of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*;

therefore, it is said, “Thus have I heard. The seat upon which the Tathāgata sits takes the *dharmadhātu* as its substance, and is adorned with the fruit of reliance—the retributive attainment of all the Tathāgata’s myriad practices. The Tathāgata is the body of great wisdom; this is his seat.
All the adornments above are the spontaneous rewards obtained through the natural functioning of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom.
It is like clouds arising when a dragon moves or wind blowing when a tiger roars; such is the response of karmic retribution, not something that can be produced by external objects.

One who has attained supreme perfect enlightenment is distinguished from non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, as well as from those within the provisional teachings who rely on wooden trees and grass seats out of weariness [with the world].
