Transcending worldly entanglements, he causes sentient beings of inferior understanding to give rise to the seeds of the three vehicles and provisionally uproot the suffering of the limited分段 (duḥkha-pratibhāga).

This is not yet the perfect awakening of ultimate realization; rather, it is distinguished from such [inferior] awakenings. Therefore, it is said that he "attains supreme perfect awakening" (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). This is a brief explanation of the major characteristics.

There are ninety-seven kinds of marks of a great man, with secondary characteristics that are inexhaustible. He wears a flower crown upon his head, a necklace around his neck, and bracelets and rings upon his hands;
he is not like those of the Three Vehicles who weary of the mundane world to leave the household life.

Because he exhorts all bodhisattvas to be born in the pure lands of the buddha-fields of other directions—and because he is distinguished from such as these—it is said that he has attained supreme perfect enlightenment and is named Vairocana.
At that time, the World-Honored One sat upon this seat, having attained supreme perfect enlightenment, together with the assembly of the ten Samantabhadras.
This constitutes the section on "the manifestation of the fruit as the cause for generating faith. Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata is the fruit of perfect enlightenment;

the assembly of Samantabhadra and others are the fruits of the Buddha’s practice; and the Flower Treasury Pure Land where the Tathāgata dwells is the fruit of the Buddha’s retributive attainment, serving as his support.

All sentient beings, by means of their own faculties and natures, contemplate the three kinds of cause and effect of the Tathāgata and practice the gate of Samantabhadra—the self-conduct of the Buddha—and thereby give rise to faith. If it were not thus, from what would faith arise?
Second, the nine classes of deities, beginning with the Vajradhara deity, clarify the cause and effect of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Why is this so? Because of the Moonlight of the Ocean [Samādhi].
The Great Illumination Bodhisattva is likewise a member of the assembly of Samantabhadra and others.

Since all Buddhas within the stage of Buddhahood collectively practice the Dharma of Samantabhadra to enter the mundane world and benefit sentient beings, those who are capable of being benefited receive their former dharmas; however, they do not benefit from their former practices.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva Ocean Moonlight (Sāgaracandra), who exists within the stage of Samantabhadra under a different name, is established as the Ten Abodes.
The Initial Mind: It clarifies that from the stage of an ordinary person, one cultivates and studies the ten levels of faith.

One believes that the fruit of the Buddhas' perfect enlightenment is no different from the various practices performed by one's own mind—namely, the conduct of Samantabhadra. The wheel of Dharma that is turned is identical and non-different from the wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Therefore, because Samantabhadra enters into the mundane through the practice of the fruit, it is named "Sea Moonlight. This has already been explained.
The lower grade [of deities], together with [the others], completes the assembly of ten. This serves to establish the gateway to the stage of the Ten Abidings Bodhisattva.

From this point downward, it includes the nine classes of various spirits, extending down to the Lord of Medicinal Herbs (Bhaiṣajyarāja) and others. This clarifies that these are the practices resulting from entering the Ten Abidings, for the purpose of entering the Ten Abidings as a *arhat* (one who has attained truth).
It is called "divine" (shen), yet it is not the ghosts or spirits of the mundane world. When one's own mind realizes the principle and does not conjoin with delusion, its wisdom is inherently divine;
it is not a state of non-thinking, for this wisdom skillfully penetrates all phenomena.
In the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Lord," within the "Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes" under the "Abode of Skillful Means," there are ten *pāramitās*.
These take the *dhyāna-pāramitā* as their essence. The meaning of the "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) is the removal of the defilements of the aggregates (*skandha-kāluṣya*).
This is because it clarifies that *dhyāna* is capable of treating the aggregates, just as a worldly threshing floor is used for processing grain. Thus, by means of the *dhyāna-pāramitā*...
The field is the essence; the *prajñāpāramitā* is the human effort; the myriad practices of Samantabhadra are the transport;
the Palace of Universal Radiance Wisdom of the Dharma-realm is the great capital residence; and all manner of various wisdoms constitute the great treasury.

In the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Lords," from the deity who presides over crops (*sasya-adhipati*) down to the deity who presides over the day (*divasa-adhipati*), these ten classes of deities clarify the causes and effects of the ten practices for benefiting sentient beings.

The deity who presides over crops serves as the representation of the practice itself, acting as the necessary provision (*sambhāra*); just as in the world, one relies upon grain crops [for sustenance].
The provisions (*sambhāra*) nourish the conditioned body; the Buddha-dharma takes the practice of the ten *pāramitās* as its provisions to nourish the *dharmakāya*.

Within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), one fully believes that one’s own mind and the nature-characteristic and great wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions are of an undifferentiated essence.
At the initial moment of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), one perceives the Path through the power of cultivating the *upāya-samādhi*. From the beginning...
The stage of the Initial Resolve (*cittotpāda-vihāra*) and all subsequent stages are collectively termed the position of the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*).

The ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), and the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*) are collectively termed the stage of Preparatory Application (*prayoga*) and collectively termed the stage of Provisions (*sambhāra*). Like the Bodhisattvas of the three vehicles, they mostly take birth in the pure lands of other directions.

Furthermore, above the fourth dhyāna, there are distinct Pure Lands of Bodhisattvas. Even if they were situated within the desire realm, it would be said that they remain there by the power of their compassionate vows to moisten birth with lingering afflictions;
this is not like the Dharma-gate of this sutra, which rides upon the Tathāgata’s Dharma-realm vehicle.

From the first stage of generating the mind of enlightenment, through the nature-fruit of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom Dharmakāya and the fruit of Samantabhadra’s practice, it universally pervades the cycle of birth and death.
Movement and stillness are equal and balanced; principle and phenomena advance together everywhere.

Therefore, the state where one removes delusions through the path as it is perceived is designated as the name of the Buddha, and the place where the mind attains awakening is designated as the world.

In total, the names of the Buddhas and the lands of the bodhisattvas—based on the causes and effects of entering the path according to their respective stages—are not something existing externally; they collectively clarify the practices performed within one's own cultivation.
It is as follows: within the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśabhūmi*), there are ten worlds of wisdom and ten names for the Buddhas, all of which are termed "Eyes" (*cakṣus*).
These constitute the fruit of Buddhahood. The ten forest-dwelling Bodhisattvas, such as Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha (Forest of Merit), serve as the causes for these practices.

To state the essential point: the ten Buddhas of their respective positions constitute the fruit of their own fundamental positions, while the ten Bodhisattvas of their respective positions constitute the cause for the practice of those respective positions.
Thus, within this first assembly, the Tathāgata serves as the fruit of the five respective positions.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, along with the various deities and spirits, serve as the causes for practice in the five stages.
Furthermore, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and the various deities and spirits take the fundamental wisdom of Vairocana as the primary cause for initiating practice.
Taking one's own body of practice as the fruit of the Buddha’s differentiated wisdom, and taking the fruit of the Buddha-nature wisdom as the cause;
since the presently practiced body is itself the fruit of the nature of principle-wisdom, they are mutually cause and effect, and mutually essence and function.
Therefore, within the *Devatāpraśaṃsā*, the virtues of the Buddha are praised first, followed by the praise of one’s own identity with the Buddha in both wisdom and virtue;
this serves as the model for entering the Dharma. It causes all practitioners to realize that they are ordinary beings when deluded and Buddhas when awakened.
Thus, wisdom and compassion advance together, as in the case of Sudhana, who dwelt at the stage of the "Joyful Practice" (*pramuditā-caryā*) among the ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*).

That land is named the Three Eyes. It is identical to the worlds inhabited by Bodhisattvas of the Ten Practices, such as the world named *Cakṣuḥ-prajñā* (Intimate Wisdom), *Dhvaja-prajñā* (Banner Wisdom), and *Ratna-prajñā* (Jewel Wisdom)—the ten worlds of wisdom.
As for the "Three Eyes": first is *mahāprajñā* (Great Wisdom), second is liberation (*vimukti*), and third is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Alternatively, they are also the three: the eye of knowledge (*jñānacakṣus*), the eye of wisdom (*prajñācakṣus*), and the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*).
Because it is the eye. It is like the syllable *sva*; it is like the three eyes on the face of the celestial king Maheśvara.
Because all Buddha-dharmas do not depart from this Dharma-body of great knowledge and great wisdom (*mahājñāna-mahāprajñā*), the meaning of these ten wisdoms pervades these three eyes.
For this reason, among the ten practices of Sudhana, the first spiritual friend’s country is named "Three Eyes" (*Treyakṣa*). This is comparable [to the present case].

The name of the mountain is Sudarśana; it corresponds to the stage of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi*). The names of the Buddhas are the Buddha Constantly Abiding Eye (*Nityasthita-cakṣus*) and the Buddha Unsurpassed Eye (*Anabhibhūta-cakṣus*);

he who is named Sudarśana is endowed with the three eyes. Because, within the ten practices, he knows the faculties of sentient beings through the eye of wisdom and acts in accordance with them, the Buddha is named "Eye.
The Good Spiritual Friend is named Sudarśana; his eyes and hair are deep blue, and his skin is azure.

The skin is golden in color, the halo extends one fathom, and the marks and signs are like those of a Buddha. This clarifies that within the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the cause and result of the practice of the three eyes is itself the Buddha.

For this reason, within the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*), the fifty kinds of provisions (*sambhāra*) and the fifty kinds of Buddha-fruits are mutually primary and secondary, mutually cause and result, and mutually essence and function, by virtue of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and principle (*jñāna-dharma*).

The nature-fruit (*dharmatā-phala*) constantly relies upon the practices of Samantabhadra to ensure they remain untainted; the practices of Samantabhadra constantly rely upon the Tathāgata’s nature-fruit to bring forth the perfection of compassion and wisdom.
If either side is discarded, nothing at all will be accomplished. All such gateways of practice are merely the causes and effects of humans and devas;
even if one attains transcendence, it remains the level of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as that of the Bodhisattvas of the supramundane Pure Land.
Including the retention of afflictions to moisten rebirth and so forth—these ten practices serve as the provisions for the fruit of Buddhahood, just as the gourd and its flower emerge together;
the flower and fruit mutually support one another, functioning with effortless mastery.

In the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Lord," the Dharma-gate of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) ranges from the Asura King to the Sun Deity. Within this, there are ten assemblies used to symbolize the ten dedications. Why is this so?
It is because the Asuras dwell within the great ocean yet do not sink their bodies; this symbolizes the perfection of the ten dedications.

Fusing the ultimate and the conventional, he dwells constantly within the great ocean of birth and death without his body sinking. While the preceding stages of the ten abodes and ten practices were merely the cultivation of world-transcending [wisdom], now his mind of compassion and wisdom increases;
further, through dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), he turns toward the ultimate to enter the conventional. Having attained the ultimate, he does not realize it as a final cessation;

knowing the ultimate to be identical with the conventional, he dwells in the conventional without defilement, acting freely to benefit sentient beings—just as an asura, though dwelling in the great ocean, [remains unsoaked].

The seawater does not submerge it. Although they share the same celestial realm, because they lack the wondrous bliss of the heavens, these bodhisattvas at this stage, while abiding in birth and death, possess none of the five sensual pleasures found therein;
and while abiding in nirvana, they possess none of the bliss of quiescent extinction found therein.

Therefore, this is called the "Dedication of Protecting and Delivering Sentient Beings While Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings. Furthermore, as stated in the Dharmadhātu-parivarta: "Accomplishing suchness..."
He comes forth as the transcendent Asura King. Furthermore, "King" (*rāja*) signifies mastery;
this indicates that the Bodhisattva in this stage has attained mastery over both *nirvāṇa* and *saṃsāra*. Moreover, "Asura" is also called "Asura. "A" means "non-" and "sura" means "to roam";
thus it is also called "wondrous" (*miao*). Furthermore, "ra" means "play," as explained in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. For...
He is not a deva. Although he is included within the deva realm, because he possesses much guile and deceit, he lacks the sublime bliss of the devas.
This bodhisattva of the [tenth] stage performs the myriad practices of great compassion and skillful means; these appear like guile and deceit, and appear like birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

He possesses none of the five desires of humans or devas, nor does he possess the bliss of the eternal, abiding nirvāṇa or the transcendental peace of cessation (*śānti*). He presides over the perfection of giving (*dāna*) among the ten stages of transference (*daśa-pratipatti*).
This is the gate of the *pāramitās*.
Second, it clarifies the indestructible dedication (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*). Because its true nature is without deficiency, it flows together with the mundane; this is called "indestructible.
Now, this is manifested through the symbolic event of the Garuḍa King. It clarifies that upon the great ocean, he observes with his pure eyes.
The Garuḍa King— here translated as the "King of the Golden-Winged Bird"— who seizes a dragon whose life is at its end with his two wings,

represents the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage of Dedication (*daśama-pratipatti*). He constantly surveys sentient beings within the great ocean of birth and death with the eye of pure wisdom regarding the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā-jñāna*),
and seizing them with the two wings of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), he establishes them in [the state of] himself.

The nature of pure nirvāṇa is the shore. This *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* takes the *dharmatā* as the essence of *śamatha*, and the wisdom of the self-nature of non-substantiality (*niḥsvabhāva*) as the essence of *vipaśyanā*.
It does not consist of two distinct entities, such as the observer and the observed. It is governed by the *śīla-pāramitā*;

because its precepts are pure, it is like the great ocean that does not harbor a corpse. It clarifies the precepts of great compassion and great wisdom, which do not harbor [the rebirths of] humans or devas.

Furthermore, because it [destroys] the corpses of the two views—defiled and pure—of the three vehicles, this garuḍa, when seizing a nāga, plunges its body into the ocean waters in a single thought-moment;
before the waves have even closed together, it seizes the nāga and emerges. This is called the power of swiftness.
A bodhisattva who has attained the Way is likewise so: by the power of observation through meditative concentration and wisdom, from the great ocean of ignorance...
At this juncture, one binds the mind to its duration; when a single thought accords with the Truth, the three periods of time—past, present, and future—are seen all at once.

To see the Way in this manner and to cultivate the Way in this manner is called "arousing the mind" (bodhicitta). Such an arousal of the mind is more difficult than the preceding stages; it clarifies only the initial mind of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*).

This is because it is difficult for one to accord with the Truth in a single thought from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and it does not yet constitute the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood.

Because it is difficult [to realize], yet upon reaching the ultimate, it is not different from the initial mind; therefore, it is clarified that the Dharma is not different, wisdom is not different, and time is likewise not different.
This can be seen by illuminating it with concentration and wisdom; however, to contemplate it with ordinary emotion is to become deluded.
The third is the Kinnara King. He represents the dedication of all Buddhas, such as Vidyutprabha.

Because all Buddhas abide within birth and death, they take the gate of *dharmakṣānti* (patience with the Dharma) as the sovereign of the myriad practices, so that all sentient beings may attain the unsurpassed Dharma-bliss of Bodhi.
Therefore, he is represented by the Kinnara King, which here means "Doubting Spirit. He is also [a manifestation of] practice.
The Lord [is] like a human being, yet has horns upon his head; his mouth resembles that of an ox. When people see him, they all doubt:

"Is he a human, or is he not a human? Therefore, he is called the "Doubtful Spirit" (Yishen). This clarifies that the Bodhisattva at this stage, through the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), achieves a mind of great compassion.

By the power of the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*), he takes birth within the six realms of existence to practice together with others and benefit them. When people see him, they all doubt whether he is an ordinary person or a sage. If it were...
Ordinary beings possess wisdom equal to that of a Buddha. If they were sages, their conduct would be identical to that of worldly affairs;

therefore, a divine spirit is invoked to manifest their practice. This spirit can act as the master of conduct, playing with the heavens, and presides over the gate of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Taking patience as the master of all practices, if one lacks patience, the myriad practices will not be accomplished. Thus, patience is the master of conduct. This...
This belongs to the category of the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*).
The fourth is King Mahoraga, here translated as "Great Python" (*mahā-bhujaṅga*) or "Great Belly. *Luo-jiā* (*Rāga*) means "one who moves by chest and belly.

He presides over the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). As for "moving by chest and belly," this clarifies that he crawls on his belly to seek those who delight in the benefits of the Dharma.

Humility is reverence; this is the meaning of diligence (*vīrya*). It clarifies the dedication to reaching all places. There is nowhere among the six realms and four modes of birth that it does not enter.
This refers to the Guardian of the Monastery Deity (*Kṣetrapāla*), who is able to protect the Dharma.
Within this, the ten kings clarify the ten *pāramitās* within the *vīryapāramitā*.
The fifth yakṣa king is the one who dedicates the treasury of inexhaustible merit and wisdom; he presides over the perfection of dhyāna.
By means of the yakṣas of meditative concentration, he protects the minds of all sentient beings, causing their minds not to be deluded, so that they may attain the great treasury of merit.
The yakṣa is here translated as "suffering existence" (kǔhuó) or alternatively named "investigation" (sìchá).

This clarifies that through the gate of dhyāna, he protects and investigates the "suffering existence" minds of all sentient beings, causing their minds not to become deluded. This Heavenly King leads the host of yakṣas and resides on the northern face of Mount Sumeru.
The sixth is the Dragon King Virūpākṣa, who presides over the host of dragons and dwells to the west of Mount Sumeru.
This Dragon King presides over the firm dedication that accords with reality; he illumines the gate of the Prajñāpāramitā.

Like a dragon roaming through the sky, he can manifest or become invisible and send down rain to moisten sentient beings. By means of the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he exercises mastery over existence and non-existence, raining down all dharmas.
It rains, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
The seventh [stage] and those equal to it are presided over by the Kumbhāṇḍa kings. These are the yakṣas and bhūtas who cause nightmares and enchantment, and who consume vital essence;
they are also called "pumpkin ghosts" (tenggua gui). Toward such evil beings, the Bodhisattva likewise accords with them in all respects; therefore, this is called "equal accordance."
He dedicates [merit] in accordance with all sentient beings, entering everywhere even into the hells.
This deity is the Heavenly King of the South, who leads two classes of beings: the first is named Kumbhāṇḍa, and the second is named Preta. As for these Kumbhāṇḍas...
His scrotum was as large as a winter melon; when walking, he would lift it and place it upon his shoulder, and when sitting, he would squat down upon it.

Clearly manifesting defiled craving and greed like a hungry ghost, the Bodhisattva of Great Compassion followed him everywhere, in order to sever all craving and seeking (this is the mastery of the *upāya-pāramitā*).

The eighth is the dedication of the mark of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Gandharva King—here translated as "Seeker of Fragrance"—seeks his food by finding places where there is fragrance to enjoy himself.
This symbolizes the Bodhisattva in the stage of the mark of True Suchness, who constantly delights the assembly with the undefiled fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body:
the True Suchness Dharma-realm, ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
[This is] birth. Because it causes [beings] to love and delight [in it], the ten kings therein clarify the ten pāramitās within the pāramitā of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
The ninth, the dedication of liberation that is unbound and unattached, relies upon the moon deity as its objective support to symbolize the pāramitā of power (bala-pāramitā);
by means of the wisdom of the space-like dharmatā that is unbound and unattached, it illuminates sentient beings and purifies the heat of their afflictions.

Because one attains the coolness of the Dharma, the tenth is the dedication of entering the infinite realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). This is symbolized by the Sun Deity (*Sūryadeva*) through the use of an illustrative object.

It clarifies the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) within the ten dedications. Just as the sun abides in the sky and shines downward upon the myriad existents, its position becomes increasingly sublime and its merit ever greater.
"Benefiting those below. This refers to Bodhisattvas at this stage whose wisdom is exceedingly high, yet whose conduct reaches ever lower.

They penetrate down to humans, devas, spirits, ghosts, followers of external paths and heterodox practices, animals, and those in the hells, fully identifying with their conduct. It is like the sun and moon:

while their form is above, their function is below, for they illuminate both the good and the evil alike. The ten kings mentioned above correspond to the ten stages within the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pratipatti*).

The perfections (pāramitās) are concluded. As with the ten abodes (bhūmis), the ten practices (caryās), the ten transferences (pariṇāmanās), and so on up to the tenth ground, the perfections within each respective stage should be understood according to that specific stage;
one may grasp them by taking a single example as a model, yet if one does so, one will not know their true direction.
In this way, the Sun and Moon Devas both symbolize the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), forming the gateway to the practice of the path of great compassionate vows.

They clarify that compassion and wisdom are without dependence, constantly taking the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) as their essence. Shining universally according to the faculties [of beings], they have no purposeful action;
they allow the sun of non-effortful wisdom to function, bringing benefit in accordance with the myriad existents.

The Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World-Rulers, the Dharma-Gate of the Ten Stages, and the Ten Abodes and Ten Practices are metaphorically represented as being like spirits. The stage of the Ten Transferences is metaphorically represented as being like kings.

Within these Ten Stages, they are metaphorically represented as being like devas, clarifying their progressive cultivation and gradual mastery of excellence. This deva realm is named the Sublime High Heaven (Sumeru).
That mountain is situated in the great ocean; it rises eighty million yojanas above the water and extends eighty million yojanas below the water.
It is composed of four precious substances: its northern face is of gold, its southern and western faces are of lapis lazuli, its western face is of crystal, and its eastern face is of white silver.
Its shape is like that of a waist-drum. It has four tiers above, with the Four Great Kings each residing on one of its four sides according to their respective directions.
On the summit of the mountain are four peaks; on these peaks dwell the Eight Heavenly Kings, each with their own retinue.

On the central peak resides Śakra, adorned with all manner of precious jewels. For this reason, it is named Sumeru, also called Mount Wonderful Peak (Miaofengshan), and also called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. This...
It is said that the clouds can govern the heavens, for Śakra is able to act as the Lord of Devas. Below this are seven layers of oceans, each surrounded by a distinct mountain of gold.
A garuḍa must fly for seven days before it can finally reach them. On these golden mountains dwell devas, all of whom are under the jurisdiction of the Four Great Kings.
Above them are the Thirty-three Heavens; the bodies of all the devas there are one yojana in height, and their garments are likewise [one yojana long].
It is two *yojanas* in height and one *yojana* in width; it weighs six *zhu*. Its lifespan is one thousand years.
One day and night there is equal to one hundred years in this human world. Thirty days constitute a month, and twelve months constitute a year.

The above is according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, the *Tri-dharma-śāstra*, and other treatises. This Heavenly King has five names: the first is "The Capable Lord" (*Śakra*), and the second is... [text truncated]
Śakra Devānām Indra is also named Kauśika, Śakra Devendra, and Indradeva; these names signify "Lord of the Gods.
In full, he is called Śakrendra. "Śakra" means "hundred," as he attained the status of Lord of the Gods by previously performing a hundred unobstructed *vaiyāvṛtya* (unrestricted) offerings.
This corresponds to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) within the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
In this stage, the Bodhisattva practices the counteractive contemplation that the worldly dharmas of suffering, emptiness, and impermanence are not real;

they all arise from the twelve links of dependent origination and are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic essence or characteristics. Thus, he achieves equanimity toward his own dharma-body, life, and wealth, and likewise toward all Buddha-dharmas.
Practicing with faith and compliance, one first remedies the coarse karma of stinginess and avarice within the desire realm by practicing the *dāna-pāramitā*.

Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), one has not yet fully mastered them; it is only at the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī bhūmi*) that a bodhisattva clearly understands the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination.
This is illustrated by the analogy of refining pure gold, which must repeatedly enter the fire, to clarify the remedy for the obstacle of stinginess.
Second, there are further immeasurable Suyāma Heavenly Kings who represent the Stainless Ground (vimalā-bhūmi).

Because these devas have transcended the terrestrial limits, they dwell in the void and possess manifold sublime pleasures. Correspondingly, for the Bodhisattvas at this stage, the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) increases and excels, and they possess the joy of the Dharma;
because the Dharma-body is the essence of their ethical discipline, they progressively advance and leave behind the worldly states of the preceding ground.

Because of being bound [to the world], the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is preeminent in the first stage (*bhūmi*). In this stage, the progressively superior pure morality (*śīla*) of the ten wholesome paths of action is preeminent;
thus it is named "Stainless" (*vimalā*). The summit of Mount Sumeru in the first stage is connected to the world and its inhabitants, and is thus associated with the mundane.

This stage, however, dwells in emptiness and is associated with the supramundane; therefore, it is called "Stainless. The first stage is likened to refined gold, yet it is not yet said to be further enhanced.
It is like medicinal ore that, when repeatedly entered into fire, becomes increasingly bright and pure. This refined true gold is further treated with alum to make it even more brilliant and clear;
because the precepts serve as the alum, [it becomes so]. The Yāma Heaven—here translated as the "Time-Division" Heaven—is so called because this heaven has neither sun nor moon.
The celestial radiance illuminates one another, such that day and night are not distinguished; one knows them only by the opening and closing of the lotus flowers.
Due to the distinction between day and night, the bodies of these devas are two *yojanas* in height; their robes are four *yojanas* long and two *yojanas* wide, weighing three *zhu*.
Their lifespan is two thousand years, with the calculation of days, months, and years being double that of the preceding heaven.

In this stage, they cultivate the ten wholesome precepts (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*) of the highest degree, thereby counteracting the coarse afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) currently active in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). In the third stage, they cultivate the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).

In the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is finally free from the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms and is born into the family of the Tathāgata, sharing the same nature as the Tathāgata.
Third, there is the inconceivable King of the Tuṣita Heaven; this is named the Heaven of Contentment (*Tuṣita*).

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that Bodhisattvas in their final birth (*caramabhavika*) provide instruction here. This is as described in the *Yingluo benye jing* (Sutra on the Original Acts of the Garland) regarding the eleven stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth.

Upon awakening to the ground (bodhi-bhūmi), one is first called "one who is to be reborn only once more" (*ekajātipratibaddha*) and is then designated as being in their "final body" (*paścima-deha*). This is assigned to the third dhyāna.

These gods of the Heaven of Contentment (*Sudṛśa*) who serve as the final-body Bodhisattvas therein are all instances where the Tathāgata, according to the occasion, employs skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to establish the Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings;

they cannot be fixed definitively. The preceding stage clarifies that, through the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśala-karmapatha*) and pure precepts (*śīla*) of the highest order, one becomes detached from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Because of the manifestation of coarse afflictions and defilements, the Bodhisattva in this stage purifies the mental habituation of the form realm, the formless realm, and the desire realm by means of the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).
Thus, they obtain a mind that transcends the three realms. This is illustrated by the analogy of refining gold:

through skillful refinement, not even a *zhu* or two is lost, and it becomes increasingly bright and pure. One should understand that the mind is refined by the nine successive meditative attainments and observed with the Dharma-eye.

One applies oneself to practice so as not to impair the fundamental Dharma, but rather to make it increasingly clear and pure. Cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the desire realm serves to remedy the obstacles of desire;

cultivating wisdom (*prajñā*) in the higher realms serves to remedy the obstacles to concentration. Through such counteractive measures, one accords with the practice of the Dharma and benefits sentient beings through skillful means without any attachment;
this is called the Ground of Radiant Light (*Prabhākārī-bhūmi*). It has the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) as its essence. The height of the bodies of these devas is four... [yojanas].

The yojana [is the unit of measure]. Their robes are eight yojanas long and four yojanas wide. Their lifespan is four thousand years; the number of days, months, and years is all double that of the preceding heaven.
These gods of the Heaven of Contentment (Tuṣita) should cultivate three dharmas to be born therein:

namely, morality (śīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (prajñā). If one cultivates only morality and generosity, one will be born in other heavens. However, within the One Vehicle Dharma (Ekayāna), the matter is not thus. Because...

Because all-pervading wisdom constitutes the very body of this heaven, the fourth, the King of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*), represents the Bodhisattva of the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī*). Like this celestial realm, they constantly delight themselves through emanations;
thus it is also called the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations. There are no objects external to the mind, as they arise from the transformations of the mind. This heaven...

The assembly of kings consists of ten celestial kings; these are the ten pāramitās within the pāramitā of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), and they always take the pāramitā of diligence as their essence.

This stage employs the metaphor of refining true gold to create ornaments, illustrating how diligence clarifies the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*).
It serves as an antidote to the habitual tendencies of erroneous karma within the three realms; such is the body of these devas.
The body is eight *yojanas* tall; the robes are sixteen *yojanas* long and eight *yojanas* wide. Their lifespan is eight thousand years.
The number of days, months, and years is double that of the preceding heaven. Their clothing weighs one *zhu*, and they consume the flavor of ambrosia (*amṛta*).
Fifth, there are again countless kings of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven who, by means of their circumstances, symbolize the Ground of Difficult Victory (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).

This is because this heaven is at the summit of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), illustrating that the objects of the bodhisattva’s desires are difficult to transcend; hence it is called the Ground of Difficult Victory.
Bodhisattvas at this stage constantly take the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) as the essence of their contemplation. Māra Pāpīyān dwells within this heaven.
To cultivate the contemplation of the ten truths is itself the stage of a Bodhisattva; those who do not cultivate this contemplation are the retinue of Māra.
Furthermore, this heaven is named Paranirmita-vaśavartin, because they take the transformations produced by others as their own enjoyment. A Bodhisattva in this stage is like this:

they constantly teach and transform sentient beings, taking the attainment of happiness for others as their own happiness. The bodies of the gods in this heaven are sixteen yojanas in height, and their garments...
It is thirty-two *yojanas* in length. The lifespan in years and months is all double that of the preceding [level].

On the sixth [level], there is again an incalculable number of Great Brahmā Kings who clearly manifest the Stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*). Since the first dhyāna belongs to the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), no women are born there;
furthermore, because it is free from the defilements of the desire realm (*kāma-dhātu*), the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because it is free from desire and is tranquil."
It is named Brahmapāriṣadya. Furthermore, according to the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it is called "Brahma" because within the assembly of Brahmās, they speak with the Brahma-voice.
As for Śikhin, he is sometimes called "Holding the Topknot," sometimes "Conch-like Topknot," or "Fire-Crested," because the calamity of fire reaches this heaven.
Those who have cultivated and attained the first dhyāna are born in this heaven. This heavenly king is among the assembly of Brahmās.
They emit the great Brahma-voice. Each of the devas thinks to themselves, "He is speaking only with me; he has attained the highest sovereignty within the great trichiliocosm.
His countenance is like that of a youth, his body is the color of white silver, and he is half a yojana in height. His garments are golden in color, and he lacks male sexual characteristics.
He takes the joy of dhyāna as food and his lifespan lasts for one kalpa. Within this realm, there are ten Great Brahma Kings who are proficient in the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Regarding the ten *pāramitās* within the *pāramitās*, the seventh is further characterized by the King of Gods of Immeasurable Light and Sound (*Apramāṇābhāsvara*). This clarifies the stage of the Far-Reaching (*Dūramgamā-bhūmi*). These two belong to the heavens of the second *dhyāna*.

In the first *dhyāna*, sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is extinguished; in the second *dhyāna*, suffering (*duḥkha*) is extinguished. This clarifies that the Bodhisattva at this stage resides in the seventh ground, wherein all conditioned activities have come to an end, yet Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) remains.

The four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) are perfected. The thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) are constantly active.
Personal suffering has already ceased, and one constantly delivers others from suffering. Both the afflictive and cognitive obscurations (*kleśajñeyāvaraṇa*) are traversed in this stage.

It is like pure gold adorned with various exquisite jewels, becoming even more sublime. Here, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is understood as the essence of gold, while compassion and wisdom are the ornaments.

The perfection of the myriad practices serves as a treasury of wondrous jewels, mutually adorning one another. Because they constantly transform all sentient beings through the light of the teachings and the net of practice, they resemble this deva realm.
Having extinguished sorrow and suffering because their minds are pure, light is emitted from their mouths as they speak.
Herein lie the ten Great Light-Sound Heavens (*Mahāprabhāsvara*), which clarify the *pāramitā* of skillful means (*upāya*). This is the body of these devas.
It is two yojanas in height, and its lifespan is two kalpas. When the calamity of water reaches this heaven, there are again immeasurable Śubhakṛtsna devas in the eighth [heaven].
It clarifies that for Bodhisattvas on the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi), once the sorrow and suffering of this heaven have ceased, there remains only the joy of dhyāna;
likewise, for Bodhisattvas at this stage, once their functional effort (*prayoga*) has come to an end, there remains only the joy of the Dharma (*dharma-prīti*). The Dharma...

The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of delighting in meditative joy (*dhyāna-sukha*) first cease at the tenth stage. When this celestial wind-disaster arrives, it is because [the lower stages] have their natures agitated by the joy of meditative delight.

For a Bodhisattva in this state, non-conceptual wisdom (*anabhoga-jñāna*) manifests; yet, there still remain the pure habitual tendencies of the wisdom that delights in the dharma of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

In the ninth [stage], there are furthermore immeasurable gods of the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) heaven, which clarifies the Good Wisdom (*Sādhumatī*) stage. This is because there is no emergence from the fourth dhyāna.

The three calamities do not reach this realm of inhalation. Furthermore, these ten heavens all take the dharma-gate of tranquility as their palaces, symbolizing the adornment of the excellent wisdom of the ninth stage (*bhūmi*).
With palaces of the Dharma-treasure consisting of hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* dhāraṇī-gates, they transform and guide sentient beings;
they are able to expound various teachings for all sentient beings through a single utterance of speech.
There is no mind, thought, or consciousness. Just as this deity lacks the thinking-consciousness capable of speech, so too this deity lacks the consciousness of the lower realms.

From the consciousness of the form realm up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception, all possess subtle consciousness. If perception and consciousness were to be exhausted, [there would be nothing].
Because they are not subsumed under the karma of the three realms, there are therein ten celestial kings who represent the ten pāramitās within the pāramitā of the power of clarity (*vidyā*).
The bodies, garments, and lifespans of these deities are all double those of the preceding heavens. It is understood that the bodhisattvas at this stage always take the Dharma-palace as their abode.
Because their merit and virtue are vast and great, they are called the Vast-Fruit Heaven (*Bṛhatphala*).

The tenth Great Lord of the Heaven of Sovereign Power (*Maheśvara*) symbolizes the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*). This clarifies that at this level, the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-jñāna*) is perfected.
As the *Bodhisattva-mūla-karman-avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "In the tenth stage, the two habitual tendencies of mind and form are simultaneously and completely exhausted.
In the eleventh stage, within the dual conditions of mind and objects, one attains unimpeded sovereignty. From the eighth stage through the tenth..."
Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*): within the eleven stages of the Universal Worthy (*Samantabhadra*) gate, one has not yet attained mastery.

This refers to the case described in the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" (*Daśadhyāna-parivarta*), where one seeks for Samantabhadra but does not see him. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

Beyond the ninth heaven, there is another distinct class of Bodhisattva gods belonging to the ten stages, named Maheśvara. These gods have eight arms and three eyes, ride a white ox, and know all in a single thought-moment.
The number of raindrops in a trichiliocosm is the skillful means employed by this introductory Bodhisattva to establish the Dharma;

it relies upon phenomena to manifest the Dharma, for the scope of his transformative guidance gradually increases in excellence. Thus, in the single-vehicle Dharma-realm, principle and phenomena are integrated;
within a single mote of dust, the Buddha-lands of all Buddhas and the realms of humans and devas coexist, their bodies and pores appearing like reflections of one another.
Entering. Those who cultivate the truth must know things as they truly are and not follow along with phenomenal appearances.
From this "Chapter on the Manifestation of Signs" up to the "Chapter on Samādhi of Samantabhadra," the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of Worlds," and the "Flower Treasury World."
Chapter [Title]. Vairocana Chapter. These five chapters of the sutra collectively answer the previous thirty-seven questions, clarifying the section on "Manifesting the Fruit and Exhorting Practice.
Samantabhadra Samādhi Chapter.

Wisdom and principle are boundless; thus they are called "Universal" (*Samantabhadra*). Wisdom that benefits according to the faculties [of beings] is termed "Worthy" (*Bhadra*). To clarify the three [wisdoms], it is called "Correct" (*Samyak*);

to clarify their depth, it is called "Concentration" (*Samādhi*), also known as "Right Reception" (*Samāpatti*). Because it is right concentration that is undisturbed and capable of receiving, retaining, and discerning all phenomena, it is named "Right Reception.
As Samantabhadra, he is the heir to the Buddhas and the house of the great wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*. The ten thousand... of all Buddhas...

The eldest son of the Universal Sovereign (Samantabhadra) skillfully discerns all dharmas to cause sentient beings to resolve their delusions; therefore, he must enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Yet, because the essence of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is free from both concentration and distraction, he manifests such [a practice] to demonstrate the Dharma-standards.

This clarifies that Samantabhadra Bodhisattva is constantly in *samādhi*, wherein stillness and distraction are universally the Truth. Nevertheless, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, it is clarified that one must first enter the Dharma.

Furthermore, there are ten thousand nāgas established in fixed karma who occupy the status of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), signifying that there are those among ordinary beings who are able to enter [the path].

If anyone were to say, "This sutra is not within the realm of ordinary beings; it is the practice of bodhisattvas," such a person should be known as one who extinguishes the Buddha’s insight and destroys the True Dharma, causing his correct teaching not to circulate in the world and bringing ruin to the world.
Right view will not arise, and the lineage of the Buddhas will be severed. Those who possess wisdom should not act in such a way.

Even if they do not exhort others to practice, or even if they themselves do not attain it through practice, they do not lose the seeds of goodness; for this samādhi serves as a superior condition for the accumulation of habitual tendencies in future lives.
It takes the fundamental wisdom of the dharma-realm as its essence and the wisdom of differentiation as its function.

Furthermore, it takes the fundamental wisdom of the dharma-realm as its essence and acts in accordance with the conduct of sentient beings as its function. Moreover, it takes the entry into samādhi as its essence and the emergence from meditative concentration as its function.
Furthermore, taking non-entry and non-exit as its essence, both entry and exit constitute its function.

Alternatively, taking both entry and exit as its essence—to state the essential point—this serves as the principle for transforming sentient beings. By using entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to clarify the essence, one subsequently arises from that concentration to manifest the ten names of concentration;
these constitute the function. Within these ten names of concentration, they are collectively based on the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). No... [text ends]
It takes the nature of wisdom as its essence. This essence is also called the Śūraṅgama Samādhi.
It serves as the essence for all unspeakable samādhis and gateways of wisdom. As a sutra says: "There is nothing among the whirlpools of the oceans of worlds that it does not enter.
"Ocean" signifies vastness, and "whirlpool" signifies profundity; this clarifies that the essence and function of this samādhi are both vast and profound.
Profound and inexhaustible, because their practice pervades all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all sentient beings within the six realms of existence throughout the ten directions. —
Chapter on the Accomplishment of the World.

Now, this chapter is explained to clarify that the world-oceans—their bases, their forms, their suffering and happiness, and their purity and impurity—are all adorned by the karmic retribution of the sentient beings themselves and do not arise from anything else.
The world-oceans of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are accomplished through the power of inconceivable transformations;
therefore, it is named the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of Worlds. This is intended to cause those who have first resolved [to attain enlightenment]...

The mind knows the realm of sentient beings to be as vast as the dharma-realm and the space-realm, entering one another like reflections, infinitely layered yet distinct in their respective abodes, for it is completely filled by the practices of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
thus, it causes bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds [to realize this].
Because one knows that within the ocean of the realms of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the identity or difference of the realms of sentient beings cannot be apprehended;

therefore, as the realms of sentient beings transform according to their own karma, the oceans of lands transform. As they undergo formation and destruction according to their own karma, the oceans of lands likewise undergo formation and destruction.
If one does not explain that the realm of sentient beings, the dharma-realm, the Buddha-realm, the bodhisattva-sphere, and the realm of empty space are non-dual, inexhaustible,

and abide in a layered manner like reflections within reflections, then all those who have resolved their minds— even if they do not enter the path of the two vehicles and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva—

will merely attain the status of a bodhisattva of the provisional teaching; their minds will remain subject to constant defilement and purity, limited and obstructed, and they shall not enter the state of Buddhahood.

Regarding the realm (*viṣaya*): there are distinctions between one's own Buddha and other Buddhas, as well as between their respective lands (*kṣetra*). This is because it serves as the basis for coming and going;
it is as described in the Three Vehicles, where pure lands exist in other directions, and Bodhisattvas aspire to be born therein.

The intent behind teaching this chapter is to cause those who have first resolved to attain bodhicitta to understand that the realms of sentient beings and the realms of the Buddhas possess a vast and profound character of mutual non-obstruction.
It is intended to cause those who resolve to attain bodhicitta in the present and future to recognize the conduct of the Buddhas and the boundless ocean of the karma of sentient beings,
and how the Tathāgata universally delivers them through the practices of Samantabhadra and the Dharma.
The nature of wisdom is unimpeded in principle. From the first generation of the bodhicitta, he raised clouds of great vows; compassion and wisdom universally cover all.

Through the ocean of *pāramitās*, there is no land where his body does not appear, and no practice that does not accord with his deeds. Within lands as small as motes of dust or the tip of a hair, worlds manifest in infinite layers.
His body of equalizing wisdom enters them all without exception, causing those who study to emulate him so that their pursuit is never in error. This...
This is like the path of a great king; it is the natural order of things, always thus. To seek anything else would be eccentric and improper.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World," in order to explain this chapter, I shall briefly provide an analysis in ten sections: first, explaining the purpose of the chapter's appearance; second, explaining the title of the chapter.
3. Explaining by what karmic retribution the Flower Treasury World-Ocean is obtained. 4. Explaining the shape and structural arrangement of the Flower Treasury World.
5. Correlating the Flower Treasury World’s structural arrangement with its causes. 6. Explaining the unimpeded nature of the pure and mixed realms within the Flower Treasury World-Ocean. 7.
Explaining how the Flower Treasury World-Ocean perfectly encompasses the karmic objects and environments of the three periods of time. 8. Explaining the Flower Treasury World... [text incomplete]

The realms are fundamentally empty, yet they give rise to objects of perception. Ninth, it explains why the Flower Treasury World (*Gandavyūha-lokadhātu*) attains mastery over its concealment and manifestation.
Tenth, the meaning of the text is explained according to its phrasing. Third, regarding the explanation of how the Flower Treasury World is obtained as a karmic reward:
from the initial stage of faith up to the eighth bhūmi, one constantly sustains [the practice] through the power of great vows and resolve, ensuring that one does not regress from bodhi.
The oceans of all *pāramitās* teach and benefit all sentient beings; reaching the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), they act for the benefit of others spontaneously and without effort.
One should know that the wind-wheel is the fruition produced by the *pāramitā* of great vows.

While the world of sentient beings is sustained by the winds of the karma of false conceptualization, the world of the Tathāgata is able to sustain all realms through the wind of wisdom and the power of great vows. For...

Through wisdom, one follows according to vows; through vows, one brings wisdom to fulfillment. This, in turn, is the fruition of the great wisdom of the Dharma-body of great vows, which constitutes the substance of the wind-wheel.
If it were not for the Dharma-body, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) would be merely composite and thus lack inherent nature.

If there were no ultimate vow, the Dharma-body would have no essence and could not manifest itself, let alone manifest for others. It is by means of these three factors acting as conditions that [the wind-wheel] is established.

Only then will one be fit to benefit sentient beings, without being obstructed by the extremes of emptiness or existence. When progress in cultivation reaches maturity, one benefits others spontaneously and without effort.
For now, take the great vows of the initial cause as the primary focus, enabling one to sustain the myriad objects of experience. In total, use the wind of great vow-wisdom to sustain these objects.
Thus, all the adornments within the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu) are sustained upon this wheel of wind; this is due to various meritorious actions.

Originally arising from vows, one returns to employ that original cause to sustain all fruits. By means of this perfection of vows (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*), one is able to accomplish the ocean of all perfections.
Because the original cause is thus, cause and effect mutually sustain one another, resulting in all manner of adornments.
Through the mutual interpenetration of the essence of the perfection of vows with all other practices, one is able to sustain the various deeds above, thereby attaining retribution.
The universal adornments and the essence of the Lotus Treasury are the retributive attainment of the wisdom-body that follows the Dharma-body and is without dependence or abiding.
The palace is the retributive attainment of Great Compassion that nurtures and sustains all beings.

The pavilions are the retributive attainment of the wisdom-illumination that observes the faculties [of beings] and accords with compassion to rescue them. Its ground of vajra is the Dharma-body of the nature of equality.
It is obtained as a retribution. All that serves as adornment among these various ornaments—specifically those made of vajra—is the retribution for the practice accompanying the Dharma-body.
All that is adorned with mani-jewels is the retribution obtained from the practice accompanying the formation of the precept-substance of the Dharma-body.
The Vajra-circumference Mountains are the retribution obtained from the karma of protecting through the precept of great compassion. [The adornment of] various flowers...
"Adornment" refers to that which is obtained as a retribution for the manifestation of myriad practices that benefit sentient beings and bring forth all manner of goodness.

"Adornment with jewel trees" refers to that which is obtained as a retribution for establishing practices that benefit sentient beings and provide shelter and protection for all conscious beings. To speak briefly, it is thus;
were one to explain in detail the causes of such karmic retributions, they could not be fully enumerated. Indeed, no retribution is obtained in vain; all have their causes. If [one does not...]

Knowing the cause. What is the cultivation of the fruit? Regarding the sixth explanation—that the Flower Treasury World (*kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*) is characterized by the non-obstruction of the pure and the mixed—it is because the practices performed by the Buddha pervade both the Dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings. Since these practices are all-pervasive, the resultant support (*āśraya-phala*) that is attained is likewise all-pervasive.

However, as for those karmic factors that are not associated [with the physical body], they coexist with it yet remain unseen, much like spirits and various beings of the ghost realm who dwell together with humans but whom humans cannot perceive.
As a sutra states: "For example, within a human body, there are always two devas who follow one;

the devas constantly see the person, but the person does not see the devas. This sutra serves to demonstrate that while the Buddha’s activity is all-pervasive, his reliance upon and the environment (the *niśraya* and *āśraya*) are likewise pervasive.

Unlike the three vehicles, which project the Pure Land to other directions and thereby give rise to the notions of coming and going or self and other, this teaching was established as a provisional net for those of inferior faculties and small minds;
ultimately, one who seeks the great bodhicitta [should understand otherwise].
One must still return to this gate of non-duality to give rise to practices and vows that pervade the entire Dharma-realm.

Seventh, regarding the Huayan world’s perfect inclusion of the karmic realms of the three periods of time: this clarifies that within a single thought-moment of this teaching, the three periods of time are present.
A single thought-moment is, in fact, no-thought. No-thought is the absence of dharmas such as the three periods of time, past and present; through this, the Dharmakāya is revealed.
Because all sentient beings' deluded thoughts and the phenomena of many kalpas across the three periods of time do not depart from within non-thought,
for this reason, all the adorned realms of this Flower Bank World are able to manifest the activities of all Buddhas.
The causes and effects of the karmic actions performed by sentient beings throughout the three periods of time are all manifested therein:
either past karma appearing within the future, or future karma appearing within the past, or karma from both the past and the future appearing within the present.

Or, present karma may manifest within the past and future, just as hundreds of thousands of clear mirrors are suspended together on all four sides—front and back—with their reflections mutually penetrating one another. This is because the essence of the *dharmadhātu* is timeless;

thus, the karmas of the three periods of time, though falsely conceptualized, suddenly manifest within this timeless reality. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Wisdom enters the three periods of time without coming or going."
Regarding the eightfold explanation of why the Buddha-lands are fundamentally empty, yet the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpakaraṇḍa*) arises as their objective support:

First, it is to clarify that although those of the Two Vehicles have attained liberation from the coarse karma of the triple world, they lack merit and wisdom; thus, they do not benefit sentient beings and remain stagnant in *nirvāṇa*.

Second, it is for the sake of the Bodhisattvas of the Three Vehicles who delight in being born in pure lands where pure appearances constantly persist, [lest they] obstruct the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).

In principle, when one’s attachment to defilement or purity is based on personal sentiment, one’s knowledge and vision are not universal; when the mind clings to a pure land, one does not attain mastery.

It is not so with this Dharma, which possesses the freedom to manifest or conceal at will. For the sake of benefiting sentient beings and to reveal supreme merit, it manifests ten thousand variations of marks and features, with radiance shining forth clearly.
If one causes sentient beings to have no attachment in their minds, then—like illusory clouds dispersing—there is not even a single thing remaining. There is nothing.

Because there is something to be gained, they maintain their attachments. Third, for those sentient beings who fear the emptiness of all phenomena, [the Buddha] teaches the principle of the emptiness and signlessness of dharmas.

This is said so that they may abandon nihilistic views; lest they claim that emptiness lacks merit and wisdom, fail to delight in contemplating emptiness, and instead take pleasure in the bonds of grasping at signs, persisting in karma according to sensory objects and being unable to attain liberation.
Therefore, by manifesting the fruits of the primary and secondary bodies resulting from merit, he causes them to contemplate the dharma of emptiness.
Emptiness purifies ignorance and accomplishes meritorious deeds.

These four are collectively for the sake of all those of the three vehicles and all ordinary beings, manifesting the scale, patterns, and modes of the vast realm of merit and wisdom, so that they may emulate and study them without falling into partiality or attachment.
As the Sūtra says: "The lands of all Buddhas are like empty space—unequaled, unarisen, and without marks—for the benefit of sentient beings."

He is born into Universal Adornment and Pureness, dwelling therein by the power of his original vows. Ninth, as for why the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu) attains mastery over concealment and manifestation:
it is because it manifests in accordance with wisdom from the principle of the emptiness of all phenomena; thus, it attains mastery over concealment and manifestation.

If even worldly dragons and ghosts, who possess the three poisons, are able to conceal and manifest themselves, how much more so can that which is empty of all things through the emptiness of phenomena?
The three poisons [are such that] pure, pristine wisdom cannot manifest them with mastery. It is like when Sudhana entered Maitreya’s pavilion;
by the power of samādhi, he saw all its various adornments, but upon arising from samādhi, they suddenly vanished, leaving not a single sign behind.
Sudhana asked, "Where have these adornments gone? Maitreya replied, "They have gone back to where they came from. He said:
"From where do they come? He replied, "They come from the wisdom and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of Bodhisattvas; they abide by relying on the wisdom and spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) of Bodhisattvas.
They have no place of departure, nor do they have a place of abiding. They are neither accumulated nor permanent, being far removed from all things.
Furthermore, it is like a magician performing various illusory feats: they come from nowhere and go nowhere. Although there is no coming or going, by means of illusion..."
By the power of that [wisdom], it is clearly visible; the same applies to those ornaments. They come from nowhere, nor do they go anywhere.

Although there is no coming or going, they manifest in this way through the power of the inconceivable wisdom of illusion resulting from habitual practice, as well as through the power of former great vows.
The Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*) is likewise manifested by the Tathāgata.
The power of the wisdom of great vows and the power of the self-nature of the dharma-realm being empty and devoid of intrinsic nature allow for mastery over concealment and manifestation.

If one follows the dharma-realm, all myriad phenomena are entirely non-existent; yet if one follows the power of the wisdom of vows, all manifold characteristics appear accordingly. This concealment and manifestation occurs in accordance with conditions, and there is no creator whatsoever.
It is simply that the principle of wisdom and reality inherently possesses inconceivable efficacy and inconceivable transformations;

there is no agent who can create them, yet they manifest freely through concealment and appearance. Ordinary beings cling to this, using it as ignorance. Once these attachments and obstructions are gone, the functioning of wisdom becomes sovereign.

In accordance with the Dharma-body, the myriad phenomena are simultaneously quiescent; following the function of wisdom, the myriad phenomena are simultaneously manifest. Following great compassion, one constantly dwells within birth and death;

yet, by following the principle of wisdom alone, birth and death are eternally true. Through these three matters, the myriad modes of concealment and manifestation do not depart from the single true wisdom;
thus, the ritual displays of transformation undergo a hundred variations.
This second assembly, the Vairocana Chapter, consists of the first five sections.
These were established to manifest the fruit of Buddhahood of the present-day Vairocana; however, there was concern that faith might not be achieved. Why is this so?

Because there were no ancient precedents, one might wonder from where such a thing could have come now. Therefore, by citing the past to authenticate the present, it is clarified that the Way is... [not lost].
This is erroneous. One who has achieved faith does not harbor doubts. A question is asked: Are the Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the present one or different?

The answer is: they are both one and different. Why is this so? Because their Dharma-body, Wisdom-body, the ninety-seven marks of a Great Man, their great kindness and great compassion, and their wisdom and liberation are one;
yet, the individual sentient beings who resolve to attain Buddhahood are [different].

They are different. Furthermore, the immeasurable Buddhas of the three periods of time all attain Buddhahood in a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), with no distinction between before and after; this is their unity.
Yet, within that single thought-moment, they do not destroy the perception of the immeasurable sentient beings and the duration of the kalpas of the three periods of time; this is their difference.

Within the text, there are four Buddhas appearing in the world, collectively clarifying the single name Vairocana, each according to the conditions of the world and responding to specific circumstances.
It is not that there is any difference in the names of the Buddhas. All names in the world are names of the Buddhas, because the virtues of the Tathāgata pervade all phenomena.
It is just as empty space pervades and contains all things, for there is nothing that is not pure.
The names of all sentient beings enter into the name of the Buddha because there is nothing that is not pure. Question:

Among these, one type consists of humans who are neither devas, nāgas, nor spirits. How is it that they obtain supernatural powers as karmic retribution such that clothing, food, and drink arrive according to their thoughts?

Furthermore, how is it that the dwelling places they occupy are so sublime and adorned with precious jewels as a result of their environment? By what karma do they obtain such rewards? Answer: It is due to causes.
Because it is vast, the karmic retribution is vast; because its cause is sublime, the abode of the karmic retribution is sublime. Question:
What constitutes the vastness and sublimity of the cause? Answer:

It is when one gives rise to faith and cultivates resolute belief in the nature of the pure dharmas—the gate of non-abiding in the essence, function, and application of the Vairocana-dharmadhātu-wisdom—based on past causes.
Power. One constantly believes that oneself and others, the ordinary and the sagely, are of one essence. There is no basis for abiding; there is no self and no "mine.
Because the mind and its objects are equal and lack dualistic characteristics, and because there is no sense of "mine," all ordinary beings and sages are fundamentally nothing but the Dharma-realm.
They possess no nature of fabrication and no nature of arising or ceasing. Abiding in accordance with the Truth, they abide in non-abiding, together with the assembly of all Buddhas.
Birth. Abiding together in the true *dharmadhātu*, all conceptualization is the fundamental unmoving wisdom (*akṣobhya-jñāna*) of all Buddhas.
Ordinary beings and sages are one in this single truth, sharing this same wisdom.

Because one has full faith that one’s own mind is the Buddha’s seed-wisdom and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there is no separate mind that believes in the Buddha apart from the mind itself, nor does one perceive a self within one’s own mind.

Because the mind possesses the marks of the Buddha, one believes in such a Dharma. Due to this cause of faith—being lofty, supreme, and vast—one obtains such a sublime and wondrous retribution of both the primary and secondary fruits.
It is asked: For what reason does this Buddha manifest and appear as a transformation from a lotus flower?
Regarding the appearance of Śākyamuni from his mother’s womb, the answer is: he appears from the mother’s womb according to what is seen by the faculties [of sentient beings].

It is only those with inferior understanding who see him thus through their own faculties. As stated in the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (Lokottaraparivarta): "He appears from the mother’s womb for the sake of sentient beings with inferior understanding;
for sentient beings with great faculties, he is seen to appear from within a lotus. This concludes the six chapters of the second assembly.

This section clarifies the gate of the Bodhisattva’s faith. It takes place in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsāgrakūṭa*), wherein one achieves faith through the fruition [of Buddhahood], believing that one's own mind is the Buddha.
This passage comprises six dharmas: 1. The Chapter on the Names of the Buddhas:

To cause those with faith to believe that the names of the Buddhas pervade all worlds, knowing that the nature of names is detached from [inherent existence]. 2. The Chapter on the Four Noble Truths: To cause those with faith... [text truncated]
This refers to one’s own conviction that the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) in all worlds is itself the Noble Truth (*ārya-satya*), because there is no seeking elsewhere.

Third, the Chapter on the Awakening of Radiant Light: it causes those with faith, by means of the radiance of their own minds, to awaken to and illuminate all inexhaustible great trichiliocosms throughout all worlds as the universal realm of the Buddha.
Mind and object merge into one; internal and external views vanish. Returning to the eastern direction as...
First, light extends to the east across thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms and a hundred thousand three-thousand-great-thousand-world systems.
In this manner, it proceeds through ten layers in each of the ten directions, doubling and circling outward until the ten directions are completely illuminated.
Body and mind become of one nature, unimpeded and all-pervasive, identical to the realm of the Buddha. Having observed in this way, one then seals it with the samādhi-mudrā of non-action and enters.
At the initial stage of the ten abodes, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and becomes a true son of the Dharma King of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Just as that single light shines upon all, one cannot claim that the Buddha’s light does not extend to oneself;

rather, one must personally employ the light of one's own mind to be like the Buddha’s light, awakening the mind so that it perfectly illumines the dharma-realm. Thus, the "Chapter on the Fourfold Clarification of Questions" enables those with faith to...

The fifth chapter, "The Five Pure Practices" (Pañca-śuddha-caryā), clarifies the dharma-gates of what is to be believed; it causes those with faith to turn back beginningless deluded thoughts, thereby establishing the ocean of wisdom characterized by the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.

The sixth chapter, "The Chapter on the Worthy Head" (Bhadramukha-parivarta), causes those with faith to believe in the Buddha’s spiritual power, which universally transforms the boundless, attaining great sovereignty as well as the merit of faith. By believing in these six dharmas, one brings contemplative practice into correspondence [with the truth].
This is called "faith. The first assembly was an exhortation to practice by extolling the fruit of Buddhahood; one has faith in what all Buddhas have attained.
This second assembly, however, establishes faith through that fruit: one believes that one's own mind is the Buddha, for it is not different from the Buddha who is the fruit.

Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is not a single name that is not the name of a Buddha, because the essence and nature of names are themselves liberated. It is merely according to sentient beings...
The various accounts of his birth differ; this clarifies that the Buddha’s name is all-pervasive, which in turn clarifies that he is unattached to any names whatsoever.
The general intent is to lead sentient beings to realize that their own fundamental ignorance is, in its essence, nothing other than the Tathāgata’s fundamental great wisdom.
This causes all sentient beings to suddenly recognize their original nature and suddenly become Buddhas. Below, ten fundamental points are raised.

The Buddha of Moving Wisdom (Dongzhi) completes the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*). The ten Buddhas of the months are all named "Moon" (Yue) to complete the ten abodes (*vihāra*), clarifying that one has newly realized the fundamental wisdom of the Dharmakāya and attained mental coolness.
This indicates that at this stage, the Bodhisattva accords with principle and delusion vanishes, because they have attained the coolness of the wisdom of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatājñāna*).
Within the stage of the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten Buddhas of the eyes are all named... [as above].
He is the Eye. He is the Illuminator of the Ten Practices. Because he knows the faculties through wisdom and gathers beings for their benefit and welfare, the Buddha is titled "Eye.
Within the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), ten Buddhas share the same name, "Wondrous" (*Miao*).

This is to clarify that within the stage of the Ten Dedications, the Bodhisattvas’ progressive cultivation has matured and wondrous wisdom manifests before them; thus, the Buddha is titled "Wondrous. The Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) are likewise "Wondrous. Thus it is said.

From the stage of the Ten Faiths upward, one attains faith by realizing that the wisdom of one’s own mind’s own discrimination is fundamentally one with the fundamental immovable wisdom of all Buddhas.
To perceive phenomena as existing apart from the mind does not constitute true faith.
Therefore, all phenomena (*dharmas*) are collectively termed the name of the Buddha. This is because all phenomena and their designations are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vivikta*).
That all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature is the nature of the *dharmadhātu*; the nature of the *dharmadhātu* is the name of the Buddha.
Thus, since all phenomena and their designations are all the name of the Buddha, they are designated as such by the Tathāgata. This is the first [point].

All phenomena are by nature devoid of intrinsic essence; because they bring about the attainment of Buddhahood, Mañjuśrī is precisely the sublime wisdom of one’s own mind that skillfully discriminates the signless.
Bodhisattvas such as Buddhasena (Awakened Head) and Śrīsena (Glory Head) are the principles and wisdom perceived within the sphere of one’s own mind according to faith and understanding.
Those of the three vehicles who have not yet turned their minds toward enlightenment will certainly not believe this. Why is that?
Therefore, it is established that after three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one shall attain Buddhahood.

Consequently, one simply acknowledges oneself and one’s own mind as being entirely those of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), merely stating that the Buddha possesses immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) and so forth, rather than having confidence that one’s own mind is the fundamental immovable wisdom Buddha (*mūla-acala-jñāna-buddha*).
For this reason, within the Dharma-realm vehicle (*dharmadhātu-yāna*), fundamental wisdom is taken as the faculty of faith (*śraddhā*). This...

Having gained faith through the sutras, one should thus believe directly that the nature of one's own mind’s discrimination is the fundamental Immovable Wisdom Buddha within the nature of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
The Golden World is the principle of the non-defilement of one's own mind;
Mañjuśrī is the sublime wisdom of one's own mind that skillfully discerns; and Bodhisattvas such as Bodhirāja and Cakṣurāja are those who follow this faith.

The wisdom of the Middle Way manifests before one. Through faith, one accords with the resultant dharmas of all Buddhas within the causal stage without the slightest error; only then is true faith established.
Having attained this faith, one advances through meditative concentration and wisdom, traversing the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, the ten stages, and the eleventh stage.
Throughout the passage of days, months, years, kalpas, and time, there is no shifting; the dharma-realm remains as it was, the Wisdom of Immovability.

The Buddha remains as he was; cause and effect do not shift, and time and kalpas do not change—only then is faith truly established. If one posits the existence of *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one is certainly still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Between the two paths of the ordinary and the holy, time and kalpas would shift and change. To have a Buddha existing outside of the mind fails to constitute true faith;
