it is merely the measure of worldly human sentiment, nothing but the long-flowing stream of birth and death, constantly following the net of views. How bitter this is! For this reason...
This is like the second assembly and the first assembly, which clarify the appearance of the Tathāgata who has newly attained perfect enlightenment.

The subsequent thirty-two chapters further include the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," clarifying that those who practice with faith and progress from beginning to end appear simultaneously with the Buddhas of the three periods of time, because the entire dharma-realm appears all at once. It is like holding a precious mirror that universally reflects all things.

As for the "Manifestation": because it is suddenly and fully revealed without any sequence of before or after, it clarifies that all phenomena are suddenly manifested within the fundamental Buddha-wisdom realm of the *dharmadhātu*.
One must not employ the limited measures of the mundane mind to interpret this as having a temporal sequence of before and after.
This is based on the realm within Maitreya’s Pavilion; the Buddha who first attained perfect enlightenment in the First Assembly is the Buddha who exhorts practice by pointing to the fruit.
The Buddhas mentioned in the "Chapter on Manifestation" refer to the Buddhas at the culmination of the causal practices of the five stages through which bodhisattvas advance.

This is because they correspond to the Immovable Wisdom Buddha (*Acalamati-buddha*) within the stage of faith (*śraddhā*). Furthermore, within these five stages of cultivation, each stage possesses its own fruition of Buddhahood.

In the teachings of the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), however, as one progresses from a preceding stage toward a subsequent stage, there is only the fruition of a bodhisattva, not the fruition of a Buddha.
Furthermore, as for the names of the Buddhas spoken by Mañjuśrī below, these pertain to this chapter and throughout the entire treatise, serving collectively to inspire faith.
Only when one has total faith in the causes and effects within the five stages, and the mind is free from obstruction, can one truly engage in spiritual practice.
It is like a person who, having traversed a perilous path five hundred *yojanas* long, first recognizes the obstacles and the open passages before proceeding.

This is analogous to a Bodhisattva at the stage of the Ten Faiths, who, within that state of faith, first discerns the progress and obstructions throughout the five stages of cultivation, and preemptively guards against them through vows and practice.
By means of faith, one discerns that the nature of one's own mind is fundamentally the immovable state of all Buddhas.
The essence of wisdom functions to prevent the views of the two extremes, for it apprehends external objects as other.

Because deluded consciousness, which fluctuates according to its various stages, obstructs true wisdom, for this reason, the mind of the ten levels of faith universally encompasses all five stages and constitutes complete faith.
Now, this single scripture suddenly presents the cause and effect of the five stages; the gateway to the fruition of all Buddhas is entirely constituted by faith. From this totality...
Having attained faith, one enters the stages of practice; only then does one no longer lose sight of the principle of wisdom (*prajñā*). It is like a person preparing food:

only when the five flavors have simultaneously reached full maturity does one begin to eat it. From the first moment of eating until the meal is finished, the five flavors are consumed together, and throughout, those flavors never depart from the five.

This clarifies the cause and effect of the five stages (*pañca-vasthā*); they are fully elucidated within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), and even as time passes, they ultimately lead to Buddhahood.
The fruit does not depart from the dharma of the initial faith, like painting a portrait according to a model. Question: All sentient beings inherently possess immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*).
Why do they not spontaneously realize the true, eternal, and pure state? Why do they instead follow along with defilement? Answer:
It is because all sentient beings, by virtue of this very wisdom, are born into the three realms; for this wisdom lacks a fixed nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and thus they are unable to know it themselves.

Wisdom is neither wisdom nor non-wisdom, nor are it phenomena such as good and evil, or suffering and pleasure; for the essence of wisdom is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), appearing only in accordance with conditions.
It is like an echo in an empty valley that forms sound in response to an object. Wisdom, being without intrinsic nature, merely discriminates in response to conditions.

Because of this discrimination, delusion and craving arise accordingly. Due to delusion and craving, the sickness of "mine" (*mamakāra*) arises. Because there is "mine," the karma of grasping at self and other is produced.
It then arises; because it firmly grasps, it is called *manas*. Because the *manas* grasps, it is termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
Due to the seeds of consciousness, birth and death continue in succession. Because of birth and death, the various sufferings are immeasurable; thus one seeks the path that is free from suffering.

Those who are deluded and do not know suffering cannot give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment. Those who know suffering and seek the truth, however, possess what is none other than their original wisdom.
Only by encountering the conditions for suffering can one come to know suffering; without encountering the conditions for suffering, one cannot know it.

Because of knowing the conditions for suffering, one is able to resolve to seek the unsurpassed path. Among Bodhisattvas of the spiritual lineage, those whose resolve and faith-understanding are strong possess a powerful disposition.
Although one may experience the fruits of happiness in the realms of humans and devas, one can still resolve to seek the unsurpassed path.
Therefore, wisdom follows delusion; wisdom follows awakening. Thus, it is like a person who falls because of the ground and rises because of the ground.

When precisely following delusion, it is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); when precisely following awakening, it is called wisdom (*jñāna*). In the state of being entangled in afflictions, it is called consciousness; in the state of enlightenment, it is called wisdom.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) originally have no names of their own; they are merely established as such names according to delusion and awakening.
Therefore, one must not calculate them as eternal or calculate them as annihilated. This wisdom and this consciousness are merely given names according to delusion and awakening.

If one seeks their beginning or end, it is like seeking tracks in the sky, like seeking a person in a shadow, or like seeking a self within the body—regardless of where one relies or dwells, in the end...
Because they cannot be apprehended, there are no characteristics of new growth, length, or location. Such is the case with ignorance (*avidyā*) and wisdom (*jñāna*):

they have neither beginning nor end. When one attains *bodhi*, ignorance is not extinguished. Why? Because it is originally non-existent; since it does not exist, there is nothing further to be extinguished.

Likewise, when one follows along with ignorance, the Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) is also not extinguished. Because it is originally non-existent, there is likewise nothing further to be extinguished.
There is cessation. However, when it merely follows along with the conditions grasped through form, sound, and fragrance, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

When it serves as the condition for knowing suffering and giving rise to the resolve [for awakening], it is called wisdom (*jñāna*). Because these are merely designated according to their conditions, their essence has no beginning or end.
This can be seen by reflecting upon it, like an echo in a valley.
From the "Chapter on the Names of the Buddhas," it is asked: Since the eastern direction represents the Dharma, it serves as a metaphor for the beginning of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*).

Just as the position of gold is in the western direction, why is the eastern direction the Golden World (*Suvarṇabhūmi*)? It is because the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is represented as golden, thereby manifesting the fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*).
Acala-jñāna replied: "This question is highly illustrative of the underlying principle. As stated in the sūtras, one takes faith as the womb;

upon reaching the stage of the ten abodes, one is said to have been born into the Buddha-family for the first time. Now, regarding why the eastern direction is designated as the Golden World (Suvarṇabhāsa-lokadhātu):"

The clarity of gold: in the first month it is the embryo; in the second month it is the fetus; in the third month it takes form; in the fourth month it is born in the Earth (Si); in the fifth month it is nurtured in the Fire (Wu);
in the sixth month it receives the cap and girdle in the Earth (Wei); in the seventh month it is the minister; in the eighth month it is the king. The ten stages of faith are like the fetal stage;
therefore, they are symbolized by the "Golden Fetus" of the East, such as the Golden World. This cites the initial cause of the ten stages of faith. As...
The Southern World of Wondrous Form, the Western World of Lotus Color, and so forth—these are the superior functions of advancing through the ten stages of faith.
As for what is called "sitting in the full lotus posture" (*paryaṅka-bandha*): to unify all worldly conditions into a single Dharma-realm is termed "binding" (*bandha*).
To designate many conditions by means of a single Dharma is termed "lotus" (*paryaṅka*). Furthermore, as for sitting in the full lotus posture, it is...
Because it represents the aspect of majestic deportment that is tranquil and unmoving, the Sūtra refers to the south.

Within the symbolism of the directions, the south signifies correctness, the sun, illumination, and emptiness, as it is empty in the center. Sudhana’s entry into the Way and his progressive cultivation involve traveling south to visit various spiritual friends;
this symbolizes the south as correctness, the sun, illumination, and the principle of emptiness. Therefore, he pays homage to the Buddha.
All recite "Namo," which clarifies that the south is empty and void.

The "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" constitutes the fundamental essence of this entire scripture and is the source of all ordinary beings and sages. In the first assembly, one gains faith in the Buddha-fruit;

here, with the Tathāgata and Samantabhadra as the primary figures, it clarifies the fruit already attained by the Buddha and the fruits realized through his practice, thereby engendering faith. Now, one enters into oneself.
Regarding the gate of faithful practice: one takes the names of Mañjuśrī and the Tathāgata, along with the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths, as the causes and effects to be believed in.
This clarifies that one should cultivate and study by means of the Dharma-gate of wondrous wisdom and through verbal designations.
Question: Why does the Tathāgata not himself proclaim his teaching? What is the purpose of emitting light and causing a Bodhisattva to speak? Answer:

The intention of the Tathāgata is to have the Bodhisattvas of each respective stage expound the Dharma-gates of that stage, so that those who practice and study may understand their respective limits and find it easy to comprehend.
Mañjuśrī constantly acts as the cause for the faith of all Buddhas and all sentient beings, and serves as the mother of wondrous wisdom.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva constantly acts as [the cause] for all Buddhas and sentient beings...

The causes for the practice of cultivation. By means of these two individuals, they bring to fruition the ocean of great compassion—the fruit of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirnimitta-jñāna*) of Bodhi—and cause the two to question one another, thereby expounding the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata.

This clarifies that for such practitioners, the beginning and end of cause and effect are perfected; the causal conditions of the past and present, the fruit of nature, the fruit of wisdom, and the fruit of practice are mutually penetrating as a single essence, so as to enable future...
Because it is easy for learners to understand,

the Chapter on the Four Noble Truths explains that "truth" (*satya*) means reality. It clarifies that the Tathāgata has spoken of four kinds of reality, causing all sentient beings to give rise to faith and understanding.
Therefore, it is asked: Why are many not mentioned, but only four? The answer is: Because these four types of truths (catvāri satyāni) comprehensively encompass all [others].

This is to clarify that all worldly existence is not apart from suffering (duḥkha) and its origin (samudaya), and all supramundane existence is not apart from cessation (nirodha) and the path (mārga).

The total exhaustion of all sufferings is called the truth of cessation; the total exhaustion of nirvana is called the truth of the path. [This applies to] the nirvana of the three vehicles (triyāna)...
In all other [vehicles], there is something further to be attained; in this Great Nirvāṇa, there is nothing further to be attained, and it is therefore called the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
This is because those of the Two Vehicles who seek quiescence mostly take birth in pure lands, and furthermore, they infer that these pure lands exist elsewhere in other directions.

Moreover, it is said that Bodhisattvas retain afflictions (*kleśa*) to moisten their rebirths; if they did not intentionally retain these afflictions, they would surely have to realize a nirvāṇa for themselves. Or...
There are pure lands in other directions where one may be reborn; therefore, the nirvana of the three vehicles is all attainable.

Furthermore, the Buddha who attains perfect enlightenment in Jambudvīpa under a wooden tree or upon a grass seat is a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*); the Buddha upon the red lotus flower in the Mahesvara heaven above is the Buddha of true retribution (*vipākaphala*).
Because both involve the feelings of delight and aversion, the four truths of the three vehicles lead to the aversion toward suffering.

The gathering [of wisdom] that rejoices in cessation and the path is called the Dharma-wheel of the Four Noble Truths. This Sūtra of the One Vehicle speaks of the "Four Noble Truths" in their ultimate sense. Why is this?
Because one who penetrates the true nature of suffering has neither longing for nor aversion toward it; because there is no other Buddha-field or separate pure land elsewhere;
and because there is no path of cultivation involving longing for or aversion toward the defiled and the pure, or toward nirvāṇa and saṃsāra. As for...

The practitioner of the path abides in accordance with the Dharma-abiding and cultivates the path in accordance with the Dharma. Without weariness or attachment, without delight or grasping, it is all one with the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), possessing neither the nature of coming or going nor the nature of a place of abiding.
From the pores of the body’s dust to the mind and its objects, all accord with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
With such faith and understanding, one thus cultivates the path. For this reason, there is the One Vehicle and the Four Noble Truths.

The three vehicles and the four truths each have their distinct differences, and each has its own corresponding faith and understanding. The Tathāgata, relying on the faculties [of beings] and employing skillful means, established these teachings;

none of them could have been formulated by ordinary worldlings. As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he taught the Dharma of the Four Truths for the sake of those who are śrāvakas, the twelve links of dependent origination for the sake of those who are pratyekabuddhas, and the six pāramitās for the sake of all bodhisattvas. This, too, is the work of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the discourse on adapting to the times, the essential summary is as follows:

This Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths and the Twelvefold Dependent Origination is such that all noble ones and all ordinary beings who give rise to a mind of faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma, yet whose path is not yet perfected, all begin from the initial mind by contemplating the suffering of themselves and others.
Thus, they resolve upon Bodhicitta and joyfully seek the methods of the Path, relying solely upon the distinctions of the Great and Small Vehicles, or the superior and inferior capacities.
They are not the same. The Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are each distinct;

however, the meaning of the Four Noble Truths encompasses all worldly dharmas without exception, as stated in the *Sūtra of the Garland*. Regarding the establishment of the ninefold vehicle (*navayāna*) dharma-gates:
first, the śrāvaka-śrāvakayāna; second, the śrāvaka-pratyekabuddhayāna; third, the śrāvaka-bodhisattvayāna. Within these three vehicles, there are respectively three types of penetration. For...
The Ninefold Pervasion. This inconceivable vehicle of the Dharma-realm consists of ten vehicles within the path of liberation;

through all of them, one attains the ultimate state where there is no suffering of the three realms. All other paths and gates are merely the phenomena of birth and death belonging to the mundane world of humans and devas.

Even if one attains a small measure of happiness, in the end one does not depart from the root of suffering. Although those of the Three Vehicles may transcend the three realms, their path is not yet true, for it is not the vehicle of the Buddha-fruit.
In the "Chapter on the Awakening of Radiance," in all places, Mañjuśrī simultaneously spoke these verses to clarify the nature of faith: "From the very beginning,
one should have self-confidence that these ten-colored worlds, the ten Tathāgatas of wisdom, and the ten-headed Bodhisattvas are, in their entirety, the fruit and practice of one's own Dharma."

The nature is great wisdom; the myriad practices are all-pervasive. Because they are established through faith, one proceeds from this point to practice, passing through the five stages without ever departing from it.
Therefore, the initial aspiration and the ultimate goal are not two different things. Such an aspiration is more difficult than the former [stages].
To seek to save others before one has saved oneself—to bow to such an initial aspiration is my homage. This initial aspiration serves as the teacher for devas and humans.
This surpasses the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; it clarifies that it is difficult for an ordinary person to enter the stage of faith (*śraddhā*).
This is because ordinary beings generally identify themselves only as ordinary beings, and are unwilling to recognize their own minds as the immovable wisdom (*akṣobhya-jñāna*).

Therefore, entering the ten stages of faith is difficult. This explains the accomplishment of the ten stages of faith, which leads spontaneously to the ten abodes (*vihāra*), beginning with the first, the Abode of Initial Resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda-vihāra*), and continuing until the ultimate [stage].

Because it culminates in the fruit of Buddhahood. Just as in the Three Vehicles one cultivates the ten stages of faith for ten thousand kalpas, in this teaching, because the Dharma-realm of fundamental wisdom is taken as the essence of the teaching, one attains realization immediately upon being capable of perceiving reality, without regard for the duration of kalpas.

This is like the assembly of two thousand people from the City of Enlightenment, headed by Sudhana, who were those who resolved their minds [for enlightenment] while on the road—six thousand in total.
This assembly of bhikṣus is likewise all of sharp and penetrating wisdom, extraordinary among humanity;

they understand much upon hearing it once, are humble, forgiving, and compassionate, and are single-mindedly intent on seeking the Great Way to benefit all living beings. They are all people who have fulfilled their faith in one lifetime, resolved their minds, and entered the stages of realization.
If one does not believe that one’s own mind is fundamentally the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom, then one will drift for eternal kalpas.

How could one who is submerged [in afflictions] be able to benefit others or rescue all things? As stated in the sutras, it is impossible for one who is themselves bound to be able to untie the bonds of others.
Therefore, there are two types of generating the bodhicitta: first, generating the mind through the cultivation of faith and understanding;

this refers only to those who cultivate the ten levels of faith and understanding, such as the aforementioned Ten Wisdoms Tathāgatas and the Ten Heads Bodhisattvas. Second, generating the mind upon the fulfillment of faith. The ten...
Because the first stage of abiding is named the "Abiding of Initial Aspiration," it corresponds to the ten months of the Buddha of the Ten Wisdoms Bodhisattvas;
this is their cause and effect. Question: For what reason is it that the establishment of the Ten Faiths gate is entirely the teaching of Mañjuśrī? Answer:
This clarifies that Mañjuśrī is the sublime wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions, which skillfully discriminates between the correct and the erroneous.
Once the correct and the erroneous are definitively established, one then practices through conduct; this is precisely what is called the conduct of Samantabhadra.

It further clarifies that Mañjuśrī is the Bodhisattva Youth, who, because he first initiated the cause and began his education, stands at the head of entering into faith; thus, he is named according to his causal practice.

The "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Clarity" (Bodhisattvapraśnaprajñāparivarta) is precisely that which clarifies the practices for the ten stages of faithful mind (*daśa-śraddhācitta*) and serves to sever doubt.
Mañjuśrī skillfully inquires into the causes and effects of good and evil in the world, which are otherwise mutually unknown; he is able to bring to fulfillment the causes of both good and evil.

Fruit. Bodhisattva Jñānacakra (Awakened Head) then answered with the truth of reality, based on the principle that dharmas do not cognize one another: "It is simply because of delusion regarding the truth that one creates karma for oneself.

One who knows the truth understands that all karma is itself the truth; by clearly awakening to this, one realizes that the essence of the karma of birth and death following the stream is, in its fundamental nature, eternally true and without transmigration.
Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are at all times known according to the Dharma."
Because it is not of the nature of transmigrating through birth and death, it is neither false nor is it real.
It is called "true" only because it is free from greed, hatred, delusion, and craving, and is genuine wisdom.

Therefore, such dharmas are taught to benefit sentient beings, so that by taking this very essence—the ignorance, karmic actions, causes, and effects—as the basis, one may awaken oneself and awaken others, causing them to know the self-nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Ultimate Truth. When both truth and falsehood have vanished, it is called the "Head of Enlightenment. Because one begins by believing in this Dharma, it is called the "Head.
This clarifies the initial mind of the Ten Faiths: fully believing that one’s own eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as all sentient beings, [are inherently enlightened].
When both the real and the false have entirely vanished, there remains only the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom;
therefore, the ten wisdoms of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya are taken as one's own fruition within the stage of the ten faiths.
The ten worlds of color—such as the Golden World, the World of Wondrous Color, and the Lotus-Color World—are the principles to be believed within these ten faiths. This is the awakening of Mañjuśrī.

The ten bodhisattvas, beginning with Śrīmatī and Samantabhadra, represent the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā-caryā*). Question: For what reason does the verse at the beginning state, "Mañjuśrī’s Dharma is always thus"?
Answer: It is because Mañjuśrī is the wisdom (*prajñā*) of all Buddhas. Immovable Wisdom (*Acalajñāna*) is the essence (*tattva*), while Mañjuśrī is its function (*vṛtti*).
This is done by means of this fundamental essence and function of the primordial wisdom of all Buddhas and all sentient beings.
Gate: Because it acts as the essence and function of cause and effect for all those with faith; because it causes them to rely upon the fundamental source;

and because, until the ultimate fulfillment of the fruit is reached, it is not different from the cause due to its non-dual nature—it is only then called the "initially aroused mind" and the "ultimate mind.
These two are not distinct. This clarifies that these ten stages of faith are difficult to arouse, difficult to believe in, and difficult to enter. Upon hearing this, everyone says: "I..."

Such a person is an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*); how could they possibly [attain it]? For this reason, the Buddha established that even for those with a small measure of faith, he praised the power of spiritual faculties and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Therefore, one should know that one must first possess such right faith; only then, through the power of right faith and right view, [can one proceed].
Practicing the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) in accordance with the Dharma, the world is named "Golden" (*Suvarṇa*), which clarifies that for two months the golden embryo (*garbha*) develops;

this represents the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) as the sacred embryo (*āryagarbha*). The Buddha’s title is "Immovable Wisdom" (*Acalajñāna*): because ignorance is fundamentally empty and lacks a substance that could be moved, it is called Immovable Wisdom.
It merely knows phenomena in response to objects and knows faculties in response to vessels, like an echo responding to a sound, without any fixed location.

That which has a discernible form is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). That which is beyond acceptance or rejection is called "immovability. Regarding the correspondence of cause and effect to their respective positions:
because wisdom skillfully discriminates phenomena to manifest *jñāna*, sublime wisdom (*prajñā*) is the cause and immovable wisdom is the fruit.
If, however, it is held that wisdom arises from *jñāna*, then immovable wisdom is the cause and sublime wisdom—Mañjuśrī—is the fruit.
They are either cause and effect, or wisdom and insight (*jñāna* and *prajñā*).

Taken collectively, they are neither cause nor effect, because their essence and function are the single reality, being non-dual dharmas; furthermore, because their essence has no beginning or end and nothing upon which it depends or by which it is attained.
This is the sovereign knowledge and vision of the nature-dharmadhātu, for it cannot be attained through worldly analogies of cause and effect.
Thus, when Mañjuśrī first gave rise to the mind of faith before Akṣobhya Buddha, he did not depart from this; so it was until the end of his faith.
Even until his own practice was perfected and he manifested the attainment of perfect enlightenment, he likewise did not depart from it. Therefore...
By means of the Buddha’s wisdom, he instructs and awakens sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
As for this "Buddha’s knowledge and vision," it is Mañjuśrī of Wondrous Wisdom, the Immovable Wisdom Buddha. This is that which is equally shared by both ordinary beings and sages;
the Buddha reveals it to ordinary people so that they may awaken and enter it.

In this "Chapter on Pure Conduct," by means of fundamental pure wisdom (*prakṛti-viśuddha-jñāna*), one inquires into sublime insight (*prajñā*). It sets forth one hundred and forty pure vows (*praṇidhāna*) to purify the afflictions and non-afflictions of ignorance within the six stages beginning with pure faith,
as well as the active manifestation of dharma-grasping (*dharma-abhiniveśa*) from the seventh stage through the tenth stage.
The two delusions regarding habitual tendencies and the Buddha-ground are purified simultaneously and in their entirety.

Within this state of faith, one must not allow for partial attachment, but guard against it through aspiration, ensuring that quiescence and activity are unimpeded. By means of this gateway of the Buddhas' primordial purity, wisdom, and sublime insight—
One hundred and forty great vows are taught to prevent the two obstacles of defilement and purity.

Therefore, by means of the correspondence across the six stages—namely, the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh ground—one cultivates the path according to each stage;

all afflictions therein arise from the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*). These two views comprise twenty types, totaling one hundred and forty, which are to be prevented.
To remove obstacles, he gave rise to one hundred and forty vows, so that those who practice this path may, from their initial faith, achieve the perfect integration of principle and phenomena;
and may those with faith realize the essence of these vows—the wondrous wisdom of discernment within the fundamentally pure wisdom of their own minds, free from deficiency.

Movement and stillness are both true, for there is no partial cultivation. For this reason, upon the mind of faith, the Dharma-nature, compassion, wisdom, sublime insight, and the myriad practices all rely upon the Buddha for their existence as they are cultivated;

they cannot exist apart from him. If one were to separate from the Buddha and claim that there is a self-dharma, then the mind of faith would not be established, the ten kinds of resolute conviction would not be established, and spiritual practice would not be established—even if one were to undergo suffering.
To practice with diligence in this manner is wrong diligence.

In the "Chapter on the Honorable Head," there are two types of faith: first, that of the Three Vehicles; second, that of the One Vehicle, as described in the *Awakening of Faith*. There are three kinds of arousal of the mind: first...

First is the awakening of the mind through the perfection of faith (*śraddhā-sampanna-cittotpāda*). After ten thousand *kalpas*, the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) continue in succession until one finally reaches the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).

Second is the awakening of the mind through practice and understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-cittotpāda*). This occurs by generating the mind through the instructions of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; or by spontaneously possessing great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*);

or by generating the mind to protect the True Dharma when it is about to perish. The Treatise states: "When such faith is perfected, one enters the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*)."
Ultimately non-retrogressive, it is called abiding in the true cause within the lineage of the Tathāgata. The two preceding types constitute the non-retrogressive arousal of the mind.

As for the third, the arousal of the mind through realization: if there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness are slight and whose afflictions have been deep-seated for a long time, even though they encounter a Buddha and receive offerings from him, they nevertheless give rise to the seeds of humans and devas, or the seeds of the two vehicles.

If one seeks the Mahāyāna, one’s faculties are not yet fixed; one may advance or retreat. One’s great resolve depends on others to arouse the mind, or one may be instructed by the teachings of the Two Vehicles to arouse the mind.
One’s practice through understanding and conduct is not genuine; there is attainment and realization, and there is abandoning and grasping. In sum, such a person dwells in a stage of regression.
Second is the arousal of the mind according to the One Vehicle, as in the arousal of the mind during the Ten Faiths of this sutra. At the moment of first arousing the mind, because of the initial...

Within this assembly, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, who has realized the fruit of the Tathāgata’s initial attainment of perfect enlightenment, manifests through every pore of the atoms of the dharma-realm in infinite layers.
Following the conduct and fruits of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), he gives rise to faith.

He believes that the Buddha-wisdom of his own mind is identical in essence and function to that of all Buddhas of the three periods of time—past, present, and future—without the slightest discrepancy. Only when one reaches this state can it be called the "arousing of the mind through faith" (*śraddhā-cittotpāda*).
From this point of faith, the "Chapter on the Buddha’s Name" clarifies that the names of the Buddhas who have attained perfect enlightenment throughout the ten directions are all-pervasive;
the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths" clarifies that the Dharma-gates taught by the Buddhas of the three periods of time pervade the realm of sentient beings;
and the "Chapter on the Radiance of Enlightenment" clarifies that the sphere of the Tathāgata’s wisdom-light universally illumines the entire dharma-realm, leaving nothing unilluminated.

To bring those who have not yet developed faith to their ultimate fulfillment, one should observe them through contemplation, so that their minds may become as vast and expansive as the realm of the Buddha.

In the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Clarification," the ten kinds of practices performed by a bodhisattva of the ten stages of faith are explained as the very practices one must cultivate for oneself.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on Pure Practices" details the one hundred and forty great vows, which are precisely what are generated during the stage of the ten levels of faith.

The Great Vow. This forms the gateway of great compassion and contains the "Chapter on the Virtuous Head" (*Bhadrapāla-paṭala*), which sets forth the merits of the Buddha-fruit as rejoiced in by those of the ten levels of faith;

these are inexhaustible and limitless. It clarifies that the merit of reciting and upholding this chapter upon first giving rise to the ten levels of faith surpasses that of making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields for the duration of an eon, let alone practicing according to one's understanding and conduct.

And thus they cultivate it. Just as in this sutra, at the very moment the initial mind of the ten stages is first aroused, by the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), the body pervades the ten directions and manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
The general meaning clarifies that this sutra’s arousal of the ten minds of faith does so solely by means of the inconceivable vehicle of the *dharmadhātu* and the vehicle of omniscience;
it does not rely on a Buddha, nor on the Buddha-dharma, nor on Bodhi.
Sāfa. He does not give rise to his mind by relying on the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, nor the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas, nor worldly dharmas, nor supramundane dharmas;
rather, he gives rise to the bodhicitta without any reliance. He gives rise to the bodhicitta solely through omniscience (sarvajñatā).
Unlike those of the three vehicles who give rise to the bodhicitta by relying upon material things, he does not rely on the existence [of a self] after three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
One generates the bodhicitta because the fruit of Buddhahood exists; one generates the bodhicitta because the fruit of Buddhahood does not exist [only] in the present or the three periods of time.
For this reason, those who enter this faith shall all be without regression. Even if their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet matured, they may momentarily think of regressing;
however, once they reach the stage of faith and its abiding, they do not regress from that single abiding. This is because they have attained correct faith in their own body and mind.
All is always the Buddha-dharmadhātu, for there is no nature of self or other.

Since the wisdom-bodies of the Buddhas of the ten directions are like reflections and their speech is like echoes, one who understands with such faith shall attain Buddhahood. I, who now have faith, also know it to be thus.
How could there be any regression in such faith and understanding? The entire body, the entire mind, and all objective realms are, in their totality, the single dharmadhātu.
Regarding the true Dharmakāya—its essence and function, its principle and wisdom—where does it abide? To what place does it retreat?
If the body and mind have something upon which they rely and dwell, then by relinquishing that basis, there will be loss and regression.

When one realizes for oneself that the body and mind fundamentally have no abode and fundamentally nothing to be attained, then all speech and conceptual discrimination are like echoes in the sky; they should respond without deliberate effort, functioning spontaneously in accordance with conditions.
Sound has no basis or abode from the beginning. To realize such a dharma and give rise to faith and understanding is to be without regression.
However, for those who resolve their minds based on something that can be relied upon, they will regress once they let go of what was attained and the point of attachment to that reliance.

Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* says: "Those who resolve their minds through realization mostly abide in a state of regression, because there is something to be attained that can be realized. For this reason...
Riding upon this inconceivable vehicle—the vehicle of omniscience that abides in no dependence—one generates the bodhicitta and proceeds without ever retreating.

If there should be anyone who retreats, it is solely because their faith has not been perfected; because they perceive something to be attained within the Buddha’s teachings and the vehicle of the Tathāgata;
because they engage in acceptance and rejection; and because, having not yet perfected their faith, they have not entered the stream of faith.

Chapter on the Summit of Mount Sumeru; this is the third assembly.
Within these Ten Abodes, there are six chapters of the sutra: first, "Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru"; second, "Verses of Praise on the Summit";
third, "The Ten Abodes"; fourth, "Pure Conduct"; fifth, "The Merit of Arousing the Mind"; and sixth, "Clarifying the Dharma.
These six chapters together constitute the Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes.
The Chapter on Verses of Praise at the Summit of Mount Sumeru:
This chapter is titled "Verses of Praise. It clarifies that all Buddhas of the past and present have gathered together in this Hall of Wisdom and Palace of Compassion.
Because one's own person is a Buddha of the future who accords with the path of the ancient Buddhas, it is said that [they come] from as many Buddha-lands as there are atoms of dust.
Regarding those who come from worlds outside the [present] land: "outside the land" refers to delusion, while "come" refers to the resolution of delusion.

This is because the obscurations of the darkness of delusive ignorance are as vast and numerous as the atoms of all worlds; conversely, the practices of awakening and resolution are likewise vast and numerous.
This is also compared to the dust of the world. Wisdom and ignorance are similar, differing only by the interval between delusion and enlightenment.

Therefore, these ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) constitute the initial mind of entering the true path of vision (*darśanamārga*), while the subsequent ten practices (*caryā*), ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh ground constitute the fruit of perfect enlightenment.
It is like a person who is one hundred years old; because they were born first, that [initial] birth is considered the "longer" [duration]. Thus it is with human life.
The Ten Sons: the first-born is the eldest. Regarding the "Ten Abodes" in the *Daśabhūmika* chapter:
they are so called because one dwells within the great wisdom born of all Buddhas; having entered this stage, one never again falls back. Thus it is named.

This constitutes their mode of abiding. Although there are ten kinds of antidotes, they differ from the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles which, for the sake of sentient beings of inferior understanding, maintain the existence of the nature of the three periods of time within the mundane world and state that the Buddha-fruit is attained beyond three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

[In contrast, our teaching holds that] as in the case of the Dragon Girl attaining Buddhahood in an instant, or Sudhana attaining the Buddha-fruit in a single lifetime—wherein the "single lifetime" refers to the non-nature and non-arising of the Dharma-realm—it is not a matter of temporal extension.
Because it transcends the dimensions of extension and contraction, length and shortness, and past, present, and future, it constitutes the essence of the *dharmadhātu*.

All those with faith should understand it thus: attaining Buddhahood now is the same as all Buddhas of the past and future attaining Buddhahood simultaneously, because the essence of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu* is devoid of temporal distinctions. It is like a single drop of water entering the great ocean.

In the midst [of this realization], it is identical to the great ocean, for there is no distinction between new and old water. Thus, one must set aside ordinary emotions to see it; it is not something known by the conscious mind.

It is like the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes within the Three Vehicles, who still undergo the segmented birth and death of the triple world and have only partially cultivated the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena.

This serves as the remedy for the obstacle of lack of faith in those who follow the icchantika path. Furthermore, within the Three Vehicles, Bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness prior to the ten bhūmis attain the Patience of Subjugation (kṣānti).
Those in the ten bhūmis and the Buddha-bhūmi attain the Patience of Quiescence (śānti-kṣānti).

Moreover, according to the Śrīmālā-sūtra, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas of the Pure Land are all considered to possess the Patience of Subjugation, because they do not yet recognize the afflictions of the Dwelling Place of Ignorance (avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi). Thus, they remain...

What is meant by "severing afflictions"? It refers merely to suppressing their active manifestation so that they do not arise, thereby attaining the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*) and undergoing the transformation-death (*pariṇāmikī cyuti*) beyond the three realms.
Such Bodhisattvas practice the six *pāramitās* and attain the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Their merit and supernormal powers both surpass those of humans and devas; however, because they have not yet cultivated the gateway of the Buddha-fruit *dharmadhātu*, this is [only] that gateway.

The three outer vehicles are like grass huts. Regarding the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*): those of the first, second, and third stages are called the mind-made body of the bliss of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and the Dharma;
those of the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages are called the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of phenomena;

and those of the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth stages are called the mind-made body that is spontaneously born and acts without effort. In this teaching of the One Vehicle, none of these [three vehicles] exist at all.
The destinations of the three vehicles mentioned above are based upon the afflictions of the ground of fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*).

This [ground] is, in fact, the immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) of all Buddhas, which all sentient beings inherently possess. It is only because the essence of this wisdom is without self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and without dependence that it cannot realize itself;
it realizes itself only by encountering conditions (*pratyaya*). How does it encounter conditions? There are three ways of encountering conditions. First, encountering...
First, the condition of suffering: it is only upon encountering suffering that one can resolve to attain enlightenment. Second, the condition of happiness:
having long dwelt among humans and devas, when the inner mind’s clarity and wisdom realize that worldly fruits of happiness are impermanent, one then begins to seek the Truth.

Third, seeing the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle, one is able to resolve to seek the Buddha’s seed-wisdom (*buddhajñāna*). By meeting these three conditions and drawing near to a true and virtuous spiritual friend, one is able to awaken oneself.
The clarity of this is fundamentally the Buddha-wisdom; it is the same for all three vehicles.

It is only because the inclinations and capacities of their minds differ in depth that they give rise to faith through fundamental wisdom and enter into realization by means of fundamental wisdom, never departing from it. Therefore, at the stage of the initial arousal of the bodhicitta, [it is so].

Thus, the five stages are simultaneously perfected. Although the dharma-gates of the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, ten stages, and the eleventh stage are set forth as the rules for progressive cultivation, they are like a king’s precious seal: a single impression leaves no discrepancy.

By means of the seal of the great wisdom of the one mind, one seals the beginningless three periods of time, such that all boundless dharmas are entirely encompassed within a single moment; the seal of wisdom pervades them all.
Because wisdom is equal to all Buddhas; because wisdom is equal to the minds of all sentient beings; because wisdom is equal to all phenomena (*dharma*);
because wisdom has no center or periphery, interior or exterior, nor the three periods of time, long or short, near or far; and because wisdom transcends the measure of empty space.
Just as worldly empty space has nothing that can be cognized, so too does non-conceptual wisdom, like a single moment of empty space, yet is able to perform discernment.
This dharma-gate surpasses even the measure of empty space. Therefore, a sutra says: "All empty space may still be measured, but the Dharma taught by all Buddhas cannot be measured.
Because of this, at the very first moment of generating the mind [of enlightenment], one dwells in the household of the Buddha’s *sarvajñajñāna* (all-encompassing wisdom).

At the mere moment of generating the mind, one manifests the attainment of Buddhahood throughout the ten directions. As the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī stated in verse: "In a single thought-moment, one universally observes the infinite..."
Regarding the measure of eons: there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. Thus one thoroughly understands the events of the three periods of time.

Transcending all provisional means, one accomplishes the Ten Powers. It is clearly known that the attainment of Buddhahood through the three vehicles over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is a teaching of expedient means.

This teaching, based on the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), does not speak of attaining Buddhahood through the power of vows and so forth. Even if one were to accomplish practice through the power of vows, it would still [be as follows]...
This refers to attaining Buddhahood according to ultimate reality; it does not refer to a temporary attainment through the power of vows.

Therefore, those who give rise to faith and advance in practice should not harbor views of the three periods of time as being near or far, extended or contracted, regarding the realm of great wisdom, for such views contradict the realm of wisdom.

One loses the realm of fundamental great wisdom because one pursues emotional consciousness and follows after appearances. This sequence of severing delusions across the five stages is like space, which has no temporal divisions;
it is like a perfect mirror that reflects all at once; it is like a mani jewel that can manifest in all colors;
it is like a single drop of water entering the great ocean, becoming identical and non-dual. By means of the perfect mirror of great wisdom, [one universally...]
All seals and all actions are accomplished without exception, because they possess the great function of non-action and because there is no distinction between the three periods of time.
As for the samādhi of immeasurable skillful means, it clarifies that emotional consciousness is obscured while correct wisdom is inherently luminous;
it is like the samādhis of the form and formless realms, all of which are attained by ceasing discursive thought. The samādhis of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas involve cultivating aversion.
One contemplates suffering as an antidote; one who delights in contemplating emptiness extinguishes both compassion and wisdom.
Bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings delight in contemplating emptiness while practicing the six perfections, thereby departing from the root of suffering to be born in a pure land.

Even if some remain in this realm, claiming they stay behind with delusions to transform sentient beings, none of these are in accord with the natural law (*dharmatā*). For this reason, this samādhi of skillful means is singular.

All sentient beings are deluded regarding the essence and function of the Dharma-realm; they therefore take the fundamental state of meditative concentration to purify their false attachments, which is termed "expedient means" (*upāya*).
This does not mean that there is a separate, conventionally established concentration existing apart from reality that is called expedient means.
For example, a water-clearing jewel can purify turbid water; acting as a pure condition for the pearl, it manifests the water as it originally was, pure by nature.

It is not that the jewel itself is able to produce the pure water. Expedient means (*upāya*) and samādhi are likewise so: they act as the condition for the fact that all phenomena are non-active and inherently pure from the beginning.
Because one manifests the attainment of the power of wisdom that is inherently non-active from the beginning, it is called "expedient means. Whether it be devas or humans...
The causes and effects of the non-Buddhists and the three vehicles all involve intentional action (*abhisamskāra*).

Because they are produced by such action, they all have specific locations and possess various distinctions regarding their results—such as being extensive or narrow, pure or impure. In this Dharma-gate of the Buddha’s *Avataṃsaka* One Vehicle, however, there is no abiding and no intentional action.
All that arises therein occurs spontaneously through non-reliant wisdom; it is born from the mind-illusion of non-abiding wisdom.
The body accords with the true *dharmadhātu*. Before all sentient beings, it manifests a physical form;

yet its essential nature and characteristics neither come nor go, nor does it perform acts of supernatural transformations. Nevertheless, it universally manifests all karmic fruits of the three periods of time within a single instant (*kṣaṇa*).
Yet, it does not abide in the views of the three periods of time, nor in [notions of] distance, proximity, or even the instant itself. Thus...
The practice of the wisdom of samādhi and all vows and conduct is entirely the functioning of principle and wisdom (*li-zhi*). It is not that something non-existent is made existent;
rather, it is the method of cultivating joy and aversion. Within the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*), it is said to be as numerous as the atoms of ten buddha-fields;

within the ten stages of transference of merit (*daśapariṇāmanā*), it is said to be as numerous as the atoms of a million buddha-fields. This is because, in contrast to the state of delusion, the atoms of fields of affliction are unspeakable.
Regarding "affliction" (*nirvṛti*): at the time of awakening, it is impossible to describe the Buddha-lands as numerous as atoms in a *kṣetra*, nor the Buddha’s wisdom.

In the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Brahmacarya-varga*), "Brahma" means purity. Because one benefits sentient beings through this pure conduct, one constantly dwells in the world and practices all deeds.
To transform and benefit sentient beings, there is no practice that can be apprehended; thus, there is no practice that is impure. Therefore, it is called the "Brahma-conduct" (*brahmacarya*).
Abiding in the Buddha’s gate of non-abiding, one returns to practicing the practice of non-practice, the dwelling of non-dwelling—this is called the "Buddha-dwelling.
The practice of non-practice benefits those who are not sentient beings—this is called "pure conduct. Now, as for the Buddha...
Wisdom is not profound; it is simply that when the deluded mind pursues appearances, the emotions diminish and wisdom is hidden. When the [mind and phenomena] are of one essence, wisdom manifests.
By knowing all dharmas through non-thought and non-deliberation, and by accomplishing great merit through non-creation and non-action, the Tathāgata established the teachings of pure practice.
Thus, the observation of dharmas reaches its consummation: the True Dharma shall flourish and all [erroneous] views shall perish. This is the Buddha-wisdom.

Just as he was about to rise, he beheld the deceased Zhisheng, who had attained awakening without depending on others. Therefore, those of later generations should practice in accordance with the Dharma;
they must not pursue sensory objects until they sink into ruin and wander lost in the stream of transmigration for eternal kalpas.

However, the scriptures mentioned above, whether read more or less, naturally hit the mark. Thus, when all conditioned phenomena are pure, wisdom is pure; when wisdom is pure, the mind is pure. Its...
When the mind is pure, all phenomena are pure. The purity of all phenomena is called the purity of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). The purity of the dharma-realm is the purity of sentient beings.
The purity of sentient beings is the purity of the Buddha-land. To practice this equality of dharmas is what is called "pure conduct."
Chapter on the Merit of First Resolving the Mind:
Now, as for those who have first resolved their minds upon awakening, their merit is difficult to measure; it is equal to empty space, and there is nothing with which to compare its kind.
Even if one were to grind away as many atoms as there are in all lands, there would be nothing with which to repay even a fraction of it. Empty space merely illustrates the greatness of formlessness;
all the atoms of the lands merely illustrate the vastness of physical obstruction. How could these possibly match the sphere of the merit, wisdom, and境 (*viṣaya*) of the bodhicitta?
As for that wisdom, in a single kṣaṇa, it fills the ten directions, manifesting bodies like clouds, appearing like Indra’s net, with wondrous forms.
They interpenetrate one another; light and shadow layered upon layer, each with a single voice, pervading the entire Dharma-realm to proclaim teaching-gates equal in number to all sentient beings.
Like rain falling upon sentient beings, their minds attain the joy of cool clarity—such is the nature of that merit. Their wondrous marks are magnificently adorned.

It shares the same essence as the *Avataṃsaka*. At the moment of first generating the bodhicitta, one dwells for an ocean of inexhaustible eons equal to those of the Buddhas of the ten directions, enters into the stream of the great wisdom of all Buddhas, and becomes equal to the merits of all Buddhas and all sentient beings.
One must, in all cases, awaken to this Dharma before one can attain Buddhahood; one must not grasp at the words of the Tathāgata’s skillful means that accord with the world within the Three Vehicles.
[From] the "Chapter on Clarifying the Dharma."
This clarifies the dharmas previously attained so that they become even more luminous; it clarifies the subsequent advancement so that it becomes manifest.

This is the stage of "Tending Toward" (*pratipannaka*) within the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), which nurtures the dharmas of the fundamental stage of the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*). Regarding the Bodhisattva "Vigorous Wisdom" (*Vīryaprajñā*): "Wisdom" (*prajñā*) has the meaning of illuminating and shining;
"Vigor" (*vīrya*) has the meaning of non-conceptualization (*acintya*). By means of this wisdom of non-conceptualization, one illuminates the function of conditioned activity.
There is that which is originally without effort; the myriad dharmas are originally pure. That the myriad dharmas are inherently pure is called "purity" (*śubha*).

The response of wisdom to this state of no-effort, whereby one knows the faculties and benefits sentient beings, is called "diligence" (*vīrya*). As for those who enter deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and attain the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of a Buddha as described in the sutras, it is because their minds accord with principle (*tattva*).
By following principle, they are naturally true; neither arising nor being suppressed, principle is true and wisdom responds accordingly. Following [this]...
To transform the multitudes through wisdom in accordance with their needs—without coming or going, and without transformation—is called the Buddha’s supernormal power (*abhijñā*).

This wisdom has no point of reliance; it has no form, color, or substance; it has no nature of coming or departing. Its nature is inherently all-pervasive and is not subsumed within the three periods of time, yet it is able to universally respond to the phenomena of the three periods of time;
this is called supernormal power. Therefore, a sutra says: "Wisdom enters the three periods of time, yet..."
Coming and going—these three periods of time are falsely established by the sentiments of sentient beings, for they do not truly exist.

Because the essence of wisdom is formless and lacks physical shape, yet responds to all classes of beings without deliberate effort, it is called "spiritual" (*shen*). It is perfectly complete throughout the ten directions;
there is no phenomenon it does not know and no root of perception it does not recognize; thus it is called "penetration" (*tong*).
The Fourth Assembly: The Chapter on Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven.
Why is it called the Palace of the Yāma Heaven? It is explained that the name of the place indicates the Dharma. This heaven is named the Time-Portion Heaven (*Kāmadhātu-deva*).

Because this heaven has neither sun nor moon, nor the alternation of darkness and light, the opening of the lotus flowers constitutes the day, and their closing constitutes the night; therefore, it is called the Time-Portion Heaven.

The "Heaven" (deva) represents the Dharma-gate of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*). Because one must not fail to know the proper time when responding to and transforming sentient beings according to their capacities, one knows whether they possess the seeds of humans or devas, or the seeds of the two vehicles, three vehicles, or the single vehicle (*ekayāna*). One thus knows by which roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) they may be guided and led.
Therefore, the "Heaven of Time" (*kāla-deva*) symbolizes that the practices one performs must be undertaken with knowledge of the proper timing.

In the "Chapter on Verses of Praise" within the *Yāma-deva-palace* section of the *Ten Abodes*, the Dharma-body is taken as the essence of the precepts. Within these Ten Practices, wisdom is taken as the essence of the precepts.
Regarding the act of gazing upward at the void and causing all necessary objects to descend from space for the benefit of sentient beings: this is "Clear Wisdom."
It is like space. Space is the root of wisdom, for wisdom is not distinct from space. Therefore, space is the root of all phenomena.
Viewed in this light, all merits arise collectively from the wisdom of emptiness.

In the "Chapter on the Ten Practices," these devas illuminate one another with their own radiance; there are no sun or moon. They distinguish day and night merely by observing the opening and closing of lotus flowers.

They are called the *Kāmadivaukas* (Time-Division Devas). A Bodhisattva in this stage likewise knows when the time has come to develop the inclinations and minds of sentient beings, and should [act accordingly].
At this time, for those who have been guided but are not yet ready for liberation, he provides the causal conditions for their attainment of liberation;
therefore, ten types of practice-gates are explained in this section. The first two chapters have already clarified this, and here it is praised.

By citing Buddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten thousand Buddha-lands, all named Guṇakūṭa (Virtue Forest), it is made clear that if one is deluded regarding the mind and its objects, ignorance pervades infinite lands.
The dust is no different [from the mind]. If one thoroughly realizes the source of the mind, then wisdom and merit will be equal to the ten directions and inexhaustible.

In this "Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries," the ten types of practice have already been explained; by means of these ten inexhaustible treasuries, one accomplishes the subsequent ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
This causes them to advance forward, ensuring that their practice of the gates of action does not stagnate.
This fifth assembly, the "Chapter on Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace," is the gate of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

At the time of first generating the mind of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), one advances in cultivation through true wisdom; yet, within this compassion, there are degrees of superiority and inferiority.
They are different. In the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) and ten practices (*daśacaryā*), wisdom is cultivated concurrently, yet the mind directed toward transcendence (*lokottara-citta*) predominates.

In this stage, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) brings the mind of transcendence to its conclusion; it transforms the compassionate aspect of the wisdom of the ten births-and-deaths into [worldly] compassion. Within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one nurtures great compassion, making it even more profound and deep.
Question: Why is the dharma of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) taught in this celestial realm? Answer: It is like the summit of Mount Sumeru.
The preceding exposition of the Ten Abodes clarifies being born into the Buddha-family, taking the pinnacle of the Buddha’s wisdom as one's own burden without ever regressing or wavering.
The Ten Practices were taught in the Yāma Heaven to signify that practice accords with the emptiness of phenomena, remaining entirely unattached.

Now, arriving at this Tuṣita Palace, it signifies that although one does not depart from the Desire Realm, while abiding in the gateway of great compassion, one always practices contentment regarding the objects of desire. There is no...
Though there is that which is stained and attached, one dwells in the world solely for the benefit of sentient beings; therefore, this is called "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*).
This is an advancement expressed by means of a location; yet, it is not that the body itself undergoes coming, going, ascending, or descending, but merely clarifies the reliance upon a location.

It represents a Bodhisattva in their final birth who, dwelling within this heaven, has fulfilled the fruits of their practice. Thus, it clarifies the very beginning of the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), just as one is first born.
One comes to the house of wisdom. By practicing the gate of great compassion through the wisdom of the Buddha, one attains the fruition of the Tathāgata;
thus, the fruition is ever-full and the practice is ever-active. Because this fruition and practice are mutually adorned, it is called the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*. As the Sūtra says:

"He who well knows the proper time preaches the Dharma for the sake of the assembly," meaning he understands whether the faculties [of beings] are mature or immature and delivers them according to what is appropriate. Question:
What is meant by the Buddhas knowing the minds of sentient beings at the proper time and the improper time? The answer is:

because the mind of the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, is fundamentally not different from the minds of all sentient beings, the Buddhas have awakened to this and realized that it is shared with sentient beings.
Sentient beings, however, are deluded and claim for themselves that there is a separation. All Buddhas, therefore, accomplish [their work] through the wisdom of the minds of all sentient beings.
Perfectly Awakened One. All sentient beings are deluded regarding the wisdom of all Buddhas and thus become sentient beings.

When they eventually attain Buddhahood, they still remain Buddhas who are deluded regarding the principle—that is, Buddhas who are themselves sentient beings. The Dharma-gates they preach further resolve the delusions within the minds of sentient beings regarding Buddhas and sentient beings.
Because there is no difference between them, one knows that the mind of a sentient being possesses such great compassion and such wisdom.

These are the myriad practices. They are undertaken solely to cause the wisdom and great compassion born at the inception of the Buddha-family to grow, so that one may become habituated to their accumulation and attain mastery.
In this process, time does not change, phenomena do not differ, and wisdom does not shift. It is like bamboo or reeds, which grow according to their natural course;

from the initial sprout to the final state, there is no difference in essence between the coarse and the fine. It is also like a child who grows from infancy to adulthood; there is [no change in substance].

This is distinct from the [ordinary] Great Elements. It is simply because the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), and the eleventh stage are the skillful means for cultivating the Path that the fruit of Buddhahood resides in the initial arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*).

Within the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), the ten practices, the ten dedications, and the ten stages—taken collectively within the ten abodes—it is fully and completely present. It is like a divine dragon or a king of horses giving birth to a divine colt; it is born therein.

The stage [of the Bodhisattva] resembles that of the father in terms of speed and slowness; however, its power and function have not yet reached those of the parents. It is like a Bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment:

by mounting the vehicle of the Tathāgata’s omniscience, they are born into the Buddha-family and possess wisdom equal to that of a Buddha, yet their supernatural powers and spiritual strength have not yet reached theirs.

This is because they must await the nourishment provided by the myriad practices of great compassion. Although the merit of this nourishment is ultimately complete, the Dharma... [is not yet fully realized].
There is difference, yet time does not shift. One never departs from the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

When the power and effort are completed, it is like the Dragon Girl who did not pass beyond a single *kṣaṇa* to attain Buddhahood in one lifetime; this is like Sudhana attaining the fruit of Buddhahood in one lifetime.

"One lifetime" means non-arising (*anutpāda*). Regarding non-arising, there are eleven aspects: first, the self-nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) is non-arising; second, all views are non-arising... [and so forth].
1. Non-arising of essence; 2. non-arising of the two emptinesses; 3. non-arising of the four natures; 4. non-arising of the non-transmigration of time and kalpas;
5. non-arising of nirvāṇa and saṃsāra; 6. non-arising of the silence of the sound of preaching the Dharma; 7. non-arising of the discrimination of wisdom; 8.
non-arising of the nature of supernatural powers and spiritual strength that is inherently all-pervasive; 9. non-arising of manifesting in response within the limit of a single kṣaṇa.
Throughout the three periods of time, across all kalpas from antiquity to the present, the prior births of all sentient beings are non-arising.

Because there are these ten kinds of non-arising, it is called "attaining Bodhi in a single birth. This sutra employs the dharmas of the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten stages, and the eleventh stage as skillful means to support the fruit of Buddhahood from the very first aspiration.
Thus, the provisions and the fruit of Buddhahood are simultaneous and mutually interpenetrating.
Because essence and function mutually support one another, it is termed "the Adornment of Enlightenment and Practice. By means of the fruit supporting practice, practice becomes free from attachment;
by means of practice supporting the fruit, great compassion and great function are accomplished.

This is as the Bodhisattvas of the *manomayakāya* in the Three Vehicles maintain that the Buddha-fruit lies after the eleventh stage (*bhūmi*), at the conclusion of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, taking the three stages of worthiness prior to the stages (*pūrvabhūmi*) as the provisions (*sambhāra*) and the ten stages as...
The path of seeing and the fruit of Buddhahood occur after eleven stages and three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Such a teaching differs from the characteristics of the five stages within the Three Vehicles by being ten times more inverted in its characteristics.

The Chapter on Verses of Praise in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace concludes the section above, wherein each has explained a single dharma, collectively forming the ten minds of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*). Alternatively, it may simply be said that sentient beings are attached to existence.
Alternatively, one might speak only of non-existence, yet sentient beings become attached to this non-existence. As the verse of the Bodhisattva Star-Host Banner (*Tārakadhvaja*) in the sutra says:

"Sentient beings engage in false conceptualization, [thinking] 'this is the Buddha' or 'this is the world. Those who thoroughly understand the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) perceive neither Buddha nor world.

And as the verse of the Bodhisattva Dharma-Banner (*Dharmadhvaja*) in the following section says: "One would rather constantly endure all the sufferings of the world than ever depart from the Tathāgata."
Come! You do not yet behold the power of mastery.
Why is this chapter titled "The Ten Dedications" (*Daśapariṇāmanā*)? The answer is: because at the beginning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the wisdom of all Buddhas is first produced.

In the stage of the Family (gotrabhūmi), although one possesses the seventh skillful means, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), which accomplishes the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), because this is the initial stage, the mind directed toward world-transcendence (*lokottara-citta*) is predominant.

Within the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśa-pratipatti*), one observes the faculties of sentient beings with the eye of wisdom (*jñāna-cakṣus*), the eye of insight (*prajñā-cakṣus*), and the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) to benefit them and transform them so that they may leave the mundane world.

In these ten stages of Dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), it is clarified that in the preceding two stages, the mind directed toward world-transcendence is predominant, while the practice of great compassion is [less so].

Inferior. This is because the wisdom of all Buddhas attained at the initial stage of the Ten Abodes, as well as the supramundane practices within the Ten Practices—practices that dwell in the secular world to benefit sentient beings and turn back from the ultimate truth to enter the mundane—are called "Dedication" (pariṇāmanā).

This is because these ten stages of Dedication encompass everything from the preceding to the succeeding, universally collecting and integrating them. Furthermore, they represent the Tuṣita Heaven Palace among all the three realms.
This deva realm is preeminent. Why is this? Because all Buddhas of the three periods of time in the world have all brought their bodhicitta to full maturity here in this heaven.
Above it lie the Nirmāṇarati and Paranirmitavaśavartin heavens, where beings are prone to indulgence in pleasure.
Above those are the heavens of the Form and Formless Realms, where beings mostly delight in tranquility. Below these, the Yāma and Trāyastriṃśa heavens are abodes attached to sensual pleasures.
It is not because they are content with little. Furthermore, this heaven is a place where those who have cultivated the three types of merit are born together.
What are these three? First, the cultivation of giving; second, the observance of precepts; and third, the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Other devas do not cultivate all three merits, but only the two merits of precepts and giving. Therefore, those other devas are either largely negligent or largely inclined toward tranquility; for this reason, they are reborn above.
The Sūtra says: "Those who desire to long for the bodhicitta will be reborn in this heaven. For this reason, this heaven expounds these ten gates of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
There are ten dharmas of dedication: first, dedicating non-active dharmas (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) toward active dharmas;
second, dedicating active dharmas toward non-active dharmas; third, dedicating a single dharma toward many dharmas; fourth, dedicating many dharmas..."
1. Dedication to a single dharma. 2. Dedication of all existent dharmas to non-existent dharmas. 3. Dedication of non-existent dharmas to existent dharmas.
4. Dedication of worldly dharmas to supramundane dharmas. 5. Dedication of supramundane dharmas to worldly dharmas. 6.
Using the dedication to the non-existence of all intrinsic natures as a skillful means for the dedication to the existence of dharmas.
Tenth, by means of the dharma of dedication that encompasses all existence, one takes the dharma of non-dedication as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

This is for the sake of enabling those who are stalled in existence or non-existence to attain mastery. Having attained great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), because there is no dharma that can obstruct them, they make offerings to all Buddhas and transform sentient beings.
Because they attain mastery over both unity and multiplicity, as well as identity and difference, how could their dharma not be equal to the infinite realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)?
Dedication. Just as the dharma-realm has no center or periphery, the mind of dedication has no center or periphery.

Just as the dharma-realm has no agent, the mind of dedication has no agent. As the dharma-realm has no coming or going, nor distance or proximity, the mind of dedication has no coming or going, nor distance or proximity.
As the dharma-realm is like space, the wisdom of dedication is like space. As the dharma-realm is inconceivable, so is dedication.
Wisdom is inconceivable. The dharma-realm has no basis; the wisdom of dedication has no basis.
The dharma-realm is that wherein all Buddhas dwell together, just as the basis-less wisdom is that wherein all Buddhas dwell together.

The dharma-realm is not encompassed by the three periods of time or by any temporal divisions of arising and ceasing; likewise, the wisdom of dedication is not encompassed by the temporal divisions of the three periods.

The wisdom of dedication that encompasses the dharma-realm and brings the activities of the three periods of time to manifestation; the wisdom of dedication that brings the activities of the three periods of time to perfect completion and manifestation;
the mastery over existence and non-existence within the dharma-realm; and the mastery over existence and non-existence through the wisdom of dedication.
It is for the sake of causing oneself and others to all become like the *dharmadhātu*—unimpeded, sovereign, and identical to all Buddhas.

For this reason, it is called the "Infinite Dedication Equal to the *Dharmadhātu*. Its general meaning is to cause all who have resolved upon *bodhicitta* to become, in every respect, like the *dharmadhātu*:
with all virtues and functions spontaneously present, sovereign, perfectly fulfilled, vast, infinite, free from the natures of "great" or "small," and not belonging to the categories of one or two.

Because three hundred million and other such numbers are finite, whereas worldly and supramundane great wisdom, great compassion, joy, and equanimity are equal to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of sentient beings.
If one does not perform dedication in this manner, even if one seeks bodhi, one will only attain the quiescent bodhi of the two vehicles.
Bodhisattvas who delight in being born in pure lands all remain outside the gate with the three carts, like those in the open space under the white [canopy].
If one does not accord with their proper portion, there will be obstructions for oneself and others; compassion and reverence will not be genuine; knowledge and vision will not be extensive;
the heart of compassion will not be universal; the mind will not be vast; and it will not correspond to the infinite dharma-realm. If one does not do so, the dedication will not be infinite.
To make a vow for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the infinite dharma-realm while remaining personally within the gate of truth and being reborn exclusively in a pure land—

because this does not accord with the unimpeded, equalizing, and infinite great compassion of the dharma-realm where defilement and purity are identical in essence— one will fail to achieve the fruit of Buddhahood.
These ten dedications encompass the practice gates of the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten stages, and the eleventh stage;
they are all contained therein.
This sixth assembly, the "Ten Stages" chapter, was preached in the palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
Why is this chapter titled "The Ten Grounds" (Daśabhūmi)? It is said that it clarifies how the Tathāgata, by means of the Wisdom of Universal Radiance, establishes the essence of the grounds.
Although the various Bodhisattvas have ascended through the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications, they do not depart from this essence; therefore, it is called the "Ten Grounds.
These dharmas of the ten grounds are identical to the ten fruits of Buddhahood that are the objects of faith for those in the ten stages of faith. Thus, by means of universal radiance...
Regarding the ten fruits of Buddhahood explained in the Hall of Illumination (*Myōdō*), the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom (*Fudōchi-Butsu*) is designated as the first stage of faith (*shin*).
