Within the process of progressive cultivation, although one passes through the ten abodes (*jūjū*), the ten practices (*jūgyō*), and the ten stages of dedication (*jūkō*), one nevertheless takes the ten fruits of wisdom from within the ten stages of faith to constitute the essence of the ten grounds (*jijichi*).
These ten Buddhas of Wisdom take the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom as their fundamental source; thus, the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom is the root.
Universal Radiance Wisdom takes as its foundation the Wisdom of Non-Abiding;
furthermore, the Wisdom of Non-Abiding takes all sentient beings as its foundation.
This is the meaning of how, when Sudhana saw Maitreya Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva in turn led Sudhana back to see his first spiritual friend, Mañjuśrī.
Up until the fulfillment of the five stages, one does not depart from the Buddha-fruit of the initial faith.
Because this Dharma of the ten stages penetrates from beginning to end as a single-limit gateway (*ekānta-dvāra*), it is titled the "Chapter on the Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmi-varga*). To speak briefly:

if the essence of the ten stages lacked the ten faiths capable of believing that one's own mind is the initial Buddha-fruit, the ten stages themselves would not be established. Thus, [the ten faiths are essential].
In the initial mind of faith, there is no Buddha-fruit of the tenth or eleventh stage (*bhūmi*), nor is there any [separate] attainment of the mind of faith.
This is because from beginning to end, it is entirely the fruit of immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*).

For one who can believe in their own mind is already the Buddha-fruit, that which is believed—the Buddha-fruit—is itself the Buddha-fruit, and the body of the practitioner is likewise the fruit-Buddha. Only such a mind of faith is truly...
Because one attains faith, faith is also the Buddha; awakening is also the Buddha. This is because one practices with the body and function of the Buddha’s wisdom as being non-different from it.
When forming this faith, one universally perceives that all the mental measures (*cittamātra*) of all sentient beings arise from the Great Wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Ordinary beings and sages are of one essence, sharing the same wisdom, without two distinct natures—just as stated in this sutra.
The "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" states: "The various pleasures of sentient beings, as well as all wisdoms of skillful means, all arise based upon the Buddha-wisdom.
It further states: "One should believe that within one's own mind, Buddhas constantly appear in the world to turn the wheel of the true Dharma."
Having attained such faith, one enters through the samādhi of skillful means, manifesting primordial wisdom that accords with that of the Buddha;

this is called being born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and becoming a true son of the Buddha. From this first stage (*bhūmi*), one dwells where the Buddhas dwell and plants the seed of the Tathāgata-nature, which is termed "pure wisdom.
Following this wisdom, one passes through the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten...
Dedication. Within each stage, ten types of practitioners are assigned to ten world-realms.

Within each stage, by means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom-born body (*jñāna-nirmāṇa-kāya*), which is equal to the realm of sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, he manifests before all sentient beings in their respective bodies.
This is not merely a matter of the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) traveling wherever it pleases; rather, it is [manifested] solely through fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
They accomplish the ocean of all-knowledge. Throughout all worlds and in all places, they manifest forms, appearing in accordance with the various types of beings.
They do not undergo the transformation-death (pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa) apart from the three realms; rather, they employ wisdom to skillfully master the nature of mind and objects.

Their wisdom is unimpeded in nature and equal to the nature of the Dharma-realm. It is devoid of coming or going and devoid of volitional construction. They do not perceive the past as being ordinary.
Now, the future is subject to transformation, and the present is subject to segmentation. Those who possess such a mind are all deluded, for it is not right view.

If, within the severing of afflictions, one employs the five hindrances, the ten entanglements, and the ten proclivities as the function of wisdom, one will not separately undergo the birth and death of transformation outside the three realms; rather, within every pore and atom, there are oceans of lands.
Ordinary beings and sages dwell together like shadows; how could there be a distinction between the interior and exterior of the three realms?
Since even the "unchanging" is fundamentally non-existent, how could there be a separate delight in transformation?
It takes all worldly realms—humans, devas, māras, and brahmās—as a single buddha-field to perform the buddha-work; there is no other pure land elsewhere. [The Five Hindrances]

The five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are: first, sensual desire; second, ill will; third, sloth and torpor; fourth, restlessness and remorse; fifth, doubt. The ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are: first, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*);
second, lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*); third, sleep; fourth, remorse; fifth, stinginess; sixth, envy; seventh, restlessness; eighth, lethargy; ninth, anger; [tenth, concealment].

The ten obscurations. Possessing penetrating wisdom and compassion—these constitute the ocean of wisdom. For the sake of the Buddhas’ knowledge and vision of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity;

for the sake of vast faith and understanding and vast rebirth; and by means of the methods for repentance and purification as taught in the *Ghoṣadatta-parivarta* (The Chapter on the Merit of the Light of the Minor Marks) within the *Devendra-garjita-sūtra*, one repents with as many virtuous actions of body, speech, mind, and tongue as there are sentient beings throughout the entirety of the Dharma-realm.
It eliminates all karmic obstructions. The devas asked, "How does one repent and eliminate them?
The celestial drum replied, "Observe that karma does not come from the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, or from above or below; yet it accumulates within the body and mind.
Even when sought throughout the ten directions, it is entirely unfindable. While the celestial drum was thus preaching the Dharma for the assembly of devas, hundreds of thousands of millions...

Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms within a hundred billion nayutas of Buddha-fields, as well as the sons of the Tuṣita devas, attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and reach the tenth stage (bhūmi).
This stage is attained as the fruit of the tenth bhūmi after three births.

However, those who have faith and understanding regarding the non-creation of evil karma become Buddhas in a single lifetime, such as Sudhana. As for the expression "one lifetime," it refers to the nature of non-arising seen upon the Path of Vision (darśana-mārga).

One always enters the Dharma-realm because there is no time of birth. Just as in the teachings of the Three Vehicles, where [the path] is carved and trimmed of its crookedness, yet the principle remains obstructed and difficult to realize—yet one can still believe in and practice them—this Single Vehicle Dharma is upright in both principle and wisdom. It neither carves nor trims;

by penetrating one's own fundamental ignorance, one immediately becomes the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom (*acala-jñāna*). All things are naturally rectified, and through this wisdom, one benefits others.

Because birth itself is the Buddha. Furthermore, by integrating the vast and limitless compassionate vows of the Ten Dedications, one causes the function of wisdom to be effortless and practice to be complete without dependence;
this is because the conduct of Samantabhadra is fully realized. Worldly people are greatly deluded:

they do not believe that what is easily accomplished can have such vast merit, yet they instead spend many kalpas practicing in a crooked manner, finding it difficult to achieve even inferior merit through their carving away [of faults].

Preserve their dispositions; after many lifetimes, they must ultimately return to this. As stated in this sutra, by giving rise to even a small measure of faith and joy, one obtains boundless and vast benefit.
Regarding the "three lifetimes": the first is the lifetime of practicing the path of seeing (darśana-mārga) in the distant past.

Second, there is birth through the perfection of attaining the fruit in the present; third, there is birth through manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment and appearing in the world in the future.
These are all within the pavilion, manifesting right now. Because they cannot be apprehended as having past, future, or present—neither ancient nor modern—they are beyond such temporal distinctions.

Nevertheless, the characteristics of the three lives are not discarded; they exist therein, but are known only through wisdom. This is because, for the sake of conforming to worldly conventions and benefiting sentient beings, there are these three lives.

If discussed from the perspective of ultimate truth (*tattva*), there is no time when the bodhicitta is generated, no time of practicing or realizing the Path, no time of attaining the fruit in the present life, and no time of manifesting perfect enlightenment in the future. This is because the three periods of time and...

The Mind-Only (cittamātra) is called the time of attaining Buddhahood because it is devoid of intrinsic nature, because there is no establishment [of phenomena], and because there is no location or basis for abiding.
If one perceives within one's own mind that there is a capacity to give rise to the bodhicitta, this is merely the arising and ceasing of emotional consciousness;
it is not called the time of giving rise to the mind. For this reason, the faith-mind and the fruit of Buddhahood—
They never depart from the Universal Radiance Hall; indeed, they constantly practice the conduct of Samantabhadra, which has no beginning and no end.

In the "Chapter on Leaving the World," they likewise never depart from the Universal Radiance Hall, because cause and effect share the same fundamental source. At that time, phenomena have no substance and wisdom has no basis.
Maitreya causes Sudhana to see his first friend, Mañjuśrī, once again, thereby clarifying that upon reaching the ultimate fruit, one does not shift from the original state.
The Cause. When Sudhana thought of seeing Mañjuśrī, he immediately heard the name of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and saw his own body enter the body of Samantabhadra.
This clarifies that the cause of perfect enlightenment does not depart from the fruit of practice.

That the three assemblies are all together in the Hall of Universal Radiance (Samantaraśmyabhāsadhvaja) clarifies that the cause and fruit of practice, as well as the fulfillment of the conduct of Samantabhadra, are all one and the same beginningless Universal Radiance.

Because they ultimately abide nowhere and possess sovereign great wisdom, if sentient beings who have resolved upon bodhicitta do not perceive this wisdom, it cannot be called the "arousing of the mind.
If one perceives a Buddha outside of the mind or grasps at signs while seeking the Truth, such a person merely performs good deeds for the time being.

Because one has not yet clearly awakened the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñā-citta*). As the Sūtra says: "Riding upon the vehicle of omniscience, one proceeds directly to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Since one rides upon the vehicle of the great wisdom of universal radiance (*samantaprabhā-mahājñāna-yāna*), one does not depart from the site of enlightenment of the great wisdom of universal radiance;

this is what is meant by "arriving. Therefore, among the various stages of generating the mind, the initial generation of the mind is difficult. This clarifies that this wisdom is difficult to believe in; yet once one attains faith, one is able to enter it.

Indeed, it is easy to give rise to the mind through realization, but difficult to give rise to the mind through first awakening faith, for when faith reaches its ultimate limit, one enters the stages [of the bodhisattva path].

For example, by practicing the ten wholesome deeds with outflows (*sāsrava*) for a single lifetime, one may still be reborn in the heavens and attain supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) as a karmic retribution; yet, the fulfillment of even ten recitations [of the Buddha's name] achieves this same result.

One can still attain rebirth in the Pure Land; how much more so for one who resolves their mind based on wisdom? After a single lifetime, would they not attain the body of wisdom and the sovereign supernormal powers?

This is like the sixteen contemplations of the Western Pure Land, all of which involve mental visualization. Once these visualizations are perfected, one attains supernormal powers through the transformation of one's own karmic retribution.
How much more so for one who penetrates the principle of wisdom, which is non-reliant, luminously pure, and universally illuminating, thereby fully comprehending both body and mind?

There is no substance. Is it not the case that internal and external views have perished? By means of the dharma of non-abiding, one follows non-abiding wisdom to make offerings to the Buddhas and benefit sentient beings.
Practicing in this manner, why worry about not attaining great power and supernormal faculties? The Master of the Treatise says in verse: Universal radiant wisdom is equal to space;
Space is merely empty, while wisdom is sovereign. From the first aspiration, one relies upon this [wisdom] to arise; In the end, one returns [to it].
Based on this fulfillment of the locus, the three assemblies in the Hall of Universal Radiance all take the fundamental wisdom of the universally radiant dharma-realm as their essence and function.
There are five types of bodhi: first, the bodhi of the Hīnayāna; second, the bodhi of the two vehicles;

third, the bodhi of the Bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās through the contemplation of emptiness; fourth, the cultivation of the ten kinds of contemplation of semblance-tathatā; [and fifth, the cultivation of true tathatā].
Regarding the ten pāramitās, there are ten obstacles to true suchness (*tathatā*) and eleven kinds of heavy impediments (*dausthulya*).
There are twenty-two kinds of ignorance regarding bodhi. Based on the ten kinds of Tathāgata wisdom, one cultivates the ten pāramitās.

Taking inexhaustible eons as a single momentary limit (*kṣaṇa-koṭi*), one accords with inexhaustible many lifetimes as a single lifetime. In a single thought-moment, delusion and awakening are the very wisdom and bodhi of the Buddha.
Tí. As stated in the *Awakening of Faith*, it is said that one may attain Buddhahood by transcending kalpas.
When it says, "I have cultivated the path to Buddhahood for immeasurable kalpas," this is all for the sake of providing countless skillful means for indolent sentient beings.

Alternatively, when it says that one must pass through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before attaining Buddhahood, these are all explanations following worldly sentiments; they are for the sake of the Three Vehicles and do not rely upon the fundamental [truth].
The awakening of wisdom. If one discusses this from the perspective of wisdom, one does not follow deluded sentiments; rather, one takes incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as being "no time.
Using this "no time" as a provisional designation, a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) encompasses the infinite three periods of time.
The infinite kalpas of the three periods of time do not, in total, transcend a single moment. As the Sūtra says: "Wisdom enters the three periods of time..."
There is no coming or going. Thus, throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, although there is emotion (*qing*), wisdom (*zhi*) is without it; wisdom subsumes emotion, and emotion dwells within wisdom.

The emotions of immeasurable eons exist within the wisdom of a single momentary limit (*kṣaṇa*). If one takes emotion to be empty and wisdom to be real, then from the beginning they are both entirely devoid of temporal substance.
From start to finish, there is no time that can shift. When comparing these two matters, one may only follow the real and not the empty.

Furthermore, the Sūtra states: "All those who have gathered from other worlds" refers to the fact that by proceeding from the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) to achieve the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), they are designated as being from "other worlds.
Within the nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), there are no distinct other worlds; they are called "other worlds" only because they have not yet reached their ultimate destination.
As for the Eightfold Noble Path: right view, right thought, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
These are right speech, right action, and right livelihood. The commentary explains: entering the Buddha’s wisdom is called right view;
observing phenomena with that wisdom is called right thought; practicing and advancing according to the five stages of the Dharma is called right effort;

being constantly united with wisdom and not associated with worldly passions is called right mindfulness; and the mind, though devoid of arising and ceasing, being able to give rise to all Buddhas [is right concentration].

Wisdom and the arousal of immeasurable great supernormal powers are called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Skillfully discerning between humans, non-Buddhists, the three vehicles, and the one vehicle;
between wrong views and right views; and between wrong concentration, right concentration, wrong practice, and right practice is called right speech (*samyag-vāc*).
It skillfully distinguishes all wrong actions of oneself and others, and skillfully manifests the Buddha’s wisdom as equal toward all sentient beings.
To share equally with all is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).

To cause all sentient beings—including humans, devas, non-Buddhists, and those in the world of birth and death—as well as the liberation dharma-gates of the three vehicles of the supramundane, to all dedicate themselves toward the Tathāgata’s fundamental mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), which is inherently free from emotional agitation, is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*). This is like the thirty kinds of vast aspirations and practices of the Dharma.
Although extensive, this is the single seal of a Buddha’s wisdom (*buddhajñānamudrā*), for it is neither prior nor posterior;

therefore, these ten stages (*bhūmi*) are in fact the fulfillment of the preceding ten abodes (*vihāra*), ten practices (*caryā*), and ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*). It is not that there are separate dharmas that come into being within these ten stages.

It is like a radish: from the root the leaves grow, and the leaves in turn nourish the root. It is also like sowing grain: from the fruit the sprout grows, and from the mature sprout the fruit arises.
It is accomplished; this is returning to the first fruit (*srotāpatti*). It is like when Sudhana saw the Tathāgata Maitreya, yet the Tathāgata Maitreya caused him to see Mañjuśrī once again;
this clarifies that the fruit does not depart from the fruit within the cause. Furthermore, it is like a person who is born and grows until they reach thirty years of age:
it is simply because one considers the growth from birth as "great" that there is no separate "greatness" that arrives. Thus, from birth to old age, it is the same.
At that time, there is no priority or sequence. Taking wisdom as the precursor, it is not encompassed by the realm of insentient things; thus, there is no distinction of priority or sequence.

Although one may establish differences such as ascent and descent, these merely clarify the stages within the single Dharma-realm wisdom; they are not like the stages perceived through the views of ordinary beings.
Those of the three vehicles do not realize the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*—to bring provisional teachings into accord with the ultimate reality—and instead speak in opposition to it.
Transformation. One must pass through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before attaining Buddhahood. This is the view from the outer gate of the Great Wisdom Mansion of the Dharma-realm;

it is like still dwelling in a grass hut, yet enjoying the pleasure of being temporarily free from the coarse sufferings of the triple world and attaining the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*).

Dwelling outside the gate of the burning house, he provisionally sets forth three vehicles; thus, there are vehicles upon which one may rely, as there is a distinction between the Pure Land and the defiled land.
One must therefore reform the net-like views of the Three Vehicles, so that those with impaired vision may attain wholeness.

Only by extinguishing and retaining the delusions of existence, as well as the outflowing bodies of the Pure and Defiled Lands, can one truly be said to possess the vastness of the Wisdom Body (*jñānakāya*). —The Treatise Master.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse: "Boundless wisdom and compassion constitute the Buddha's virtues; The Buddha, through wisdom and compassion, perfects the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

In turn, by means of these ten stages, all positions are perfected; The preparatory gates (*prayoga*) of the five preceding stages Do not depart from the arising of the wisdom and compassion of the ten stages.

Therefore, at the very first arousal of the mind in the ten abidings (*vihāra*), That arousal of the mind immediately enters the wisdom of the ten stages. Although the skillful means (*upāya*) of the five stages differ,"
It is solely for the sake of maturing the wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Like a swift breath flying through space, it does not cease its wandering yet reaches nowhere;
like fish and dragons swimming in water, they do not cease their movement yet do not leave the water.

Thus, the distinctions among the practices of the five stages do not cease their differentiation, yet they do not depart from wisdom. All the distinctions of days, months, and years are [subsumed] by the seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*) of wisdom.
There is no difference. The Master of the Treatise further states in verse:

"The golden realm of all sentient beings, Pure, stainless wisdom, indestructible— The jewel of wisdom lies within the inner garment, Yet they remain outside the gate, desiring only long-term poverty. The vast jeweled vehicle stands at the crossroads;
Mañjuśrī guides and Samantabhadra supports it, Drawn by many powerful, fat, white oxen. In a single thought, it pervades everywhere."

Wandering through that which has neither contraction nor expansion, such a precious vehicle cannot enter it; one merely delights in the gate of diligent toil and stands before it, unaware that one’s own body abides eternally within.

One sends forth constant words saying, "I am not capable. For those shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, "shrouding" means covering over the fundamental wisdom (*jñāna*) of one's own *tathatā* (suchness).
Since this wisdom is itself without intrinsic nature, it becomes deluded by pursuing objective conditions; thus, it follows [along with them].
Delusion regarding suffering is extreme; when one awakens to this for oneself, delusion is eliminated. Delusion regarding the self becomes false, while awakening to the self becomes wisdom.
Awakening and delusion fundamentally possess no dual nature; as for wisdom and delusion, each lacks an intrinsic nature and both arise entirely from conditions.
Because the fundamental wisdom has no inherent nature, it does not itself cognize whether it is wisdom or not-wisdom; it merely arises in accordance with objects and pursues them.

Sentiment arises from the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). Unless one reaches the ultimate limit of suffering and, weary of suffering, seeks the Truth, even if a Sage were to transform them, they would not believe or follow;
thus, this [realization] does not arise. There are two kinds of generating the mind (*cittotpāda*): the first is generating the mind out of weariness with the suffering of saṃsāra after a long time;
this is called the "Noble Wisdom of Self-Awakening" (*svapratyātmāryajñāna*), and is also called the Buddha-wisdom, the spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*), and the non-... [omitted].

The Master’s wisdom [is as follows]: Second, one relies on the exhortation of those who have attained prior awakening to understand the root of suffering; only then can one give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

If one says that the aspiration must rely on previous Buddhas to arise, this is identical to the eternalist view (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). If so, by whom did those who attained prior awakening take their teachers?

If they were passed down through successive transmission, they would not escape the eternalist view. If there were an ancient, eternal Buddha to serve as the teacher in this succession, then that ancient Buddha himself—
As for the statement that "the essence is itself true and does not follow delusion," this means that one must not tread upon its ancient traces. This is because the True is itself eternally true;
it cannot follow along with birth and death by means of being "true. Thus, birth and death are themselves eternal birth and death, for the Buddha is himself the eternal Buddha.
If sentient beings were definitively subject to birth and death, then birth and death would be inherently eternal and could never be realized as true;

this would constitute the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). Both of these [extremes] are incorrect, for they do not transcend the extremes of nihilism and eternalism. This is for the sake of all sentient beings.
Birth and death have no intrinsic nature; fundamentally, there is no birth and death. One falsely conceptualizes birth and death, yet fundamentally they are not birth and death.
All Buddhas fundamentally have no self-nature; in reality, there is no bodhi, nor is there nirvana. Yet sentient beings delusively claim that the Buddhas possess bodhi and nirvana.
If there are sentient beings who can know it thus, this is called "arousing the mind," and this is called [the awakening of] all [Buddhas].
The Buddha is named the One Who Sees the Path; he is able to awaken all sentient beings. He is the one who has reached the end of ignorance.
Ignorance is fundamentally non-existent, and the Buddhas are likewise non-existent; thus he is named the Awakened One.

Relying solely on wondrous wisdom that is without dependence, without dwelling, without substance, and without intrinsic nature, he is able to respond like an echo, manifesting form-bodies to teach and transform sentient beings; this is named Great Compassion. It is inconceivable.
There is attainment and realization; there is delight and aversion; there is grasping and relinquishing; there is ancient and modern;
there is true and false—this is the arousal of the bodhicitta. Arousing the bodhicitta in this manner is so that one is not shrouded by the ignorance of the long night.
Within the gate of diverse characteristics, there are in total fifty kinds of bodhi; regarding the general essence and common characteristics, they are categorized solely according to these ten.

The differentiation of the stages (*bhūmi*) constitutes the primary substance for spiritual advancement. Within these ten stages, enlightenment (*bodhi*) is collectively characterized by five types of enlightenment as its primary substance.
These five types of enlightenment are: first, the enlightenment of emptiness and signlessness (*śūnyatā-animitta-bodhi*).
2. The Bodhi of universal radiance and non-reliant abiding wisdom; 3. The Bodhi of the great vows that can give rise to great wisdom and great compassion to extensively benefit sentient beings;
4. The Bodhi that, by means of great compassion, can follow along with both defilement and purity without being stained by either;
5. The Bodhi of the effortless perfection of the myriad practices of wisdom and compassion. "Bodhi" means awakening (*bodha*). As for why it is called "unsurpassed," it is simply...
The One Vehicle is not the Three Vehicles. First, there is the enlightenment of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, which is attained by both the Three Vehicles and the One Vehicle.

Second, there is the enlightenment of universally radiant, non-abiding wisdom, which belongs solely to the One Vehicle and not to the Three Vehicles. This refers to the Bodhisattva of the One Vehicle.
At the beginning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), abiding in this wisdom is called "dwelling where the Buddhas dwell" and being born into the family of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.

By means of this ground of wisdom, one advances in the cultivation of all practices, following differentiated wisdom and following differentiated practices, yet never departing from the ground of the universally radiant, non-reliant wisdom obtained at the initial resolve.
This is because the ultimate goal of such an awakening mind is not distinct [from its beginning]. Thus is the awakening mind generated.
Regarding the difficulty of the preceding mind: it is because this stage of wisdom is difficult to attain.

Through the three great vows, one can give rise to great wisdom and generate great compassion to extensively benefit sentient beings. It clarifies that all phenomena do not arise from themselves; rather, wisdom arises by relying on the great vows and accomplishes compassion.
Nor do they arise from another, because both wisdom and the vows lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). As for "not arising together": [it means they do not arise from both].

Because phenomena lack any inherent combination, they are not without causes. Rather, wisdom must arise through aspiration; because one practices compassion, it is said that "the seed of Buddhahood arises from conditions.
For this reason, the One Vehicle is taught. Furthermore, when the effortless wisdom of a Bodhisattva in this eighth stage manifests, there is still the fear of stagnating in quiescence;
therefore, the eighth *pāramitā* of aspiration serves as a defense, causing them to remain mindful of their original vow.
Therefore, fourthly, because of their great compassion, they are able to follow along with both the defiled and the undefiled, yet remain unstained by them,
regarding the bodhi [enlightenment] of the six perfections practiced in the preceding six stages— which attains supramundane, mundane, and both supramundane and mundane bodhi—
and, upon reaching this seventh stage, they employ that supramundane, mundane, and both supramundane and mundane bodhi to enter into the world, being identical [with it].

All the activities of ordinary beings are transformed into the practice of great compassion. Although they appear identical to worldly defilement, because their wisdom possesses an undefiled nature, they dwell in the world without attachment, like a lotus in water;
for though it constantly grows within the water, it remains unsullied. Furthermore, the essence of clear wisdom is without dependence and without intrinsic nature;
thus, it can follow great vows to abide amidst the secular stream, remaining sovereign by neither belonging to defilement nor purity.

This seventh stage dharma-gate is not within the reach of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), nor is it known by those bodhisattvas who practice the six pāramitās while still harboring delight in or aversion toward afflictions (kleśa).
Through the five wisdoms, compassion, and the myriad practices, one attains the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta) bodhi.

If one considers it through the gate of general and specific characteristics, the essence of wisdom is not different, and time is likewise not different; this is the totality of the initial mind of the ten abidings.

[End of] section. If, by way of the gate of distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), one attains a portion of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom of identical essence (*sahaja-jñāna*) during the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), ten practices (*caryā*), and ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*);
attains a portion of the Tathāgata’s conduct of identical essence;

and attains all the Tathāgatas’ great vows of transference that harmonize compassion and wisdom—from the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) up to the sixth stage—one relies upon the dharmas of the three preceding stages of worthiness (*pūrva-śaikṣa*).
Through this nourishment and fulfillment, they cause one to emerge from the entanglements. Although there is compassion, it is the vow that causes all sentient beings to transcend the world;
it is through this that, upon reaching the seventh stage, one takes the previously attained mind of supramundane liberation and only then dwells within the entanglements without being defiled.
From the gate of the three emptinesses and non-action, one enters the skillful practices that accord with the world while remaining amidst its entanglements. Yet, there still remains...

There are two kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*): those of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and those of action (*abhisaṃskāra*). These still involve volitional activity and development until the eighth and tenth stages (*bhūmi*), when compassion and wisdom are perfected.

At that point, one spontaneously benefits sentient beings according to their needs, and the state of non-action finally culminates. Upon reaching the eleventh stage, the beings benefited are equal in extent to the *dharmadhātu*.
According to their faculties and the timing, one manifests form-bodies (*rūpakāya*) so that there is no birth that is not benefited. Not...
Acting for the sake of others, one employs universal luminous wisdom (*samantāloka-jñāna*).

Because this is of the same essential nature as the deluded minds of all sentient beings, one is able to know the karmic actions performed by all sentient beings and manifest accordingly. In the first stage of the eighth bhūmi, one attains wisdom that is effortless (*anābhoga*);
in the ninth bhūmi, one clarifies effortless wisdom and attains mastery in teaching the Dharma; in the tenth...
Because on the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākārī*), wisdom and compassion are fully perfected within effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*), the tenth ground is the fruition within this stage.

It is clear that causal practice is difficult to initiate, whereas fruitional practice is easy to accomplish—just as water entering a current flows spontaneously to the ocean, how much more so when this practice does not depart from the ocean?
As the Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha, it is like a world-system where one place is defiled and another..."
"Pure. This refers to the interval between these two states, which is difficult to transcend. This clarifies that the sixth stage is pure and the seventh stage is purely defiled;
within these two positions, one may stagnate in either defilement or purity, making it difficult to pass beyond them.

The intent is to clarify that by means of great compassion and great wisdom, one does not depart from these two practices, but rather teaches and transforms all sentient beings, causing them to ultimately achieve Great Bodhi and be endowed with all [virtues].

The wisdom of wisdom (*jñānajñāna*). By means of the wisdom of application (*prayogajñāna*), one manifests the fundamental wisdom (*mūlajñāna*); by the power of contemplation through fundamental wisdom, one accomplishes the wisdom of differentiation (*viśeṣajñāna*).
Because this wisdom has no basis, it does not undergo constant defilement; because defilement has no basis, it cannot stain or purify.

It exists solely as a skillful means arising from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to benefit sentient beings. As for the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), they are called the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). This cessation...

There are four kinds of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). First, the extinction concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of the *śrāvaka*: by means of the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, consciousness and the mind cease;

both active afflictions (*kleśa*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) are extinguished. Second, the extinction concentration of the *pratyekabuddha*: the twelve links of dependent origination cease; active afflictions are extinguished, and wisdom is also extinguished. Third, the provisional teaching bodhisattva:
contemplates the Four Noble Truths and the twelve links of dependent origination, clarifying suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.

There is no person, no sentient being, and no life-span. Their nature and characteristics are empty and quiescent; they are entirely without bondage. Practicing the six *pāramitās*, they are born in the Pure Lands.

Alternatively, by means of a body born at will (*saṃcintyabhavopapatti-kāya*), they dwell in this Sahā world. Or it is said that they remain in the world out of compassion, retaining their afflictions (*kleśa*).

Even if they enter the state of tranquil concentration (*śamatha-samādhi*), they merely cease according to the principle of signlessness (*animitta*); they do not undergo cessation through the loss of the great functional power of the *dharmadhātu*.
Fourth, like the Bodhisattvas of the One Vehicle, they resolve their minds based on the Tathāgata’s wisdom of universal radiance.

They realize that fundamental ignorance is itself the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance of all Buddhas. Taking this great wisdom as the substance of their progressive cultivation, all aspects of quiescence and function follow the gates of this wisdom:
the quiescence of a single body is the function of many bodies, and the quiescence of many bodies is the function of a single body.

Functioning through the quiescence of the identical body, and functioning through the quiescence of the distinct body; likewise, the quiescence and function of the identical and distinct bodies are sovereign.
Equal to the empty dharma-realm, they are unimpeded and infinitely layered.
This eighth assembly, the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis," was held in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantāloka-maṇḍala*) and expounds the Dharma-gate of the ten samādhis.

The seventh assembly was held in the Heaven of the Third Dhyāna (*Tṛtīya-dhyāna-svarga*) and expounded the Dharma-gate of the eleven stages (*ekādaśa-bhūmi*); its text has not yet arrived. The "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" clarifies the manifestation of the Buddha.

The arising [of Mañjuśrī] signifies transcending the entanglements of worldly existence; the perfection of practice [of Samantabhadra] signifies that Mañjuśrī is the master of wisdom that transcends entanglement, while Samantabhadra is the master of conduct that enters into the mundane world.
In the "Chapter on Departing from the World," it is stated that after all Buddhas have themselves attained the fruit of Buddhahood, [they manifest these two aspects].
Constantly employing one's own fruits and practices, one perpetually acts for the benefit of sentient beings; this is also called the "Chapter on Benefiting the World.
It is not a detachment characterized by withdrawal. All Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment through this great wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*;
it is also called the "Chapter on the *Dharmadhātu* of the Great Wisdom Hall of Universal Radiance. This is the ultimate fruit of the realm of bodhi-wisdom.
This encompasses the entire section. Regarding the threefold search for Samantabhadra through the power of samādhi:

it clarifies that although the samādhi possesses compassion, it is predominantly a supramundane mind; therefore, one does not see the gate of Samantabhadra’s entry into the mundane world to benefit sentient beings throughout the eleven stages.
Only by performing the threefold search does one finally behold Samantabhadra, which clarifies the ascent from the tenth stage.
Advancing, one enters the stage of the fruit of Samantabhadra’s conduct, because one accomplishes the gate of Samantabhadra’s sovereign mastery over quiescence and activity.

Therefore, the subsequent text uses the analogy of the king of wish-fulfilling maṇi jewels, which can respond to whatever is sought and take on the same color as objects without losing its own inherent quality as a jewel;
this clarifies that the Tathāgata, as the king of omniscience—the ultimate fruit—never abandons the various [virtues] of the bodhisattvas.
The practice of skillful means follows the various inclinations and desires of all sentient beings, guiding them accordingly so that they may attain happiness.

The general meaning clarifies that from after the stage of the ten faiths until before the tenth bhūmi, one accomplishes the fundamental wisdom of the dharmakāya through the practices of Samantabhadra, thereby attaining the differentiated wisdom within the supramundane.
Within the eleventh bhūmi, one purely accomplishes [the fruit] by means of the fundamental wisdom of the dharmakāya.
The gate of Samantabhadra possesses infinite great functions within the midst of birth and death;

it is equal to the deluded thoughts of all sentient beings, sharing the same perceptions and the same functions, and liberating them according to their capacities. For this reason, the Tathāgata instructs one to contemplate Samantabhadra.

In the "Chapter on Leaving the World," it is said that these are the practices of Samantabhadra following the attainment of Buddhahood; they are called "universal observation" because, though observing everywhere, one neither perceives Samantabhadra nor his seat.

As for "the seat": this clarifies that from the initial stages of the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten bhūmis, one has already ascended by means of the conduct of Samantabhadra.
One seeks extensively the supramundane mind of the Tathāgata’s liberation, compassion, and wisdom, attaining the sovereign, effortless path of Buddhahood.
Once this is perfected and all-pervasive, there remains the conduct of Samantabhadra following the fruition of the ten bhūmis, as well as all [that follows].
Samādhi is purely an entry into the mundane world because there is no seeking of the supramundane fruit of Buddhahood; thus, within this samādhi, the three types of seeking are not perceived.
It is purely great compassion, devoid of practices for self-benefit, and therefore "mutual non-perception" occurs.

This is because prior to the fruit of Buddhahood at the tenth stage, one practices the conduct of Samantabhadra with a mind that seeks both self-benefit and the benefit of others, and thus seeks supramundane liberation. Therefore...
On the eleventh stage, one practices the conduct of Samantabhadra.

Because this is exclusively the practice of benefiting sentient beings without seeking one's own liberation, it is clear that the path of self-liberation is already fulfilled and there is nothing further to be sought.
Therefore, on the eleventh stage, one acts solely for the benefit of all sentient beings, without accumulating merit for oneself. Thus, having [completed] the ten stages...

Regarding the previous practices of Samantabhadra for one’s own benefit and the benefit of others, although one seeks the practices of Samantabhadra within the eleven stages (*bhūmi*), they have not yet been fully perceived.
For this reason, the great assembly looked everywhere, yet in the end, they were unable to see the body or the seat of Samantabhadra.

However, those who entered into contemplation attained what was appropriate: first, they must enter the concentration of no-thought and no-mind, realize the principle of the *dharmakāya*, and accord with the void.
Only when one has realized the nature of emptiness can one skillfully give rise to wisdom and cultivate a mind of offering;

this must be done with mastery, in accordance with the principle of wisdom. If one merely cultivates the dharma-body of emptiness and signlessness, one will be unable to manifest the function of wisdom.
If one only generates conceptualizations in a one-sided manner and fails to perceive the signless dharma-body, then it is purely conditioned existence.

The Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers (*Daśābhijñā*) thus concludes the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), including the ten concentrations (*samādhi*), the ten supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), and the ten patiences (*kṣānti*). These are the skillful means for entering into birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to benefit sentient beings.

They also constitute the five positions (*pañcasthāna*): the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), the ten transferences (*daśapariṇāmana*), the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*).
General Cultivation.

Regarding the Ten Patiences (*daśa-kṣānti*), if one follows the provisional teachings for Bodhisattvas, those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) constitute the Patience of Subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*); it is only upon reaching the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) on the stages that one enters the Patience of Accordance with Non-arising (*anutpatti-anuloma-kṣānti*).

Regarding patience (*kṣānti*): if one takes the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) as penetrating the initial mind of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one attains the gate of mindfulness of the light of wisdom of all Buddhas;

this is called being born into the family of Buddha-wisdom, and it is called attaining the patience of sound (*ghoṣānugakṣānti*). It is also called the patience that accords with non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).

Since there were already the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) previously, this refers to the possession of patience based on those powers. If one lacks the supernatural intelligence of thorough penetration, one merely achieves the patience of subduing (*viśeṣa-kṣānti*) and the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).

It is non-arising. Prior to the tenth stage, one accomplishes the supernormal powers (abhijñā) through patience (kṣānti). Within the eleventh stage, one accomplishes patience through the supernormal powers.
This is because these ten concentrations (samādhi), ten supernormal powers, and ten patiences are the functional manifestations of a single virtue.

The three chapters preceding the "Asaṃkhyeya" chapter— namely, the ten concentrations (*dhyāna*), the ten supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), and the ten forbearances (*kṣānti*)— clarify that cause and effect encompass the beginning and end,

the commencement and conclusion, without shifting even for the duration of a single *kṣaṇa*. As stated in the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra), ninety *kṣaṇas* are contained within a single thought-moment (*cittakṣaṇa*), and one *kṣaṇa* passes through...

Nine hundred cycles of arising and ceasing. Thus, because the fruit of Buddhahood throughout the three periods of time, as well as the skillful means and practices of Samantabhadra, are such that time does not shift, they are measured solely by the *kṣaṇa* (instant), and the designation "arising and ceasing" is not established.

Even if one were to discuss arising and ceasing, it is established only within the *kṣaṇa*, with no further duration of length or brevity. From this point downward, up to the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," the Buddha is elucidated.

Regarding the three types of karma within the fruition, why does the Tathāgata himself explain this chapter? It is to clarify that these numerical dharmas are so vast that they are beyond the reach of the wisdom of those in lower stages;
only a Buddha can fully comprehend them. These are two types of ignorance regarding the fruit of Buddhahood, which cannot be understood until one reaches the perfection of discriminating wisdom.
This refers to the *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* and the *Anuvyañjana-prabhāsa-guṇa-parivarta*.
These two chapters of the Dharma were spoken by the Tathāgata himself. There are five further stages, each of which was spoken by the Bodhisattvas according to their respective positions:
the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Faiths spoke the Dharma of the Ten Faiths; the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abidings spoke the Dharma of the Ten Abidings, and so on for these various chapters.
The distinction of the fruit of non-attainment wisdom is clarified only upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood; this was likewise spoken by the Tathāgata himself.

Therefore, the one who asks the question must be the Tathāgata, the sovereign king with mastery over mind and intellect, who alone is capable of such inquiry. Furthermore, regarding these numerical dharmas:
The fruit of Buddhahood is finalized only when wisdom is perfected; because wisdom is all-pervasive, it knows spontaneously, not through the application of effortful attention (*prayoga-manasikāra*).
This is because the Buddha himself has so stated.
Since the preceding chapter was the "Asaṃkhyeya," this one naturally follows as the "Life Span. Regarding the teacher who expounds this chapter:
it is taught by the Bodhisattva Mind-King (Cittarāja). This clarifies that the Buddha’s life span has the mind-king as its essence, and that the mind-king represents his life-force.

Because of its sovereignty, this clarifies the life-force of the Tathāgata’s mind-king. It extends or contracts, lengthens or shortens, according to the faculties [of beings], acting with mastery over phenomena;
yet in reality, the Tathāgata has no life-span and no length or brevity. This is established as a graduated sequence for the sake of those who have not yet awakened.
This causes them to know that the lifespan of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible; it uses the few to manifest the many, and the short to manifest the long.

Were it not so, how could one know the lifespan of the Buddha? In reality, however, the Tathāgata has no lifespan of either length or brevity; the life-span of the Tathāgata is like fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
Chapter on the Abodes of Bodhisattvas:
The Kingdom of Kāśmīra (formerly called Jibin). This is translated as "Who Enters.
Formerly, before this kingdom was established, there was a great dragon lake that no one dared to approach. Later, an arhat beheld its magnificent landscape.
"It is a suitable place for people to dwell. He then requested from the dragon enough space for one knee. The dragon granted his request.
The Arhat transformed himself to become large, and his knee gradually filled the pond. Believing the dragon's word, he withdrew and departed.
The Arhat used his supernatural powers to dry up the water, allowing the common people to settle there and build their houses. Everyone said, "We..."
Without relying on the Holy Teacher, who could enter this place? Therefore, based on these words, its name was established.

This chapter, "The Inconceivable Dharma of the Buddha," derives its name from the three karmas of the Tathāgata’s body, speech, and mind. Why is it called "inconceivable"? Because it transcends the sphere of conceptualization and the mind.
It cannot be reached; thus it is called "inconceivable. Because emotional consciousness and verbal designations cannot reach it, it is said to be "inexpressible.

This clarifies that within the activity of the three karmas of this Buddha-fruit, the phenomena of both the ultimate and conventional truths are fully perfected; therefore, the Buddha is titled the "Unsurpassed Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings.
This clarifies that the three types of karmic activity and the two wisdoms are all-pervasive, universally encompassing all dharmas. [This is] the Blue Lotus.
This is the wisdom of ultimate truth (*tathatājñāna*). The Lotus Treasury (*padmagarbha*) is the wisdom that accords with worldly convention (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
By means of these two wisdoms—ultimate and conventional—he himself proclaims his own threefold activities as vast, sovereign, and inconceivable.

In the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata," the preceding chapter explained the three karmas and two wisdoms of the Buddha himself, which enter the inconceivable limit and universally pervade all things to bring infinite benefit to sentient beings.
This chapter, concerning the three karmas and two wisdoms, explains how they enter the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) within inconceivable wisdom.

Therefore, in the "Chapter on the Merit of the Tathāgata’s Minor Marks and Radiance," the preceding chapter has already clarified the ocean of the ten bodily marks; there are oceans of marks as numerous as the atoms within ten lotus-treasury worlds.

Adorning the body: this chapter, based on the merit of the Buddha’s physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*) being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), symbolizes the wondrous wisdom and luminous nature of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

It is established in order to attract and guide all sentient beings. For what reason does the Tathāgata himself proclaim this chapter? To clarify two types of ignorance within the state of Buddhahood:
first, ignorance regarding the vastness of the numerical categories of dharmas; second, ignorance regarding the minor marks (*anuvyañjana*) and their radiance.

The two categories of phenomena—the merit of qualities (*guṇa*) and the ignorance (*moha*)—are not within the reach of the wisdom of bodhisattvas; they become manifest only upon the fulfillment of the fruit of Buddhahood.
The "Chapter on the Incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya-varga*) concerns the vastness of numerical phenomena.

The "Chapter on the Merit of the Radiance of the Minor Marks" concerns the merit of the self-nature and non-reliance of the Dharmakāya and Jñānakāya, which are devoid of intrinsic nature. These two types of phenomena are neither attained through conditioned activity nor by means of effort.

This is the extent reached by the practices of Samantabhadra; because it serves as the basis for those practices, it is the dharma that culminates at the stage of Buddhahood when the practices of Samantabhadra are perfected.
Therefore, the Tathāgata himself spoke of it, clearly teaching the dharma-gate of his own stage from within that very stage.

This is intended to prevent later students from being confused. The meaning clarifies that the Dharma-body and fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) do not belong to what is produced through the cultivation of practices;

rather, it is only great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and discriminative wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) that must rely upon this fundamental wisdom. This is because it is the constant basis for all bodhisattva practices and the fruit of Buddhahood.
Therefore, the Tathāgata himself spoke of this. Without this wisdom, the fruit of virtue—[one... (Note: The source text appears to be truncated at the end.)

Because all conditioned phenomena are impermanent. Just as the essence of space serves as the very substance for all that exists, yet space itself does not belong to the realm of cultivation or birth.
— From the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra."

In the preceding chapter, the ultimate fruit was reached; the nature of wisdom (*dharmatā-jñāna*) was first elucidated so as to benefit sentient beings. This chapter elucidates that the practices of Samantabhadra (*Samantabhadra-caryā*) are able to benefit all things.
If one possesses the principle and wisdom (*jñāna*) but lacks practice, then that principle and wisdom will not be perfected while dwelling in the mundane world.

If one possesses practice but lacks principle and wisdom, there is no means by which that practice can transcend the mundane. Therefore, only when the essence of principle and practice is thoroughly penetrated does one achieve the gate of non-dual sovereignty. As the Sūtra says:
To know the mental activities of all sentient beings is called the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

Because one is without a [separate] mind of one's own and because the obstructions between self and other have been severed, one's own mind and the minds of all sentient beings are of one essence and non-dual. It is by means of this that one can know the minds of all sentient beings;
for since one's own mind and the minds of sentient beings are non-dual, there is no distinction between the interior and exterior of the body.
One sees. Because there is no view of internal or external, the boundless world-realm and the realm of space are equal;
one’s own mind and the realm of space are equal. Thus, there is neither large nor small, neither far nor near, nor any intermediate point.

Since one’s own mind is without large or small, far or near, nor any intermediate point, wisdom is constantly and universally pervasive throughout the worlds of the ten directions, yet without coming or going. Since wisdom is thus constantly and universally pervasive...
In the worlds of the ten directions, there is no coming or going. Thus, one is able to manifest form-bodies in accordance with the faculties of beings with sovereign ease.

Being able to manifest form-bodies in accordance with the faculties with sovereign ease, one then possesses the sovereignty of preaching the Dharma in accordance with those faculties. One then possesses the sovereignty of the mutual interpenetration of one body and many bodies.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," why is it titled "The Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata"? It is because, following the second assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance, ten levels of faith were established.
With the Buddha Immovable Wisdom as the head of the first faith, one proceeds from these ten faiths to advance in practice through faith. Not...
Departing from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), the essence of immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*) gives rise to the vows and practices of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
By cultivating discriminative wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), one perfects great compassion; when this stage is fulfilled, it is called the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata.

This clarifies that the one who first appeared at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) in the first assembly as having newly attained perfect awakening was the manifestation of Vairocana Buddha; he is the one who appears within this chapter.

This Bodhisattva advances through the five stages (*pañca-bhūmi*), and when the realization, wisdom, and compassion of these stages are perfected, he appears; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Appearance.
Its general meaning clarifies that Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra represent the gates of the wisdom and practice that accomplish the fruit of Buddhahood.
It further causes [the Buddha] to expound the Dharma of the Buddha’s appearance: the Buddha is fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), whose essence is wordless; whatever possesses words is all deviation.
This is distinct wisdom. Thus, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are the common dharma of all Buddhas of the past and present.

For those who have first resolved their minds toward enlightenment, from the moment they first give rise to the mind of faith, they have all traversed these two practices of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra;

it is only upon reaching this point that they are fully perfected. Practicing and advancing in this manner, they never depart from the ten wisdoms of the Immovable Wisdom Buddha within the initial mind of faith.

Because this is the essence [of the Tathāgata], it is clear that at all times there is no movement: wisdom does not move, practice does not move, and one is able to travel everywhere throughout the ten directions without moving.
Entering the many from the one does not move; entering the one from the many does not move; entering the large from the small does not move.

These five stages of ascending progress represent the Dharma of transcending the heavens, or the body pervading the ten directions, yet ultimately never departing from the Hall of Universal Radiance (Puguangming-dian).

The essence of wisdom is a single moment; therefore, this Dharma, which has already reached its consummation as its own fruit, is taught without departing from the place where faith was established—the Hall of Universal Radiance.
It is just as when Sudhana went to the Tathāgata Maitreya and again saw Mañjuśrī, his initial friend of faith, entering into a state similar to the body of Samantabhadra.
This is done lest later students become confused regarding the Dharma, point by point.
The journey of Sudhana is used to symbolize this, so that it may be easily understood.

Upon reaching this "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," it clarifies that once the five stages of the sūtra have been practiced and cultivated until their merit is matured, one then discusses its dissemination and entrustment. This is when we speak of the fundamental dharma-realm.
The nature itself is neither deluded nor awakened; it has no arising and no ceasing, no formation and no destruction, and no flowing out or penetrating through.

This is the intent of the entrustment for its circulation, because it is taught from the state of an ordinary person who has not yet awakened, until the ultimate point of the completion of the power of preparatory practice.
Just as in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," which directly discusses the ultimate fruit of the meritorious efforts of all Buddhas, it is self-circulating and requires no formal entrustment;

so too, in this "Tathāgatotpatti-parivarta," it clarifies that for those with faith, it is only when the power of the five stages of preparatory practice reaches its culmination that they become truly authentic.
Having newly ascended to the completion of their merit and brought the two practices to full perfection, the teaching of entrustment and circulation is then proclaimed. This makes it clear.
Because the fruition is initially fulfilled, one then enters the eternal Way of the Dharma-realm; it is not a measure of antiquity or modernity, nor of beginning or end.
To circulate this Dharma is called "circulation," which refers to the Chapter on the Dharma-realm.

This is a metaphor for the appearance of the Tathāgata—the realm of body, mind, wisdom, and the ten immeasurable matters—which, being beyond all metaphors, is expressed through metaphor. This is but a brief and partial path of the mind and intellect.
It is absolute. It functions through the inconceivable, natureless, unconditioned, and limitless sovereignty that cannot be expressed by words, measures, or metaphors.

Thus, in the entrustment for the circulation of this chapter, it is said that this Dharma-gate shall not fall into the hands of other sentient beings—namely, those who delight in studying the two vehicles or three vehicles, such as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who take pleasure in emptiness and non-self, and who aspire to be born in pure lands.

"Earth" refers to other sentient beings who, because they have not yet turned their minds [toward enlightenment], abide in the cycle of death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*).

Because they are these "other sentient beings," if there are ordinary persons of great resolve or those of the three vehicles who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment], that which is entrusted by the Buddha is called "circulation.
Even if this Dharma were expounded by a Bodhisattva at the stage of sainthood (*ārya-bhūmi*), there would be no ordinary persons who would delight in studying it. It is not so.

This is called an entrustment (*parindanā*), not a circulation (*pravartana*). Furthermore, it cites the analogy of a wheel-turning monarch’s (*cakravartin*) son who possesses all the marks of a king;
after the king’s death, his seven treasures do not disperse or perish because this son is capable of governing the king’s rightful position.
If this son were not present, after the king’s death, all these treasures would vanish and be scattered within seven days. Son of the Buddha, this sūtra-treasure is likewise:

it does not fall into the hands of any other sentient beings, except for the true sons of the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, who are born into the family of the Tathāgata and have planted roots of goodness that bear the marks of the Tathāgata. If this [son] were not present...

They are the true sons of the Buddha. Such a Dharma-gate will not long remain before it perishes. It is clearly understood that this is intended only to cause ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) to resolve their minds and enter into realization.
Even if noble ones (*ārya*) were to constantly preach it, if there are no ordinary persons who delight in practicing and entering into realization, the Dharma will naturally perish.
It is said that there are no ordinary beings who practice the path of cessation; phenomena have neither arising nor ceasing. As the Sūtra says:
"Those who plant the various roots of goodness for the marks of a Tathāgata" clarifies that the Tathāgata takes the wisdom of liberation as his home.

Just as in a single thought-moment, when non-conceptuality arises and all views regarding body and mind have perished, one is born into the home of the Tathāgata’s sublime principle of non-substantiality and correct wisdom. Thus, the Tathāgata perceives all things.

The Dharma has non-existence as its nature and non-characteristic as its characteristic. It is without characteristics while not destroying characteristics, because the characteristics of the object of clear wisdom are inherently true;

this is called the Tathāgata’s characteristic of names and kinds. It clarifies that the objective realm of one's own mental wisdom is neither arising, abiding, nor ceasing—this is the Tathāgata’s characteristic.
It clarifies that the wisdom of one's own mind is equal to the wisdom of all Buddhas and all sentient beings. All...
One nature is non-nature; one mark is markless. Like the realm of empty space, it can manifest shadow-like bodies according to the dispositions and inclinations of sentient beings.
Its arising has no place of origin, and its cessation has no place of departure. To realize that the mind and its objects are like illusions—this is the characteristic of the Tathāgata.
Those who realize such a Dharma as this are born into the family of the Buddha and plant the seeds of the Tathāgata’s marks.
When ordinary beings hear this Dharma and cultivate and study such true wisdom-seeds of the Tathāgata, it is called the non-interruption of the Buddha-lineage;
it is termed the entrustment for circulation.
The ninth assembly of this "Chapter on Leaving the World" was preached in the Hall of Universal Radiance.
The "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" clarifies that one's own realization and practice are perfected;

thus, the Buddhas of the ten directions all share the same name, Samantabhadra, to demonstrate that within the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten dedications, even a single portion of the awakened mind is capable of subduing all things.
Among the afflictions, there is a portion of coarse delusions; in practice, one attains a portion of compassion.

Although one may tread upon a portion of Samantabhadra’s path, one has not yet fully perfected the entirety of Samantabhadra’s conduct. Therefore, according to their respective stages, the fruits of Buddhahood are merely designated by the same names—Moon, Eye, or Wondrous.
It is only when reaching the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," where enlightened conduct is revealed as perfectly complete and equal, that it cannot be described [in such limited terms].
There are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field, all bearing the same name, Samantabhadra Buddha.
Therefore, in the first assembly, the Dharma-gates taught were all caused to be expounded by Samantabhadra; this is because the essence follows from its function.

In the second assembly, the wisdom-function of Samantabhadra follows from the essence, continuing thus up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), where in every case the function follows from the essence, thereby causing fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) to be perfected and made luminously clear. However—
At the conclusion of the final ten stages, one relinquishes the bliss of samādhi and nirvāṇa; like a dense forest of afflictions, one then possesses the great function of Samantabhadra.

Only then can one be said to have established the universal teaching and attained mastery within the cycle of birth and death. Those who resolve their minds [on enlightenment] must deeply grasp this essential meaning.
Only then is one fit to cultivate the Way; to seek it through many previous and subsequent lifetimes would be inconsistent with this principle.
This tenth chapter, the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta," was preached at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Why is this chapter entitled "Entering the Dharma Realm" (*dharmadhātupraveśa*)? For those who clearly understand and take delight [in the truth], the initial realization of what was previously obscured is called "entering.

The nature of the realms of body and mind is inherently without dependence; this is called "Dharma" (*dharma*). When the one and the many are mutually penetrating, and the barriers of true and false, right and wrong, have vanished, it is called the "Realm" (*dhātu*).
Furthermore, realizing that the seeds of ignorance and consciousness are purely the functioning of wisdom is "non-dependence."
The realm of wisdom is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Furthermore, with a single sublime sound, it is heard throughout the ocean of benefits;

with a single fine hair, its measure is equal to the boundless. By transcending the views of large and small, things and self are of one substance. When consciousness ceases and emotions are extinguished, wisdom penetrates without obstruction;
this is called "entering the Dharma-realm. Question: Why is it that at the beginning of all the preceding assemblies, it is stated that [the Buddha] does not depart from Bodhi?
The site of the assembly was the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*). Furthermore, the three assemblies resided together in the Hall of Universal Radiance;

this is a single assembly within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). For what reason, then, does it directly state: "At that time, the World-Honored One was in Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, in the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada"?
Answer: To restate that the three assemblies were all present in the Hall of Universal Radiance is to clarify and promote the five [qualities].

The stages of practice have already been completed. Without departing from the essence of the fundamental immovable wisdom of universal radiance, this assembly of the Dharma-realm is stated directly to be at the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī.
This clarifies that one’s own Buddhahood is fully realized and that the practice of delivering sentient beings is perfected;
therefore, one manifests within human realms, cities, and gardens to transform those of the two vehicles—śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—as well as those in the Pure Lands.

The Bodhisattva takes the sovereign Dharma-realm alone as his essence. There are no five stages of bodhi-practice to be cultivated, nor are there any distinct wisdoms or Samantabhadra vows and practices to be studied.
The dharma that universally benefits sentient beings throughout the ten directions does not require further synthesis.
For this reason, it is directly called the Jeta Grove; just as when all rivers flow into the sea, the names of the individual streams vanish, it is designated solely by this.
The Dharma-realm serves as the name.
In the "Entering the Dharma-realm" chapter,
Sudhana seeks fifty-three spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to represent the five stages and three kinds of causes.
The fruit is the fundamental wisdom within the Dharma-body, which functions within the differentiated wisdom of Samantabhadra. Within these two, the wisdom that abides nowhere is called the Buddha.

This Buddha—Mañjuśrī and the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra—along with the fifty spiritual friends, act as cause and effect through their practice, yet they themselves possess no cause or effect; for within the stage of one's own Buddhahood, there is none.
Because there is nothing to be practiced and no place for practice, that which is cultivated serves as the antidote for practitioners within the five stages;

it is designated as "cause and fruit" in reference to the points where the latencies of the two obscurations—defilement and purity—are respectively matured and eliminated. However, the Dharma-body, the wisdom of principle, and the myriad practices themselves possess no cause or fruit.

It is simply because, within the five stages, one employs the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) to counteract afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), that the names "Tathāgata cause" and "Tathāgata fruit" are established. Question:
Why is it said only that one "seeks the bodhisattva path," rather than saying one "studies the bodhisattva mind"? Answer:
Because for Bodhi there is nothing to be attained, nothing to be cultivated, nothing to be studied, and nothing to be practiced; therefore, one only seeks the bodhisattva path. One studies...

The Bodhisattva Practice: In the first stage, the Dwelling of Initial Resolve, one uses the samādhi of non-thought and non-action, along with preparatory skillful means, to assist in the manifestation of bodhi.
Because bodhi has no substance and no intrinsic nature, it acts as the condition for non-abiding in relation to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
One seeks the various practices of a bodhisattva through this, because these practices are themselves bodhi and lack substance or intrinsic nature. If, regarding...
To practice enlightenment separately from the external [path] refers to the enlightenment of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who practice the contemplation of emptiness;
it is not the enlightenment of the One Vehicle, which is the sovereign enlightenment of the wisdom and principle of Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, and the myriad practices of compassion and vows.

For this reason, the Tathāgata spoke to bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" and that they are dharmas of arising and ceasing, because these bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings cultivate analytical [deconstruction].
The contemplation of the emptiness of the illumination of dharmas (*dharmāloka-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) destroys the existence of the triple world (*tridhātu*).

However, because it does not clarify that all existences within the triple world are themselves the functional manifestation (*vṛtti*) of bodhi, the Bodhisattva of this One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) true teaching merely seeks the Bodhisattva path and practices the Bodhisattva conduct;

thus, essence and function are comprehensively integrated, and there is no separate seeking. If one were to seek bodhi separately, then essence and function would be distinct, and dualistic views would persist forever.
Because it is not called "riding the inconceivable vehicle," one therefore seeks only the bodhisattva path; there is no separate enlightenment (*bodhi*).

This clarifies that enlightenment is without seeking, without the arousal of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*), without practice, without location, without question or answer, and without attainment or realization.
To practice all practices and fulfill the path of Samantabhadra is because the great function of enlightenment is thus perfected. [Verse:]
It is said that if there are bodhisattvas who do not weary of the suffering of birth and death, they will possess the path of Samantabhadra, which nothing can destroy.
This is because by clarifying that the suffering of birth and death is itself bodhi, there is nothing that can destroy it.

If, however, one abandons the suffering of birth and death to cultivate the practices of bodhi and resolve for bodhi, then there is something that can destroy it. Why is this? Because there would then be the defilement of both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa.
That which is destroyed by the two obstacles of purity is precisely that which is destroyed by the dualistic views of right and wrong, or of annihilation and permanence.

Those who, apart from their own Buddha-fruition, single-mindedly seek the truth by focusing exclusively on other Buddhas external to themselves, are fundamentally neither practitioners of the path of cultivation nor those of the path of vision.
If they reach the fruition of their own stage of practice, it is because they are in accord with the Buddhas' own realization. Since they are in accord with their own Buddha-fruition, even if...
Those who manage to see [the Buddha] through forceful striving have only a temporary manifestation; this is because it is not within the reach of their own practice.

These five stages and ten levels constitute the fruit of Buddhahood, each of which is defined according to the scope of the wisdom and compassion cultivated in practice, and the extent of what is traversed and reached therein.
The designation of the Buddha’s name is not merely a matter of forming a vow or aspiring for a temporary vision of the Buddha’s transformation body according to one's own sentiments.
"One birth" refers to birth within non-birth, for it is not a birth occurring sequentially within the three periods of time.
From this point on, Māyādevī represents the initial gate of the eleventh stage; the subsequent nine spiritual friends collectively clarify that [the Bodhisattva] takes great compassion as his mother.
The essence follows entirely the conduct of the Mother; through the illusory power of wisdom, compassion and wisdom are born, pervading the ten directions.

This pervasive presence conforms to worldly conventions, unlike the stages prior to the tenth bhūmi where one remains obstructed and fails to reach [this state]. These eleven bhūmis merely manifest the practice of the eleven stages of cultivation.
Upon fulfilling these eleven stages of Samantabhadra, the manifested virtue becomes all-pervasive, and conduct is fully prepared within the mundane world, free from seeking.
He has transcended the world. From the time of Lord Candraprabha onwards, they have all been of the same worldly stream, lacking the distinct marks and extraordinary features of the divine;

thus they appear as one with ordinary people. This signifies that his own supramundane path is perfected, and he no longer harbors a mind seeking further liberation, nor any thought of abandoning defilement or pursuing purity.
He simply boards the ship of the Dharma-nature, hoists the great sail of compassion, and takes great wisdom as his helmsman, proceeding [toward the shore].
The wind of the original vow blows through the net of the various *pāramitās*.

Constantly traversing the ocean of birth and death, it filters out all sentient beings who are like fish caught in the nets of attachment, establishing them on the shore of the wisdom of universal radiance that is free from dependence.

They dwell eternally in the unimpeded jewel palace of the *dharmadhātu*, which contains the merit of the myriad practices of illusory abiding—just as the multi-storied pavilion where Maitreya currently resides. Furthermore, it causes them to...
Regarding the contemplation of the body and the mind as being like a dream or a shadow: this causes one to penetrate their characteristics.
